repo_results and benchmark_case let the long runs (an hour of LBM, 30 minutes of 3D PINN) enter the database without being repeated: it reads what the script wrote, checks it against the reference again, and snapshots the generating script with the run.

docs.title: Curation: which experiments are good enough
docs.text:
python -m pinneapple_lab curate (also run by report) grades every run and experiment and writes lab/curation.json and lab/CURATION.md; the catalogue page shows the tier of each run, a quality filter and, in each run's sheet, the dimensions, the readiness for each use and what to do next. It uses the vocabulary of pinneapple_veriphysics.applicability: a dimension without evidence is not run, never a neutral pass, and evidence is verified (a check measured it in this run), inferred (metrics, files, names) or unsupported.

dimension what counts kind validation fraction of the run's checks that pass quantitative reference checks against an independent truth: exact solution, experiment, published value quantitative baseline checks that the method beats a simpler one (persistence, linear, nearest design, the original) quantitative physics conservation, symmetry, monotonicity, a physical range or law the method was not trained on quantitative generalization checks on unseen inputs (held-out designs, out-of-distribution cases, beyond the observed window) quantitative uncertainty an uncertainty estimate is reported (ensemble spread, sigma, intervals) quantitative reproducibility code snapshot, git commit, parameters, saved diff; agreement of repeats with other seeds quantitative data datasets with documented cards quantitative assets figures, movies, photoreal renders, a 3-D viewer qualitative documentation description, docs pages that cite the experiment, papers / references qualitative review a human review: novelty, clarity, visual appeal (1-5), a one-line story, approvals, limitations qualitative

A check says what it is evidence of with ctx.check(..., kind="reference" | "baseline" | "physics" | "generalization" | "verification" | "sanity"); left out, the kind is inferred from the name and the arguments. "reference" is kept for independent results: an exact solution of the same problem, a measurement, a published result of another group, another code that does not share the model's inputs. Agreement with a second code that shares the geometry, materials or loads (GetDP on the same machine polygons, a reduced model inside the same pipeline), and solver checks on canonical problems, are "verification": they answer the model question of the trust card ("is the solver right?") and never count toward a tier. label="drag vs Ahmed 1984" gives a check the short line that seals and showcase tiles print.

Tiers are gates, not averages, so a strong figure never hides a failed check. There are six, A to F, and every run gets exactly one: the rules below are tried in this order and the first that holds gives the letter (pinneapple_lab.curation.problem for E and F, assess_run for the rest).

letter name exact rule F not usable the run crashed; or a sanity check on finiteness or convergence failed (diverged: a check named *finite*, *nan*, *converg*, *diverg*, exits_cleanly); or a physics check failed (conservation, symmetry, equilibrium); or every reference check failed and no other independent check (reference, baseline, physics, generalization) passed: the result contradicts the reference E known problems any other failing check: a reference check failed while another independent check passed (large error vs the reference), a generalization check failed (outside the validity range), a baseline was not beaten, or a verification / unclassified check failed A flagship all checks pass; a reference check and a baseline or physics check pass; reproducible (code snapshot, commit); at least three figures or a movie / render / 3-D view; documented; for machine-learning experiments (surrogates, forecasters, neural operators) a generalization check passes. Ready to become a product, a paper or marketing once a human review approves it B solid all checks pass, at least one independent check (reference, baseline or physics) passes, reproducible. Demos, use cases, training data C plausible all checks pass and the trust card's model, physics or benchmark stage is answered by a passing check, but the B gates are not met: the only evidence is a verification against a code that shares the inputs, or the run is not reproducible D exploratory ran, no failing check, but none of those stages is answered (no checks, or only sanity checks): consistent, not validated

A and B mean what they meant before the scale had six letters, so the published showcase panel (A and B only) still shows the right items with the right tiers; it was rendered before B's seal turned from amber to light green. The old C (exploratory) is now C or D and the old D (not usable) is now E or F (pinneapple_lab.curation.TIER_HISTORY). The tier is never set by hand: it is recomputed from the run's stored checks by every curate, and the same runs give the same letters (a test re-curates the committed lab and compares).

An E or F item's headline is its main problem and the next step: the failing check (by priority: divergence, physics, reference, unseen data, baseline, then the first failing check; "+N more" when several fail) or the crash's last error line, and hint / hint_pt, the action that would lift it one letter (F → E, E → D):

rule letter next step (EN) next step (PT) crashed F E: make the run finish without an error E: fazer a execução terminar sem erro diverged F E: make the result finite and converged E: tornar o resultado finito e convergido physics F E: make the physics check pass E: fazer a verificação física passar contradicts F E: agree with the reference, or pass an independent physics check E: concordar com a referência ou passar numa verificação física independente reference E D: bring the error vs the reference within its tolerance D: trazer o erro face à referência para dentro da tolerância generalization E D: pass on the unseen inputs D: passar nos dados não vistos baseline E D: beat the baseline D: superar o baseline other E D: fix the failing check (or "the N failing checks") D: corrigir a verificação que falha

lab/CURATION.md lists every E and F item with both.

docs.title: What is missing for the next letter, and how to get there
docs.text:
Every item also records its path to the next letter (next_steps in lab/curation.json), computed from the same evidence and thresholds that gave the letter:

letter gaps it lists F, E every failing check, with the measured value against its tolerance or bound (value 1.33, max 0.05), or the crash D the trust-card stages (model, physics, benchmark) no passing check answers C no independent check passes; reproducibility score below 0.6 B each flagship gate it misses: reference, baseline or physics, unseen data (learned models), reproducibility below 0.75, figures or documentation score below 0.6 A what would strengthen it (A+): a second independent reference, a check that quantifies uncertainty, a baseline or benchmark comparison, a human review any lowered because fewer than half of its runs are A or B: that comes first

Each gap carries the PINNeAPPle actions that address it, from a curated registry (pinneapple_lab.next_steps.ACTIONS), with the item's experiment and parameters filled in: a rerun or a refinement sweep (python -m pinneapple_lab run / sweep), pinneapple check on the run folder, ctx.check(..., kind="reference" | "physics" | "generalization"), pp.compare, pp.trust_card, pp.validate, validate_pinn (PINNs), TrustGate (narrow the validity range), pinneapple_lab.uq.gci_check / coverage_check, ensemble_study, pp.benchmark.run, ctx.figure, pp.viz.field_view, Experiment.references, python -m pinneapple_lab review. A test resolves every action's import path or command and checks every gap type the curation can emit has at least one; a gap without one would print "no PINNeAPPle action yet" (none does today).

from pinneapple_lab.curation import next_steps

for gap in next_steps("solid_fem/cantilever"):          # list[pinneapple_lab.next_steps.Gap]
    print(gap.to, gap.short, gap.why, gap.measured)
    for a in gap.actions:                               # Action: id, kind, target, command, params, text, runnable
        print("  ", a.command)

Gap and Action are the stable API (to_dict / from_dict); the Flow Studio reads them to offer the suggested nodes. On the command line:

python -m pinneapple_lab seal --explain em_pinn/em_tm_cavity            # gap, why, the suggested commands
python -m pinneapple_lab seal --explain em_pinn/em_tm_cavity --lang pt
python -m pinneapple_lab improve em_pinn/em_tm_cavity                   # dry run: what --run would execute
python -m pinneapple_lab improve em_pinn/em_tm_cavity --run             # run them, then re-curate

improve executes only the registry's runnable lab commands (rerun, refinement sweep, seed sweep, pinneapple check), and only with --run; everything else is printed for a person to do. A rerun cannot fix a result whose method is wrong: the re-curation then reports the same letter.

Example (seal --explain em_pinn/em_tm_cavity, first gap):

em_pinn/em_tm_cavity: tier F
problem: Ez vs closed form (+2 more)
1. [E] agree with the reference
   why: failing check Ez vs closed form (value 1.33, max 0.05)
   -> diagnose the PINN on fresh points (residual, failure modes such as a collapsed or spectrally biased solution) before retraining
      validate_pinn(net, problem)
   -> rerun with epochs doubled and see whether the result converges
      python -m pinneapple_lab sweep em_pinn -g epochs=3000,6000 -p case=em_tm_cavity -p n_collocation=2048 -p seed=0 -p tolerance=0.05
   -> compare on the same points with a reference or a baseline solver at equal budget
      pp.compare(problem, [result, "fem"], reference="exact")

Reports (HTML, Markdown, PDF) and the catalogue's roadmap and report sheet show the same list.

Lab items per letter. Measured by python -m pinneapple_lab curate over the committed lab runs (lab/curation.json, 2026-10-18); an item is an experiment, or one case of it when the experiment declares case_param.

letter items runs items by their tier before the six-letter scale A flagship 19 19 19 from A B solid 50 170 50 from B C plausible 0 0 none D exploratory 6 7 6 from C E known problems 1 1 1 from D F not usable 5 11 5 from D total 81 208

The E item is the benchmark arena import (a dataset-audit check fails: one effective sample pattern in 54). The F items are three getting-started example scripts that did not finish within the example runner's time limit (crashed) and two electromagnetic PINN cases whose every closed-form reference check fails (contradicts).

An experiment takes the tier of its best run, one level lower when fewer than half of its runs are usable. The score (0-100) is the weighted mean of the dimensions that ran, shown with its coverage, like the Veriphysics trust score. Readiness lists what each use still needs: product (generalization, uncertainty, a reference or physics check, reproducibility), paper (reference, baseline or physics, reproducibility, novelty review), marketing (strong visuals, a validated headline number, a story), training data (a documented dataset of validated runs).

The catalogue opens on What can we present?: for each use (product, publication, marketing, training data) the items that are ready or approved, and the closest candidates with their distance in effort points (S = 1, M = 3, L = 8) and what they miss. Below it, the roadmap lists every item (an experiment, or one case of it when the experiment declares case_param) with its limitations — declared by the experiment (Experiment.limitations, a list or a dict per case), by the reviewer, or detected (failed runs, inferred-only evidence, low coverage) — and the path forward: the actions that close each gap, specific to the kind of experiment (a persistence baseline for a forecast, a grid-convergence study for CFD, held-out designs for a surrogate, ...), with their effort and what each unlocks.

Reports for one item or a filtered set, as HTML, Markdown or PDF: a summary table (tier and distance to each use) and, per item, the story, description, key figures, readiness, headline metrics, every validation check with its kind, the evidence dimensions, limitations, path forward, references and the command that reproduces it.

python -m pinneapple_lab brief --item kepler_law -o kepler.html
python -m pinneapple_lab brief --tier A,B --use paper --limit 10 -o paper_candidates.pdf
python -m pinneapple_lab brief --ready marketing --format md -o marketing.md
python -m pinneapple_lab brief --experiment benchmark_case -o landing_cases.pdf

The catalogue has the same reports one click away (an item, a use's ready and closest items, or everything the current filter shows); served by python -m pinneapple_lab serve they also download from /report.pdf|.html|.md?items=...&tier=...&use=...&ready=.... The Showcase at the top of the catalogue gathers the most striking figures of the database (photoreal renders, general-relativistic views, 3-D twins, movies).

Human review is the qualitative half and is never filled in automatically:

python -m pinneapple_lab review kepler_law --reviewer "name" --novelty 4 --clarity 5 --visual-appeal 3 \
    --story "Kepler's third law and the Sun/Jupiter mass ratio recovered from planetary data" --approve paper
python -m pinneapple_lab curate

docs.title: Trust card: six questions
docs.text:
Every run and portfolio item also answers the six questions a reviewer asks of a physics or Physics-AI result, each from the run's own evidence:

stage question answered by Data and geometry Was the physical problem represented correctly? recorded inputs plus a mesh, domain or input check Model Can the model (or solver) represent the relevant dynamics? unseen-data checks (learned models); a known-answer or convergence check (solvers) Physical constraints Are the equations and the boundary conditions respected? kind="physics" checks (conservation, divergence, equilibrium) Benchmark How does the result compare with a solver or reference data? kind="reference" / "baseline" checks Uncertainty Where may the prediction not be reliable? uncertainty checks (answered); reported spread or declared limitations (partial) Engineering decision Is the result adequate for the intended use? tier A/B, readiness for a use, and the declared limitations (failed at E and F)

The status of each stage is answered, partial, open or failed (a failing check).

Uncertainty is answered only by a number. pinneapple_lab.uq provides the checks: coverage_check (a learned model's 90 % interval must hold about 90 % of unseen values) and gci_check (the grid convergence index of a solver result from two or three meshes, with the Richardson-extrapolated value). rom_study/beam_parametric and calculix_case/plate_hole use them. The card appears in the catalogue's run sheet, in every report (HTML, Markdown, PDF) and as a table in lab/CURATION.md.

docs.title: Quality seal
docs.text:
pinneapple_lab.seal stamps an item's figures, renders and movies with a small PINNeAPPle badge: the pineapple mark, the wordmark, the tier letter on a disc in its colour, the tier line and, optionally, the one-line evidence. Every letter has a seal, so a figure always says where its result stands, not only when it is good.

letter colour EN PT A green #2FBF71 INDEPENDENT REFERENCE REFERÊNCIA INDEPENDENTE B light green #A6D96A REFERENCE PENDING REFERÊNCIA PENDENTE C yellow #FFE066 PARTLY CHECKED VERIFICAÇÃO PARCIAL D orange #FDAE61 EXPLORATORY · NOT VALIDATED EXPLORATÓRIO · NÃO VALIDADO E red #F0603C KNOWN PROBLEMS PROBLEMAS CONHECIDOS F dark red #A50026 NOT USABLE NÃO UTILIZÁVEL
  • The tier is read from lab/curation.json; no argument sets it, and stamping again after curate picks up the new tier. The evidence line is the item's curation headline: the first passing reference check (✓, A), the first passing physics, baseline or unseen-data check (◐, B), the verification check (◐, C), or for E and F the failing check (✗).
  • E and F always carry the main problem and the next step (↑, from the curation), whatever reason= says, and have no compact form: the badge grows instead (the problem and the next step each wrap onto up to two lines, so neither is cut), and it is at least 56 px tall on a stamped figure.
  • Colour is never the only cue: the letter and the tier line are always printed. The badge carries its own dark panel, so it reads the same on light and dark figures; on that panel the tier line and each letter on its disc have a WCAG contrast ratio of at least 4.5 (contrast_ratio, checked by a test). F's outline and tier line use a lighter red (#FF8A80) because dark red is too dark on the panel; its letter is white.
  • The full form carries a ↑ next line: the first gap of the item's path to the next letter ("A: compare with an independent reference", "A+: quantify the uncertainty"); next_step=False (--no-next) leaves it out of an A–D seal.
  • Below 56 px tall an A–D badge drops the small print (mark, wordmark, letter) so it stays legible.
  • lang="pt" writes the tier line, the reason (the display label's Portuguese form when the experiment gives one) and the next step in Portuguese.
from pinneapple_lab.seal import seal_for, save_seal, stamp_figure, stamp_file, sealed_savefig

s = seal_for("repo_results/prius_pmsm")             # tier and evidence from lab/curation.json
save_seal(s, "seal.svg"); save_seal(s, "seal_pt.png", lang="pt")
stamp_figure(fig, s)                                 # matplotlib: keeps off colour bars, picks the emptiest corner
with sealed_savefig(s):                              # a savefig hook: every figure saved in the block is stamped
    fig.savefig("torque.png")
stamp_file("render.jpg", s)                          # PNG / JPG / WebP -> render.sealed.jpg
stamp_file("wake.gif", s, corner="tl", size=0.3, opacity=0.9)   # GIF frame by frame, MP4 by an ffmpeg overlay
seal_for("repo_results/prius_pmsm", tiers="A,B")     # SealError unless the item is A or B

corner="auto" (the default) scores each corner by the colour gradient and spread under the badge, so colour bars, axis labels and the subject push it elsewhere; for figures it also never overlaps a colour-bar axes. size is the badge width as a fraction of the image width, opacity its alpha. A plot filled to its edges has no free corner; then the badge goes in a strip added under it (extend="auto") instead of covering the axes:

Figures of Lab items at other letters, stamped by the commands below:

D: exploratory E: known problems F: not usable 
python -m pinneapple_lab seal repo_results/prius_pmsm -o seal.svg --lang pt
python -m pinneapple_lab stamp repo_results/prius_pmsm figure.png -o figure_sealed.png
python -m pinneapple_lab stamp --all --out export/sealed                    # every figure of every item, A to F
python -m pinneapple_lab stamp --all --tiers A,B --out export/validated     # validated items only, for posts
python -m pinneapple_lab legend --lang pt -o seal_legend_pt.png             # the six seals

--tiers (also --tier) filters, it never changes a letter: stamp ITEM FILE --tiers A,B on a D item writes nothing and exits with status 2. Every stamp --all writes manifest.json (item, tier, reason, next step, files).

docs.title: Experiments page
docs.text:
pinneapple_lab.explorer builds the page of every experiment, served by the Lab server at /experiments (behind the same LAB_USER / LAB_PASSWORD login) and exported as static HTML by python -m pinneapple_lab site --out <dir> (<dir>/experiments/). It reads the Lab curation and the experiment manifests (adding an experiment) and nothing else:

  • every Lab item, with its A-F seal and reason, the trust card, its best run's measured metrics, the failing check for E and F, the path to the next letter with the suggested commands, its figures stamped with the seal, movies (loaded on demand), the 3-D viewer and links to the guide, the script and the pull request;
  • every examples/* folder, from its experiment.json: the Lab items made from its scripts and the best letter among them, or "not curated" with python -m pinneapple_lab register examples/<folder>.

Filters by letter, domain, method and "ready to use", search, sort by letter or date, a bar with the number of experiments per letter (counted from the list), a page per experiment, EN / PT, lazy thumbnails, and a layout that works on a phone. python -m pinneapple_lab coverage -o docs/lab/coverage.md writes the coverage list (experiment -> curated yes / no); the committed one is here.

route what /experiments the page /api/experiments?letter=&domain=&method=&ready=1&q=&sort=letter\|date its entries, filtered /api/experiment?key=KEY one entry /api/coverage experiment -> curated yes / no /stamped/EXPERIMENT/RUN_ID/PATH?key=ITEM, /stamped-repo/PATH?key=ITEM a figure stamped with the item's seal /seal.png?key=ITEM&lang=en\|pt an item's seal /repo/PATH, /repo-thumb/PATH files an experiment manifest lists (nothing else under the checkout)

docs.title: Showcase panel
docs.text:
pinneapple_lab.showcase.panel renders the animated panel of the Lab's best results, 1080 x 1350 on #090C14: the header, a hero tile with a slow Ken Burns zoom, a 3 x 3 grid of Tier A tiles, a row of two Tier B tiles and the footer. It writes an MP4 (H.264, yuv420p, faststart), a GIF (720 wide, 12 fps, palettegen), a still PNG and a JSON of the tiles it used.

  • Tiles come from the curation: Tier A first (hero and grid), then the strongest B. picks=[(item, figure)] overrides the order and the figure; an item still lands where its tier puts it, and a C to F item is never shown.
  • Every tile's green "✓" or amber "◐" line is the item's curation headline: the display label its experiment gives the check (Experiment.check_labels, English and Portuguese, a short form for small tiles), used only when every check the line names passed, else the check's own line. Lines are fitted to one row by a smaller font or by dropping a whole " · " clause, never cut mid-word. The hero carries the full seal; grid tiles a small compact one.
  • GIF and MP4 figures play in their tiles, resampled to run once over the 8 s loop at 15 fps.
  • Framing: picks=[(item, figure, {"focus": box, "fill": bool, "rotate": bool})]. focus is the subject's box in figure fractions (or several boxes laid side by side), so axes, legends and colour bars outside it are left out whole; fill crops the tile from the box instead of showing all of it; rotate turns a tall render to fit. Without a focus, plots are cut only at empty rows and columns. The Ken Burns window stays inside the image, so no black bars appear.
python -m pinneapple_lab showcase --lang en,pt --out docs/assets/showcase

docs.title: Examples and use cases
docs.text:
Every script under examples/ (224 today, use cases included) is also a lab experiment, example_script. A run executes the script from the repository root as a user would, then keeps what it produced anywhere in the checkout: figures, JSON files (outputs, and their numbers as metrics), the name: value lines it printed (metrics prefixed stdout.), arrays from .npy / .npz / .csv (the artifacts dataset), the console output, and the script with its neighbouring Python files as the code that ran. Data files it overwrote in the checkout are restored, and untracked files it left in the working tree are moved into the run, so the checkout stays clean. A script that needs a GPU, a download or a missing optional dependency fails and is recorded, so the catalogue doubles as a health report of the examples.

python -m pinneapple_lab examples                                   # list them, grouped by folder
python -m pinneapple_lab examples --run --match use_cases --timeout 1800
python -m pinneapple_lab run example_script -p script=examples/getting_started/03_heat_diffusion_1d.py

Scripts run one at a time, and the checkout should not be edited while they run: a run attributes every file that changes during it to the script (sources and docs are never restored, but they are recorded as produced).

docs.title: Serving the catalogue
docs.text: python -m pinneapple_lab serve --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8093 serves the lab as a web app (standard library only): the catalogue page, live from the database (new runs appear on reload), every run's files (/files/...), a JSON API (/api/catalog, /api/status, /api/runs, /api/runs/<id>, /api/datasets) and each dataset over all validated runs as one .npz (/download/<experiment>/<dataset>.npz). LAB_USER / LAB_PASSWORD turn on HTTP Basic login (except /health). pinneapple_lab/deploy/Dockerfile packages it, and apps/deploy runs it as the lab service behind Caddy next to the other apps. On a fresh checkout the run records are present but the dataset shards are not: sweeping again recomputes exactly the runs whose shards are missing.

docs.title: Versioning the database
docs.text: The run metadata, metrics, validation, figures and dataset cards are small and versioned in git under lab/. Arrays, dataset shards and the SQLite index are not versioned (see .gitignore). Rebuild the index with python -m pinneapple_lab reindex. python -m pinneapple_lab report also writes lab/DATASETS.md: every dataset with its schema (shapes, ranges, units), its sample count over validated runs, and the sweep and export commands that rebuild it (runs are cached by parameters, so the sweep only computes what is missing). Large datasets are exported (export) and published separately, for example to the Hugging Face Hub with pinneapple_hub.

docs.title: Lattice Boltzmann wind tunnel and the FluidX3D bridge
docs.text:
Two pieces, both under pinneapple_simulation:

Module What it is numerical_solvers.lbm_tunnel A 3-D lattice Boltzmann solver written in PyTorch (CPU or GPU) for wind-tunnel cases: inlet, outlet, open sides, walls, moving walls, solid bodies from masks or STL files, and the force on them. external_solvers.fluidx3d A bridge to FluidX3D (Moritz Lehmann's OpenCL LBM for GPUs): it writes a wind-tunnel main_setup() into your own FluidX3D checkout, builds and runs it, and reads back forces and .vtk fields.

The solver uses methods from the LBM literature that FluidX3D also uses. No FluidX3D code is copied or shipped:

  • D3Q19 and D3Q27 velocity sets;
  • SRT or TRT collision (TRT magic parameter 3/16), with optional Smagorinsky LES (Hou et al. 1996);
  • DDF shifting: the solver stores f − w instead of f, which keeps the 16-bit rounding error small (Lehmann et al. 2022);
  • FP16 storage (storage="fp16s"), which halves the memory of the distributions;
  • Guo forcing, split into its even and odd parts so that it is correct with TRT;
  • halfway bounce-back on solids, with the moving-wall term;
  • momentum-exchange force on bodies;
  • equilibrium inlet and open faces, and a zero-gradient outlet;
  • unit conversion between lattice units and SI (Units);
  • legacy VTK output that ParaView reads, and that FluidX3D's own exports share.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
from pinneapple_simulation.numerical_solvers.lbm_tunnel import WindTunnelLBM, Units, sphere

un = Units.from_si(lbm_length=8, lbm_velocity=0.05, lbm_rho=1,      # D = 2 cm sphere at 0.1 m/s
                   si_length=0.02, si_velocity=0.1, si_rho=1260)  # in a glycerol-water mix
lbm = WindTunnelLBM((96, 48, 48), nu=un.nu(1e-4), u_in=(0.05, 0, 0), storage="fp16s")
lbm.add_solid(sphere(lbm.shape, (24, 23.5, 23.5), 4))
lbm.run(3000)
Fx = un.si_F(lbm.force_on_solid()[0])          # drag in newtons
lbm.write_vtk("out/sphere")                     # sphere-u.vtk, sphere-rho.vtk, sphere-flags.vtk

Faces are set per side with faces={"x-": "inlet", "x+": "outlet", "y-": "open", ...}. Each side is one of inlet, outlet, open, wall, moving or periodic. The defaults are an inlet at x−, an outlet at x+, and open on the other four sides. voxelize_stl(trimesh_mesh, shape, center, size) turns an STL into a solid mask.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
examples/lbm/01_sphere_wind_tunnel.py runs these cases (tests in tests/test_lbm_tunnel.py):

Case Result Force-driven Poiseuille channel, SRT and TRT < 1 % from the parabola Stokes drag on a sphere (Re ≈ 0.1), Stokes far field on the sides R = 5 cells: +2.6 %; R = 8 cells: +1.1 % against 6πρνRU Sphere at Re = 20, D = 8 cells, 96 × 48 × 48 tunnel, FP32 Cd = 3.19; Schiller & Naumann (1933) gives 2.61 (+22 %) Same, FP16 storage, half the memory (38 instead of 76 B/cell) Cd = 3.19, 0.05 % from FP32; velocity differs by at most 0.002 U

The Re = 20 drag is 22 % above the correlation for two reasons. The sphere is only 8 cells across, so its surface is a staircase. The tunnel is only 6 diameters wide, and the open sides hold the free-stream velocity, which confines the flow; at low Re the disturbance reaches far, so this matters. The Stokes case shows the method converges with resolution (+2.6 % at R = 5, +1.1 % at R = 8). For numbers you report, use bodies of 20+ cells and a tunnel 15+ diameters wide. The example is sized to run in about an hour on 4 CPU cores. FP16 storage works when the flow moves at u ≳ 0.02 in lattice units. Far below that (u ≈ 0.005), the 16-bit rounding is a few percent of the velocity.

docs.title: FluidX3D bridge
docs.text:
from pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.fluidx3d import WindTunnelSetup, run_fluidx3d, read_results, results_to_samples

s = WindTunnelSetup(stl="stl/car.stl", length_m=4.5, velocity_m_s=30, nu_m2_s=1.5e-5, rho_kg_m3=1.2,
                    box=(1.0, 3.0, 0.75), memory_mb=2000, time_s=0.5, export_every_s=0.1, floor=True)
run_fluidx3d(s)                          # needs FLUIDX3D_HOME and an OpenCL device
res = read_results()                     # res["forces"]: (t, Fx, Fy, Fz) in N; res["fields"]["u"]["data"]
samples = results_to_samples(res)        # PhysicalSamples for training

write_setup backs up src/setup.cpp to setup.cpp.pinneapple.bak and replaces the active main_setup(). enable_features switches on the defines.hpp extensions the setup needs (EQUILIBRIUM_BOUNDARIES, FORCE_FIELD, VOLUME_FORCE, SUBGRID, MOVING_BOUNDARIES for a moving floor, FP16S) and comments out BENCHMARK. The generated setup uses only the API in FluidX3D's documentation. It has not been compiled against every FluidX3D version, so check the build log the first time.

License. FluidX3D is not open source in the OSI sense: its license allows public research, education and personal use, and forbids commercial and military use. PINNeAPPle does not download or bundle it. You clone it yourself and are responsible for using it within those terms. The PyTorch solver above is independent of FluidX3D and is covered by PINNeAPPle's own license.

docs.title: Not implemented yet
docs.text:
The FluidX3D features this solver does not have yet are tracked in issue #473:

  • free surface (VOF-LBM);
  • esoteric-pull in-place streaming;
  • D2Q9 and D3Q15;
  • temperature;
  • particles and IBM;
  • multi-GPU domains;
  • ray-traced graphics.

docs.title: Lunar rover terramechanics in 3D
docs.text:
NASA's VIPER rover at real scale, driving on lunar regolith with Wong-Reece wheels and full multibody dynamics. Everything on this page is a library feature: the soil database, the wheel model, the deformable terrain, the multibody vehicle, the CAD, the renders and the PINN surrogate. The example examples/use_cases/terramechanics/lunar_rover_3d.py is a thin script that puts them together.

import pinneapple as pp
from pinneapple_simulation.vehicle import scenarios, viz

spec = pp.vehicle.viper()                                   # cited figures in spec.sources, CAD in spec.cad
spec.cad.export("viper.glb")                                # PBR materials; .stl too
site = scenarios.crater_site()                              # deformable regolith, a crater, rocks
run = pp.vehicle.VehicleSimulator(pp.vehicle.build_vehicle(spec), site,
                                  pp.terramechanics.get_soil("GRC-1")).run(45.0, speed=0.2)
run.summary()                                               # distance, slip, sinkage, energy, loads, attitude
viz.animate(run, site, "run.gif", mp4="run.mp4", field="normal_stress")
Library module What it holds pinneapple_simulation.terramechanics.soils Soil, get_soil: GRC-1, JSC-1A and the validation soils, each parameter with its source pinneapple_simulation.terramechanics.wong_reece WongReeceModel: stresses on the contact arc, forces, sinkage for a load, testbed operating points pinneapple_simulation.terramechanics.terrain DeformableTerrain (soil memory, ruts, grouser marks, stress maps), RigidRock pinneapple_simulation.terramechanics.testbed single-wheel testbed, the bundled published points, validation and (separate) calibration pinneapple_simulation.terramechanics.surrogate train_contact_surrogate: PINN of the wheel-soil contact with a held-out error report pinneapple_simulation.multibody MultibodyTree: floating base, revolute joints, linearly implicit steps pinneapple_simulation.vehicle VehicleSpec, build_vehicle, VehicleSimulator, viper(), scenarios, viz pinneapple_design.geometry.vehicle_cad parametric vehicle CAD, centre of mass and inertia from the meshes, glTF/STL pinneapple_tools.visualization.studio lighting presets, shadows (Sun shadows, Lunar-Lambert), planetary renders

Shortcuts: pp.terramechanics, pp.multibody, pp.vehicle.

docs.title: About the sources
docs.text:
Every number below either cites a source or is marked as an estimate with its reason. One caveat applies to all of them. From the environment this was built in, NASA's documents and the journal papers could only be found through a web search. The search returned text excerpts, but the PDFs, figures and photos could not be opened. So:

  • the wording of the quotes, and the slide or page they come from, should be checked against the documents;
  • the single-wheel test points are third-party readings of the published figures (see Validation), not tables from the papers;
  • the renders were compared with VIPER's published dimensions and ratios and with the layout NASA's renders and photo captions describe (arrays on three sides, a white front without arrays, the mast at the front-left, the TRIDENT drill on a vertical rail at the front). The photographs themselves could not be downloaded, so a pixel-level side-by-side comparison is still to do.

docs.title: The rover: NASA VIPER
docs.text:
Quantity Value used Source Envelope (L × W × H) 1.7 × 1.7 × 2.5 m (model: 1.69 × 1.54 × 2.50 m) Bluethmann (2024), VIPER Rover Overview and Mobility and Hardware, LSIC, NTRS 20240013903 Mass 450 kg (447 kg roving in LSIC 2024) Francis & Sobey (2025), Design and Test of the VIPER Mobility Actuators, NTRS 20250000568 Wheels 4, 0.50 m diameter, 0.20 m wide, rigid sheet metal with spokes and rim grousers Fong, VIPER briefings, NTRS 20220000441 and 20250004148 Grousers 24, 0.025 m tall Hu et al. (2025), J. Field Robotics, doi:10.1002/rob.22597 (arXiv:2405.11001); 2.5 cm also in LSIC 2024 Mobility module per corner actuated suspension, steering and drive Francis & Sobey (2025) Suspension ±40°, 200 N m Fong (2022, 2025) Steering ±50° McBryan, Francis & Sobey (2025), ICES-2025-147, NTRS 20250005201 Track, wheelbase ≈ 1.3 m, ≈ 1 m at nominal ride height; suspension changes ride height and track, steering changes track and wheelbase Investigating the geotechnical properties of the lunar south pole with NASA VIPER's mobility system, Planet. Sci. J. (2025), doi:10.3847/PSJ/add13f Speed 0.20 m/s top, 0.10 m/s prospecting Fong (2022), NTRS 20220000441 Mast tip ≈ 2.5 m above the wheel rims; NavCam pair and LED headlights on a pan-tilt head NASA (2023), VIPER team raises its mighty mast Antennas gimballed high-gain (gimbal at ≈ 2.3 m), fixed low-gain LSIC 2024 Power and thermal solar arrays on three sides, radiator on top LSIC 2024; Fong (2022) Drill TRIDENT, 1 m class rotary-percussive, vertical, 10 cm bites; integrated into the rover's belly, stows inside and extends 1 m; < 20 kg, 200 N maximum weight on bit; deployment and feed stages, brush, chute, footpad Zacny et al. (2021), LPSC 52, abstract 2400; NASA (2024), Into the Belly of the Rover; NTRS 20240000585; Chu et al., Honeybee Robotics / LSIC poster Instruments NSS on the front; NIRVSS and MSolo under the rover; one hazard camera per wheel Andrews (2020), NTRS 20205000864; Fong (2022)

Estimates (not found in the sources that could be reached). Each one is chosen to agree with the published envelope, track, wheelbase and wheel size:

  • Suspension geometry: pivots under the chassis, arm length, and a 0.15 m steering offset. These give the 1.3 m track and 1.0 m wheelbase, and ±40° of arm travel changes ride height and track as the PSJ paper says.
  • Chassis: a 1.44 × 1.48 m body with 7 cm chamfers on its edges, on a 1.20 × 0.40 m keel that carries the suspension actuators. It fills the 1.7 m envelope with the wheels outboard, and the wheels clear every chassis part when steered ±50° (tested).
  • Faces: arrays on the left, right and aft faces; the front face white radiator over silver MLI, gold MLI on the belly, a radiator and a raised rim on the deck (layout from NASA renders; sizes estimated).
  • Mast and head: a tapered square mast at the front-left of the deck, a pan-tilt head with the NavCam stereo pair (0.24 m baseline), an AftCam and a row of six LED lights, the high-gain antenna on a gimbal at ≈ 2.24 m.
  • TRIDENT position: the drill rail stands on the front face, right of centre, with the auger below the belly and the footpad 0.36 m above the ground (from NASA renders and photos; the internal bay of the belly installation is not modelled). Rail 1.30 m, auger 25 mm, footpad 0.12 m: sized for the 1 m stroke.
  • Instruments: NSS low on the front face, NIRVSS on the keel front near the drill, MSolo under the keel.
  • Other dimensions: array panels covering the body faces; high-gain dish 0.40 m across; straight grousers (the shape was not found).
  • Mass split: per corner, 12 kg wheel with its drive, 8 kg steering module and 10 kg arm; 330 kg chassis, split among structure, avionics, arrays, radiator, mast, drill and instruments. The centre of mass and the inertias are computed from the CAD meshes with these masses.
  • Actuators: drive torque limit 80 N m (more than the soil torque at 90 % slip under the static lunar load, so traction, not the motor, limits climbing); wheel speed limit 2.5 rad/s; steering torque limit 60 N m.

All of this lives in pinneapple_simulation.vehicle.viper.VIPER_SOURCES. The CAD is built by pinneapple_design.geometry.vehicle_cad: - every part is a closed mesh with a material and a mass; - the bodies (chassis, 4 arms, 4 steering modules, 4 wheels) get their mass, centre of mass and inertia tensor from the meshes (Eberly's polyhedral mass properties, checked against boxes, cylinders and tubes in the tests); - export(".glb") writes glTF with PBR materials (new studio materials: white paint, anodised black, wheel metal, solar cells, radiator, gold and silver MLI, lens, LED, regolith, rock).

Computed for the model: total mass 450.0 kg, centre of mass 0.871 m above the ground at nominal ride height, and inertias about it 162 / 177 / 172 (roll / pitch / yaw) kg m² (glTF: viper.glb).

docs.title: Wheel-soil model
docs.text:
WongReeceModel(soil, wheel, g=1.62) integrates the stresses on the contact arc with piecewise Gauss-Legendre quadrature, vectorised over wheels.

  • Normal stress: Bekker pressure-sinkage σ = (k_c/b + k_φ) h^n, with the Wong-Reece shape: maximum at θ_m = (a0 + a1 s) θ_f, and the rear arc mapped onto the front one (Wong & Reece 1967; Wong 2008).
  • Shear: Janosi-Hanamoto τ = (c + σ tan φ)(1 - e^(-j/K)), with the shear displacement j = R_s[(θ_f - θ) - (1 - s)(sin θ_f - sin θ)].
  • Slip-sinkage: the exponent of the pressure-sinkage law grows with driving slip, n = n0 + n1 s (Ding et al. 2010, 2011, who identified it from single-wheel tests on lunar simulant). Skid (s < 0) leaves it at n0 by default (slip_sinkage="drive"; "both" uses |s|, "none" turns it off). A larger exponent means a softer response at the few-centimetre depths of a wheel, so the wheel sinks deeper as it slips and digs.
  • Grousers: shear on the equivalent radius R_s = R + λ h (Ding et al. 2011, λ = 1 by default). The visual grouser marks come from the vehicle simulation (below).
  • Multi-pass: Wong's repetitive loading. The soil remembers the deepest sinkage it carried, z_u. A later wheel reloads it elastically (p = k_u h, k_u = k_u0 + A_u z_u) up to p_u = k z_u^n, then follows the virgin curve. As in Wong's treatment of consecutive wheels in one track, the shear displacement left by the wheel in front is carried over. A rear wheel in a rut therefore sinks deeper in total but needs less extra compaction, and its traction builds over a shorter arc. Both effects are tested.
  • Bulldozing: passive earth pressure on the soil wedge, R_b = b(0.67 c z K_pc + 0.5 z² γ K_pγ), with Terzaghi's bearing-capacity factors (Bekker 1969; Wong 2008). It is applied on the side face by default. Ahead of the wheel it is optional (bulldozing="both"), because Wong-Reece's σ sin θ term already contains the compaction resistance.
  • Lateral force and side slip: lateral shear with j_y = R(1 - s)(θ_f - θ) tan β (Ishigami et al. 2007), plus sidewall bulldozing. The force opposes the side slip.

The model reproduces the library's earlier Bekker-Wong solver to 2e-6 relative error when the extensions are off.

docs.title: Soils
docs.text:
get_soil(name) returns the parameters with soil.sources (and soil.provenance() as a table). Status of each parameter:

Soil c [kPa] φ [°] k_c [kN/m^(n+1)] k_φ [kN/m^(n+2)] n ρ [kg/m³] K [m] Status GRC-1 0.25 38 0.7 505 0.8 1620 0.018 c, φ, k_c, k_φ, n, ρ: secondary (the RoverDevKit catalogue, MIT, which attributes them to Oravec et al. 2010); K: estimate JSC-1A 1.0 45 1.4 820 1.0 1600 0.018 secondary (RoverDevKit, attributed to Zeng et al. 2010). k_c, k_φ, n equal the classic Apollo lunar-soil set, so they are probably not a JSC-1A bevameter fit; K: estimate Ding2011-TYII 0.25 31.9 15.6 2407.4 1.10 1605 0.011 secondary (Ding et al. 2011, Table 2, via RoverDevKit) FJS-1/Hurrell2025 2.4 38 1.37 820 1.0 1740 0.018 c, φ secondary (Hurrell et al. 2025); pressure-sinkage proxied by catalogue FJS-1 KLS-1 1.716 40.6 −44.06 3581.8 1.26 1600 0.018 secondary (Wang & Han 2016; Lim et al. 2021)

Other values, not measured for these simulants: - Wong-Reece coefficients: a0 = 0.40, a1 = 0.15, exit-angle ratio 1/3 (estimates, the library's earlier values). - Unloading modulus: k_u0 = 2e8 N/m³. Almost all of the sinkage stays plastic. - Slip-sinkage: n1 was not published for any of these simulants. The validation soils keep n1 = 0 (the cited state, the "before" of the calibration below). GRC-1 and JSC-1A use n1 = 0.8, an estimate: the rounded mean of n1 fitted on the training points of the five single-wheel series (0.64–0.94).

The Oravec et al. (2010) GRC-1 paper and the Zeng et al. (2010) JSC-1A paper are the primary sources to check these against. The parameters the library used before under the name "GRC-1" (SoilParams(): c = 1.4 kPa, φ = 30°, k_c = 1.37, k_φ = 814, n = 1) are kept as "Apollo-lunar". Their source was not recorded, and they are not the GRC-1 values above.

docs.title: Validation against single-wheel tests
docs.text:
testbed.validate(testbed.load_dataset(name, wheel)) runs the wheel at the measured slips. It finds the sinkage for the test load, then the drawbar pull and the torque, using the soil parameters cited for that test. The bundled points (terramechanics/data/single_wheel_tests.csv) are readings of the published figures made by RoverDevKit (MIT licence, status digitised_approx). They are not tables from the papers, and they are used unchanged. No tabulated single-wheel data for GRC-1 or JSC-1A could be obtained here; the NASA Glenn and WES reports that hold such tables could not be opened.

With the cited soils (nothing fitted, n1 = 0), errors over all points:

Test (load) Drawbar pull RMSE RMSE / load Sinkage RMSE Torque RMSE ding2011 smooth (80.0 N) 7.7 N 0.096 4.2 mm 0.58 N m ding2011 grousered (80.0 N) 4.0 N 0.050 7.7 mm 0.53 N m wanghan2016 smooth (58.9 N) 14.4 N 0.244 16.1 mm 0.82 N m wanghan2016 grousered (58.9 N) 9.2 N 0.156 13.6 mm 0.54 N m hurrell2025 grousered (24.5 N) 3.0 N 0.122 4.7 mm not reported

With a constant exponent the model's sinkage is almost flat with slip (≈ 10, 12 and 20 mm), while every test series rises, from ≈ 5 mm at zero slip to 15–27 mm at 0.6 slip, and the model over-predicts the sinkage at low slip.

Slip-sinkage calibration with held-out points. testbed.calibrate_holdout(data) fits the two coefficients of the slip-dependent exponent n = n0 + n1 s (Ding et al. 2010, 2011) and the shear modulus K, by least squares on the drawbar pull and sinkage of every other point (sorted by slip, starting with the lowest: testbed.holdout_split). The other points are held out: they do not enter the fit or its scaling (a test moves them and checks that the fit does not change). Errors on the held-out points only:

Test Fitted n0, n1, K Sinkage RMSE before → after Drawbar pull RMSE / load before → after ding2011 smooth 0.91, 0.65, 16 mm 4.9 → 0.5 mm 0.116 → 0.101 ding2011 grousered 0.88, 0.84, 10 mm 10.2 → 3.1 mm 0.061 → 0.067 wanghan2016 smooth 0.53, 0.82, 50 mm (bound) 15.7 → 1.3 mm 0.232 → 0.045 wanghan2016 grousered 0.63, 0.94, 31 mm 13.9 → 0.4 mm 0.109 → 0.117 hurrell2025 grousered 0.77, 0.74, 25 mm 3.3 → 0.8 mm 0.092 → 0.139

What this says: - Sinkage: the slip-dependent exponent reproduces the rise of sinkage with slip in all five series; the held-out sinkage error falls by a factor of 3 to 37. The largest remaining miss is the 27 mm point of the Ding grousered wheel at 0.6 slip (model 22 mm), where the grousers dig more than the exponent law follows. - Drawbar pull: much better for the Wang & Han smooth wheel (0.232 → 0.045 W, 0.244 → 0.043 W over all points), about unchanged for the Ding wheels and the Wang & Han grousered wheel, and worse for the Hurrell wheel (0.092 → 0.139 W): there the fit trades pull for sinkage, and the model's pull keeps rising past 0.3 slip while the measured pull levels off. For the Wang & Han smooth wheel K ends at its 50 mm bound. - The fitted n0 are 0.53–0.92 and n1 0.64–0.94. Every fitted value and the held-out errors are in results.json (slip_sinkage_calibration).

docs.title: Multibody vehicle
docs.text:
build_vehicle(spec) makes a floating-base tree:

chassis -> 4 × (suspension arm -> steering module -> wheel)

That is 18 degrees of freedom, with the bodies' masses and inertias taken from the CAD.

  • Dynamics: MultibodyTree.step takes a linearly implicit Euler step on M(q) v' + h(q, v) = Q. Each force provider returns its generalised force and the derivative with respect to the velocities, so stiff slip dynamics and servo gains stay stable at 2 ms. The tree is checked against free fall, a pendulum's period (0.004 % off), and momentum and energy conservation of a tumbling free tree.
  • Wheels: at each step the simulator finds each wheel's sinkage below the undisturbed surface, its slip (from the wheel's angular velocity and its centre velocity) and its slip angle. It then evaluates Wong-Reece with the soil memory ahead of the wheel, and applies the forces at the axle and the soil torque about it. Slip is regularised below 0.02 m/s.
  • Vertical damping: c = ζ 2√(k m) (soil_damping, ζ = 0.7). Granular soil dissipates the energy of a bouncing wheel, and the quasi-static laws have no damping of their own. This is a model setting, like the damping of Chrono's SCM soil, not a measured property.
  • Rocks: rigid. The rim and its grousers get a penalty contact with Coulomb friction (μ = 0.6), so a wheel climbs a rock and the vehicle bounces off it.
  • Drive: per wheel, a PI speed loop with an 80 N m torque limit. The wheels turn at the commanded rate, and the slip is whatever the soil gives.
  • Steering: PD heading hold (±20° command), front and rear steering opposite.
  • Suspension: PD to a set point, 200 N m limit, plus an assumed load-levelling loop. On four wheels only the diagonal ("warp") share of the loads can be equalised by the arms; the front/rear split is fixed by the centre of mass.
  • Slip-sinkage in the dynamic run: the slip that sets the exponent follows the wheel's slip with a lag of 0.15 m of rim travel (sink_length, about one contact length). Slip-sinkage builds up as the wheel turns and digs; a stopped wheel neither builds nor loses it, so the slip ratio of a nearly stopped wheel, a ratio of noise, cannot feed back into the sinkage. Without the lag, a wheel held on a 20° slope dug itself in and the run diverged. This is a model setting, not a published law.
  • Terrain: DeformableTerrain keeps the soil memory on a 1 cm grid. Every wheel writes its rim trace and the shear it leaves, and the rut gets a real cross-section: a floor as wide as the wheel at the computed sinkage, walls at the angle of repose (38°) and rounded berms on both sides holding 30 % of the rut cross-section (the rest is compaction). A rear wheel in a front wheel's rut reloads the compacted soil (multi-pass) and deepens the rut only where it sinks deeper; a wheel running over a berm flattens it. Each time a grouser passes the bottom of a loaded wheel it writes a mark across the track, so the marks are spaced by the grouser pitch times (1 − slip) (tested). Ruts keep the peak normal and shear stress for optional colour maps.

docs.title: Results (full vehicle, GRC-1, lunar g)
docs.text:
Grades (wheel-rate command 0.1 m/s, mean over the second half of a 14 s run):

Grade [°] Slip Speed [m/s] Sinkage [mm] Drive torque per wheel [N m] End heading [°] 0.0 -0.007 0.101 14.8 4.8 (peak 10.1) 0.0 5.0 0.001 0.100 15.2 9.3 (peak 19.0) 0.0 10.0 0.020 0.098 16.0 14.0 (peak 28.3) 0.0 12.5 0.031 0.096 16.5 16.3 (peak 35.3) -0.0 15.0 0.054 0.093 17.2 18.8 (peak 39.1) -0.0 17.5 0.080 0.090 18.2 21.9 (peak 47.9) 0.0 20.0 0.125 0.085 20.0 25.0 (peak 54.4) -0.0

On level ground the mean slip is -0.007: the rear wheels, running in the front wheels' ruts, carry slightly more traction and push. The slip grows with grade, to 0.05 at 15° and 0.13 at 20°, the sinkage with it (slip-sinkage), and the vehicle holds its heading on every grade. The averaging window straddles a change of regime: the rear wheels drive on virgin soil until they reach the start of the front wheels' ruts, one wheelbase (≈ 1 m, ≈ 11 s) after the start; there the slip is ≈ 0.17 on 15° and ≈ 0.26 on 20° (all four wheels). In the ruts the shear carried over from the front wheels lets the rear wheels push and the slip of all four falls to ≈ 0. A longer run would report the in-rut value. This is more optimistic than NASA's published figures. LSIC 2024 lists 15° slopes as a design requirement, and a limit of 40 % slip on 15° is quoted for VIPER in the literature (secondary source). Pavlov et al. (NTRS 20220005373) give about 18° as the safe limit with a 50 % slip cap, and Hu et al. (2025) extrapolate about 85 % slip at 30° for the full-scale rover. Likely reasons: - the GRC-1 parameters are secondary and describe a dense, firm state (φ = 38°, n = 0.8); - the shear carried over between wheels in one rut (Wong's multi-pass treatment) helps the rear wheels, and its size is not calibrated for lunar simulants (VehicleSimulator(multipass_shear=False) turns it off); - slip-sinkage on GRC-1 uses an estimated n1 (0.8), not a measured one.

Treat these grades as model results, not as predictions of VIPER's performance.

Cross slope 10° at 0.1 m/s (heading hold): slip angles -3.2 / -3.0 / -5.7 / -5.6° and lateral forces 32 / 45 / 20 / 30 N per wheel (FL, FR, RL, RR). The steering crabs into the slope to hold the heading.

Crater crossing at 0.2 m/s. The crater is 4 m across and 0.32 m deep, degraded (depth 0.08 D; Pike's 0.2 holds for fresh craters), and a 12 cm rock sits under the left wheels:

Distance Mean slip Max sinkage Energy Max pitch Max roll Max rock force Max drive torque 8.63 m 0.018 36.6 mm 794 J (92.0 J/m) 10.5° 3.8° 490 N 31.4 N m

What the run shows: - the left front wheel climbs the rock, leaves the soil and spins up (slip 1); - the wheel loads swing between 0 and about 300 N; - the rear-left wheel, pushed against the rock with the front-left wheel lifted, slips up to ≈ 0.3 and digs to 37 mm (slip-sinkage), the deepest point of the run; elsewhere the sinkage stays at 11-20 mm; - the chassis pitches down into the bowl and back up; - the arms move to keep all four wheels loaded; - slip rises on the climb out.

docs.title: PINN surrogate
docs.text:
train_contact_surrogate(WongReeceModel(GRC-1, VIPER wheel), slip -0.4 to 0.9, sinkage 2-60 mm) trains a Fourier-feature residual MLP on Wong-Reece data, with four physics terms: - dF_z/dz ≥ 0; - dF_x/ds ≥ 0 below 0.3 slip; - the Mohr-Coulomb traction limit; - M_y ≥ R F_x.

Each term is first checked on the reference over the box, and a term the reference violates would be dropped. All four hold. The error is measured on 2000 held-out Latin-hypercube points that were never used in training:

Output Held-out RMSE Max error RMSE / range R² Fx [N] 0.916 5.340 0.066 % 0.999985 Fz [N] 1.473 13.873 0.108 % 0.999982 My [N m] 0.196 1.110 0.052 % 0.999989

Along the crater run, at the (slip, sinkage) states the wheels actually met (same inputs to both): drawbar pull RMSE 0.79 N, load 2.83 N, torque 0.28 N m, with 0.2 % of the states outside the training box (they are left out of these errors). sur.save(stem) writes TorchScript + JSON in the format rover.SurrogateContact.from_torchscript reads.

docs.title: Pictures
docs.text:
vehicle.viz and studio.planetary render with PyVista: - Pose: the CAD posed by the multibody state, so the wheels roll with their joint angles. - Terrain: replayed to each instant. Ruts, walls, berms and grouser marks are deformations of the terrain mesh, so their shading and shadows come from the geometry under the low Sun. - Ground to the horizon: a 1 cm patch around the vehicle, a 4 cm field with the ruts out to 14 m, and a curved annulus out to 4 km whose height follows the Moon's curvature. The camera (≈ 2 m up) sees the real horizon, ≈ 2.6 km away, and never the edge of a mesh. studio.planetary.border_visibility projects the mesh border through the camera and checks that every point inside the frame is hidden by the ground; the tests and the dashboard example run it for every camera used. - Shadows: Sun shadows of the vehicle, rocks and terrain, baked into the terrain and applied to the vehicle's vertices. - Regolith: shaded with McEwen's (1991) Lunar-Lambert function, which keeps it lit at grazing Sun angles. - Colour maps (optional): contact stresses on the wheel arcs and in the ruts, with a colour bar (field="normal_stress"). The default view shows the ruts by their geometry only.

The lighting presets (studio.lighting) are shared by PyVista, Blender (render(..., background="lunar_south_pole")) and the browser viewer (Scene.set_lighting(...)):

Preset Sky Sun lunar_south_pole black 5° high, 0.53° disc. At ≈ 86° S the Sun stays within ≈ 5.5° of a level horizon: 90° − 86° + the 1.54° lunar obliquity lunar_low_sun black 12° high: shadows ≈ 4.7 times the object height, and small crater floors stay partly lit (used for the animation) lunar_day black 30° high

Earth can be shown in the sky (earth=True) at its 1.9° apparent size.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• The renders and the CAD were checked against published dimensions, not against photographs (see About the sources). The geometry details marked as estimates may differ from the real rover.
  • The Wong-Reece laws are quasi-static and per wheel. Transient soil flow, grouser-by-grouser force oscillations (Irani et al. 2011) and wheel-wheel soil interaction beyond the rut memory are not modelled.
  • Soil parameters are secondary or estimated (see the table). The single-wheel validation uses digitised figure points. The slip-sinkage coefficients are calibrated per test series (on half of its points); for GRC-1 n1 is an estimate, so the vehicle's sinkage at high slip carries that uncertainty.
  • The load-levelling suspension law, the controllers' gains and the vertical soil damping are model choices.
  • Rocks are rigid ellipsoids. The terrain grid is 1 cm, so grouser marks are drawn about 1 cm wide.

The previous quasi-static six-wheel rocker-bogie model (pinneapple_simulation.rover) is still in the library with its verification tests. Its generic 40 kg rover is no longer used by the example.

docs.title: Model
docs.text: A Model maps coordinates to predicted fields — u = model(x). It knows nothing about the PDE it is being used to solve; physics enters later, as a loss computed on top of the model's output. This separation is what lets you swap a SIREN for a Fourier neural operator without touching the physics code, and swap the PDE without touching the model code.

docs.title: Where it lives
docs.text:
Architectures live in pinneapple_neural.architectures (re-exported at pinneapple_neural and, for legacy imports, pinneapple_models). Every model subclasses BaseModel(nn.Module) (pinneapple_neural/architectures/base.py), which adds framework-wide conventions on top of a normal torch.nn.Module:

  • forward(x) — the actual coordinate → field mapping (subclass-defined).
  • forward_batch(batch) — a default dict-based entry point used by the Trainer/Arena: it reads batch["x"] (or batch["x_col"] for PINN collocation batches) and calls forward.
  • save_checkpoint(path, metadata=None) / a matching load path — writes a dict with state_dict, class_name, and user metadata so a checkpoint can be reloaded without knowing which class produced it ahead of time.
  • family / name class attributes used by the model registry for discovery and reporting.

docs.title: Building a model
docs.text:
Rather than importing architecture classes directly, use the registry:

from pinneapple_neural import build_model

model = build_model("SIREN", in_dim=2, out_dim=1, hidden_dim=64, n_layers=4)

build_model is a thin wrapper over ModelRegistry.build (pinneapple_neural.architectures.registry), which looks the name up in the ModelCatalog and instantiates it with the given kwargs — the same registry the benchmark suite (pinneapple_tools.benchmark_suite) uses to build every model in a comparison run from a plain string name.

docs.title: Available architecture families
docs.text: pinneapple_neural.architectures ships several families, all subclassing BaseModel: PINN-style MLPs (SIREN, ModifiedMLP with Fourier feature embeddings), coordinate encodings (HashGridMLP), neural operators (AFNO and others under neural_operators), graph networks (MeshGraphNet), plus transformer, ROM, reservoir-computing, and classical time-series model families under the same registry. Which family you pick affects only how coordinates map to fields — everything downstream (loss compilation, training, benchmarking) is architecture-agnostic.

docs.title: What a Model is not
docs.text: A Model does not know about boundary conditions, PDE residuals, or optimizers. Those responsibilities belong to ProblemDefinition, PINN / Physics, and Solver respectively. The only contract a Model has to satisfy is: given a batch of coordinates, return a batch of predicted field values.

docs.title: PhysicsModule: composing models and solvers
docs.text:
pinneapple_core.module (also pp.PhysicsModule, pp.Sequential, pp.SolverModule, pp.Hybrid) treats a neural network, a numerical solver and a mix of the two as the same kind of component. Everything is a torch module.

Class Use PhysicsModule base class: subclass it and write forward; gives describe(), num_parameters(), a small fit(x, y) Sequential chain modules, solvers and plain functions; (name, module) pairs name them SolverModule(fn, params, trainable) a differentiable function as a component, e.g. a finite-element solve; autograd flows through it, and the names in trainable become parameters (calibration, identification) SolverModule.from_method(problem, "fem") any pp.solve method (FEM, external code, ...) as a component; not differentiable, so only what follows it trains Hybrid(solver, corrector, mode) residual (u0 + c), multiplicative (u0 (1 + c)) or replace (c); corrector_input chooses what the corrector sees; return_parts=True returns solver output and correction separately 
model = Hybrid(SolverModule(coarse_fem_solve), corrector, corrector_input=lambda args, u0: torch.stack([u0, k(args[0]), x], 1))
model.fit(theta, fine_solution, epochs=600, lr=1e-2, batch_size=32)
print(model.describe())

examples/physics_module/01_coarse_fem_plus_neural_correction.py builds a coarse 6-cell finite-element solve of -(k(x) u')' = 1 with oscillating k plus a dilated convolutional corrector, trained end to end through the solver: held-out relative error 0.31 for the coarse solve alone and 0.10 for the hybrid. Hybrid(..., detach_solver=True) stops gradients into the solver. Model discrepancy decomposition and neural-closure workflows are separate roadmap items (X27, X28).

docs.title: Modelica models as Physics AI data
docs.text:
pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.modelica takes a Modelica model, written as a .mo file, to training data and checked surrogates:

  1. OpenModelica compiles the model into an FMU (FMI 2.0, Co-Simulation or Model Exchange), or simulates it directly.
  2. fmpy runs the FMU over a parameter sweep.
  3. The runs become a dataset, split by run, so the test runs are parameter combinations the model never saw.
  4. The surrogates are trained on that dataset and checked against the physics.
Function What it does omc.build_fmu(models, name, out_dir, fmi_version="2.0", fmu_type="cs") .mo file(s) to an .fmu, via buildModelFMU omc.simulate_mo(models, name, stop_time, parameters=...) Simulates with omc and returns {variable: array} including time. Parameters are applied with -override, so nothing is recompiled omc.omc_available() Returns "local" (omc on the PATH), "docker" (the image openmodelica/openmodelica:v1.24.4-minimal, or PINNEAPPLE_OMC_IMAGE) or None sweep.fmu_sweep(fmu, ranges, n, stop_time, output_interval, outputs, step_size=...) Latin-hypercube sweep on one output grid. Returns an FMUDataset (params, time, outputs, split, save / load) simulate_fmu, fmu_to_upd One FMU run, as arrays or as a PhysicalSample fmi_compat.check_fmus(fmus, exporter) Run FMUs in every interface they offer (CS, ME) and tabulate what passed; see FMI import compatibility

OpenModelica does not need to be installed. If Docker is available, the helpers run omc from the official image and mount only the working directory.

from pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.modelica.omc import build_fmu
from pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.modelica.sweep import fmu_sweep

fmu = build_fmu("LadleCooling.mo", "LadleCooling", "build/")
ds = fmu_sweep(fmu, {"k_lin": (1.5, 4.0), "d_lin": (0.15, 0.35)}, n=80, stop_time=14400,
               output_interval=120, outputs=["T_melt", "T_shell"], step_size=10.0)
train, test = ds.split(16)

Step size of Co-Simulation FMUs. A Co-Simulation FMU from OpenModelica integrates with explicit Euler on the communication step. fmpy uses the output interval as that step, so a coarse output grid can make the FMU inaccurate or unstable. fmu_sweep(step_size=...) simulates on the fine step and interpolates onto the output grid. The tests include a case that fails without it.

docs.title: Examples (examples/modelica/)
docs.text:
The models are in examples/modelica/models/: - DrainingTank.mo: a tank with an inflow, emptying through an orifice by Torricelli's law; - LadleCooling.mo: a hot-metal ladle as three lumped masses (melt, refractory lining, steel shell). The model includes conduction through the lining, radiation from the slag-covered surface, and convection plus radiation from the shell.

Example Result 01_modelica_to_fmu.py FMU and omc agree within 0.13 K on the melt and 0.76 K on the shell over 4 h (fixed-step FMU against DASSL). The run is packed as a PhysicalSample 02_ladle_surrogate.py MLP over 5 inputs and time, trained on 64 FMU runs and tested on 16 unseen ones: see below 03_tank_inverse_pinn.py Discharge coefficient identified from 21 noisy level readings by a PINN: see below

docs.title: Surrogate of the ladle model
docs.text:
The sweep has 80 Latin-hypercube runs over five inputs: lining conductivity and thickness, surface emissivity, tapping temperature and shell convection. The trajectories last 4 h. On the 16 held-out runs:

Neural surrogate Nearest training run Melt temperature RMSE 0.81 K (max 4.0 K) 19.1 K Shell temperature RMSE 1.23 K (max 4.6 K) 27.7 K Time for the melt to reach 1350 °C, mean error 0.6 min 19.0 min Steps where the predicted melt warms up 0 of 1920

The nearest-run baseline shows how much the sweep alone gives. The physical check is that the melt never warms up in the predictions.

docs.title: Discharge coefficient by a PINN
docs.text:
Setup. The FMU runs with the true Cd = 0.62. The readings are 21 levels over the first 300 s, with 5 mm noise. The PINN fits the readings and the mass balance A dh/dt = q_in − Cd a √(2gh) at 200 collocation points over 0–900 s, with Cd as a trainable parameter.

Results.

Cd Level error over 300–900 s (no readings) PINN 0.627 (1.2 % off) 2.9 mm Finite differences on the readings, averaged 0.628 ± 0.020 Network fitted to the readings only 57 mm

On Cd alone, the PINN is no better than averaged finite differences. What it adds is a level model that follows the mass balance where there are no readings.

Tests: tests/test_modelica_omc.py and tests/test_fmi_runner.py. The omc tests check the Torricelli equilibrium, the parameter override, the sweep and the Latin-hypercube strata. They skip when neither omc nor the Docker image is present.

docs.title: Molecular visualisation: proteins on metal surfaces
docs.text:
pinneapple_tools.visualization.molecular (also pp.molecular) shows molecules alone or adsorbed on metal surfaces. It covers the visual side of a protein-on-metal molecular dynamics (MD) pipeline, such as RoyalMD Gold (TheVisualHub/RoyalMD_Gold) runs with OpenMM. It contains no MD engine: anything that gives atom positions can be shown, such as a PDB file, an OpenMM or mdtraj trajectory, or the torch MD of pinneapple_simulation.

Function What it does Molecule.from_pdb, Molecule.from_mdtraj Read atoms, elements, residues and chains; multi-MODEL PDB files give the frames. Also provide the CA backbone trace and the residue class (hydrophobic, polar, positive, negative, special) fcc_slab(metal, facet, nx, ny, layers) fcc slab of Au, Ag, Cu, Pt, Pd, Ni, Al or Pb, with a (111), (100) or (110) top facet, in whole lattice repeats so a periodic box does not strain it slab_for_footprint(xyz, ...) Size the slab from a molecule's footprint plus padding, centred under the molecule orient_on_surface(xyz, masses, active_site, gap) Turn the thinnest principal direction toward the surface normal (broadest face down), turn the active site away from the surface, place the lowest atom gap Å above it render(...) Off-screen still with pyvista: space-filling or backbone tube, coloured by residue class, element, chain or height, on a metallic slab with three-point lighting render_frames(...) + encode_mp4(...) Trajectory as PNG frames (fixed camera or slow orbit, time labels) and an H.264 MP4 (imageio-ffmpeg) md_dashboard(...) Potential energy, temperature, backbone RMSD, height above the surface and contacts over time rmsd, height_above, contacts The analysis behind the dashboard to_glb(...) glTF scene (one mesh per residue class and the metal), for the PINNeAPPle web viewer or any glTF viewer StepLog Numbered, optionally coloured, step-by-step console log of a pipeline

pinneapple_tools.visualization.studio.particles.compose_video adds live charts next to the rendered frames.

from pinneapple_tools.visualization.molecular import Molecule, orient_on_surface, slab_for_footprint, render

mol = Molecule.from_pdb("protein.pdb")
xyz = orient_on_surface(mol.xyz, mol.masses, gap=3.0)
slab, cell, _ = slab_for_footprint(xyz, "Au", "111", padding=6.0)
render(mol, "protein_on_gold.png", xyz=xyz, slab=slab, color_by="residue")            # or style="cartoon"

docs.title: Example: carbonic anhydrase II on Au(111) with OpenMM
docs.text:
examples/molecular/protein_on_gold.py protein.pdb --ps 12 runs these steps:

  1. Repair the structure with pdbfixer.
  2. Orient it on the surface and build an Au(111) slab under its footprint.
  3. Set up Amber14 with GBn2 implicit solvent. Gold acts on every protein atom through the INTERFACE Lennard-Jones parameters (σ = 2.629 Å, ε = 5.29 kcal/mol; Heinz et al. 2008), summed over the lattice as a Steele 10-4-3 wall.
  4. Minimise, then run Langevin dynamics at 300 K.
  5. Write stills, an MP4, the MD dashboard and a glTF scene.

The example uses a flat wall and not explicit gold atoms: on a CPU, explicit atoms inside the implicit solvent cost far more. The pictures still show the explicit slab. A run of tens of picoseconds shows thermal motion and the first contacts. It is a visualisation demonstration, not an equilibrated adsorption study. The OpenMM bridge with verified equilibration is issue #460; explicit slabs, restraints and orientation sampling are issue #461.

Result of the run in the picture: 12 ps of dynamics on 4 CPU cores (about 20 minutes).

  • Temperature settles at 300 K within 4 ps. The early dip comes from the constrained degrees of freedom absorbing the initial velocities.
  • The backbone RMSD rises to 1.9 Å.
  • The number of atoms within 3.5 Å of the gold grows from 1 to 48 while the centre of mass barely moves: side chains reach down to the surface.
  • MP4 of the trajectory, with a slow orbit and a time label.

Tests: tests/test_molecular_viz.py. They check PDB reading, slab geometry (nearest-neighbour distance a/√2 and layer spacing for each facet), orientation, RMSD invariance to rigid motion, renders, glTF and MP4.

docs.title: Audit: electric-motor magnetics and topology optimization
docs.text: Status: merged with the electromagnetics package (user guides: electromagnetics, topology optimisation). Numbers below come from runs of the code (tests in tests/test_motor_magnetics.py, tests/test_topology_optimization.py, examples in examples/motor_magnetics/ and examples/topology_optimization/).
