docs.title: Added (status: exists and verified unless noted)
docs.text:
pinneapple_simulation/electromagnetics/: polar ring mesher with moving band, gmsh importer, P1 A_z solver with Newton (nonlinear B-H), magnets, coils, Dirichlet and (anti-)periodic BCs, Arkkio Maxwell-stress torque and co-energy torque, flux linkage, back-EMF, cogging, Steinmetz/Bertotti iron loss, magnet eddy loss (resistance limited) and a time-harmonic eddy solver with net-current constraints, SPM/reluctance machine model, adjoint torque sensitivities.

pinneapple_design/topology/: density filter, Heaviside projection, OC, MMA (written from Svanberg 1987, dual solved with L-BFGS-B), compliance (MBB, cantilever), thermal compliance, Stokes/Brinkman double pipe, reluctance-rotor torque problem.

Verification (measured): - Wire: A error 1.3e-3 (second order); magnetized cylinder: inner B within 0.14 %; anti-periodic half model identical to full. - Nonlinear iron ring around a wire: B vs B-H curve within 0.3 % (three current levels). - Slotless SPM vs exact subdomain solution: torque within 0.05 % (Maxwell stress) and 0.02 % (co-energy) at n=360, rotor off-grid. - Skin effect in round wire: R and X within 0.1 % of the Bessel solution; low-frequency eddy loss within 0.09 %. - Slotted SPM (4 poles, 24 slots): on-load torque 16.80 vs 16.82 N m (Maxwell vs co-energy); cogging within ~0.01 N m of a ~0.37 N m peak; cogging exactly periodic. - Adjoint torque sensitivities vs finite differences: rel. error < 1e-5 (linear and nonlinear iron). - MMA vs SLSQP on Svanberg's 5-variable problem: same optimum (1.33995636). - MBB 60x20: OC 233.7, MMA 233.5; double pipe: two pipes for 1x1, merged channel for 1.5x1 (qualitative Borrvall-Petersson result).

docs.title: Open points
docs.text:
• Cogging: the original disagreement between Maxwell stress and co-energy came from the moving-band elements (shape changes with angle). Fixed by excluding the band from the Arkkio annulus and differencing co-energy at whole grid steps; remaining difference ~3 % of the peak at n_theta=360 and mesh-pattern dependence of a few % when the slot pitch has an odd number of steps.
  • Optimized reluctance rotor: Maxwell 46.2 vs co-energy 47.1 N m (1.9 %) on the thin-featured design; nonlinear re-evaluation drops mean torque from 38.1 (linear) to 13.4 N m (saturation), so the optimization should use nonlinear iron.
  • Done since: user guides, CHANGELOG, CI step; the Newton solver's stall at a 1e-7 residual (Armijo test below round-off) is fixed.
  • Not done: TEAM benchmark references, transient eddy currents, geometry-parameter surrogate.

docs.title: Multiscale ensembles: scales, filters and closures
docs.text:
An adaptive ensemble (Adaptive ensembles of physics models) picks a model from the errors it made and the physics of the current case. In turbulence that is not enough. Every model answers at a scale:

  • a surrogate is trained on fields at one resolution, with one implicit or explicit filter;
  • an LES resolves the field down to its filter width and models the rest with a closure;
  • a DNS resolves everything down to the dissipation scale.

A question asks for a scale too: the field filtered at some width, a spectrum up to some wavenumber, a time scale. A model that does not resolve those scales cannot answer, however small its validation error. And when it can answer, its output is filtered in a particular way, which the question may not share.

pinneapple_physics.multiscale deals with filtering and closure first and explicitly, then uses the scales to choose models. It is plain numpy, except multiscale.learned (PyTorch).

Module Contents filters box, Gaussian and sharp spectral filters with exact transfer functions; restriction and prolongation between grids; post-filtering from one width to another and how much of the target filter it can reach; filters whose width varies in space, and their commutation error ns2d pseudo-spectral 2-D vorticity DNS and LES (ETDRK4, 2/3 dealiasing), energy spectrum, residual of the vorticity equation closures Smagorinsky, dynamic Smagorinsky, gradient (Clark) model; a-priori and a-posteriori tests; label-free closure health residuals residuals of the filtered equations at several widths, split into subfilter, commutation and model parts consistency cross-scale consistency: the fine prediction, filtered, against the coarse one scales ScaleProfile, ScaleQuery, scale_compatibility, ScaleAwareRouter with a fidelity ladder learned scale-conditioned FNO with a filtering-consistency loss; differentiable LES; closure trained a posteriori viz animation of a run: requested scale, chosen model, spectra, weights

docs.title: Filters
docs.text:
A filter of width Δ acts on each Fourier mode through its transfer function. On a periodic grid it is applied mode by mode, so the transfer function is exact to round-off (tested on single modes). Filters with a uniform width commute with derivatives. In 2-D the filter is the tensor product of the 1-D filters.

kind transfer function Ĝ(k) remarks box sin(kΔ/2) / (kΔ/2) top-hat average; changes sign, with zeros at k = 2πn/Δ Gaussian exp(−k²Δ²/24) same second moment as the box; positive; two Gaussians compose (Δ² = Δ₁² + Δ₂²) sharp 1 for |k| ≤ π/Δ, else 0 spectral cut-off; idempotent 
from pinneapple_physics.multiscale import Filter, apply_filter, refilter, realizability_mismatch, restrict

g = Filter("gaussian", 0.2)
w_bar = apply_filter(w, g)                              # periodic, last two axes
w_coarse = restrict(w_bar, 32)                          # Fourier restriction: integrals preserved to round-off
w_wide = refilter(w_bar, g, Filter("gaussian", 0.5))    # exact: a wider Gaussian from a narrower one
realizability_mismatch(Filter("sharp", 0.3), Filter("gaussian", 0.3), kmax=32)   # > 0: content beyond the cut-off is lost

refilter(u, source, target) applies Ĝ_target / Ĝ_source where that ratio is at most 2. Beyond that ratio the scales are treated as lost: recovering them would only amplify the source's errors. realizability_mismatch measures, weighted by a model spectrum, how much of the target filter cannot be reached. The router uses it.

filter_variable_width(u, kind, delta_field) and commutation_error(u, kind, delta_field, axis) handle a width that varies in space. The commutation error ∂(ū)/∂x − (∂u/∂x)‾ is zero to round-off for a uniform width and non-zero otherwise (Ghosal & Moin 1995). A residual of the filtered equations picks it up from filtering alone, so it must not be blamed on the model.

docs.title: Closures and how to test them
docs.text:
Filtering the momentum equations leaves the subfilter stress τᵢⱼ = (uᵢuⱼ)‾ − ūᵢūⱼ. In 2-D vorticity form the filtered equation gets the tendency −curl(div τ) = −div σ, with the subfilter vorticity flux σⱼ = (uⱼω)‾ − ūⱼω̄. Each closure below is a callable closure(omega, solver) -> tendency for VorticityNS2D(n, nu, closure=...), with a stress(omega, solver) method:

closure model reference Smagorinsky(cs=0.17) τ = −2 (C_s Δ)² |S̄| S̄ Smagorinsky 1963; Lilly 1967 DynamicSmagorinsky() coefficient from the Germano identity between grid and test filter, least squares, domain average, clipped at 0 Germano et al. 1991; Lilly 1992 GradientModel() τ = Δ²/12 ∂ₖūᵢ ∂ₖūⱼ Clark, Ferziger & Reynolds 1979 learned.LearnedClosure periodic CNN that returns the flux σ, so the tendency −div σ conserves circulation trained a posteriori, see below

Tests:

  • apriori_test(w_fine, filter, closure, n_coarse) filters a resolved field and compares the closure, computed from the filtered field, with the exact subfilter terms. It reports the correlation of the stress components and of the tendency, the mean subfilter energy transfer Π = −τᵢⱼS̄ᵢⱼ, and the backscatter fraction (Π < 0), which no eddy viscosity can represent.
  • aposteriori_test(les, w0_bar, ref_bar, times) runs the LES from the filtered initial field. It returns the energy-spectrum error, the field error, the resolved-energy dissipation rate against the reference, the long-run stability and the enstrophy growth.
  • closure_health(w_les, w0_bar, kc, closure=..., solver=...) needs no reference, so it can run in operation:
  • the field must stay finite;
  • resolved enstrophy must not grow in unforced 2-D flow. Advection conserves enstrophy, and viscosity and the forward enstrophy cascade only remove it;
  • the spectrum near the cut-off must not pile up or collapse against the power law of the resolved range;
  • the Germano-identity error germano_error must stay below 1.05. This error is the resolved stress between the grid filter and a test filter, as the closure predicts it, compared through the tendency it produces: 1 means no better than no model, above 1 means worse than no model.

A 2-D result to keep in mind: for Gaussian and box filters the leading-order subfilter stress is τ ≈ Δ²/12 ω (−S̄₁₂, S̄₁₁), the strain rotated by 45° times the vorticity. It is orthogonal to S̄, so an eddy-viscosity stress has near-zero correlation with the true stress (measured −0.03 to 0.00 below), the gradient model has 0.97 to 0.99, and the gradient model's mean energy transfer is zero. The vorticity tendency, which is what the resolved equation sees, correlates 0.1 to 0.4 for all of them. Stress correlations of 0.3 to 0.4, quoted for Smagorinsky in 3-D channel flow, do not carry over to 2-D.

docs.title: Multiscale residuals
docs.text:
from pinneapple_physics.multiscale import ns2d_multiscale_residuals, Filter

r = ns2d_multiscale_residuals(w_t0, w_t1, dt, nu, [Filter("gaussian", d) for d in (0.1, 0.2, 0.4)],
                              subfilter="exact")      # or "dynamic", a closure, or None
print(r.to_markdown())                                # raw | subfilter | commutation | model, per width

The residual of an exact field, filtered, is the subfilter term, not a model error. The table splits it: raw = subfilter + commutation + model. For a resolved DNS pair (64², ν = 10⁻³, Gaussian filters), the model part is 10 % of the raw residual at Δ = 0.2 and 0.3 % at Δ = 0.4. On an exact steady Taylor-Green vortex every part is zero at every width. With white noise added, the residual follows the filter's transfer function (sqrt(mean Ĝ²)), as the tests check. multiscale_residuals(state, residual_fn, filters, subfilter_fn=..., commutation_fn=...) is the generic version for any equation.

docs.title: Cross-scale consistency
docs.text:
from pinneapple_physics.multiscale import cross_scale_consistency

rep = cross_scale_consistency(fine, coarse, coarse_filter=Filter("sharp", L / 16), tol=0.05, gci=None)
rep.passed, rep.field_error, rep.spectrum_error, rep.failed      # e.g. ['circulation (mean)']

The fine prediction is refiltered and restricted to the coarse grid. It is then compared with the coarse prediction on the field, on the spectrum over the shared wavenumbers, and on integrals (circulation, energy, enstrophy, or any {name: fn}). Tolerances can be scaled by a known discretisation error (gci). Restricting an exact field keeps its integrals to round-off. A 32² solver started from the same state as a 64² solver passes. The same 32² solver with a biased source term fails, and the report names the broken integral, circulation (mean). In the ensemble, the scale-conditioned FNO checks itself this way: its prediction at Δ, filtered to 2Δ, against its prediction at 2Δ.

docs.title: Scale-aware selection and adaptive fidelity
docs.text:
from pinneapple_physics.ensemble import PhysicsEnsemble
from pinneapple_physics.multiscale import ScaleAwareRouter, ScaleProfile, ScaleQuery, Filter

profiles = [
    ScaleProfile("fno", Filter("gaussian", 2 * h), h, re_range=(150, 300), fidelity=0),
    ScaleProfile("les_dynamic", Filter("sharp", pi / 16), L / 48, closure="dynamic Smagorinsky", fidelity=1),
    ScaleProfile("dns", Filter("sharp", 0.0), L / 128, re_range=(0, 6000), fidelity=2),
]
router = ScaleAwareRouter(profiles, query_fn=lambda case: ScaleQuery(case["filter"], re=case["re"]))
ens = PhysicsEnsemble(experts, mode="select", router=router,
                      prediction_checks={"les_dynamic": lambda pred, case: les_health(pred, case)})
router.route(ScaleQuery(Filter("sharp", h / 4), re=3000)).reasons[0]   # 'not covered: ... a resolved solver ...'

For each case:

  1. Models whose resolved width (filter width or grid spacing) is larger than the requested width sleep. So do models whose time step is longer than the requested time scale.
  2. Every other model gets a compatibility of exp(−(mismatch/0.25)²) times a Reynolds-range score, where mismatch is the realizability mismatch of the requested filter from the model's own output filter. This compatibility is a prior on the learned weights.
  3. Fidelity ladder: only the lowest rung with a compatible model (≥ 0.3) is awake. A question about small scales goes straight to the solver; a question about large scales stays on the surrogates.
  4. Prediction checks: the label-free closure health of each LES and the consistency check of the scale-conditioned FNO. A failing model is left out of the case, and when every model on the rung fails the ensemble moves up a rung.
  5. The residual look-ahead uses the residual of the filtered equations with the subfilter term removed, at the requested width and at twice it.

docs.title: Models that connect scales
docs.text:
• learned.ScaleConditionedFNO2d(conditioned=True) takes Δ as input: FiLM modulation of every Fourier layer by log Δ. It is trained on one dataset filtered at several widths with fit_scale_conditioned. The filtering_consistency_loss makes its prediction at Δ₁, filtered to Δ₂, equal its prediction at Δ₂. conditioned=False gives the scale-blind network for comparison.
  • learned.TorchVorticityLES2D + LearnedClosure + train_closure_aposteriori: the closure is trained through the solver. The LES is rolled out 60 steps, the loss compares its trajectory and spectra with the filtered DNS, and the gradient goes through every step. as_numpy_closure plugs the result into VorticityNS2D.

docs.title: Experiment: decaying 2-D turbulence with shifting Reynolds number and requested scale
docs.text:
examples/physics_ensemble/multiscale_turbulence.py (benchmark: multiscale.turbulence.DecayingTurbulence2D).

Case. 2-D decaying turbulence on [0, 2π)² at three Reynolds bands, Re = 1/ν = 150-300, 700-1400 and 2800-5000. Each case starts from a random field with its energy spectrum peaked at k = 6, run for 0.5 time units so the cascade develops. A query gives that state and asks for the vorticity 0.28 and 0.30 time units later, filtered at a requested width Δ/h ∈ {1, 2, 4, 6, 8} (h = 2π/64) with a box, Gaussian or sharp filter, on a 64² grid. The independent reference is a 256² DNS filtered at that width. Training data come from a separate 128² DNS (600 cases).

Query streams. Three seeds of 60 queries each, 180 in all. The Reynolds regime shifts low → high → mid. The width and the filter are drawn per query. The initial states are never in training, and the width 6h is not used to train any model.

Experts.

Expert Filter of its output Re range How it was built FNO Gaussian 2h 150-300 supervised CNN Gaussian 4h (32²) 2800-5000 supervised DeepONet sharp 8h 700-1400 supervised MeshGraphNet box 4h (24² torus graph) 700-1400 supervised PINN sharp 8h 150-300 Fourier-Galerkin physics loss only LES 48², three variants sharp, k ≤ 16 any Smagorinsky (C_s 0.17), dynamic Smagorinsky, gradient model DNS 128² ≤ 6000 resolved solver SC-FNO Gaussian 2h..8h (Δ is an input) 700-5000 scale-conditioned, with the filtering-consistency loss LES-learned sharp, k ≤ 16 700-5000 closure trained a posteriori through the solver

Configurations. A is the original ensemble: scale-blind, it filters every output again with the requested filter, and it learns from past errors plus the residual look-ahead. B adds the scale-aware router, realizable post-filtering, and the fidelity ladder with an error tolerance. C adds the closure and consistency checks and the closed multiscale residual. D adds the two scale-linking experts.

Each configuration has a cost/accuracy setting: the weight of the cost for A, the tolerance for B-D. The table sweeps it over all 180 queries.

Configuration (setting) Error, all Error, 1h (n=28) Error, 2h (n=47) Error, 4h (n=47) Error, 6h (n=26) Error, 8h (n=32) Spectrum error Above 25 % Coarser than asked Cost of chosen model (s) Share sent to the DNS A, cost weight 0.1 1.3 % 4.3 % 1.0 % 0.5 % 1.0 % 0.4 % 0.005 1 1 0.85 97 % A, cost weight 0.5 22.3 % 32.1 % 27.0 % 19.9 % 16.8 % 15.1 % 0.199 57 25 0.073 4 % A, cost weight 5 23.7 % 36.0 % 29.6 % 20.0 % 16.8 % 15.1 % 0.326 61 29 0.036 0 % B, tolerance 0.1 7.1 % 3.3 % 4.8 % 7.9 % 9.7 % 10.4 % 0.021 6 0 0.59 42 % C, tolerance 0.1 7.0 % 3.3 % 4.8 % 7.8 % 9.4 % 10.1 % 0.018 6 0 0.59 42 % D, tolerance 0.1 7.2 % 3.3 % 6.2 % 8.3 % 7.6 % 10.3 % 0.018 5 0 0.69 34 % B, tolerance 0.25 11.1 % 3.3 % 15.6 % 12.1 % 10.2 % 10.5 % 0.031 11 0 0.42 23 % C, tolerance 0.25 10.8 % 3.3 % 15.4 % 12.1 % 9.8 % 9.6 % 0.025 16 0 0.45 24 % D, tolerance 0.25 12.8 % 3.3 % 19.9 % 13.5 % 9.7 % 11.9 % 0.032 15 0 0.43 16 % B, tolerance 0.5 17.3 % 3.3 % 22.8 % 16.3 % 18.6 % 21.8 % 0.057 42 0 0.32 16 % C, tolerance 0.5 17.9 % 3.3 % 25.2 % 16.2 % 18.6 % 22.1 % 0.055 54 0 0.33 16 % D, tolerance 0.5 16.6 % 3.3 % 24.5 % 16.8 % 14.9 % 17.5 % 0.056 52 0 0.18 16 % Always the DNS (also the best expert in hindsight) 0.9 % 0.87 100 %

Errors are relative L2 against the filtered reference. The spectrum error is the mean |log₁₀ E/E_ref| up to the requested cut-off. "Above 25 %" counts queries whose error is above 25 %. "Coarser than asked" counts queries answered by a model whose resolved width is larger than the requested one. Costs are median CPU wall times.

What the numbers say:

  • The scale-blind ensemble does not know when it cannot answer. With any weight on cost it moves from the DNS to the surrogates for every query, including the finest ones. It then answers 25-29 queries with a model coarser than the request, and its error at the finest width is 32-36 %. The scale-aware configurations never answer below a model's resolved scale, and keep 3.3 % at 1h at every tolerance, because those queries go to the DNS. Their tolerance gives operating points between "always DNS" and "always surrogate" (7 % error at 0.59 s, 17 % at 0.18-0.33 s), which the cost weight of A does not reach: it jumps from 1.3 % to 22 %.
  • In mean error per unit cost they do not beat the scale-blind ensemble here. On this small 2-D problem on a CPU, the 128² DNS costs 0.87 s, about the same as an LES with the dynamic or learned closure (1.2-1.5 s with closure overhead), so the LES rung saves nothing. The DNS is also the best model on almost every query. With 3-D turbulence, where an LES is orders of magnitude cheaper than a DNS, the ladder pays off; this experiment does not show that.
  • The closure checks work on the closure that is wrong. The label-free check flags static Smagorinsky (C_s = 0.17) on all 180 queries. Its Germano-identity error is 1.35, worse than no model, and a posteriori it dissipates 1.5×, 3.5× and 7.9× too much resolved energy in the low, mid and high bands. The check never flags the dynamic, gradient or learned closures, which are not over-dissipative here. The gradient model did not become unstable before t = 2 in these cases, so nothing was flagged for it. C's gain over B is small (10.8 % against 11.1 % at the 0.25 tolerance; the same at 0.1), because the Smagorinsky LES was rarely the model chosen anyway.
  • The scale-linking models are mixed.
  • The closure trained a posteriori is the best LES in every band. Its spectrum error is 0.008-0.013 against 0.038-0.052 for the classical closures. Its field error is 10-18 % against 17-37 %, and its dissipation ratio is 0.98-1.41.
  • The scale-conditioned FNO beats the scale-blind network at large widths: 16.1 % against 16.7 % at the held-out 6h, and 16.1 % against 20.1 % at 8h.
  • But it loses to separate fixed-width FNOs post-filtered exactly: 11.2 % at 6h, 9.5 % at 8h. #604's acceptance criterion is therefore not met.
  • In the ensemble, D gives the cheapest point at the 0.5 tolerance (0.18 s, 16.6 %) and no gain elsewhere.

Closures on held-out cases (8 per band, LES 48², sharp filter k ≤ 16, a posteriori to t = 0.3, stability to t = 2):

Re band Closure Stress corr. Tendency corr. Germano error Spectrum error Field error Dissipation LES/DNS Flagged low no model 0.039 17.0 % 0.99 0 % low Smagorinsky 0.17 -0.00 0.13 1.37 0.047 17.3 % 1.55 100 % low dynamic Smagorinsky -0.00 0.13 1.00 0.038 16.8 % 1.02 0 % low gradient 0.29 0.20 0.97 0.040 19.5 % 0.99 0 % low learned, a posteriori 0.32 0.008 10.1 % 0.98 0 % mid no model 0.046 28.0 % 0.91 0 % mid Smagorinsky 0.17 -0.00 0.15 1.36 0.055 26.4 % 3.47 100 % mid dynamic Smagorinsky -0.00 0.15 1.00 0.044 27.7 % 1.00 0 % mid gradient 0.32 0.21 0.98 0.051 33.3 % 0.88 0 % mid learned, a posteriori 0.34 0.011 16.3 % 1.07 0 % high no model 0.046 31.1 % 0.62 0 % high Smagorinsky 0.17 0.00 0.15 1.35 0.051 28.9 % 7.94 100 % high dynamic Smagorinsky -0.00 0.15 1.00 0.045 30.8 % 0.88 0 % high gradient 0.33 0.20 0.99 0.052 37.0 % 0.46 0 % high learned, a posteriori 0.32 0.013 18.3 % 1.41 0 %

The true backscatter fraction (Π < 0) is 0.49 in every band. The eddy viscosities have none; the gradient model has 0.46-0.48. In 2-D the dynamic coefficient comes out almost zero, so dynamic Smagorinsky behaves like no model. The field errors at t = 0.3 are dominated by the loss of correlation of the small scales, which a closure cannot recover. The spectrum is the measure that tells the closures apart.

Scale-conditioned FNO on held-out cases (n = 80, Gaussian targets; the training widths were 2h, 4h and 8h):

Width Scale-conditioned Scale-blind Best fixed-width, post-filtered Spectrum error Consistency (Δ vs 2Δ) 1h (extrapolation) 38.0 % 32.5 % n/a 0.731 18.8 % 2h 26.1 % 24.0 % 26.0 % 0.077 8.9 % 4h 17.6 % 15.5 % 15.3 % 0.029 11.9 % 6h (held out) 16.1 % 16.7 % 11.2 % 0.034 8h 16.1 % 20.1 % 9.5 % 0.039

Limits of this experiment.

  • It is 2-D, decaying and small.
  • Several surrogates are weak, with CPU-sized training: the DeepONet's relative training MSE was 0.66 and the PINN's relative Galerkin residual 0.51.
  • The output horizon (0.3 time units, about two eddy turnovers) decorrelates the small scales.
  • One training run per model.
  • Re-running with more training, a 3-D LES/DNS pair or forced turbulence is the next step.

Every number above is regenerated by python examples/physics_ensemble/multiscale_turbulence.py, then --stage sweep --seed s for s = 0, 1, 2, then --stage sweep-report.

docs.title: Rigid bodies with NVIDIA Newton
docs.text:
pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.newton_physics runs rigid-body scenes with Newton (Apache-2.0, built on NVIDIA Warp). Newton runs on CPU or GPU and offers several rigid-body solvers; PINNeAPPle wraps them behind one scene description, records the trajectory in SI units and checks a solver setting against closed-form results before it is used in a study.

pip install newton                 # core: XPBD, semi-implicit, Featherstone
pip install "newton[examples]"     # adds the viewer, mesh/URDF/USD importers and MuJoCo-Warp

docs.title: Scene, run, result
docs.text:
from pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.newton_physics import RigidScene, simulate

scene = RigidScene(gravity=9.81).ground(mu=0.4)
scene.box("crate", (0.1, 0.1, 0.1), pos=(0, 0, 0.1), vel=(2.0, 0, 0), mu=0.4)   # half extents [m]
bob = scene.sphere("bob", 0.05, pos=(0.17, 0, 1.0))
scene.revolute(-1, bob, anchor=(0, 0, 2.0), axis=(0, 1, 0))                    # hinge to the world

traj = simulate(scene, duration=2.0, dt=1e-3, solver="xpbd", record_every=10)
traj.pos, traj.quat, traj.vel, traj.omega      # (T, N, 3|4), quaternions (w, x, y, z)
traj.energy()["total"]                         # kinetic + potential [J]
traj.to_upd()                                  # PhysicalSample for datasets and surrogates
traj.to_rigid_body_state()                     # torch state for the differentiable rigid_body module
  • Shapes: sphere, box, capsule, cylinder and mesh (closed triangle mesh, e.g. from an STL). Mass comes from density (default 1000 kg/m³) or is set exactly with mass=.
  • Joints: revolute (hinge through an anchor about an axis, both given in world coordinates at t = 0) and fixed. Joints form trees; a body that is the parent of a joint but has no parent itself gets a free joint to the world.
  • scene.check() lists problems (non-positive sizes, a body with two parents, invalid friction) before any solver is touched; the description imports without Newton installed.
  • Solvers: "xpbd" (default), "semi_implicit", "featherstone" and "mujoco" (needs newton[sim]). Initial body velocities are set for the maximal-coordinate solvers (XPBD, semi-implicit).

docs.title: Check the solver before trusting it
docs.text:
validate(solver) runs six scenes with a closed-form answer and reports simulated value, reference, error and pass/fail. Results on CPU, dt = 1 ms (bounce 0.1 ms), Newton 1.6.1:

check reference XPBD Featherstone semi-implicit free fall, max error / drop height z0 − g t²/2 0.20 % ✓ 0.20 % ✓ 0.20 % ✓ box sliding with friction μ = 0.4 stops at v0²/(2μg) = 0.510 m 0.509 m, 0.20 % ✓ – 0.282 m, 45 % ✗ pendulum period, 5° 2π√(I/(mgL)) = 2.007 s 2.010 s, 0.17 % ✓ 2.008 s, 0.05 % ✓ unstable ✗ rebound with restitution e = 0.5 e² h = 0.250 m 0.250 m, 0.05 % ✓ – 0.068 m ✗ torque-free spin, angular momentum drift 0 0.30 % ✓ – 0.29 % ✓ box resting on the ground for 2 s no sinking, no drift 2 µm ✓ 8.2 mm ✗ 8.2 mm ✗

What the table says:

  • XPBD passes all six and is the default for contact-rich scenes. It is slightly dissipative: a 10° pendulum loses about 2.6 % of its swing energy in 2 s at dt = 1 ms.
  • Featherstone is the most accurate for joint chains (pendulum period within 0.05 %), but with its default penalty contact a 0.2 m box sinks 8 mm into the ground; use it for articulated mechanisms, not stacking or impacts.
  • Semi-implicit uses penalty contacts and needs a much smaller step and tuned contact stiffness (ke, kd) for friction, restitution and hinges; with the defaults at 1 ms it fails four checks, and validate says so.

Checks marked "–" need initial body velocities, which are set only for the maximal-coordinate solvers.

  • runner.py: simulate(), RigidTrajectory (energy, UPD export, .npz save).
  • validation.py: the six analytic checks and validate().
  • Tests: tests/test_newton_rigid.py (scene checks run without Newton; the solver tests are skipped when it is not installed).

docs.title: Non-Hermitian physics: PT-symmetric dimers and exceptional-point tuning
docs.text: pinneapple_physics.non_hermitian (also pp.non_hermitian) models PT-symmetric dimers and chains, finds their exceptional points (EPs), and checks whether a control parameter can move an EP along a desired law. It implements and verifies the no-go theorem of "A No-Go Theorem for Exceptional-Point Tuning in PT-Symmetric Dimers" (Zenodo record 23287622).

docs.title: The dimer and its exceptional point
docs.text:
H = [[ε + iγ, b], [b*, −iγ + ε]] is PT symmetric: P H* P = H, with P = σx. Its eigenvalues are ε ± sqrt(|b|² − γ²).

  • For γ < |b| the spectrum is real (unbroken phase).
  • At γ = |b| the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors coalesce. This is the EP.
  • Beyond it the eigenvalues form a complex-conjugate pair (broken phase).

PTDimer returns the following:

Quantity Method Closed-form EP location ep_gamma EP found from the matrix alone (independent check) ep_gamma_numeric Phase (unbroken, EP or broken) phase Eigenvector overlap, which goes to 1 at the EP eigenvector_overlap Petermann factor, which diverges at the EP petermann_factor Square-root splitting near the EP splitting

PTChain does the same for N sites. There the EP can be of higher order: the trimer's is an EP3 at γ = √2 |b|.

docs.title: The no-go theorem, checked symbolically
docs.text:
import sympy as sp
from pinneapple_physics.non_hermitian import analyze_ep_tuning
from pinneapple_physics.non_hermitian.ep_tuning import _symbols

lam, J, G = _symbols()                      # lam real, J > 0, G real; target gamma_EP^2 = J^2 + lam J G
print(analyze_ep_tuning(J + sp.Symbol("c") * lam))
# gamma_EP^2(lam) = J**2 + J*c*lam + J*lam*conjugate(c) + c*lam**2*conjugate(c)
# class: reciprocal polynomial; exact target realised: NO; degree in lam: 2
# no-go theorem APPLIES: exact linear tuning is impossible in this class
print(analyze_ep_tuning(sp.sqrt(J**2 + lam*J*G)).exact)   # True  (route A, PT symmetric)
print(analyze_ep_tuning(J, J + lam*G).exact)               # True  (route C, PT broken)

For a reciprocal coupling b(λ) = J + c₁λ + … + cₙλⁿ, the EP law γ_EP² = |b(λ)|² is a polynomial of degree 2n whose leading coefficient |cₙ|² is positive. It therefore cannot equal the linear target. The report gives:

  • the EP law and its degree;
  • the residual against the target;
  • the class of the coupling;
  • which of the four assumptions hold (A PT symmetry, B dimension 2, C polynomial coupling, D reciprocity);
  • whether the theorem applies.

The classes and the ways around the obstruction:

Coupling EP law Exact linear tuning? PT symmetric? Phase only, J e^{iφ(λ)} J², fixed no yes Reciprocal polynomial, J + cλ + … degree ≥ 2 no (no-go) yes Route A, √(J² + λJ⟨G⟩) J² + λJ⟨G⟩ yes yes Route B, state-dependent feedback (conjecture) see note yes Route C, non-reciprocal: b_ab = J, b_ba = J + λ⟨G⟩ J² + λJ⟨G⟩ yes no

Note on route B. feedback_coupling updates the coupling from a measurement of itself with a polynomial map, b ← (b + (J² + λJ⟨G⟩)/b)/2. Its fixed point is the route-A coupling. This shows that feedback can produce the non-polynomial dependence the theorem rules out for static couplings. It is an illustration, not a proof of the paper's Conjecture 1 for any physical feedback mechanism.

docs.title: The hypothesis map as a physics audit
docs.text:
theorem_profile() states assumptions A–D as a physics_audit.ModelProfile, and design_features(H, polynomial) reads them from a device Hamiltonian. Auditing a design then says whether the theorem constrains it:

  • all assumptions VALID: linear tuning is out of reach for this design;
  • an assumption VIOLATED: the theorem does not apply, and the violated assumption names the route that opened up.
from pinneapple_physics.physics_audit import audit_assumptions
from pinneapple_physics.non_hermitian import theorem_profile, design_features, PTDimer, route_c_asymmetric

ab, ba = route_c_asymmetric(1.0, 0.5)
print(audit_assumptions(theorem_profile(), design_features(PTDimer(ab, ba).hamiltonian(0.5, 1.0), polynomial=True)))
# no_go_ep_linear_tuning: VIOLATED ... [VIOLATED] pt_symmetry ... [VIOLATED] reciprocal_coupling ...

docs.title: Beyond the dimer
docs.text:
For a chain with uniform coupling, H(γ, b) = |b| H(γ/|b|, 1) after a gauge transformation. So γ_EP = κ_N |b| exactly, and the dimer's obstruction carries over to every N. Numerically, κ_N² is:

N κ_N² EP order 2 1 EP2 3 2 EP3 4 1 EP2 5 1.5 EP3

This scaling argument does not cover chains where the control parameter changes only some bonds. That case is the paper's open question Q2 (Conjecture 2).

Tests: tests/test_non_hermitian.py. Figure: pinneapple_physics.non_hermitian.viz.ep_tuning_figure.

docs.title: Faster implicit pressure solves in OpenFOAM
docs.text: pinneapple_simulation.accelerated_foam makes the pressure solve of an OpenFOAM run cheaper. It changes only the initial guess of the linear solve. OpenFOAM's own solver (PCG, GAMG, ...) still iterates, with the same tolerance and the same stopping test, so the converged fields pass the same convergence test as a plain run (section 2 shows why an equal residual is not always an equal error, and compares at matched accuracy). Every number on this page comes from a run made with the code in this package, and each one is compared with plain OpenFOAM on the same case at the same settings.

docs.title: Where the time goes
docs.text:
In a pressure-based solver (PISO in icoFoam/pisoFoam, PIMPLE in pimpleFoam/interFoam, SIMPLE in simpleFoam) every corrector assembles and solves a Poisson-type equation for the pressure (p, or p_rgh with gravity): fvm::laplacian(rAU, p) == fvc::div(phiHbyA). The matrix is symmetric and negative definite, it is new at every corrector because rAU changes, and it is solved by PCG (DIC or FDIC preconditioner) or GAMG. Momentum, turbulence and phase-fraction equations are much cheaper to solve. They are diagonally dominant and need a few smoother sweeps. The pressure equation is elliptic, so its iteration count grows with the mesh.

The logs of the runs below show this directly. On the 128 x 128 cavity with PCG-DIC, the pressure needed 34 239 iterations over 256 solves, while the velocity components needed 1 478 + 1 492 symmetric Gauss-Seidel sweeps over 128 solves each. At 256 x 256 the figures were 74 261 against 2 540 + 2 579. Each pressure iteration also costs more than a smoother sweep, because it adds a preconditioner application and two global reductions. Profiling studies by GPU-solver vendors also treat the pressure solve as the part worth offloading. One NVIDIA presentation reports that the pressure solve is still "about 35% of total" after offloading it to AmgX (OpenFOAM workshop 2020; we could not open the slides, so this figure comes from search excerpts). We found no peer-reviewed CPU breakdown for PISO/PIMPLE that we could verify, so this page relies on our own logs.

docs.title: What exists, and what it costs to use
docs.text:
Tool What it does Licence Use here PETSc4FOAM (gitlab.com/petsc/petsc4foam, upstream develop.openfoam.com/modules/external-solver) ldu2csr conversion and PETSc/Hypre solvers behind solver petsc; (BoomerAMG, GPU back-ends, matrix caching) GPL-3.0-or-later (README and LICENSE) Not used. It is a separate build against PETSc. AmgX (github.com/NVIDIA/AMGX) GPU algebraic multigrid and Krylov BSD-3-Clause Not used: there is no GPU here. amgx4Foam (github.com/SimFlowCFD/foamExternalSolvers) OpenFOAM to AmgX bridge No LICENSE file in that repository; the Cineca original was not reachable Not used: the licence is unknown. Ginkgo (github.com/ginkgo-project/ginkgo) Portable sparse linear algebra (CUDA/HIP/SYCL/OpenMP), including mixed precision BSD-3-Clause Not used. OGL (github.com/hpsim/OGL; Olenik et al., Meccanica 2024, doi:10.1007/s11012-024-01806-1) Ginkgo solvers as OpenFOAM lduMatrix solvers GPL-3.0 Not used. RapidCFD (github.com/Atizar/RapidCFD-dev) OpenFOAM fork with everything on CUDA GPLv3 Not used. It is a fork, not a plugin. pyamg Smoothed-aggregation and classical AMG in Python MIT Optional, for the Python benchmarks

None of these is a dependency of PINNeAPPle, and no code from them is copied into the repository. The pinneWarmStart plugin is our own code. It is written against OpenFOAM's public lduMatrix::solver interface, the same runtime-selection mechanism that PETSc4FOAM and OGL use. OpenFOAM is GPL-3.0-or-later: this repository contains no OpenFOAM source, and the plugin binary you build links against your installed libOpenFOAM.so, so that binary falls under OpenFOAM's licence if you distribute it.

Ideas from the literature, and which ones were tried. Learned multigrid and preconditioners: Greenfeld et al. 2019 (arXiv:1902.10248), Luz et al. 2020 (arXiv:2003.05744), Li et al. ICML 2023 (PMLR 202), and Häusner et al. "Neural incomplete factorization" (arXiv:2305.16368). Learned pressure predictions or initial guesses: Tompson et al. 2017 (arXiv:1607.03597), CFD-GCN (arXiv:2007.04439), and a neural initial guess for pressure-velocity coupling (arXiv:2409.07175). Projection of a new right-hand side on earlier solutions: Fischer 1998, CMAME 163:193-204, which PETSc implements as KSPGUESSFISCHER. POD/ROM predictors as initial guesses: Markovinović & Jansen 2006, IJNME 68:525-541. Mixed-precision iterative refinement: Carson & Higham 2018, SISC 40:A817. The arXiv and DOI pages could not be opened from the build environment, so these references were checked through their abstracts and listings, not read in full.

We tried four of them, all measured below:

  1. Fischer projection on past solutions, in C++ inside OpenFOAM.
  2. POD of earlier runs.
  3. A learned graph-network correction of the guess.
  4. Mixed-precision CG.

We also tried AMG through pyamg, offline only.

docs.title: What this package does
docs.text:
OpenFOAM pressure corrector
   fvMatrix::solve -> lduMatrix::solver::New("pinneWarmStart")
      1. x_prev = incoming p (what plain OpenFOAM starts from)
      2. guess x0:  projection on the last k solutions  (C++, k mat-vecs)
                    or a Python guesser via named pipes (POD of earlier runs, learned network, ...)
      3. safeguard: keep x0 only if sum|b - A x0| < sum|b - A x_prev|
      4. inner OpenFOAM solver (PCG/DIC, GAMG, ...) from x0, same tolerance;
         relTol measured against the residual of x_prev, so a run stops where a plain run would
      5. store the solution; optionally write A, b, x_prev, x to disk

plugin/pinneWarmStart.C is the solver wrapper (about 500 lines). To use it, set this in fvSolution:

p
{
    solver          pinneWarmStart;
    innerSolver     PCG;            // or GAMG, with its usual entries
    preconditioner  DIC;
    tolerance       1e-6;
    relTol          0.05;
    guess           projection;     // none | projection | external
    nSnapshots      8;
    snapshots       all;            // all | converged: keep only solutions of relTol 0 solves
    applyTo         all;            // all | converged: change the guess of relTol 0 solves only
    dumpDir         "";             // write every system (lduMatrix arrays) to this directory
    pipeDir         "";             // guess external: request/reply FIFOs served by Python
}

Also load the library from controlDict with libs ("<path>/libpinneWarmStart.so");.

The projection guess is the Galerkin projection on the span of the last k solutions and the current field: x0 = X (X^T A X)^-1 X^T b, built with the matrix and right-hand side of the current solve. Because x_prev is in the span, the A-norm error of x0 is never larger than that of x_prev. This is the default guess that plain OpenFOAM uses. The cost is k matrix-vector products, k(k+1)/2 dot products and a k x k solve, which is a few inner iterations' worth. The C++ code does a symmetric elimination with diagonal pivoting that drops linearly dependent snapshots. It runs in parallel, because the reductions use gSumProd/gSumMag and the history is kept per processor.

relTolReference previous (the default) handles the case where OpenFOAM's relTol is relative to the initial residual. With a better guess, the same relTol would ask for a smaller absolute residual. That makes the solve more accurate but not cheaper, and the run would no longer be comparable with a plain run. The wrapper therefore turns relTol into the absolute tolerance max(tolerance, relTol * r(x_prev)), the point where a plain run stops.

Building. build.build_plugin() compiles the wrapper with the installed compiler against libOpenFOAM.so:

  • With a full OpenFOAM installation ($FOAM_SRC/OpenFOAM/lnInclude), it uses those headers. wmake libso also works with plugin/Make.
  • With a binary-only package such as Ubuntu's openfoam (v1912), there are no headers. Use the source of the same version instead (apt-get source openfoam with a deb-src entry), passed as openfoam_src or $PINNEAPPLE_OPENFOAM_SRC. The headers are only read at build time.

Python side:

  • ldu: reads the dumped systems and converts them to SciPy CSR or PyTorch sparse matrices. It also computes OpenFOAM's normalised residual (normFactor).
  • solvers: PCG with Jacobi, DIC (the same algorithm as OpenFOAM's), or pyamg AMG preconditioners, plus a PyTorch CG. The PyTorch CG runs in float64, or in mixed precision with float32 inner CG and float64 refinement. All of them use OpenFOAM's stopping test.
  • warm_start: ProjectionWarmStart (the same algorithm as the C++ code) and PODWarmStart (a POD of earlier runs plus recent solutions).
  • learned: LearnedWarmStart, the projection plus a graph-network correction. It is trained on dumped systems and safeguarded.
  • guess_server: serves any of these guesses to a running solver through named pipes.
  • case: writes the cavity case, runs and parses logs, and compares fields.
  • benchmark: the comparisons on this page, including tutorial_comparison for an installed tutorial.

FreeSurfaceFlow (numerical_solvers/free_surface.py) accepts pressure_solver= and libs=, so its p_rgh solve can be warm-started.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
Extraction is exact. A run with guess none; dumpDir systems; writes every pressure system as OpenFOAM handed it to PCG. Re-solving those systems in Python with the DIC-PCG of solvers.pcg, starting from the dumped x_prev, gives:

  • the same iteration count as the OpenFOAM log, solve by solve;
  • the same initial residual to about 1e-15 relative;
  • a solution within about 1e-14 (relative L2) of OpenFOAM's.

test_openfoam_dump_is_reproduced_by_python checks this on a 16 x 16 cavity.

Fields are unchanged within solver tolerance. Every comparison runs three versions of the same case:

  1. plain OpenFOAM;
  2. the same inner solver wrapped by pinneWarmStart;
  3. a reference whose pressure is solved to tolerance 1e-11; relTol 0 (1e-12 for damBreak).

The tables report the relative L2 difference of the final fields between runs. "vs plain" is the warm-started run against plain OpenFOAM. "vs ref" measures each run against the tightly converged reference. The plain run's own "vs ref" value is the size of the error that the solver tolerance allows.

All runs used one core of the same machine (4-core VM, no GPU) with OpenFOAM v1912 from the Ubuntu 24.04 package. Wall times are the best of two runs of the solver process.

docs.title: 1. Lid-driven cavity, PISO (icoFoam), standard settings
docs.text:
Settings: Re = 100, Courant number 0.5, 128 time steps, 2 PISO correctors. Pressure tolerance 1e-6 with relTol 0.05, and relTol 0 for pFinal. pinneWarmStart uses projection on the last 8 solutions around the same inner solver.

case inner run p solves p iterations wall [s] dp vs plain dU vs plain dp vs ref dU vs ref cavity 128x128 PCG-DIC plain 256 34 239 13.11 - - 2.8e-4 1.2e-7 cavity 128x128 PCG-DIC warm 256 11 197 7.19 2.6e-4 1.8e-7 3.8e-5 1.5e-7 cavity 128x128 GAMG plain 256 1 590 5.02 - - 9.9e-4 1.2e-6 cavity 128x128 GAMG warm 256 501 4.32 9.8e-4 1.7e-6 1.8e-5 5.5e-7 cavity 256x256 PCG-DIC plain 256 74 261 112.8 - - 3.2e-3 1.5e-7 cavity 256x256 PCG-DIC warm 256 30 041 61.3 3.1e-3 4.1e-7 5.8e-5 3.6e-7 cavity 256x256 GAMG plain 256 2 955 32.8 - - 4.5e-3 1.3e-6 cavity 256x256 GAMG warm 256 979 25.9 4.4e-3 2.3e-6 3.9e-5 1.1e-6

How the speed-ups break down:

  • Iterations: 3.1x fewer (PCG, 128), 2.5x fewer (PCG, 256), 3.2x fewer (GAMG, 128) and 3.0x fewer (GAMG, 256).
  • Whole-run wall time: 1.83x and 1.84x with PCG, 1.16x and 1.27x with GAMG.

The pressure difference to plain OpenFOAM (2.6e-4 to 4.4e-3) is the same size as the plain run's own distance to the tightly converged reference (2.8e-4 to 4.5e-3). That distance comes from relTol 0.05, not from the warm start.

The warm-started run is 7-115x closer to the reference in pressure. This is because it stops at the same absolute residual as plain but starts from a much better point in the non-final correctors. The velocity agrees with the reference to 1e-6 or better in every run.

docs.title: 2. The same cavity with relTol 0 everywhere: matched accuracy
docs.text:
With relTol 0, both runs stop at the same absolute normalised residual. Even so, the warm-started solution carries more algebraic error. The projection leaves error in smooth, low-eigenvalue modes, which the L1 residual under-weights.

In this closed cavity, most of that error is the pressure level (the near-null mode fixed only by pRefCell). Re-solving the dumped 64 x 64 systems offline against exact solutions (spsolve) gives a relative error of 5e-7 for plain and 4e-6 for warm at the same residual, mostly in the mean level. The fair comparison is therefore at equal accuracy: tighten the warm start's tolerance until its error against the reference is no larger than plain's.

case run p iterations wall [s] dp vs ref dp vs ref (mean removed) dU vs ref cavity 64x64 plain PCG-DIC, tol 1e-6 11 796 1.34 9.2e-7 9.2e-7 1.2e-8 cavity 64x64 warm, tol 1e-6 5 054 0.89 4.1e-5 8.2e-6 3.1e-8 cavity 64x64 warm, tol 1e-7 7 370 1.09 4.2e-6 5.2e-7 3.4e-9 cavity 64x64 warm, tol 1e-8 9 616 1.33 1.1e-6 9.8e-8 4.7e-10 cavity 128x128 plain PCG-DIC, tol 1e-6 46 844 17.52 1.5e-6 1.5e-6 5.3e-9 cavity 128x128 warm, tol 1e-6 11 435 7.92 4.6e-5 3.3e-6 1.1e-8 cavity 128x128 warm, tol 1e-7 19 782 10.35 2.2e-6 2.7e-7 9.9e-10 cavity 128x128 warm, tol 1e-8 29 227 13.36 2.5e-7 1.2e-8 1.2e-10

At equal or better accuracy in every field, the warm start is 1.31x faster on 128 x 128 (13.4 s vs 17.5 s, tolerance 1e-8 vs 1e-6). On 64 x 64 it gives nothing (1.33 s vs 1.34 s). At the same tolerance it is 2.2x faster on 128 x 128 (1.5x on 64 x 64), but with a 30x larger pressure error (still at the 1e-5 level) and the same velocity to 3e-8.

Recommendation: pair pinneWarmStart with a tolerance about 10-100x tighter than the plain run's when the pressure itself is a quantity of interest. Settings with relTol > 0 in the non-final correctors, the usual PISO/PIMPLE practice (table 1), do not need this.

docs.title: 3. Free surface: damBreak (interFoam, p_rgh), refined 2x
docs.text:
The case is the v1912 tutorial, refined 2x to 9 072 cells, run to t = 0.25 s. It uses PIMPLE with 3 correctors. p_rgh uses PCG-DIC with tolerance 1e-7 and relTol 0.05, and relTol 0 for p_rghFinal. The reference uses tolerance 1e-12 with relTol 0.

run p_rgh iterations wall [s] dp_rgh vs plain dp_rgh vs ref dU vs ref dalpha vs ref plain PCG-DIC 23 355 9.24-10.03 - 1.5e-2 2.3e-2 7.8e-3 warm, all solves 31 964 12.32 1.0e-2 6.9e-3 1.0e-2 3.8e-3 warm, snapshots converged 25 429 10.82 7.8e-3 8.5e-3 1.5e-2 4.3e-3 warm, snapshots converged; applyTo converged 23 346 9.41 2.6e-7 1.5e-2 2.3e-2 7.8e-3

No gain here. The interface moves through the mesh and changes the density in the matrix from step to step, so old solutions are a poor basis. In the second corrector, the projected guess has about the same residual as the field it replaces, but its error is smoother: PCG needed 58 iterations where plain needed 12 for the same reduction (read from the logs).

Restricting the projection to the final solves (applyTo converged) makes the wrapper neutral (23 346 vs 23 355 iterations, fields identical to 3e-7). The overhead of the wrapper is then 1.8% of wall time (9.41 s vs 9.24 s).

The differences to the reference are at the 1e-2 level for every run, including plain. This transient is sensitive to the pressure tolerance itself.

docs.title: 4. Offline: Python solvers and guesses on the same systems
docs.text:
The systems are the 128 pressure systems of a 64 x 64 cavity (lid speed 1, relTol 0 everywhere), dumped by guess none. Each is re-solved to tolerance 1e-6 starting from each guess. Times are Python times, which are only comparable within this table: the NumPy DIC uses SciPy triangular solves and is far slower per iteration than OpenFOAM's C++.

The POD basis comes from the 256 systems of two other runs, at lid speeds 0.8 and 1.2 (a two-point design of experiments), and keeps rank 9 for 99.9999% of the energy. The last 8 solutions of the current run are added to it.

The graph network has 4 layers and a width of 32. It was trained for 150 epochs (390 s on the CPU) on 128 systems of those two runs. Its mean training residual ratio went from 1.0 to 0.53.

guess solver iterations solve [s] guess [s] mean initial residual previous field (OpenFOAM) PCG-DIC 11 796 31.8 0 1.9e-2 previous field PCG-Jacobi 39 762 3.29 0 1.9e-2 previous field PCG-AMG (pyamg) 695 3.72 0 1.9e-2 previous field Jacobi-CG, PyTorch f64 39 762 22.1 0 1.9e-2 previous field Jacobi-CG, PyTorch f32 + f64 refinement 48 508 6.49 0 1.9e-2 projection, last 8 PCG-DIC 2 743 8.92 0.12 1.2e-2 projection, last 8 PCG-AMG (pyamg) 282 3.31 0.12 1.2e-2 POD of 2 earlier runs + last 8 PCG-DIC 2 128 6.88 0.34 3.8e-4 POD of 2 earlier runs + last 8 PCG-AMG (pyamg) 253 3.42 0.34 3.8e-4 projection + learned correction PCG-DIC 2 683 7.85 1.99 8.7e-3 projection + learned correction PCG-AMG (pyamg) 273 3.27 1.90 8.7e-3

What the table shows:

  • Projection. It cuts DIC-PCG iterations 4.3x and AMG-PCG iterations 2.5x on the same systems. Every solution in this section agrees with OpenFOAM's to 7e-5 or better.
  • POD of earlier runs. It removes another 22% of iterations relative to the projection alone. Its initial residual is 30x smaller.
  • Learned correction. It removes 2% of DIC iterations relative to the projection alone, and its guess costs more than it saves. A local graph network acts like a learned smoother: it reduces the residual, but the iteration count is set by global, low-frequency error that it cannot see. We report it as no practical gain.
  • AMG (pyamg). It cuts iterations about 17x relative to DIC. In Python, its setup on every new matrix dominates the time.
  • Mixed-precision PyTorch CG. On the CPU it needs more iterations than float64 and is not faster per useful iteration. Without a GPU we make no GPU claim.

docs.title: 5. Python guesses inside a running OpenFOAM (guess external)
docs.text:
The 64 x 64 cavity from section 4, run by icoFoam with the guesses served through the pipes:

run p iterations wall [s] Python guess time [s] dp vs ref dU vs ref plain PCG-DIC 11 796 1.20 - 9.2e-7 1.2e-8 projection in C++ (guess projection) 5 054 0.90 - 4.1e-5 3.1e-8 Python projection (guess external) 4 999 1.34 0.29 3.4e-5 6.9e-8 Python POD of earlier runs + last 8 4 237 1.35 0.43 3.9e-5 2.6e-8 Python projection + learned correction 5 088 3.82 2.71 1.9e-5 5.2e-8

The Python projection reproduces the C++ one (4 999 vs 5 054 iterations; the small difference comes from round-off in the elimination order). This confirms that the coupling loop works end to end. POD of earlier runs saves the most iterations, but on a 4 096-cell case the pipe and Python overhead outweighs the saving. These Python models belong inside the C++ wrapper, or on much larger meshes where an iteration costs more than a round trip.

docs.title: Summary of measured speed-ups
docs.text: setting pressure iterations wall time (whole run) Cavity, PISO with relTol 0.05, PCG-DIC (128², 256²) 3.1x, 2.5x fewer 1.83x, 1.84x faster Cavity, PISO with relTol 0.05, GAMG (128², 256²) 3.2x, 3.0x fewer 1.16x, 1.27x faster Cavity, relTol 0, matched accuracy, PCG-DIC (128²) 1.6x fewer 1.31x faster Cavity, relTol 0, matched accuracy, PCG-DIC (64²) 1.2x fewer none damBreak, interFoam p_rgh none (worse unless restricted to final solves) none

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• The gain comes from time correlation. The projection helps when consecutive pressure systems are alike, as in transient PISO/PIMPLE runs with small time steps. For steady SIMPLE with relTol 0.1-0.01, each solve is short and the right-hand side changes a lot, so expect little.
  • Equal residual does not mean equal error. At the same tolerance, a warm-started solution can have a larger algebraic error in smooth modes (section 2). Tighten the tolerance 10-100x when the pressure itself matters, and compare at matched accuracy, as done above.
  • Multiphase cases with a moving interface (damBreak) did not benefit. Use applyTo converged there, or leave the plain solver.
  • It works with any symmetric inner solver. With GAMG, iterations drop, but a GAMG cycle costs much more than the projection, so the wall-time gain is smaller (see the tables).
  • guess external blocks the solver until the Python server answers. Start the GuessServer before the solver. For production use, prefer the in-process C++ projection; the pipes are for experimenting with Python models.
  • Systems with coupled interfaces (processor, cyclic) are handled by the C++ wrapper. In Python, LduSystem.to_csr refuses them because the interface coefficients are not in the dump.
  • No GPU was available, so the GPU paths (torch_pcg on CUDA) were only run on the CPU. No GPU speed-up is claimed.

docs.title: Reproducing
docs.text:
from pinneapple_simulation.accelerated_foam import build, benchmark
lib = build.build_plugin(openfoam_src="/path/to/openfoam-OpenFOAM-v1912.200626")   # or with FOAM_SRC set
rows = benchmark.openfoam_comparison("work", lib, n=128, end_time=0.5, repeats=2)
print(benchmark.markdown_table(rows))

The tests are in tests/test_accelerated_foam.py. The OpenFOAM tests skip when icoFoam is missing or the plugin cannot be built.

docs.title: OpenFOAM parameter campaigns on several machines
docs.text: pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.openfoam.campaign runs one verified OpenFOAM case many times with different inputs. The runs can be spread over workstations, cluster nodes or cloud sessions. A study that takes days on one machine finishes in the time of a few runs, and its results come back in a form a surrogate model can be trained on.

docs.title: What a run does
docs.text:
1. Copy the base case. The base is a case directory or a .tar.gz. A run can swap in another mesh, such as a geometry variant. After a swap, fields sized for the old mesh are reset, and setFields or the solver rebuilds them.
  2. Apply the parameters.
  3. Dictionary edits by path, such as boundaryField/inlet/value in 0/U. Their values are templates filled with the parameters and with derived values ("Uy": "U*cos(radians(theta))").
  4. An optional patch rebuilt to an area (area_patch). It takes the boundary faces of a plane that are nearest to a centre point until they add up to the area, which makes an inlet diameter an input.
  5. An optional Python hook ("setup": "module:function") for anything else.
  6. Run. The pre-processing commands run (checkMesh, setFields, ...). The case is decomposed with scotch when the OpenFOAM installation has it, otherwise simple along the longest side. The solver then runs with mpirun.
  7. Sample lines while the solver runs (LiveLineSampler). The sampling reads the written fields, so it does not depend on the function objects of the OpenFOAM version. Sampled times can be deleted, keeping one every keep_every seconds, which bounds the disk use of long transients.
  8. Write <results>/<id>.json with:
  9. the parameters and the values derived from them;
  10. the solver health read from the log: last time, Courant number, phase-fraction bounds, phase volume history, whether the run reached End, and the first fatal error;
  11. the time-mean profiles on the lines;
  12. the host and the wall time.

docs.title: Splitting the work
docs.text:
Every machine runs the same command on the same plan file and takes its share:

Option Share --worker W the runs tagged "worker": "W" in the plan --shard i/n every n-th pending run, starting at the i-th run ids only those runs
  • Runs already done (their result file exists) are skipped, so a stopped worker restarts where it was.
  • Claims: a run is claimed with a lock file next to the results, so machines that share a disk never run the same case. --force clears a lock left by a worker that died.
  • Machines that share nothing, such as cloud sessions, use --publish-git. Each result is committed and pushed to the current branch as soon as it is written, with a rebase on what other workers pushed meanwhile. The author can be set with --git-name and --git-email.
M="python -m pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.openfoam.campaign plan.json"
$M --commands 5            # prints the command to start on each of 5 machines
$M --shard 3/5 --procs 4 --publish-git
$M --status                # done / running / pending, on any machine
$M T07 --stage-only cases  # write a case without running it, to inspect it

docs.title: The plan
docs.text:
{"name": "jet sweep", "base": "base_case.tar.gz", "solver": "interFoam", "procs": 4, "end_time": 30,
 "pre": ["checkMesh", "setFields"],
 "derived": {"Uy": "U*cos(radians(theta))", "Uz": "U*sin(radians(theta))"},
 "edits": [{"file": "0/U", "key": "boundaryField/inlet/value", "value": "uniform (0 {Uy} {Uz})"}],
 "area_patch": {"patch": "inlet", "area": "pi*(d/1000)**2/4", "centre": [0, -7.4, -1.3], "normal": [0, -1, 0],
                "from": ["inlet", "wall"], "rest": "wall"},
 "sample": {"fields": ["k", "alpha.water"], "keep_every": 10, "average_from": 0,
            "lines": [{"name": "L1", "start": [0, -7.4, -2.2], "end": [0, 15.3, -2.2], "n": 101}]},
 "results": "results",
 "runs": [{"id": "T01", "params": {"U": 8.6, "theta": 5.0, "d": 109}, "worker": "1"},
          {"id": "D1", "params": {"U": 10, "theta": 10, "d": 85}, "mesh": "mesh_variant.tar.gz", "group": "deflector"}]}
  • Paths are relative to the plan file.
  • Expressions accept the parameters, earlier derived values, numbers, arithmetic and the functions of math. Nothing else is evaluated, so a plan received from someone else cannot run code. The setup hook is the exception: it imports a Python module, so use it only from plans you trust.
  • In edit values, {Uy} writes the number in full, {Uy:.4f} formats it, and a list is written as an OpenFOAM vector.
  • area_patch exposes the area it actually reached as patch_area, so an edit can use it, for example to set a flow rate.

From Python:

from pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.openfoam.campaign import Campaign, GitPublisher
c = Campaign.from_json("plan.json", procs=8)
c.run(shard=(1, 3), publish=GitPublisher("me", "me@example.org"))

docs.title: Requirements and limits
docs.text:
• OpenFOAM is sourced from FOAM_BASHRC (default /usr/share/openfoam/etc/bashrc), with MPI for procs > 1. Tested with OpenFOAM v1912.
  • Meshes must be in ASCII format: area_patch, the decomposition box and the line sampler read them directly. Run foamFormatConvert once on a binary base case.
  • Lines are sampled with the value of the nearest cell, without interpolation. Points with no cell nearby, such as points inside an obstacle, are dropped.

Example: examples/openfoam_campaign/ (a jet into a bath in a 2-D trough, six runs on two workers). Tests: tests/test_openfoam_campaign.py. It covers: - dictionary edits and safe expressions; - shards, workers, claims and the plan file; - log parsing and field reset after a mesh swap; - a patch cut to half its area; - two short parallel interFoam runs.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
These primitives appear across the framework:

  • PhysicalSample
  • ProblemDefinition
  • Geometry & Domain
  • Model
  • PINN / Physics
  • Solver
  • Backend
  • Training Pipeline
  • Researcher & Benchmarking

docs.title: PhysicalSample
docs.text: PhysicalSample is the framework's unified container for a piece of physical data — a UPD-aligned (Unified Physical Data) record used consistently across modeling, simulation, and PINN training so that data coming from a numerical solver, an experiment, or a synthetic generator all look the same to the rest of the pipeline.

docs.title: Where it lives
docs.text:
pinneapple_data.physical_sample.PhysicalSample (re-exported at pinneapple_data). It's a dataclass with five fields:

  • state: xr.Dataset | Dict[str, Any] — the core physical state, preferably an xarray.Dataset for structured grid data, or a dict for other layouts.
  • geometry: Optional[Any] — an optional geometry asset describing the spatial structure the state lives on.
  • schema: Dict[str, Any] — governing equations, boundary/initial conditions, forcing terms, unit policies.
  • domain: Dict[str, Any] — domain interpretation metadata (grid, mesh, graph, points, ...).
  • provenance: Dict[str, Any] — lineage metadata: identifiers, source, tiling, time span, and other traceability information.
  • extras: Dict[str, Any] — an open-ended slot for feature caches, mesh labels, SDFs, and anything else that doesn't fit the above.

It also has small helper methods, e.g. domain_type() (reads domain["type"], defaulting to "grid" for an xarray.Dataset state) and is_grid().

docs.title: What else lives in pinneapple_data
docs.text:
• Storage — UPDZarrStore / ZarrUPDIterable for Zarr-backed datasets (plus HDF5 and PyTorch-native storage elsewhere in the package).
  • Collation — collate_upd_supervised, collate_pinn_batches, move_batch_to_device for turning a list of samples into a training batch.
  • Collocation & active learning — CollocationSampler/ CollocationConfig for drawing collocation points, and ActiveLearningConfig/ResidualBasedAL/VarianceBasedAL/CombinedAL/ AdaptiveCollocationTrainer for residual- or variance-driven adaptive sampling during training.
  • Transforms — Normalizer, StandardScaler, MinMaxScaler.
  • Splits — SplitSpec/split_indices for train/val/test partitioning.
  • PINN batch builders — build_from_bundle, build_from_solver, build_from_real_data produce a PINNBatch from a data bundle, a pinneapple_simulation solver run, or real measured data respectively.
  • STLMesh/load_stl/load_stl_bytes for mesh import, and UPDItem/ ConditionSpec/SamplingSpec/Batch as the lower-level typed containers PhysicalSample-based datasets ultimately produce.

docs.title: How it's used
docs.text: A numerical solver run (Geometry & Domain sampling + pinneapple_simulation), an experimental measurement, or a pinneapple_pdb-built dataset can all be wrapped as one or more PhysicalSample objects. From there, pinneapple_data's collation and collocation utilities turn them into the batches that Model/PINN / Physics/Solver consume — PhysicalSample is the hand-off point between "where did this data come from" and "how do I train on it."

docs.title: Physics audit: which model to use, when to trust it, when to revisit the physics
docs.text:
"It is in the fundamental knowledge that we must look for the cause of a model's imperfections."

An adaptive ensemble picks the best model from the errors each one made on earlier cases. That leaves two questions open:

  • Is the current case still inside the physics each model was built on?
  • When a model fails, why did it fail?

pinneapple_physics.physics_audit (also pp.physics_audit) adds those layers on top of the predictive models. It is plain numpy and does not import torch.

Layer What it does Module 1. Predictive models PINN, FNO, GNN, DeepONet, CNN, solvers, closed forms pinneapple_physics.ensemble experts 2. Physical evaluation Residuals, conservation, bounds, boundary conditions and invariants, without ground truth. Each model's assumptions and the regime of the case monitor, assumptions, regime 3. Adaptive decision Compatibility of the case with each model's physics, used as a prior on the ensemble weights. Models outside their physics sleep, and the router escalates to the solver routing 4. Diagnosis and evolution Probable cause of a failure, with its evidence and a confidence. Next experiment or change of highest value. Graph of phenomena, equations, assumptions and models attribution, improvement, knowledge

docs.title: Assumptions and their validity (Physics Assumption Auditor)
docs.text:
A ModelProfile is the model card that the audit reads. It holds:

  • the model's equations;
  • its assumptions, taken from the catalogue or written by you;
  • the mechanisms it represents;
  • its training envelope.

Each assumption holds inside a range of dimensionless numbers, with a soft band around the edges. Near a transition the audit says MARGINAL; it does not flip from valid to violated. A feature that is not given is UNKNOWN, never a silent pass.

from pinneapple_physics.physics_audit import ModelProfile, Envelope, laminar, audit_assumptions, regime_features

f = regime_features(velocity=0.12, length=0.05, nu=1e-6)          # {"Re": 6000, "Fr": ...}
lam = ModelProfile("laminar", "closed form", ("Hagen-Poiseuille / laminar correlations",),
                   (laminar(2300), "incompressible"), envelope=Envelope({"Re": (1, 2300)}))
print(audit_assumptions(lam, {**f, "Ma": 0.05}))
# laminar: VIOLATED (compatibility 0.00)
#   [VIOLATED] laminar: Re <= 2.3e+03 (Re = 6e+03): VIOLATED
#   [VALID] incompressible: Ma <= 0.3 (Ma = 0.05): VALID
#   [OUTSIDE] training envelope: Re = 6e+03, trained on 1 .. 2.3e+03 (outside)
#   probable phenomena: turbulence

Catalogue. ASSUMPTIONS lists the common simplifications. The factory functions build them with other thresholds.

  • Flow regime: laminar, turbulent, hydraulically_smooth, creeping_flow, attached_flow
  • Fluid behaviour: incompressible, continuum, boussinesq, constant_properties, shallow_water
  • Structures: small_strain, linear_elastic
  • Heat and transport: lumped_capacitance, forced_convection, diffusion_dominated, advection_dominated

Features. regime_features and the functions in regime compute these numbers:

  • Re, Ma, Pe, Kn, Ri, Ra, Gr, Pr, Bi, Fr, St and Da;
  • β·ΔT (beta_dT) and ΔT/T (dT_over_T);
  • the roughness Reynolds number ε⁺.

Training envelope. An Envelope can come from training samples (Envelope.from_samples). It then also measures the distance to the nearest training case, so a case that sits in a hole of the data is flagged even when it is inside every range.

docs.title: Validity monitor (no ground truth needed)
docs.text:
PhysicsValidityMonitor runs the checks below on every prediction:

Check What it measures residual_check Norm of the residual of the governing equations conservation_check Conserved total against its expected value bounds_check Admissible values, such as non-negative density (critical by default) boundary_check The prediction against the boundary condition constitutive_check Violation of a material or constitutive law invariant_check Change of a quantity that must stay constant envelope_check Distance outside the training envelope (extrapolation)

The status goes from OK to WARN and then ALARM. An alarm is raised when:

  • a critical check fails;
  • the same check fails persistence times in a row;
  • a residual drifts to drift_ratio times its own baseline, even while it is still below its tolerance.

docs.title: Physics-aware routing
docs.text:
PhysicsAwareRouter turns the compatibility of the current case with each model into a prior on its weight:

w_i ∝ w_learned_i · max(c_i, floor)^strength · exp(-cost_weight · cost_i / max cost)

  • Sleeping models. A model below abstain_below is asleep. It is not used for that case, and inside the ensemble the case does not change its weight: its loss is set to the mixture's. A laminar correlation is therefore not punished for the turbulent cases it was never meant for. It is ready again as soon as the flow returns to its regime.
  • Escalation. When no model fits (best compatibility below escalate_below), the router escalates to the solver named in escalate_to.
from pinneapple_physics.ensemble import PhysicsEnsemble
from pinneapple_physics.physics_audit import PhysicsAwareRouter

router = PhysicsAwareRouter(profiles, features_fn=lambda case: case["features"],
                            escalate_below=0.9, escalate_to="solver")
ens = PhysicsEnsemble(experts, mode="select", router=router)
out = ens.predict(case)          # also returns "prior", "awake" and "escalate"
print(router.route(case))        # standalone decision, with the reasons

The learned weights, the residual look-ahead and the cost term of the ensemble still apply on top of the prior. So history and the current residual can correct a compatibility estimate that is wrong.

docs.title: Failure attribution
docs.text:
attribute_failure weighs the evidence of one case and returns the probable causes, each with a probability and its evidence. The confidence of the diagnosis drops when evidence types are missing, and the report lists which ones were.

Cause Evidence pde_violation The residual fails its tolerance or jumps above its in-domain level conservation A conserved total is off boundary_condition The prediction does not meet the boundary condition regime_change The case violates an assumption of the model extrapolation The assumptions hold, but the case is outside the training envelope, far from the training cases, or the models disagree numerical_resolution Grid convergence index, change under refinement, CFL above its limit, or non-finite or out-of-bounds values measurement The reference reading failed its own physical consistency check missing_physics The model satisfies its equations, inside its assumptions and envelope, and still disagrees with the reference (model-form error)

Low residuals do not guarantee a correct prediction, and high residuals alone do not identify the cause. The last row is the case where the residual misleads. When there is no reference, a low residual comes with a note that it does not prove the prediction right.

docs.title: Knowledge graph and guided improvement
docs.text:
default_graph(profiles) links phenomena, equations, assumptions, parameters, mechanisms and models. It answers questions such as:

  • unrepresented(model, features): Re went up, so is turbulence represented in this model?
  • models_for(mechanism): which models represent this mechanism?
  • explain(model, features): a readable account of what the model misses for this case.

to_mermaid() draws the graph.

recommend(attribution, audit, graph, features, model) ranks the next steps by probability × confidence × gain / cost:

  • switch to a model or equation that represents the missing mechanism (the graph names it);
  • run high-fidelity simulations in the new regime, with design points around the case;
  • train a specialised model;
  • add collocation points or change the loss;
  • add a conservation projection;
  • enforce the boundary condition exactly;
  • refine the mesh;
  • check the sensor;
  • add the missing term or fit a discrepancy model.

improvement_plan(cases) aggregates many cases, so the actions that fix the most frequent and most confident causes come first.

diagnose(profile, features, prediction, query, monitor, error) runs all of this for one case and returns a Diagnosis with trusted and a Markdown report().

docs.title: Example: pipe friction across regimes
docs.text:
examples/physics_audit/pipe_regimes.py predicts the Darcy friction factor of a rough pipe (ε/D = 1e-3) for 160 cases. The Reynolds number goes through the laminar, transitional, turbulent and high-Re rough regimes, then back to laminar. The truth is Churchill's correlation. The models:

Model Formula or source Assumes Training envelope Cost laminar 64/Re Laminar flow Re ≤ 2300 1 blasius Smooth-pipe Blasius Turbulent flow, smooth wall 4000 ≤ Re ≤ 1e5 1 surrogate Learned surrogate Turbulent flow 4000 ≤ Re ≤ 2e5 1 solver High-fidelity, 1 % noise — — 100

Mean relative error over the 160 cases:

laminar transition turbulent high Re, rough laminar again all solver share History only (PhysicsEnsemble) 0.01 % 5.9 % 0.33 % 1.0 % 1.9 % 1.49 % 21 % History + physics router 0.01 % 2.1 % 0.03 % 0.59 % 0.00 % 0.38 % 25 % Physics router alone 2.27 % 27 % Best single model (surrogate) 12.3 %

Back in laminar flow. On the first five laminar cases, the history-only ensemble keeps the turbulent surrogate, with errors of 17 %, 11 % and 47 %, and then falls back to the expensive solver. With the router, the laminar law answers from the first case, with no error, because it was asleep through the turbulent segment and kept its weight.

Physics and history complement each other. The router alone is worse than the router with history. Inside its envelope, Blasius looks compatible with the case, but the pipe is rough. Only the errors it makes reveal that.

The example then diagnoses three failures:

  1. laminar at Re = 6000. Regime change: the laminar assumption is violated. Turbulent transport is not represented. The recommendations are to use a model that represents it (solver or surrogate) or to run high-fidelity simulations in the new regime.
  2. blasius at Re = 5e5. Regime change: hydraulically_smooth is violated with ε⁺ = 25, so the flow is in rough-wall turbulence and the model lacks the wall-roughness mechanism. The case is also outside the training envelope, and the smooth-pipe law residual fails.
  3. blasius at Re = 6e4. Every assumption is valid, the case is inside the training envelope and the residual of the smooth-pipe law is 0.3 %, yet the error is 14.5 %. The cause is missing physics (p = 0.87): the model satisfies its own equations, but they do not describe this case. A residual check alone would have trusted this prediction.

docs.title: Adaptive ensembles of physics models
docs.text:
pinneapple_physics.ensemble.PhysicsEnsemble (also pp.ensemble.PhysicsEnsemble) selects and combines physics models case by case: neural operators (FNO, DeepONet), graph networks (MeshGraphNet), PINNs, numerical solvers and closed forms. It uses the same prequential core as the adaptive forecaster (pinneapple_physics.online_learning): Fixed-Share weights, AdaHedge over the learning and switching rates, adaptive conformal intervals. Every case is predicted with weights learned from earlier cases only, so the model choice cannot overfit.

from pinneapple_physics.ensemble import PhysicsEnsemble, from_callable, from_solution, from_torch

experts = [
    from_torch("fno", fno_model, to_input=lambda case: make_fno_input(case), from_output=lambda y, case: y[0]),
    from_torch("gnn", meshgraphnet, to_input=lambda case: make_graph(case), from_output=lambda y, case: y[0]),
    from_solution("pinn", pp.solve(problem, "pinn"), points=lambda case: case["points"]),
    from_callable("solver", lambda case: run_solver(case), cost=50.0),
]
ens = PhysicsEnsemble(experts, mode="select")      # or "combine"
for case in stream:
    out = ens.predict(case)                        # field, interval, per-expert fields, weights, active model
    ens.update(case, reference=high_fidelity(case))  # when a reference exists

docs.title: What the weights can learn from
docs.text:
Signal Argument When to use Reference field (sensor, experiment, high-fidelity run) update(case, reference) relative L2 error; validation campaigns, digital twins with sensors Physics residual, no reference residual_fn, residual_weight operation without ground truth: models that violate the PDE lose weight Cost cost_weight, Expert(cost=...) adaptive fidelity: the cheap surrogate while it is good enough, the solver when it is not Physics residual of the current case, before predicting residual_fn, residual_lookahead regime changes: the choice reacts on the first new case instead of after past errors pile up

With mode="select" and predict(case, select_only_leader=True) only the leading model runs, except every explore_every cases, when all run so their errors stay current. Experts that raise or return non-finite values are left out of that case and scored with the worst loss.

router= adds physics-aware routing (pinneapple_physics.physics_audit.PhysicsAwareRouter): each expert's assumptions and training envelope are checked against the current case, the compatibility tilts the weights before predicting, and experts outside their physics sleep for that case without losing weight. See Physics audit.

prediction_checks={name: fn(prediction, case)} runs label-free checks on each model's prediction for the current case before choosing: a closure check of an LES, a cross-scale consistency check, a conservation check. Each returns a score in [0, 1] (or (score, reason)). A model whose score is below check_threshold is left out of that case but still scored, so its weight learns from the failure. The others are tilted by score ** check_strength. When every awake model fails, the router's escalate_from moves up a fidelity ladder. predict reports checks, failed_checks and escalated_by_checks.

docs.title: Scales: which model can answer the question at all
docs.text:
A model trained or run at one resolution and filter represents the field at that scale and nothing finer. A small validation error does not make it fit for a question about smaller scales. pinneapple_physics.multiscale lets every expert declare its scales and every case declare the scales it needs:

  • ScaleProfile: output filter (kind and width), grid spacing, closure, Reynolds range, time step and fidelity rung;
  • ScaleQuery: the filter of the requested output, the Reynolds number and the time scale;
  • ScaleAwareRouter: a model asked for scales below the ones it resolves sleeps. A filter it cannot reproduce by post-filtering its own output is tilted down. The lowest fidelity rung that covers the case is used (surrogate, then LES with a closure, then a resolved solver), and the router moves up a rung when the closure checks fail.

The filters, the closure tests, the multiscale residuals and the experiment on 2-D turbulence are described in Multiscale ensembles: scales, filters and closures.

Other options: conserve=(weights, target_fn) projects the combined field onto a conserved total; min_weight keeps near-zero weights out of the "combine" average; point_weights gives quadrature weights for the norms. fit_static_weights(predictions, references) fits fixed convex weights on a validation set and reports their cross-validated error next to each single model.

docs.title: Results (advection-diffusion with exact solutions, pinneapple_physics.advection_diffusion_1d)
docs.text:
150 cases whose diffusivity moves through three regimes; every learned model was trained on one regime only (examples/physics_ensemble/fno_pinn_gnn_solvers.py):

low nu mid nu high nu all cases FNO (trained on low nu) 0.57 % 4.4 % 40 % MeshGraphNet (trained on mid nu) 19 % 16 % 38 % PINN (high nu, physics loss only, no data) 16 % 13 % 6.5 % upwind FD 4.1 % 3.4 % 2.5 % Lax-Wendroff FD, coarse grid 2.5 % 1.2 % 0.10 % 1.25 % (best single model) Adaptive ensemble, select 0.57 % 2.0 % 0.10 % 0.88 %

Relative L2 error of the space-time field. 90 % intervals covered 93 % of the points. In the tests (tests/test_physics_ensemble.py) the residual-only mode (no reference at all) removes the out-of-distribution FNO in the high-diffusion regime, and the cost-aware lazy mode cuts the compute by more than 70 % against running every model while keeping the error low. With CPU-sized training the MeshGraphNet stays the weakest expert; the ensemble learns to ignore it. In "combine" mode a model that fails badly still costs a little during a regime change, so "select" is the better default when some experts can be far off.

The PDE residual is a good detector of failure (it flags the out-of-distribution FNO at once), not a ranking of the most accurate model: a learned field can have a larger residual than a slightly less accurate numerical solution.

docs.title: Five model families and an animated view
docs.text:
examples/physics_ensemble/five_model_families_gif.py puts an FNO, a MeshGraphNet (multiscale ring graph), a DeepONet, a PINN (physics loss only) and a dilated 1-D CNN in one ensemble. Each is trained on its own regime of advection speed and diffusivity; the stream of 80 cases drifts through the five regimes. Relative L2 error per regime (select mode, 16 cases each):

regime (training data of) FNO GNN DeepONet PINN CNN ensemble FNO (c = 1, low nu) 1.2 % 240 % 38 % 45 % 72 % 1.2 % GNN (c = 0.5, high nu) 18 % 5.4 % 18 % 26 % 74 % 10 % DeepONet (c = 0, mid nu) 37 % 63 % 11 % 18 % 29 % 16 % PINN (c = -0.5, high nu) 39 % 28 % 16 % 4.2 % 51 % 7.0 % CNN (c = -1, low nu) 128 % 153 % 37 % 27 % 0.96 % 4.7 % all cases 24 % (best single) 7.8 %

The ensemble switches to the right family 2 to 6 cases after each regime change (the gap to the diagonal is that delay); no single model comes close over the whole stream. 90 % intervals covered 90 % of the points.

docs.title: Detecting the regime change before the errors pile up
docs.text:
