docs.title: Results (generic example, measured on 4 cores)
docs.text:
• 105 designs (feed gain 10–22 dBi × side 2.4–4.8 m × F = 3, 4, 5 m), median 106 s per design (both polarisations, λ/8 mesh), 11 520 s of PO in all.
  • F = 4 m: one grid design meets the spec, 16 dBi with a 4.8 m reflector (usable 1.006 m). The optimiser found 15.7 dBi with a 4.53 m reflector and PO verified it: usable diameter 1.05 m for V and H, ripple 0.24 dB, taper 0.84 dB, phase ripple 1.7°, cross-pol −28.8 dB. The GP predicted 1.00 ± 0.21 m (95 %) there: its mean met the spec, its lower bound did not, and PO settled it in one solve.
  • Pareto front (PO, F = 4 m): 0.90 m from 2.4 m (19 dBi), 0.97 m at 4.4 m (13 dBi), 1.01 m at 4.8 m (16 dBi). The usable diameter is not monotone in size or gain: a low-gain feed lights the edge and the diffraction ripple breaks the ±0.5 dB band; a high-gain feed tapers the amplitude past it (22 dBi: taper 2.08–2.21 dB and usable 0.67–0.69 m at every size from 2.8 m).
  • Focal length is a strong lever: best usable diameter 0.91 m at F = 3 m (no design meets the spec, cross-pol up to −23.2 dB), 1.01 m at F = 4 m, 1.12 m at F = 5 m (16 dBi, 4.0 m; four designs meet the spec). The optimiser searches at the base F only; at F = 5 m the grid already holds a 4.0 m design that meets it.
  • Surrogate (all 105 designs, inputs gain, side, F): held-out RMSE / 95 % coverage: usable diameter 0.14 m / 0.85, ripple 0.060 dB / 0.94, taper 0.44 dB / 0.90, phase ripple 0.67° / 0.90, cross-pol 0.48 dB / 0.93. The usable diameter is a threshold quantity (the first radius where a tolerance breaks) and the GP under-states its uncertainty (0.85, not 0.95): use the maps to choose where to solve, and PO to decide.

docs.title: Limits of physical optics
docs.text:
PO leaves out the fringe edge currents (PTD) and multiple reflections; the feed is an ideal cos^q pattern with no back radiation, no feed or strut blockage and no chamber; the edge diffraction it gives is that of the truncated PO current. The optimiser's verification is PO only: no MoM solver is wired in. The issue's textbook comparison (Hemming, Electromagnetic Anechoic Chambers) was not done here: the book was not available to check numbers against, so no value from it is quoted.

Flow nodes: antenna.compact_range_design (the study; quick by default) and antenna.compact_range_check (one design against a spec).

docs.title: Dataset physics audit: does the data solve its PDE?
docs.text:
A model trained on wrong data inherits the error, and model-level checks may never see it. Two open bugs of a widely used Physics AI library show how training data can be silently wrong: generated Darcy data that did not solve the documented equation (NVIDIA/physicsnemo#2036) and permeability samples with far less diversity than documented (NVIDIA/physicsnemo#2035). pinneapple_data.audit checks the data itself, before anyone trains on it.

import pinneapple as pp

card = pp.datasets.audit("heatsink_forced_convection")      # a zoo dataset, with the constraints its card states
print(card)                                                 # one line per check: PASS / WARN / FAIL / NOT-APPLICABLE

from pinneapple_data.audit import audit_dataset
card = audit_dataset({"train": {"a": a_train, "u": u_train}, "test": {"a": a_test, "u": u_test}},
                     physics="darcy", generator=my_permeability_sampler, units={"a": "-", "u": "-"})
card.to_json("audit_card.json")

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
Check What it measures Fails when finite infinities and missing values any infinity (NaN is a warning, marked "documented" when the metadata says the value was not recorded) physics.solve per sample: ||u - A^-1 f|| / ||A^-1 f||, the distance to the solution of its own discrete problem (the residual in the A^-1 norm) above 2 % physics.bc, physics.flux boundary values against the exact discrete solution's; net boundary flux against the source integral above 2 % constraint: ... declared relations between columns ("r_base_k_w > 0", "source_width_mm == source_frac_w * base_width_mm") any row breaks one diversity.duplicates exact and near copies inside the train, validation and test splits (closer than 1e-3 x the median nearest-neighbour distance) any diversity.effective effective number of distinct samples: participation ratio of the principal-component spectrum, against freshly drawn samples of the stated generator when there is one below half the generator's (without a generator: below 2) diversity.spectrum mean radial spectrum of the inputs against the generator's off by more than a factor 2 in a shell leakage nearest training sample of each test sample any test sample closer than 1e-3 x the median training spacing units units in the metadata parse, and match the problem's when stated otherwise

The physics check is built in for "darcy" (-div(a grad u) = f, u = 0 on the unit square, cell-centred, the discretisation of operator_benchmarks.darcy_2d and of darcy_2d_li2021); any other problem passes a DatasetPhysics(name, columns, check, tolerances). Each solve check runs on up to 64 random samples per split by default (max_physics_samples).

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
Zoo datasets (cards stored in pinneapple_hub/zoo/audit_cards/ and shown in each dataset's Hub card):

Dataset Decision Notes heatsink_forced_convection PASS 4 constraints on 6000 rows, no duplicates or leakage heatsink_natural_convection PASS 3 constraints on 5000 rows rover_contact_grc1_viper PASS airfoil_rans_cst_re4e6 WARN Cm is NaN in the 340 training rows: documented ("Cm not recorded in the campaign table") single_wheel_tests WARN 5 torque values NaN: documented ("NaN = not reported"); one split, so no leakage check burgers_1d_li2021, darcy_2d_li2021 not audited yet Hub-only; the test downloads and audits them where the network allows

Defects (tests/test_dataset_audit.py, Darcy on 32 x 32 cells, coefficient from the Li et al. 2021 generator):

  • data generated by an independent finite-difference solver of the expanded equation -a lap u - grad a . grad u = f pass (physics.solve below 1 %: the two discretisations differ by their truncation error); the same solver with the cross term scaled by 0.5 (the #2036 defect) fails on every sample (solve above 10 %, flux imbalance too);
  • permeability samples whose Fourier coefficients share one value per sample (the #2035 defect) fail diversity.effective (below 0.1 of the generator's) and diversity.duplicates, while still solving the PDE;
  • one test sample of 20 copied from the training set (5 %) fails leakage, with the pair listed.

docs.title: In pinneapple check
docs.text:
[[dataset]]
path = "datasets/darcy.npz"          # <split>__<column> arrays (the zoo layout); or zoo = "darcy_2d_li2021"
physics = "darcy"
constraints = ["u > 0", "u < 1 / 24"]

Rules: PC451 (physics and constraints), PC452 (diversity), PC453 (leakage); infinities report as PC403, units as PC501.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Without a stated generator, diversity can only flag a collapse (an effective sample count below 2); a set that is merely narrower than documented needs the generator.
  • Leakage and duplicates are measured in the space of the declared inputs (standardised for tabular data). A copy that was transformed (shifted, rotated, resampled) is not a near copy in that space.
  • The physics check is as good as the stated discretisation: data generated by another consistent scheme differ by its truncation error, so the tolerance must be above it (0.5 % at 32 x 32 for a contrast-20 coefficient).

docs.title: Derivative trees across physics
docs.text:
In thermodynamics one fundamental potential in its natural variables — the Helmholtz energy A(T, V), the Gibbs energy G(T, p) — generates every property by differentiation. Organised by order, the derivatives form a tree: depth 1 gives the "forces" (entropy, pressure), depth 2 the response functions (heat capacities, compressibility, expansion, speed of sound), and so on. Legendre transforms move between potentials; Maxwell relations tie the branches together. Because every property comes from one function, the properties are consistent by construction.

The same structure appears across physics, and pp.potential (pinneapple_physics.potential) treats it once:

Domain Potential Natural variables Depth 1 Depth 2 Adapter Thermodynamics, EOS A(T, V), a(T, rho), G(T, p) T, V (or rho), p S, p, U, H, G c_v, c_p, kappa_T, alpha_p, w thermo Hyperelasticity W(F) deformation gradient P = dW/dF, Cauchy stress tangent d2W/dFdF hyperelastic Electric machines co-energy W'(i, theta) currents, rotor angle flux linkages, torque differential inductances machines Analytical mechanics L(q, qd), H(q, p) coordinates, velocities / momenta momenta, generalised forces, energy mass matrix, coupling mechanics

docs.title: A potential and its tree
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from pinneapple_physics.potential import thermo, tree, maxwell_relations

A = thermo.van_der_waals(a=0.3640, b=4.267e-5, c=2.5, molar_mass=0.0440098)   # CO2 constants, SI, per mole
t = tree(A, depth=2, at={"T": np.array([280.0, 320.0]), "V": np.array([2e-4, 4e-4])})
print(t)                                    # every node: depth, symbol, unit, value
print(t["p"], t["cp"], t["w"])              # named quantities and responses
print(t.symbolic_agreement())               # autodiff against SymPy derivatives, per node
print(maxwell_relations(A)[0].text)         # (dS/dV)_T = (dp/dT)_V

A potential is any differentiable function written in torch (Potential(fn, {"T": "K", "V": "m3/mol"}, names=..., responses=...)) or a SymPy expression (Potential.from_sympy). Variables can be tensors: for W(F) the tree holds P with shape (3, 3) and the tangent with shape (3, 3, 3, 3) per point.

docs.title: Legendre transforms and where they fail
docs.text:
legendre(potential, swap={"V": "p"}, conjugate_sign=-1) gives G(T, p) = A + p V (thermo.gibbs(A) is the same call with the Gibbs names), and mechanics.hamiltonian(L) gives H(q, p) = p qd - L. The transform is one-to-one only where the potential is convex (or concave) in the swapped variables. With bounds= the convexity is checked on a grid and reported: for van der Waals below its critical temperature, A is not convex in V between the two spinodals, and ConvexityReport.intervals("V") gives that interval at each temperature — the test suite checks it against the closed-form spinodal.

from pinneapple_physics.potential import convexity
rep = convexity(A, "V", {"T": (250.0, 330.0), "V": (6e-5, 6e-4)}, n_grid=81)
print(rep)                                  # convex in V: no (share of stable grid points)
print(rep.intervals("V")[0])                # ({'T': 250.0}, [(V_lo, V_hi)]): the unstable interval

docs.title: Is a model or a table consistent with one potential?
docs.text: consistency_check(model, family, at=...) evaluates the identities a potential satisfies — the Maxwell relation, c_v = T (ds/dT)_v, the energy equation, the Mayer relation, the speed of sound — on anything that predicts the properties separately: a multi-output surrogate, a lookup table, or measurements on a grid ({"axes": ..., "values": ...}, differentiated with np.gradient). Each identity is reported with its relative violation (median, 95th percentile, maximum). It is to thermodynamic consistency what the conservation checks of the trust layer are to conservation laws.

docs.title: Known answers
docs.text:
tests/test_potential.py (must pass in CI):

Case Reference Measured Ideal gas: p, S, c_v, c_p, kappa_T, alpha_p, w closed forms 1e-13 relative G(T, p) by symbolic and numeric Legendre transform each other, to third order; A + pV 1e-9 (relative to the node scale) Van der Waals: p, (dp/dV)_T, c_p - c_v, critical point, spinodal closed forms 1e-11; spinodal within one grid step Peng-Robinson, CO2, 4 states: p, (dp/dT)_V, residual c_v CoolProp PR backend (optional) 1e-15 to 2e-13 relative Neo-Hookean: P and the 3x3x3x3 tangent Bonet & Wood (2008) closed forms 1e-9 relative; major symmetry 1e-14 Double pendulum: accelerations, energy, Hamiltonian closed-form equations of motion; T + V 1e-11; RK4 drift 6.9e-8 over 5 s Surface-PM machine (linear iron): torque from the co-energy potential Maxwell-stress (Arkkio) torque of the same FEA 16.854 vs 16.837 N m (0.10 %); flux linkages to 1e-14 Wb

docs.title: Measured study: a potential-based surrogate against a direct one (CO2 near the critical point)
docs.text:
surrogate.PotentialSurrogate learns the Helmholtz energy a(T, rho), and every property is a derivative of it. Its MLP and input-convex (convex=True, convex in v) variants were compared with surrogate.DirectSurrogate, which has one output per property, on mixed CoolProp data for CO2 (Span-Wagner): each training sample carries one of p, s, u, c_v, c_p, w. The data, loss, optimiser and steps were the same for every model (examples/potential_co2, full tables in results/report.md).

The table gives the RMS error divided by the standard deviation of the property, averaged over the six properties, as the mean and 95 % t-interval over seeds. The training region is T 305-335 K, rho 100-800 kg/m3.

configuration (seeds) direct potential (MLP) potential (ICNN) all six properties, 3000 steps (5): training region 0.10 [0.07, 0.13] 1.61 [1.60, 1.62] 1.24 [0.79, 1.69] the same, extrapolated to T 335-365 K 0.25 [0.20, 0.30] 1.97 [1.91, 2.02] 3.24 [1.43, 5.05] the same, extrapolated to rho 800-950 kg/m3 0.66 [0.62, 0.71] 3.20 [3.19, 3.21] 2.69 [2.27, 3.10] no c_p in training, 3000 steps (5): training region 0.22 [0.21, 0.23] 1.57 [-0.89, 4.02] 3.49 [0.72, 6.27] all six properties, 9000 steps (2): training region 0.04 [-0.04, 0.11] 1.51 [-1.08, 4.10] 1.30 [-7.03, 9.62] Maxwell relation, 95th percentile of the violation (first row) 0.41 2.8e-5 1.1e-6

The potential approach lost on accuracy. The direct surrogate was more accurate in every region of both 5-seed configurations, and no region favoured the potential. What the potential bought was consistency: its identities held to between 1e-7 and 1e-4, where the direct surrogate's were off by 0.3 to 14.

Two failure modes showed up:

  • With c_p in the mixed data, the MLP potential collapsed to near-zero pressure. Near the Widom line the c_p peak needs a nearly flat isotherm, and fitting it pulled the potential away from p.
  • The input-convex network keeps (dp/drho)_T > 0, but nothing keeps c_v > 0, and in the hotter region it was not.

Training took 4 to 10 times longer per step, because the loss differentiates twice.

Not measured:

  • tuning for each model;
  • longer budgets with five seeds;
  • subcritical and two-phase states, other fluids and noisy data.

docs.title: Flow nodes
docs.text: potential.eos_tree, potential.hyperelastic, potential.double_pendulum, potential.machine_coenergy and potential.co2_surrogates (one seed at a reduced budget; the example flow potential_co2/surrogate_study).

docs.title: Not covered
docs.text:
• Mooney-Rivlin is tested at small strain only; the hyperelastic potentials are not yet wired into the FEM code.
  • The machine co-energy map has no angle-current cross terms, so it does not give dpsi/dtheta (the reciprocity with dT/di).
  • Legendre transforms of tensor variables (swap their components instead).
  • Mixtures (G(T, p, n_i)), plasticity and damage potentials: the classes take them, but no adapter or known-answer test is provided.

docs.title: Design from intent
docs.text:
pinneapple_design.intent turns a goal written in plain language into a design you can build: geometry, materials and operating conditions, with the margin to every failure mode, a trust report and the limits of what was checked. It never fills a gap with an invented number: a value it needs and cannot read becomes a question, a value it defaults says where the default comes from, and a request no template covers is refused with what would be needed.

import pinneapple as pp

pp.design("a heat sink for a 40 W chip in still air")
# NeedsInput: What is the highest allowed temperature of the chip's case (or source)? [°C]

pkg = pp.design("a heat sink for a 40 W chip in still air", answers={"t_limit": (85, "°C")}, out_dir="hs")
print(pkg.summary())        # design, verdict with probability, trust decision, model calls
pkg.files["html"]           # hs/report.html; also report.pdf, design.json, geometry/*.step|stl|glb, check/

pp.design("an electric motor for my drone")
# OutOfScope (needs): needs an electromagnetics design template: the interior-PM machine FEA and drive ...

The same call from a shell and from an agent:

pinneapple design "a bracket that holds 2 kN" --answer arm_length=100mm --out bracket
pinneapple design --templates

and the MCP tool design (pinneapple-mcp), which answers questions and refusals at once and runs the design as a job (poll job_status).

docs.title: The pipeline
docs.text:
Each stage is a typed object you can inspect, test and replace.

Stage Object What it does intent -> requirements formulate(text) -> RequirementSpec picks a template by keywords, reads every number unit pair, checks the unit's dimension and the template's range with pinneapple_data.physical_units, fills the template's slots; each value is stated (with the quote), answered, defaulted (with its source) or missing; missing critical values become Questions requirements -> physics plan(spec, template) -> PhysicsPlan governing physics, assumptions, design variables, the models at each fidelity with their availability on this machine, failure modes multi-fidelity optimisation optimise(...) -> OptimisationResult Latin-hypercube screening on the closed form, then the design-study core (pinneapple_design.design_optimizer: NSGA-II on the reduced model, or the GP surrogate-assisted loop when the reduced model costs seconds), distinct candidates (the knee of the Pareto front for several objectives) robustness robustness(...) -> Robustness Monte-Carlo propagation (pinneapple_analysis.uncertainty.tolerance.propagate) of the uncertain inputs to the probability that every margin stays >= 0, with a Wilson interval, the 5th percentile of each margin and the rank correlation of each input with the smallest margin verification verify(...) -> Verification the full solver on the chosen design, its own checks, and the comparison with the reduced and closed-form models output by output assessment assess(...) -> Assessment the trust report (pinneapple_analysis.trust.TrustReport) and the verdict: will work, likely to work (not verified by the full solver), marginal, will not work, unverified package DesignPackage geometry (STEP, STL, glTF, renders), bill of materials with cited properties, operating window, build instructions, every number with the model it comes from, model calls per fidelity, limits; report.html / report.pdf, design.json, check/ for pinneapple check

Every template designs at the worst corner of its own uncertainty (the optimum is robust, not on the nominal edge), then the Monte Carlo measures the probability of success around it. When the full solver measures something the cheap models assumed (the bracket's stress-concentration factor), the design is re-checked with the measured value and re-optimised if it no longer meets its margins.

An LLM is optional. Anything with extract(text, schema) -> dict (for example CallLLM("anthropic"), which wraps pinneapple_llm.call_llm) can propose the template and values; a value is used only if its quote is in the request and contains the number, and its unit has the slot's dimension. The deterministic parser always runs and wins on conflicts, so the pipeline works offline.

docs.title: The five demos
docs.text:
python examples/design_from_intent/design_from_intent.py runs all five through the same pipeline; the outputs are in examples/design_from_intent/_out/. The numbers below are copied from _out/summary.json of that run.

request first reply design verdict (P, 95 % interval) full solver check model calls (closed form / reduced / full) (a) "I want a toy car that does a loop" complete (every value defaulted with a source) R = 8.4 cm, clothoids 2.5 R = 21.0 cm, launch 2.47 m/s, car 31 g, 1.5 mm PLA strip will work (1.000, 0.998-1.000) Newton: goes round at both time steps, v_top 1.507 m/s >= worst-case envelope 1.023 m/s 2000 / 6600 / 1 (b) "a bracket that holds 2 kN" asks for the arm length (answered: 100 mm) Al 6061-T6, t = 17 mm, w = 36 mm, mounting leg 72 mm, two M6 8.8 will work (0.9985, 0.9956-0.9995) CalculiX: peak 94.3 vs 96.8 MPa (hex FE), deflection 0.380 vs 0.380 mm 12000 / 19 / 1 (c) "a heat sink for a 40 W chip in still air" asks for the temperature limit (answered: 85 °C) copper C110, base 100 x 100 x 6.5 mm, 14 fins 1.1 x 47 mm will work (1.000, 0.998-1.000) finite volume: source (case) temperature 77.7 vs 77.6 °C (network), energy balance 1e-12 2000 / 2600 / 1 (d) "a wing for a 1.2 kg model glider, at most 2 m span" complete span 2.0 m, AR 7.69, taper 0.33, NACA 2412 will work (1.000, 0.998-1.000) fine lattice: sink 0.4409 vs 0.4406 m/s, e 0.989 vs 0.990 2000 / 6600 / 1 (e) "an electric motor for my drone" out of scope: needs an electromagnetics design template (current-density, thermal, demagnetisation limits) - - - -

The closed-form call counts include the Monte-Carlo samples when a template runs its robustness study on the calibrated closed form (the bracket). Each report also gives an estimate, not a measurement, of the time the full solver would have needed for every evaluation: the measured seconds of its one full call times the number of evaluations (about 650 h for the loop and 130 h for the bracket on the machine of this run; the measured call time varies between runs).

docs.title: (a) Loop-the-loop car
docs.text:
Nothing in the request is a number, so every value is a default with its source: the rolling-resistance coefficient and the launcher scatter are design envelopes, not measurements (the design must work for any rolling resistance up to 0.05 and a launcher 5 % slow), the drag coefficient's worst case is the bluff-body end of the range (a cube is about 1.05, Hoerner), the strip material is the printable PLA with its datasheet yield strength.

  • Closed form: v_top^2 = v0^2 - 2 g z_top - losses with the losses at the mean speed, the top condition v_top^2 >= g (R - h), the peak load at the end of the entry clothoid.
  • Reduced: the 1-D along-track ODE (d(v^2)/ds with N = m (v^2 kappa + g cos theta), rolling resistance on N, drag, the wheels' inertia), RK4, vectorised: 6600 designs in 6.6 s. The car is a point on its centre-of-mass path, the track offset inwards by the centre-of-mass height h (12.5 mm for the car, 6 mm for Newton's sphere), so kappa = 1 / (R - h) on the top arc and N / (m g) = v_top^2 / (g (R - h)) - 1 at the top: 0.49 at the worst case (1.023 m/s, R - h = 7.14 cm), not the 0.27 a radius of R would give. Without losses it conserves energy to 0.3 % and reproduces the v0^2 = 5 g R threshold of a circular loop (tests).
  • Full: NVIDIA Newton (XPBD) on the 3-D track mesh with its side rails and the helical exit, at two time steps. Newton's contact dissipates energy on the curved mesh (5.7 % of the launch energy by the top here, with no friction at all, and it does not go away with a smaller step or a finer mesh), and its Coulomb friction, correct on its flat analytic case (stopping distance 0.5087 vs 0.5097 m), takes most of the energy of a rolling sphere on the curved mesh. So the Newton run is frictionless and judged against the worst-case envelope: the car must stay on the track (largest gap to the surface 0.1 mm) and keep at least the envelope's speed at the top (1.507 >= 1.023 m/s).

The optimiser minimised the launch speed and the peak load on the car together; the knee of the front uses the longest clothoid allowed (2.5 R), which cuts the peak load to 5.0 g at the worst case, with a loop 8.4 cm in radius. Operating window (1-D model): launch 2.24 to 7.02 m/s (the upper end is the strip's yield / 2), any car from 10 g up, rolling resistance up to 0.0695 at the design speed minus the scatter.

docs.title: (b) Bracket, verified with CalculiX
docs.text:
pp.design("a bracket that holds 2 kN") asks how far from the mounting face the load acts: the bending moment depends on it and there is no safe default. With 100 mm:

  • Closed form: cantilever beam theory (M c / I, P L^3 / 3 E I).
  • Reduced: an in-house hexahedral FE model of the L (C3D8I, the fillet as a staircase), 0.53 s per design, so the optimiser fits a GP surrogate of it and checks 19 designs with the FE model.
  • Full: CalculiX on a gmsh C3D10 mesh of the exact part (filleted corner, two M6 clearance holes, ISO 273), two mesh sizes. Checks: support reaction = load (1e-7), the arm's bending stress against M c / I at mid-arm (0.05 %), mesh convergence of the peak (1.2 %). The measured stress-concentration factor of the R = t fillet is 0.97 of the nominal stress (the peak is not at the fillet for this proportion), fed back into the reduced model.

The bracket is sized at the worst corner of its stated uncertainty (load +10 %, plate -0.2 mm, yield 90 % of the datasheet value; all three labelled as assumptions in the report). The two M6 8.8 bolts (proof load from ISO 898-1) set the mounting-leg length: they are the limiting failure mode (5th-percentile margin 0.017). The STEP file is the OpenCASCADE B-rep from the gmsh script, with the exact holes and fillet.

docs.title: (c) Passive heat sink
docs.text: The request gives the power and "still air" (read as 0 m/s, quoted in the report); the allowed temperature has no safe default, so it is asked for. With 85 °C the template reuses the heat-sink sizer physics: the closed form is the hand calculation (Elenbaas / Bar-Cohen coefficient evaluated once with the fin root at the limit), the reduced model the converged resistance network, the full model the 3-D finite-volume solve of the base with its energy balance, spreading cross-check and grid convergence. The design is sized with the convection coefficient 15 % low and the interface resistance 50 % high (the engine's stated band and the paste's spread). In still air within the default 100 x 100 x 50 mm envelope only copper meets the limit at that corner: 1.23 kg, source (case) temperature 77.7 °C nominal, 83.9 °C with the coefficient 15 % low (the base underside peaks at 77.2 °C under the source; the paste's 10 K·mm²/W over 30 x 30 mm adds 0.44 K at 40 W). Operating window: up to 47.2 W at 25 °C, or 31.3 °C ambient at 40 W.

docs.title: (d) Glider wing
docs.text: The lift comes from the vortex-lattice code of pinneapple_design.aero (closed form: elliptic lifting line; reduced: a 3 x 10 lattice per half span; full: 8 x 32, with the lattice convergence of the span efficiency, Munk's e <= 1 and the lift slope below Helmbold's estimate as checks), the profile drag from turbulent flat-plate friction and Hoerner's thickness form factor. The wing is chosen for the lowest sink rate with the design speed taken at the heavy (+5 %), thin-air (-6 % density) and draggy (+25 % profile drag) corner, so the lift coefficient stays below the 0.8 design cap in every Monte-Carlo sample: span 2.0 m (the stated limit), aspect ratio 7.7, taper 0.33, NACA 2412, sink 0.44 m/s at 7.2 m/s (wing alone). No viscous solver ran: the report says so, and that a RANS check is the next level.

docs.title: (e) Out of scope
docs.text: pp.design("an electric motor for my drone") returns OutOfScope(kind="needs"): needs an electromagnetics design template: the interior-PM machine FEA and drive models exist (pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.machines), but no template sizes a machine from a request yet, and it would also need winding current-density, thermal and demagnetisation limits, which those models do not check. A motor template is the natural next one to write with the guide below. Weapons are refused outright (kind="refused"); a request no template matches lists the installed templates; a request a template matches but cannot honestly design (a loop for a roller coaster that carries people, a bracket under fatigue loading, a liquid-cooled heat sink) is refused by that template's check_scope with what it would need.

docs.title: Writing a template
docs.text:
A new domain plugs in with one class and one register call. The worked example is pinneapple_design/intent/templates/example_spring.py, a helical compression spring (Shigley, ch. 10):

import pinneapple_design.intent as I
from pinneapple_design.intent.templates.example_spring import CoilSpringTemplate

I.register(CoilSpringTemplate())
pkg = I.design("a steel compression spring that takes 50 N with 10 mm travel", verify=False)
print(pkg.summary())

What a template declares, in the order the pipeline uses it:

  1. Selection and reading. keywords (word -> weight; the best total selects the template) and slots: each Slot has an SI unit (its dimension is what the parser matches), the words that point to it in a sentence, its valid range, and either critical=True (asked for when missing) or a default with a default_source. Phrases can set values through cues (("still air", 0.0)). check_scope(spec) refuses requests the physics does not cover; extra_questions(spec) asks for "one of these two" values.
  2. Physics. physics and assumptions (shown in the plan and the report), objectives (ObjectiveChoice with the words that select each one), failure_modes (each names an output that is a margin, >= 0 when the mode does not occur, typically capacity / demand - 1).
  3. Variables. variables(spec) -> [DesignVariable]; integers and choices (materials) are integer variables, and a value the user stated is fixed rather than optimised.
  4. Models. fidelities (closed form, reduced, full; each with the modules or programs it needs) and evaluate(level, X, spec, **options), which returns every margin and objective for a batch of designs. The full solver runs through verify(design, spec) -> FullResult with its own checks (equilibrium, energy balance, mesh convergence, a closed-form reference) and the outputs to compare with the reduced model (compare; compare_kind "at_least" / "at_most" for a solver known to be biased one way). reduced_is_expensive = True makes the optimiser fit a GP surrogate of the reduced model.
  5. Robustness. uncertainties(spec, design) -> [Uncertain] (nominal, spread, distribution and why this range), design_options(spec) (the worst corner the optimiser designs at), robust_level (a closed form calibrated to the best model that ran on the design, when the reduced model is too slow for thousands of samples).
  6. Package. geometry (closed Body meshes in metres), bill_of_materials (with the cited properties from pinneapple_design.intent.materials), operating_window, build_instructions, limits, figures.

Rules that keep templates honest: every material property comes from materials.MATERIALS (each value carries its source) or from the user; every default has a default_source; an envelope that is assumed rather than measured says so in its source and in limits; a model that has no stall, fatigue, buckling or radiation says so in limits.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text: tests/test_design_intent.py: parsing offline, units and ranges, template selection, refusal, the LLM quote check, cited materials, each demo's models against closed forms (energy conservation and v_top^2 = g R for the loop, beam theory for the bracket, the finite-volume energy balance for the heat sink, Munk's e <= 1 for the wing), the CalculiX bracket when ccx and gmsh are installed, determinism with a fixed seed, the package files passing pinneapple check, the CLI, the MCP tool and a new template plugged in. The Newton loop check takes minutes and runs with PINNEAPPLE_SLOW=1.

docs.title: Design reports without an LLM: Datasheet and the self-planning study
docs.text:
A study that ends in a folder of JSON is not a deliverable. This guide documents the two modules that turn a study into a datasheet, and the one that decides what to study before it runs:

module job pinneapple_tools.reporting.datasheet layout only: KPI strip, numbered sections, table-beside-figure rows, run plan, items to confirm, limitations. Renders HTML, prints to PDF. pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.reflector.study_report plans a compact-range study from a Problem, runs and caches every step, renders the datasheet ...reflector.study_report_text / ..._figures the narrative and the figures, both computed from the stored numbers

Nothing in this chain calls a language model. Every sentence is a format string over a number that the solver produced, and every step exists because a dimensionless number asked for it.

docs.title: The datasheet
docs.text:
from pinneapple_tools.reporting.datasheet import KPI, Figure, Note, Section, Step, Table, Datasheet

d = Datasheet("3 GHz compact range", subtitle="Quiet zone by physical optics, validated",
              eyebrow="EM / reflector")

d.kpis([KPI("Focal length", "1.50", "m", "F/D = 0.62"),
        KPI("Fresnel number", "0.42", "", "a^2 / (lambda z)")])

d.note("The design does not deliver the 0.60 m quiet zone.", "bad", "Specification not met")

s = d.section("Model and resolution", lede="What the geometry is and at what resolution it is integrated.")
s.row(Table([["Focal length", "1.50 m"], ["Mesh", "18,400 triangles"]],
            header=["quantity", "value"], caption="**The design as modelled.**"),
      Figure("fig_side.png", "**Side section at x = 0.**"))
s.note("The quiet zone is in the near field.", "warn", "Fresnel number 0.42 < 2")

d.plan(done=[Step("Model", "the section is 12 wavelengths across", "done", "3 s")],
       queued=[Step("Bandwidth", "the range must cover 2-4 GHz", "queued", "")])
d.confirm(["Which tolerance, over which diameter?"])
d.limitations(["Physical optics: no fringe (PTD) edge current."])

d.build("report/cr.html", pdf="report/cr.pdf")   # HTML always; PDF when a browser exists
  • note(text, tone, title) with tone in info (neutral), warn (amber) and bad (red). The verdict is a bad note, so a failed specification cannot be styled as a success.
  • plan(done=..., queued=...) renders the run plan: what each step is, why it is there, what it cost, and where it stands. This is what makes the document auditable rather than assertive.
  • Glyphs: write $\\lambda$, $\\pm$, ° freely. build() translates them after escaping, so a token never leaks into the PDF as literal text.
  • build() prints through headless Chromium. find_chrome() probes $PINNEAPPLE_CHROME, PATH (google-chrome, chromium, microsoft-edge, headless_shell), the macOS app bundles, then Playwright's cache. With no browser it still writes the HTML.

docs.title: The study that plans itself
docs.text:
from pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.reflector.study_report import Problem, plan, run, report

p = Problem(freq_hz=3e9, focal=1.5, section=1.2, offset=0.9, roll=0.15,
            feed_gain_dbi=12.0, qz_diameter=0.6, qz_z=3.0, band_hz=(2e9, 4e9))

for step in plan(p):
    print(step.key, "->", step.reason)

study = run(p, "results", parallel=8)   # every number cached in results/study.json
report(p, study, "report")              # report/compact_range.pdf

plan() reads the geometry and returns the steps it can justify, each with the number that put it there:

step when it is planned the number that decides it model, validation always the section in wavelengths; the integrator is checked against a closed form, PO against GO, the mesh against itself, before any number is read qz always the quiet zone at the reference planes, cuts and the full disk spec always usable diameter at three tolerance tiers, so the verdict does not hang on one threshold reference reference= given published rows are compared row by row calibration reference_geometry= given how close the module's edge family can get to the published extents and area, with the residual reported rather than hidden by a fit profile the edge is thin in wavelengths the spread of every metric over the plausible profile family bandwidth band_hz= given the edge depth in wavelengths across the band tolerance always what a feed displacement of 0.25-3 lambda costs axial always the quiet zone is a cylinder, not a plane sweep qz_to_section > 0.6 or Fresnel < 2 whether any (feed gain, section size, rolled edge) in the family reaches the specification optimize same condition a grid and a surrogate-driven search on the same solve budget

Problem.from_text() parses a sentence into the same object:

p = Problem.from_text("3 GHz, focal length 1.5 m, 1.2 m square reflector, 0.15 m rolled edge, "
                      "0.6 m quiet zone at 3 m, feed 12 dBi")

The command line does the whole thing in one call:

python -m pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.reflector.study_report \
    --freq 3 --focal 1.5 --section 1.2 --offset 0.9 --roll 0.15 --gain 12 --qz 0.6 --qz-distance 3 \
    --band 2 4 --parallel 8 --out cr_study

The lengths are metres unless --feet is given, and Problem.from_text accepts either unit in the sentence itself.

docs.title: Rules the narrative follows
docs.text:
These are the ones that keep the report honest, and they are worth copying into a new study:

  1. The verdict comes from a criterion, not from a mood. usable >= qz_diameter at the declared tolerance tier, printed with the percentage of the specification it represents.
  2. A disagreement with a reference is stated with its cause. Where PO cannot represent the reference's edge, the difference is reported and the conclusions are drawn from differences between designs, which share the edge, never from absolute levels.
  3. Every absolute claim is quoted against the spread of the model family. If a conclusion does not survive the profile-family band, it is not a conclusion.
  4. A metric with a different meaning is flagged as such. The cross-polar level on the principal cuts is a feed property: with a symmetric reflector and an ideal cos^q feed it cancels by symmetry, so PO reporting -58 dB where a full-wave solve of a real horn reports -23 dB is measuring a different thing, not making an error. The report says so instead of claiming agreement.
  5. The run plan and the limitations are part of the document. What was not modelled is a section, not a footnote.

docs.title: Worked examples
docs.text:
• A full study -- the reference geometry, the full-disk metrics, the 48-design sweep and the 30-solve equal-budget search -- is examples/use_cases/antennas/compact_range_qz.py for the model side; adding run() and report() around the same Problem produces the datasheet.
  • The same datasheet applied to an audit, where an external solver's result table is read back, checked against the physical bound of the antenna class and written up without a new solve, is the pattern in docs/guides/antenna_design.md.

See also Compact range quiet zone for the underlying model and Antenna design for the Vivaldi side.

docs.title: Design studies: one problem, many optimisers, verified candidates
docs.text:
pinneapple_design.design_optimizer describes a design optimisation problem once and runs any method on it under the same evaluation budget. Every evaluated design is recorded, so the Pareto front, the convergence history, the feasibility report and the cost are computed the same way whatever produced them. Candidates found on a surrogate are re-evaluated with a reference model or solver before anyone calls them optimal.

It is the engine behind two apps: the Engineering Design Optimizer (black-box, surrogate + high-fidelity verification) and the Physics Design Optimizer (gradient-aware, method comparison, design files).

docs.title: The problem
docs.text:
from pinneapple_design.design_optimizer import (Constraint, DesignProblem, DesignSpace, FunctionEvaluator,
                                                Objective, Variable, run)

space = DesignSpace([Variable("x", -1.0, 3.0), Variable("y", -1.0, 1.0)])
f = lambda X: {"f1": X[:, 0] ** 2 + X[:, 1] ** 2, "f2": (X[:, 0] - 2) ** 2 + X[:, 1] ** 2, "g": X[:, 0] + X[:, 1]}
problem = DesignProblem("demo", space, [Objective("f1"), Objective("f2")], [Constraint("g", upper=1.5)],
                        FunctionEvaluator(f, ["f1", "f2", "g"], torch_fn=f))   # torch_fn: gradients via autograd
result = run(problem, "nsga2", budget=400, seed=0)
print(result.summary(), result.evaluations.rows(space, result.pareto())[:3])
  • Variable(kind="integer") rounds a variable (fin counts, ply counts). Gradient methods relax it when the evaluator accepts fractional values (relaxable=True), mark those iterates relaxed and evaluate the rounded end point; relaxed designs never enter a Pareto set.
  • Constraint(kind=...) labels a limit as physical, manufacturing or validity; feasibility_report lists each constraint's value, margin and status (active within 5 % of the bound, inactive, violated).
  • An evaluator may return "_valid"; False (a surrogate outside its training range, a geometry that does not exist) makes the design infeasible with that reason.

docs.title: Evaluators
docs.text: Evaluator Use FunctionEvaluator(fn, outputs, torch_fn=None) any vectorised Python model; torch_fn makes it differentiable ZooEvaluator(name, space, fixed=...) a pp.zoo model; its validity range marks designs invalid TorchModuleEvaluator(module, outputs, ...) an MLP, PINN, neural operator or differentiable physics model CommandEvaluator(command, space, outputs) an external solver: designs in a CSV, outputs back in a CSV from_model_ref(ref, space) zoo:<name>, a TorchScript file or cmd:<command> from a model reference GPSurrogate(problem, outputs) Gaussian-process surrogate trained on your evaluated designs

docs.title: Methods and budget
docs.text: run(problem, method, budget=..., seed=...) with random (Latin hypercube), nsga2, pymoo-nsga2 (optional pymoo), scipy-de, scipy-slsqp (finite-difference gradients), bayesian (GP, ParEGO) and gradient (Adam through autograd). One evaluation is one design passed to the evaluator: a finite-difference gradient costs d + 1, an autograd step costs one (and its wall time is reported). compare_methods runs several on the same budget and seeds and reports the hypervolume (normalised over all runs), the evaluations needed to reach 95 % of the best, and whether each run converged (hypervolume grew less than 1 % over its last quarter).

docs.title: Verification and active learning
docs.text:
from pinneapple_design.design_optimizer import presets, run, select_candidates, verify_candidates

problem = presets.heatsink_problem("surrogate")                 # zoo MLP of the heat-sink FVM engine
res = run(problem, "nsga2", budget=600, initial=problem.space.from_dicts([presets.heatsink_baseline()]))
chosen = select_candidates(res.evaluations, res.pareto(), 5)
report = verify_candidates(problem, res.evaluations, chosen, presets.HeatsinkEvaluator("fvm"))
print([r["status"] for r in report.rows], report.errors["t_source_c"])

Statuses: verified (the reference ran and the design is feasible under it), rejected by reference, reference failed, only surrogate. surrogate_assisted(problem, reference) fits a GP on reference runs, optimises on it with each constraint applied to a pessimistic value (mean plus or minus 2 standard deviations), verifies designs along the front and adds them to the data; the error it reports per round is measured at designs the GP had not been trained on.

docs.title: Presets
docs.text:
• heatsink_problem(fidelity): plate-fin heat sink in ducted air, minimise mass and cost (or pressure drop) within source temperature, pressure drop, fin stress and extrusion limits. Fidelities surrogate (zoo MLP, differentiable), closed_form (resistance network) and fvm (3-D finite-volume base, the reference). The cost model is an assumption the user sets (CostModel).
  • airfoil_problem(): CST airfoil at Re 4e6, minimise drag and maximise spar depth at a lift target, on the zoo ensemble airfoil_cst_rans_mlp (differentiable). No reference solver ships with it, so its candidates stay "only surrogate" until verified with OpenFOAM.
  • plate_fin_bodies, airfoil_bodies and design_file(bodies, "stl" | "step") write the chosen design as a binary STL or an AP214 faceted STEP file through the geometry library's writers; preset_bodies(preset, design) picks the right one.
  • preset_info(preset): what a form needs (variables, operating point, limits, cost model, objectives, baseline design and the reference that verifies candidates).

docs.title: After a run: what an app shows and exports
docs.text:
The design apps are built on these calls, so a run gives the same files and tables from Python:

  • verify_front(problem, ev, front, n, reference) returns the candidates spread along the front, the verification report (None without a reference) and the status of each candidate;
  • write_design_files(folder, problem, ev, candidates, status, labels=...) writes evaluations.csv, candidates.csv (with the verification status and, from a comparison, the run that found each one), candidates_to_run.csv (the variables only, to run in your solver) and parameter_space.json;
  • chart_points(problem, ev, front) thins the evaluations for a trade-off plot and keeps the front;
  • verify_uploaded_results(space, candidates, results, objectives, constraints) verifies the exported candidates against the solver results you ran offline, matching rows by their variable values;
  • MethodComparison.union_result() and .fronts(seed) give a comparison as one result (for study_result) and each method's front.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text: The heat-sink model assumes ducted laminar/developing flow without radiation; the fin stress is root bending of a cantilever fin under a uniform lateral load. The hypervolume above two objectives is a seeded Monte Carlo estimate. Bayesian optimisation refits a GP at every proposal, so it is meant for budgets of a few hundred evaluations at most.

docs.title: Dimensional analysis, Buckingham pi and curve collapse
docs.text:
pinneapple_analysis.dynamics.dimensional finds the dimensionless groups of a problem, checks that the quantities given are enough to form them, and derives the scaling laws that dimensions alone determine. It also measures whether a family of curves collapses onto one after rescaling, against controls that can expose a collapse that is not real.

All the algebra is exact rational arithmetic (fractions.Fraction), so group exponents have no round-off.

Results follow the toolkit's shared contract. They carry:

  • the assumptions, each marked checked or unchecked;
  • diagnostics;
  • the conditions under which the method does not apply.

docs.title: Two different things: dimensional analysis and empirical normalisation
docs.text:
Dimensional analysis uses only the dimensions of the quantities. Take n quantities over k base dimensions, and let D (k × n) be the matrix of exponents. A product Π = ∏ q_i^α_i is dimensionless exactly when D α = 0. The groups are a basis of that null space: there are n − rank(D) of them (Buckingham 1914).

Empirical normalisation uses the data: dividing by the maximum, z-scoring, or min-max scaling a curve and its time span. Its result is dimensionless, but it is not a pi group. Two curves that obey different laws can look alike after it.

The module keeps the two apart:

  • TrajectoryNormalizer.dimensional(...) builds its scales from quantity products and checks their dimensions. It raises DimensionError if a "time scale" is not a time.
  • TrajectoryNormalizer.empirical(...) marks every trajectory it produces as source["normalization"]["kind"] == "empirical", with the note "not a pi representation".

docs.title: Analyzing a problem
docs.text: Task Call Gives Find the groups BuckinghamPiAnalyzer(quantities, target=..., repeating=...).analyze() The n − rank(D) groups with integer exponents, named when they match a known group (Re, Pe, Fo, Pr, Ra, Gr, Nu, Bi, Ma, Fr, We, St, Sc). Diagnostics for isolated dimensions and insufficient quantities. Check a known group analyzer.express(DimensionlessGroup({...})) Exact exponents writing it as a product of the groups found, or None if it is not one. Find characteristic scales analyzer.characteristic_scales(Dimension.of(T=1)) One product with that dimension, plus the groups that make it ambiguous. For example, L/U and L²/α differ by Pe. Get the implied scaling law analyzer.scaling_law() When only the target's group exists, the exponents are exact and only the constant is unknown. Fit the constant with .fit_constant(y, values). Fit a power law freely ScalingLaw.fit(y, {"x1": ..., ...}) Least squares in log space, with t intervals per exponent and R². Check an equation check_homogeneity({"term": Dimension, ...}) Whether every term has the same dimension.

docs.title: Normalising and comparing curves
docs.text:
Task Call Gives Normalise trajectories TrajectoryNormalizer.dimensional(...) or .empirical(...), then .apply(tr) and .invert(tr) A labelled, invertible rescaling Measure a collapse CurveCollapseAnalyzer(curves).analyze(x_scales, y_scales, origin=...) The collapse measure, the raw measure, and a permutation p-value, plus degenerate and by-construction flags Find the best collapse exponents .fit_exponents(P) and .sensitivity(P, p, q) The best x / P^p, y / P^q, and the curvature at that optimum (stability) Compare two systems SimilarityMetrics.groups(groups, a, b) and .curves(a, b) Log-ratio of each group, and the distance between two curves

Units and systems. Dimension accepts any base names, so a force-length-time system works as well as SI. Dimension.from_unit("W/m2/K") and PhysicalQuantity.from_unit(name, value, unit) read units with pinneapple_data.physical_units, which converts values to SI. A unit with an offset (°C, °F) is refused for absolute values.

DimensionlessGroup.sympy() returns the group as a SymPy expression.

docs.title: How the groups are built
docs.text:
With a target, the groups use repeating variables (Rayleigh's method):

  1. Choose r = rank(D) dimensionally independent quantities, not including the target.
  2. Make one group for each remaining quantity q_j, as q_j ∏ R^a, solving D_R a = −D_j exactly.
  3. Scale the result to coprime integers.

The target therefore appears in exactly one group, which is listed first. Without a target, the groups are the integer null-space basis of the reduced row echelon form.

Either way, the groups are unique only up to products and powers of each other. express shows that two bases agree.

docs.title: When the quantities are insufficient
docs.text: Situation Status What it means A base dimension carried by a single quantity isolated_dimension:<base>, warn That quantity cannot enter any group, so either it is irrelevant (like the mass of a pendulum) or a quantity carrying that dimension is missing. The target's dimension cannot be built from the other quantities failure The heat flux q from k and L alone needs a temperature difference. The result is not applicable. rank(D) = n failure No group exists.

docs.title: The collapse measure
docs.text:
The measure is the mean across-member variance on the common support, divided by the variance of the master curve:

C = mean_x Var_k[y_k(x)] / Var_x[mean_k y_k(x)]

C = 0 means the curves are identical, and C of order 1 or more means there is no collapse. It is unchanged by a common rescaling of y.

Three controls go with it:

  1. The raw measure. The collapse is compared with the curves before any rescaling.
  2. A permutation control. The same scale factors are assigned to the wrong members. If the permuted scalings collapse as well, the scaling explains nothing. The p-value cannot go below 1/m! for m members: about 0.04 for 4 members and 0.008 for 5.
  3. origin=. It says where the scales came from:
  4. "dimensional": built from quantities, independent of these curves.
  5. "empirical": taken from the curves themselves. This raises the collapse_by_construction warning.
  6. "fitted": exponents fitted on these same curves. This raises a warning that the p-value is optimistic, and that the result should be validated on held-out members.

A rescaling that flattens the master curve is reported as degenerate, and the result is not applicable, rather than as success.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
When it works. Drag on a sphere:

from pinneapple_analysis.dynamics.dimensional import BuckinghamPiAnalyzer, PhysicalQuantity as Q

qs = [Q.from_unit("F", None, "N"), Q.from_unit("rho", None, "kg/m3"), Q.from_unit("U", None, "m/s"),
      Q.from_unit("d", None, "m"), Q.from_unit("mu", None, "Pa s")]
r = BuckinghamPiAnalyzer(qs, target="F").analyze(aliases={"d": "L"})
print(r.estimate["groups"])   # ['Pi_1 = F / (rho U^2 d^2)', '1/Reynolds = mu / (rho U d)']

Dimensions say only that F / (ρ U² d²) = f(Re). They do not give f. In the creeping-flow limit, where ρ drops out, the analysis gives F = C μ U d exactly, and the data fix C = 3π; see stokes_constant in the benchmarks.

When it tells you the list is wrong. The pendulum, with its mass:

r = BuckinghamPiAnalyzer([Q.of("T", T=1), Q.of("L", L=1), Q.of("g", L=1, T=-2), Q.of("m", M=1)], target="T").analyze()
print(r.estimate["groups"])          # ['Pi_1 = T^2 g / L']  ->  T = C sqrt(L/g)
print(r.diagnostic("isolated_dimension:M"))   # warn: m cannot enter any group

Remove g from the list and the target can no longer be formed. The result then reports insufficient quantities instead of returning a group.

When a collapse is not evidence. Take five curves that follow five different laws (an exponential, a line, a logistic, a cosine and a cubic). After min-max and span normalisation they reach a collapse measure of 0.44. That is the same value as the raw curves of the same five laws (0.44), and the result carries the collapse_by_construction warning. A true dimensional collapse is many orders of magnitude tighter: 1.6e-5 for Newton cooling, 4e-9 for the conduction profiles below.

docs.title: Assumptions, failures, limits
docs.text:
Always unchecked. The list of quantities is complete and relevant. Buckingham's theorem rewrites the relation among the quantities given, and cannot tell you which quantities matter. Dimensional constants (g, a material constant) must be listed when they matter.

Not handled. - Vector or directional dimensions (Huntley's L_x, L_y). You can declare them as separate base names, but the module does not reason about them. - Angles, which are treated as dimensionless. - Mixing unit systems in one matrix. Any base names are accepted, but nothing is converted between systems.

Collapse. - The measure is computed on the common support only, by linear interpolation of each curve. - A good collapse supports a scaling. It does not explain it.

Cost. - Exact elimination is O(k² n) in fractions, which is negligible for physical problems (n below about 20). - The automatic choice of repeating variables tries combinations in order, O(C(n, r)). - Collapse with P permutations costs O(P · m · n_grid).

docs.title: Benchmarks
docs.text:
To reproduce the table:

python -m pinneapple_analysis.dynamics.benchmarks dimensional

It uses seed=0 and 999 permutations. The values below were measured on 2026-10-31.

Case Quantity Reference Computed Error Pass reynolds Re 7.485e+04 (compute_dimensionless_numbers) 7.485e+04 0 yes peclet Pe 5.357e+05 (compute_dimensionless_numbers) 5.357e+05 1.2e-10 yes prandtl Pr 7.143 (compute_dimensionless_numbers) 7.143 0 yes fourier Fo 0.00168 0.00168 0 yes rayleigh_in_span Ra is a product of the groups found yes yes: Ra = Π₁ Π₂^½ Π₃^½ – yes pendulum_constant C in T = C √(L/g), 40 points, 1 % noise 2π = 6.2832 6.2887 ± 0.0109 0.0055 (z = 0.50) yes pendulum_free_exponent_L exponent of L, free fit 0.5 0.4998 ± 0.0024 −0.0002 (z = 0.07) yes stokes_constant C in F = C μ U d 3π 9.4248 1.8e-15 yes cooling_collapse collapse under t/τ, T/ΔT 0 1.6e-05 1.6e-05 yes (raw 11.2, permuted median 50.3, p = 0.007) conduction_collapse collapse under x/√(αt) 0 4.0e-09 4.0e-09 yes (raw 1.38, p = 0.036: 4 members, floor 1/24) fitted_exponent_x exponent of τ in t/τ 1 1.0005 4.7e-04 yes fitted_exponent_y exponent of τ in ΔT = τ^½ 0.5 0.4994 −6.2e-04 yes empirical_false_collapse 5 different laws after min-max and span 0.4387 (raw) 0.4429 – demonstration, flagged collapse_by_construction

What the rows show, and what they do not:

  • Group values. The Re, Pe and Pr values agree with an existing implementation of the same textbook formulas. That shows the groups are the right ones, not that the formulas were validated independently.
  • Collapse residuals. These come from linear interpolation of irregularly sampled curves, 81 points per cooling curve.
  • The pendulum. It uses the small-angle period. Large amplitudes add the amplitude as a group, which this case does not test.

docs.title: Critical slowing down and early-warning indicators
docs.text:
pinneapple_analysis.dynamics.early_warning computes, from a time series, the statistical signatures of a system losing stability. It reports how strongly those signatures trend, and checks the trend against a null model and against its own sensitivity to the analysis choices.

The series can come from measurements, from a simulation, or from a trained model's prediction (see the shared foundation). Results follow the toolkit's contract.

docs.title: An indicator is not a prediction
docs.text:
Near a local bifurcation the dominant eigenvalue λ of the linearised dynamics goes to zero, and perturbations decay more slowly. For dx = λx dt + σ dW with λ < 0:

Quantity Formula variance σ²/(2|λ|) lag-Δt autocorrelation e^{λΔt}

Both rise as λ → 0⁻ (Scheffer et al. 2009; Dakos et al. 2012). A significant rise is consistent with this, but it does not show that a transition will happen, nor when.

Several things produce the same rise without any loss of stability:

  • a trend left in the data;
  • noise whose amplitude grows;
  • a change of sampling;
  • slow forcing far from a bifurcation.

The benchmarks below measure the first two. Conversely, many transitions give no warning at all: noise-induced, rate-induced and global ones. Every result states this in limits, and TransitionDiagnostics keeps the indicator and the prediction apart: is_prediction is always False.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
Step Call Notes Detrend detrend(t, x, "loess" \| "gaussian" \| "linear" \| "none", bandwidth) loess (local linear) is the default: it has no first-order edge bias. The Gaussian kernel of Dakos et al. is biased near the ends by about slope × bandwidth. On the saddle-node benchmark, where the equilibrium moves, that bias swamped the fluctuations: residual variance 9e-5 against a theoretical 2.6e-6. Rolling statistics RollingStatistics(window).compute(t, x, ("variance", "std", "cv", "skewness", "kurtosis")) window is a fraction of the record (or by="time"). Missing values are skipped, and a window with fewer than min_count values gives NaN. Autocorrelation AutocorrelationAnalyzer(window, lag=1) On an irregular grid, use lag_time= and tol=: the estimate is built from pairs of samples whose spacing is within the tolerance of the lag. Recovery rate RecoveryRateEstimator.from_ar1(ac, dt) gives ln φ / dt; .from_pulse(t, x) fits an exponential relaxation The AR(1) rate approaches zero from below near a bifurcation. Spectral indicators indicators low_frequency_power and spectral_exponent Welch periodogram per window (spectral reddening). They need a regular grid. All of it, with significance EarlyWarningAnalyzer(...).analyze(trajectory) See below. Variance, AC1 and recovery rate together CriticalSlowingDown(...) The critical-slowing-down signature. Robustness .sensitivity(windows=..., bandwidths=...) and .sampling_sensitivity(factors=...) Kendall τ over a grid of choices, and over coarser sampling. Verdict TransitionDiagnostics(result, sensitivity).report() One of no signal, indicator signal (not a prediction) or inconclusive, with the doubts listed.

EarlyWarningAnalyzer.analyze returns, for each indicator:

  • its values per window and their Kendall τ against time;
  • a surrogate p-value: the share of stationary surrogates whose τ is at least the observed one.

Kendall's own p-value assumes independent points, and overlapping windows violate that, so it is kept only in the StabilityIndicator and is not used for the verdict.

The surrogates keep the autocorrelation of the residuals and remove any trend:

  • an AR(1) fitted to the residuals (the default);
  • phase-randomised or IAAFT surrogates from pinneapple_systems.time_series.predictability.

The analysis also checks the residuals. It reports:

  • the missing fraction and the regularity of the grid;
  • a Kendall trend left in the residuals, which means the detrending was incomplete;
  • a warning when no detrending was done;
  • the ADF and KPSS p-values, from pinneapple_systems.time_series.audit.tests, when statsmodels is installed.

docs.title: Benchmark series
docs.text:
ramp_series(kind) simulates stochastic normal forms by Euler–Maruyama. In every one the decay rate r of perturbations goes linearly from 1 to end (> 0), so the system approaches the bifurcation but does not cross it:

kind Equation saddle_node dx = (μ − x²)dt transcritical dx = (−r x − x²)dt pitchfork dx = (−r x − x³)dt ou_decreasing dx = −r x dt

Three negative controls keep the stability constant:

  • stable;
  • stable_trend: an accelerating trend in the mean;
  • stable_growing_noise: the noise amplitude multiplied by 3 over the record.

The saddle-node and transcritical basins shrink with r. A path that leaves the basin is reported through tipped_at, and the rest of the series is NaN.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
When it works. The OU process with decreasing stability:

from pinneapple_analysis.dynamics.early_warning import EarlyWarningAnalyzer, TransitionDiagnostics, ramp_series

s = ramp_series("ou_decreasing", seed=1, end=0.1)
an = EarlyWarningAnalyzer(n_surrogates=99)
r = an.analyze((s["t"], s["x"]))
print(r.estimate["variance"]["tau"], r.estimate["ac1"]["tau"])    # 0.89 and 0.88, both p = 0.01
print(TransitionDiagnostics(r, an.sensitivity((s["t"], s["x"]))).report()["verdict"])
# 'indicator signal (not a prediction)'

When it misleads. In both cases below the stability never changes:

s = ramp_series("stable_trend", seed=2)                          # accelerating trend in the mean only
EarlyWarningAnalyzer(detrend="none").analyze((s["t"], s["x"]))   # AC1 rises "significantly"; flagged no_detrending
EarlyWarningAnalyzer(detrend="loess").analyze((s["t"], s["x"]))  # the rise disappears

s = ramp_series("stable_growing_noise", seed=3)                  # noise amplitude x3
EarlyWarningAnalyzer().analyze((s["t"], s["x"]))                 # variance rises significantly, AC1 does not

This is why variance alone is not evidence of slowing down, and why the verdict requires the indicators that a linearisation predicts to agree.

docs.title: Assumptions, failure conditions, limits
docs.text:
Unchecked assumptions. The data cannot test these, and each result lists them:

  • the transition, if any, is a local bifurcation reached slowly;
  • the control parameter changes slowly compared with the recovery time;
  • the noise amplitude and the sampling are stationary;
  • the detrending removes the slow trajectory and keeps the fluctuations.

The analysis is not applicable when:

  • there are fewer than 3 × min_count values;
  • the grid is irregular and no lag_time is given for the autocorrelation;
  • spectral indicators are requested on an irregular grid.

Known weaknesses, measured in the benchmarks:

  • White measurement noise dilutes the autocorrelation and adds constant variance.
  • Coarse sampling leaves too few points per window.
  • The p-value has a floor of 1/(n_surrogates + 1).

Cost. - On a regular grid without missing values, the rolling statistics are vectorised: a 1000-point series with 99 surrogates and two indicators took 1.2 s here, LOESS detrending included. - With missing values or an irregular grid, the statistics loop over windows. - LOESS detrending is O(n²).

docs.title: Benchmarks
docs.text:
To reproduce the table:

python -m pinneapple_analysis.dynamics.benchmarks early_warning

It uses seed=0, 40 replicate series per row, 99 AR(1) surrogates and α = 0.05. "Detection" means that variance and lag-1 autocorrelation both rise significantly.

Case What is measured Reference Measured Pass ou_ac1 mean rolling lag-1 autocorrelation, stationary OU (40 series of 2000 points) e^(−θΔt) = 0.7787 0.7739 ± 0.0022 (z = 2.2) yes ou_variance mean rolling variance, same series σ²/(2θ) = 0.01 0.009952 ± 0.0001 (z = 0.47) yes detect_saddle_node detection rate, ramp of r from 1 to 0.1 ≥ 0.8 0.975 yes detect_transcritical detection rate, ramp of r from 1 to 0.1 ≥ 0.8 0.975 yes detect_pitchfork detection rate, ramp of r from 1 to 0.1 ≥ 0.8 0.975 yes detect_ou_decreasing detection rate, ramp of r from 1 to 0.1 ≥ 0.8 0.975 yes fp_stable false-positive rate, constant stability α = 0.05 0 yes fp_trend_raw false-positive rate, accelerating trend, no detrending — 0.65 demonstration fp_trend_loess the same, detrended with LOESS α = 0.05 0 yes fp_growing_noise_variance variance alone, noise ×3, constant stability — 1 demonstration fp_growing_noise_ac1 AC1 alone, the same series α = 0.05 0.025 yes detect_ou_obs_noise_1 detection, white measurement noise of 1× the initial std — 0.8 demonstration detect_ou_obs_noise_3 detection, measurement noise of 3× the initial std — 0.2 demonstration detect_ou_subsampled_4 detection, every 4th sample kept (250 points) — 0.625 demonstration detect_ou_subsampled_16 detection, every 16th sample kept (62 points) — 0.05 demonstration

The values above were measured on 2026-10-31. The ou_ac1 estimate sits slightly below the theory (z = 2.2). This is consistent with the known small-sample bias of the lag-1 estimator, about (1 + 4φ)/n_window. The false-positive rate of the constant-stability control was 0 of 40. The AR(1)-surrogate test is conservative here: it rejects less often than α.

The rows marked "demonstration" have no pass/fail reference: they measure a known failure mode.

What the benchmarks do not cover:

  • These are normal forms with additive noise and a linear ramp, so detection here is easier than in field data.
  • The rates depend on the record length (1000 points), the noise, and how close the ramp ends to the bifurcation (r = 0.1).
  • They do not measure how early a signal appears before a transition, and the toolkit makes no claim about lead time.

docs.title: First-passage and hitting times
docs.text:
pinneapple_analysis.dynamics.first_passage estimates when a trajectory first reaches a boundary:

tau = inf{ t >= 0 : X(t) in boundary of Omega }

It works on a single trajectory, on an ensemble of observed or simulated trajectories, or on a stochastic model that it simulates itself. Trajectories can come from measurements, solvers, closed forms or a trained network's predictions (see the shared foundation for how to load them).

All results follow the toolkit's contract. Each one carries:

  • the estimate and its uncertainty;
  • the assumptions, each marked as checked or not;
  • numerical diagnostics;
  • the conditions under which the method does not apply;
  • a reproducibility record (seed, input hash, versions).

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
Question Call Method When did this trajectory first cross the boundary? FirstPassageAnalyzer(bc).crossing(trajectory) Linear interpolation inside the sampling interval that contains the crossing. Works on irregular grids and skips missing samples. What is the distribution of τ over these observed runs? .from_trajectories(ensemble) One crossing per run. A run that never crosses is right-censored at the end of its window. The survival function is the Kaplan-Meier estimate with Greenwood log-log bands. What does this stochastic model predict? .monte_carlo(sde, x0, t_max=..., dt=..., n_paths=...) Euler-Maruyama paths, with a Brownian-bridge crossing correction and optional reflecting walls. Paths not hit by t_max are censored there. How much does the step size dt still matter? .dt_convergence(sde, x0, dts=[...]) Repeats the run at each step size. Reports the successive changes, the observed order and a Richardson estimate. What does a solved Fokker-Planck equation give? survival_from_density(t, x, p) or survival_from_solution(sol, x, t) (a pp.solve result) With an absorbing boundary, the mass of the density is the survival probability: S(t) = ∫ p(x, t) dx (trapezoid rule). The density of τ is -dS/dt, and the hazard is f / S. Diagnostics: initial mass, any increase of S, negative density. How sensitive is the answer to a parameter, or to the choice of noise model? .sensitivity(lambda v: SDE(...), values, ...) or .sensitivity({"additive": ..., "multiplicative": ...}, ...) Common random numbers (same seed for every model), plus a central-difference derivative for a parameter sweep.

Each result has a HittingTimeDistribution for every boundary (result.distribution when there is only one). It gives:

Method Returns survival(t) S(t) = P(τ > t) survival_function() S(t) with its confidence band cdf(t) P(τ ≤ t) hitting_probability(T) P(τ ≤ T) and its interval, as a CrossingProbability. .no_crossing gives the probability of not crossing within T. quantile(q), quantile_ci(q), median quantiles of τ and their intervals prediction_interval(level) interval for the τ of a new realisation mean() the mean, or the restricted mean when some samples are censored (see below) density(bins) histogram density of the event times

The probability interval depends on censoring:

  • If no sample is censored before T, it is a binomial proportion with a Wilson interval.
  • Otherwise it is the Kaplan-Meier estimate with its band.

docs.title: Boundaries
docs.text:
Boundary Call Hit when upper threshold BoundaryCondition.threshold(b, "up", component) x ≥ b lower threshold BoundaryCondition.threshold(b, "down", component) x ≤ b two-sided threshold BoundaryCondition.threshold(b, "either") x reaches b from the side it started on interval (exit) BoundaryCondition.interval(l, u) x leaves (l, u) level set, any dimension BoundaryCondition.level_set(phi) phi(x) ≥ 0, e.g. phi = |x| - R to leave a ball reflecting wall BoundaryCondition.threshold(L, "down", behaviour="reflecting"), passed as reflecting=[...] never: the state is mirrored back into the domain

A list of boundaries gives one τ per boundary on the same trajectories. Use this for several thresholds, or for the two sides of an interval separately.

Reflecting walls are supported only in monte_carlo, and only as thresholds.

docs.title: Foundations
docs.text:
Deterministic crossing. Let g(x) ≥ 0 mean "on or past the boundary", and let a crossing be bracketed by the samples i-1 and i. The crossing time is

tau = t[i-1] + (t[i] - t[i-1]) * (-g[i-1]) / (g[i] - g[i-1]).

For a twice-differentiable trajectory the error is at most |f''| h² / (8 |f'|), so it is second order in the sampling step h. This is measured in the benchmark below.

The bracket [t_{i-1}, t_i] is always reported. It is an exact bound on τ only if the trajectory does not leave and come back between two samples, which the samples themselves cannot show. That assumption is therefore always listed as unchecked.

Censoring. A run observed until time c without a crossing tells you only that τ > c. Treating c as an event time, or dropping the run, biases the distribution. In the benchmark, ignoring censoring is off by 0.15 in S(t).

The Kaplan-Meier estimator uses each run exactly up to its own end:

S(t) = prod over t_j <= t of (1 - d_j / n_j)

where d_j is the number of events at t_j and n_j the number of runs still at risk. Its variance is Greenwood's formula, and the band is built on the log-log scale so it stays inside [0, 1].

Kaplan-Meier requires independent censoring: when a run stops being observed must not depend on how close it is to the boundary.

Monte Carlo of an SDE. The model is dX = a(t, X) dt + b(t, X) dW with diagonal noise. Each Euler-Maruyama step is

X[k+1] = X[k] + a h + b sqrt(h) Z

which is weak order 1 in h.

Checking the boundary only at the steps misses paths that cross and come back within a step. This makes τ late by O(√h): the effective barrier moves out by about 0.5826 σ √h (Broadie, Glasserman & Kou 1997). For scalar thresholds and intervals, the Brownian-bridge correction adds the probability of such an excursion,

p = exp(-2 d_k d_{k+1} / (b^2 h))

where d_k and d_{k+1} are the distances to the barrier at the two ends of the step. The correction:

  • reads b at the start of the step;
  • places a bridge crossing at the middle of the step;
  • for an interval, adds the two one-sided probabilities, which is first order.

Level-set boundaries have no bridge correction. They are checked only at the steps, and the result says so in its diagnostics.

When the mean is not the mean. If some samples have not hit the boundary by the horizon T, the mean of τ cannot be estimated from the data. mean() then returns the restricted mean

integral from 0 to T of S(t) dt

labelled as such. It is a lower bound of the true mean. In that case censored_fraction is a warning, and upper quantiles may be inf.

docs.title: Closed forms
docs.text:
These functions serve as references in the tests and are available to callers. Here a is the distance to the barrier and ν the drift towards it.

Function Result Source brownian_first_passage_pdf, _cdf, _mean Inverse-Gaussian law of x0 + μt + σW reaching b. It is defective when the drift points away: total mass exp(2νa/σ²). Karatzas & Shreve (1991), sec. 3.5.C. The tests check it against scipy.stats.invgauss. brownian_exit_probability, brownian_exit_mean Exit side and mean exit time from (l, u), from the scale function Cox & Miller (1965), sec. 5.7 brownian_exit_survival P(τ > t) for an interval, by eigenfunction expansion after removing the drift The tests check that its integral equals brownian_exit_mean to 1e-6 ou_mean_first_passage Ornstein-Uhlenbeck mean first-passage time, T = √π/(σ√θ) ∫ erfcx(-(y-m)√θ/σ) dy, by quadrature Gardiner, Stochastic Methods, sec. 6.2. The tests compare it with an independent finite-difference solve of D T'' + a T' = -1.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
When it works. This is Brownian motion with drift towards a barrier, where the exact answer is known: E[τ] = a/μ = 2.

import numpy as np
from pinneapple_analysis import dynamics as dyn

an = dyn.FirstPassageAnalyzer(dyn.BoundaryCondition.threshold(1.0, name="b"))
r = an.monte_carlo(dyn.SDE.brownian(mu=0.5, sigma=1.0), 0.0, t_max=60.0, dt=2e-3, n_paths=20_000, seed=0)
d = r.distribution
print(r.summary())                   # ok; diagnostics: MC relative s.e. 0.010, dt / median tau 0.0019
print(d.mean())                      # sample mean 2.0034, s.e. 0.0204 (truth 2)
print(d.hitting_probability(2.0))    # 0.7174, Wilson 95 % interval (0.7111, 0.7235)
print(d.prediction_interval(0.9))    # (0.211, 7.137): where the tau of a new path falls 90 % of the time

When it does not answer the question asked. Here the drift points away from the barrier. The barrier is reached with probability e^{-1} ≈ 0.368 over infinite time, and the mean of τ is infinite.

r = an.monte_carlo(dyn.SDE.brownian(mu=-0.5, sigma=1.0), 0.0, t_max=20.0, dt=1e-2, n_paths=5000, seed=0)
print(r.estimate["b"])   # p_hit 0.376 by t = 20 (exact 0.3667), median inf, mean 13.2 = restricted mean up to 20
print(r.diagnostic("b: censored_fraction"))   # warn: 62 % of paths not hit; the mean is a lower bound

The number labelled "mean" in this second run is not E[τ]. The result says so in mean_kind and in the censored_fraction warning.

Observed data. A cooling test logged to CSV with units in the header:

tr = dyn.from_csv("cooling.csv", time="time")                     # "time [s]", "T [°C]" -> units kept
r = dyn.FirstPassageAnalyzer(dyn.BoundaryCondition.threshold(50.0, "down", component="T")).crossing(tr)
r.estimate, r.uncertainty            # tau, and the sampling interval that brackets it

docs.title: Diagnostics and failure conditions
docs.text:
Diagnostic Meaning censored_fraction Share of samples not hit by the horizon. Above 1 % it is a warning (restricted mean). At 100 % it is a failure, and the result is marked not applicable. mc_relative_se_mean Monte Carlo relative standard error of the mean. A warning above 2 %. dt_over_median_tau The step compared with the hitting time scale. Above 1 %, run dt_convergence. monitoring Brownian bridge, or discrete steps only, which is a warning: biased late by O(√dt). started_on_boundary The trajectory or path starts on or past the boundary, so τ = t0. crossing_across_gap, max_bracket_width Missing samples, or coarse sampling, around a crossing. The interpolated time is uncertain by the bracket width.

The method does not apply, or should not be trusted, when:

  • the SDE is not an adequate model of the system (always an unchecked assumption);
  • the noise is non-diagonal (not supported);
  • dt is not small against the hitting time scale;
  • most paths are censored;
  • in observed data, censoring depends on the state;
  • in observed data, the trajectory leaves and re-enters between samples.

docs.title: Cost
docs.text: Operation Cost Monte Carlo O(n_paths × n_steps × (d + n_boundaries)). Paths stop once they have hit every boundary. Measured: 20 000 paths with up to 30 000 steps of dt = 2e-3 took 4.8 s (bm_drift_mean row of the table below). The test suite caps 10 000 paths × 10 000 steps at 30 s. Kaplan-Meier O(n log n). 10⁶ censored samples took 0.47 s on the same machine. Deterministic crossing O(n) per boundary

docs.title: Benchmarks
docs.text:
To reproduce the table:

python -m pinneapple_analysis.dynamics.benchmarks first_passage

It uses seed=0, 20 000 paths and the full sample sizes. Each row compares one result with a reference that is independent of the code under test.

  • For a Monte Carlo row, "Pass" means |error| ≤ 4 Monte Carlo standard errors.
  • For a whole distribution, "Pass" means the error is within the 99 % Dvoretzky-Kiefer-Wolfowitz bound.

The values below were measured on 2026-10-30 (Python 3.13, NumPy 2.5, SciPy 1.18, one CPU core).

Case Quantity Reference Computed Error MC s.e. z Pass Cost [s] bm_drift_mean E[tau] 2 2.003 0.00337 0.02036 0.1655 yes 4.79 bm_drift_cdf sup_t |F_MC - F| 0 0.004586 0.004586 - - yes (DKW 0.0115) 0.00 bm_drift_mean_coarse_bridge E[tau], dt = 0.02 2 2.043 0.04286 0.02086 2.055 yes 1.03 bm_drift_mean_coarse_no_bridge E[tau], dt = 0.02, discrete monitoring 2.165 2.165 0.0002474 0.02097 0.0118 yes 1.02 bm_interval_mean E[exit time] 0.3457 0.3481 0.002359 0.002098 1.125 yes 1.83 bm_interval_p_up P(exit through upper) 0.542 0.5497 0.00773 0.003518 2.197 yes 0.00 bm_interval_survival sup_t |S_MC - S| 0 0.00631 0.00631 - - yes (DKW 0.0115) 0.00 ou_mfpt E[tau] 12.93 12.82 -0.1107 0.1268 0.8731 yes 5.12 reflect_absorb E[tau] 0.91 0.907 -0.003023 0.005786 0.5224 yes 3.60 crossing_order observed order of the interpolation error 2 2.001 0.0005045 - - yes 0.28 km_censored sup_t≤2 |S_KM - S| 0 0.006988 0.006988 - - yes 0.43

What the rows show, and what they do not:

  • Discrete monitoring without the bridge. At dt = 0.02 it gives E[τ] = 2.165, which is 0.165 late. This matches the continuity-corrected prediction 2.165. The bridge removes most of that bias: 2.043, with z = 2.1 at this coarse step. The residual 0.04 sits near the edge of Monte Carlo noise and is consistent with the first-order placement of bridge crossings in the middle of the step.
  • Kaplan-Meier. About 33 % of the samples are censored. The pointwise 95 % band covered the true S(t) at 99.5 % of the 201 points checked. The estimate that ignores censoring is off by 0.151.
  • Interpolation. The worst-case error over 16 grid offsets falls from 1.6e-3 to 2.5e-5 as h goes from 0.1 to 0.0125.
