docs.title: Identifiability, calibration and inverse problems
docs.text:
One core in pinneapple_analysis.inverse_problems answers three questions in order:

  1. Can these parameters be recovered from these measurements? analyze_identifiability. Run it before the experiment, when only the sensor positions and the noise are known.
  2. What are the parameters, and how sure are we? calibrate. It fits the measurements, gives confidence intervals only where the data determine the parameter, and checks the fit on held-out measurements.
  3. Which inversion method should I trust for this problem? compare_methods. It runs least squares, an adjoint gradient, automatic differentiation, Bayesian regularisation and a PINN on the same data, and ranks them by held-out error.

The Parameter Identifiability Lab, the Model Calibration Lab and the Inverse Model Studio apps are built on these calls.

docs.title: Models, parameters, measurements
docs.text:
Object What it holds Parameter(name, value, lower, upper, unit, log=None, fixed=False, truth=None) One unknown. Positive parameters are analysed in ln (a sensitivity is then per 100 % change). truth is used only to check synthetic studies. Observations(inputs, sigma, values=None, observable=None) One row per measurement: inputs such as position or time, the noise sigma, the measured value (or none yet), and which observable the row measures ("T", "q_base", ...). Observations.from_frame(df, ...) reads a table loaded by pinneapple_data.data_health.load_table (CSV, Excel, Parquet, JSON, sensor exports, decimal commas). ForwardModel predict(theta, inputs, observable). Ready-made models: PinFinModel (analytic fin), RodModel (finite-volume fin with h(x) zones: exact sensitivities, one-solve adjoint, torch twin), PlateModel (the Inverse Heat Lab's 2D plate), LumpedCoolingModel, ArrheniusModel. Your own model: ExpressionModel("T_air + (T0 - T_air)*exp(-k*t)", ...) (parsed safely, nothing is passed to eval), CallableModel(fn, ...) (any Python function or solver interface), or TabulatedModel(table, ...) (simulated runs interpolated over the parameters).

model_from_spec({...}) builds any of these from JSON. get_preset(name) returns ten problems with known answers, for example fin_h, fin_h_k, fin_h_k_flux, rod_h_field, rod_base_bc, plate_h, cooling_h, cooling_h_C and arrhenius_one_T / _two_T. Their measurements are synthetic: the model at the stated truth plus Gaussian noise from a fixed seed.

docs.title: 1. Identifiability before the experiment
docs.text:
import numpy as np
import pinneapple_analysis.inverse_problems as inv

fin = inv.PinFinModel(d_mm=5, length_mm=50)
params = fin.default_parameters()
params[1].fixed = False                                   # k unknown as well as h
sensors = inv.Observations({"x_mm": [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]}, sigma=0.5,
                           observable=np.array(["T"] * 5, dtype=object))
report = inv.analyze_identifiability(fin, sensors, params)
print(report.summary)

The output: 0 of 2 parameters identifiable. Moving h up and k up together leaves the predictions unchanged: the data fix h/k, not h and k separately. Most informative extra measurement: q_base at x_mm=0. The fin temperatures depend on h and k only through h/k. The base heat flow scales with sqrt(h k), so a heat-flux meter makes both identifiable.

The report combines four methods:

  • Fisher information (rank, condition number, Cramér-Rao bounds, expected correlations). The eigen-directions with zero or small eigenvalues are reported as ambiguities, with the combination the data do fix.
  • Local sensitivity of every measurement to every parameter, and the leverage of each measurement (its share of the identifiable information).
  • Profile likelihood (Raue et al., 2009) with 95 % intervals. A profile that rises only because another parameter reaches its bound is reported as such, not as a closed interval.
  • Posterior by adaptive Metropolis (flat priors inside the bounds) for cheap models.

It then gives a D-optimal design: from candidate measurements (other positions, times, temperatures or another observable), the greedy picks that most increase log det F, with the rank and the bounds each pick would give.

Limits: the Fisher rank is a local numerical test at one point, not a symbolic proof of global identifiability. The profile and the posterior are only as good as the bounds you give.

docs.title: 2. Calibration
docs.text:
b = inv.get_preset("fin_h_k_flux").build()
cal = inv.calibrate(b["model"], b["observations"], b["parameters"], holdout=b["validation"])

With the heat-flux meter, the run above gives h = 25.17 W/m²K (Jacobian 95 % interval 23.74 to 26.68, bootstrap 24.81 to 25.49) and k = 16.13 W/m·K (15.16 to 17.16, bootstrap 15.88 to 16.38). The truth is 25 and 16. The held-out RMSE is 0.41 °C for a sensor noise of 0.5 °C. Without the meter (fin_h_k), both parameters come back not estimable, with no interval and the reason.

  • Identifiability is checked at the calibrated values. A non-identifiable parameter gets no interval.
  • Jacobian intervals use the stated sigma (absolute_sigma=True, a sensor specification). They are widened by sqrt(chi2/dof) when the residuals are larger than the stated noise, and never narrowed. Pass absolute_sigma=False when sigma is only a weight.
  • Bootstrap intervals come from residual resampling and refitting.
  • Held-out measurements are never fitted. They can be given explicitly, as a random fraction, or as the last rows by an input (holdout_by="t_s", an extrapolation test).
  • warnings lists a parameter on its bound, a reduced chi-square far from 1, a held-out error much larger than the fit error, and a missing validation set.

docs.title: 3. Comparing inversion methods
docs.text:
out = inv.compare_methods(inv.get_preset("rod_h_field").problem(),
                          ["least_squares", "adjoint", "autodiff", "bayesian"])

This preset reconstructs a convection field h(x) in four zones and the temperature field T(x) from twelve thermocouples. Every method recovers the truth inside its 95 % interval. Held-out RMSE: 0.176 °C for least squares, adjoint and autodiff, and 0.180 °C for the Bayesian MAP, whose smoothness prior pulls the zones together. Forward model evaluations: 11 (least squares, exact sensitivities), 39 (adjoint, one extra solve per gradient whatever the number of zones), 48 (autodiff) and 3012 (Bayesian, of which 3000 are the MCMC chain).

Method Needs Uncertainty least_squares any model Gauss-Newton interval adjoint adjoint_gradient (e.g. RodModel) Gauss-Newton interval autodiff predict_torch Gauss-Newton interval bayesian any model (MCMC if cheap) posterior interval, flagged as set by the prior for non-identifiable parameters pinn pinn (the Inverse Heat Lab fin and plate; h only) none from one run

available_methods(problem) says which methods apply and why the others do not. With a known truth, every solution reports its parameter and field errors and truth_recovered. That flag is true when the truth lies inside the interval of every identifiable parameter, or within 5 % when the method gives no interval.

Measured on the presets (synthetic data, same seeds): the Inverse Heat Lab plate PINN (plate_h, 1500 steps, 56 s on one CPU core) gave h = 14.0 W/m²K for a true 15. Least squares on the finite-volume model gave 14.96.

docs.title: Immersed analysis on raw geometry
docs.text: pinneapple_simulation.immersed solves heat conduction and linear elasticity directly on a part given as a signed distance (SDF), a voxel mask or an STL surface, without generating a conforming mesh. The part sits in a uniform background grid of Q1 or Q2 elements; the cells it cuts are integrated by an adaptive octree; boundary conditions on the curved surface are imposed weakly (Nitsche for temperatures and displacements, surface quadrature for fluxes, convection, tractions and forces). This is the finite cell / CutFEM family (Parvizian, Düster & Rank 2007; Burman et al. 2015; Schillinger & Ruess 2015). The measured verification and the comparison against conforming FEM are in the research report.

docs.title: When to use it, and when not
docs.text:
Measured, not assumed (report, "Verdict"):

Use immersed when Use conforming FEM (gmsh + tet_fem, or CalculiX) when the input is voxels, an implicit SDF, or an STL that does not mesh (holes, flipped facets: the winding number still gives a robust inside test) the part meshes cleanly: P2 was 1.2–1.8× faster on a smooth sphere, 20× on a bracket and over 50× on a heat sink at equal accuracy the geometry changes topology across a sweep (no remeshing step to fail) the part has thin walls in bending (Q1 locks; Q2 needs 4× the unknowns of P2) the fields are smooth and unknowns matter more than wall time (Q2 used half the unknowns of P2 on a smooth sphere) sharp edges carry a change of boundary condition, or convection on many sharp edges (the edges are chamfered at the octree-leaf scale: 1.3 % of the convective area on the heat sink)

docs.title: Steady heat
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from pinneapple_simulation import immersed as im

part = im.cylinder((0, 0, 0), 0.02, 0.1) - im.cylinder((0, 0, 0), 0.008, 0.12)    # CSG of exact SDFs
disc = im.Discretization(part, h=0.004, order=2)                                   # grid + cut-cell quadrature
bore = lambda X, n: np.hypot(X[:, 0], X[:, 1]) < 0.01                              # select by point (and normal)
sol = im.solve_heat(disc, conductivity=200.0, source=0.0,
                    bcs=[im.Dirichlet(80.0, where=bore), im.Convection(h=25.0, T_inf=20.0)])
print(sol.max(), sol.balance["imbalance"], sol.info["dofs"])                      # energy balance closes to round-off
  • Geometry: im.ball, im.box, im.cylinder, im.torus, im.annulus and |, &, -; any vectorised SDF with im.SDFGeometry(fn, (lo, hi)); im.VoxelGeometry(mask, origin, spacing); im.STLGeometry.from_file(path).
  • Conditions: Dirichlet(value), HeatFlux(q) (into the body), HeatInput(power) (a total power spread over the selected area), Convection(h, T_inf). where(X) or where(X, n) selects the surface points; the first matching condition wins; unselected surface is adiabatic.
  • Options: order 1 or 2; depth (octree levels, default 2 for Q1, 3 for Q2, 2 for STL); stabilization "ghost" (default, bounded condition number for any cut) or "fcm"; condition=True reports the condition number.

docs.title: Linear elasticity
docs.text:
from pinneapple_simulation import immersed as im

disc = im.Discretization(im.box((0, 0, 0), (0.1, 0.02, 0.02)), h=0.004, order=2)
clamp = lambda X, n: (X[:, 0] < 1e-3) & (n[:, 0] < -0.5)
tip = lambda X, n: (X[:, 0] > 0.099) & (n[:, 0] > 0.5)
sol = im.solve_elasticity(disc, E=210e9, nu=0.3,
                          bcs=[im.Displacement(0.0, where=clamp), im.Force((0, 0, -100.0), where=tip)])
print(sol.max_displacement(), sol.balance["imbalance"])                           # equilibrium check

Displacement(value, components=(2,)) restricts a support to some directions; Traction, Pressure and Force (an exact total load) are the loads. Stresses and von Mises at any points: sol.stress(X), sol.von_mises(X).

docs.title: Transient heat
docs.text:
from pinneapple_simulation.immersed import verification as V
from pinneapple_simulation.immersed.transient import solve_transient_heat

c = V.sphere_cooling()                                                             # series solution available
disc = im.Discretization(c["geometry"], 0.0625, order=1)
s = solve_transient_heat(disc, c["k"], c["rho_c"], 0.0, c["bcs"], T0=c["T_i"], dt=1e-3, n_steps=50, theta=0.5)

theta 1 is backward Euler, 1/2 Crank–Nicolson; source(X, t) and bcs(t) may depend on time.

docs.title: Checks that come with every result
docs.text:
• heat: sol.balance (heat generated against heat leaving through each condition, Nitsche's consistent flux);
  • elasticity: sol.balance (applied loads against reactions);
  • verification against exact solutions: immersed.verification (manufactured solutions on curved domains, sphere / cylinder / Lamé sphere / sphere cooling in closed form, conditioning() for small cuts);
  • against conforming FEM on the same part: immersed.compare (SDF parts) and immersed.parts.study (STL parts).

docs.title: In a flow
docs.text: The Flow node immersed.heat runs steady heat with uniform generation and convection on a built-in solid or an STL file, and returns the peak temperature, the energy balance, the cost by phase and a mid-plane figure.

docs.title: Industrial presets
docs.text:
A preset is an engineering problem already set up, solved and validated with PINNeAPPle. You open it, replace the defaults with your own values and run it. Each preset carries:

  • a data sheet: the sector, the question it answers, every input in SI units with a realistic default and the source of that default, the outputs and the validity domain;
  • the pipeline: geometry, then the model, then the solver (and optionally the surrogate), then post-processing, then a decision;
  • checks on every run: a trust report with conservation, convergence, correlation ranges and the applicability domain;
  • references: comparisons against citable values with the error measured (standards, published benchmarks, analytic solutions, independent solvers). A preset with no independent reference says so on its data sheet;
  • optional capabilities, where the physics allows them: a 3-D scene of the result, a surrogate, an inversion, an optimisation checked with the solver, and design variants run side by side.
import pinneapple as pp

pp.presets.names()                                     # the catalogue
p = pp.presets.load("water_distribution_network")
p.card()                                               # data sheet (JSON-ready; the Hub shows it)
r = p.run(demand_factor=1.3, hw_c=100)                 # your values, SI units
print(r)                                               # outputs, decision, trust report
p.validate()                                           # reference cases with the measured error
p.optimize()                                           # e.g. least-cost diameters, re-solved and checked
p.invert()                                             # e.g. Hazen-Williams C from logged pressures
pp.presets.load("water_hammer_valve_closure").run(fidelity="surrogate", t_close=6.0)

Command line:

python -m pinneapple_presets list
python -m pinneapple_presets card power_pcb_junction
python -m pinneapple_presets run power_pcb_junction vias=16 t_ambient=45
python -m pinneapple_presets validate steel_footbridge_pedestrian
python -m pinneapple_presets report all            # rewrites examples/industrial_presets/ and the Hub index

In the Flow Studio, the preset.run node takes the preset name, a dictionary of overrides and the fidelity (solver or surrogate). The preset.validate node runs the references.

docs.title: Catalogue
docs.text: The table is in examples/industrial_presets/README.md. It is regenerated from the stored results, so every number in it was measured. Each preset folder holds its README: the data sheet, the measured outputs, the validation table, the surrogate hold-out error, the inversion, the optimisation, the variants and the figures.

docs.title: Surrogates
docs.text:
SurrogateSpec(inputs, outputs, n_train, n_test, bounds, log, log_outputs) declares the surrogate. python -m pinneapple_presets surrogate <name> then builds it in five steps:

  1. It draws a Latin hypercube over the inputs.
  2. It runs the real solver at every point.
  3. It fits one anisotropic Gaussian process per output.
  4. It measures the error on an independent hold-out set.
  5. It stores everything as a few-kB JSON file in pinneapple_presets/data/surrogates/.

A run(fidelity="surrogate") call returns each output with its standard deviation. When the inputs fall outside the training box, or when a parameter differs from the value the surrogate was trained at, the call raises a warning, the trust report marks the check "contradicts", and nothing is extrapolated silently. pinneapple_presets.surrogate.serve_spec(name) describes the surrogate for a model server: its inputs with bounds and units, its outputs, its error and the call that runs it.

docs.title: Adding a preset
docs.text:
1. Subclass pinneapple_presets.Preset.
  2. Set the data-sheet attributes: params as Param(name, unit, default, source, lo, hi), and outputs.
  3. Implement solve(p) -> dict, checks(p, out) -> [Check], decide(p, out) and references(). Add the optional scene, figures, invert, optimize and variants methods where the physics allows them.
  4. Register the class in pinneapple_presets/registry.py.
  5. Run python -m pinneapple_presets report <name>.
  6. Add a test.

Every default needs its source. Every reference needs its citation, plus the tolerance it must meet.

docs.title: Self-modifying brick builds
docs.text:
pinneapple_design.bricks builds structures from interlocking toy bricks, judges every build with physics and redesigns it until it meets a goal: the longest cantilever past a table edge, a bridge that carries a load with the fewest parts, the tallest tower that survives a push. The geometry follows the LDraw unit system, so builds open in LDraw-compatible editors and real part shapes can be loaded from the LDraw parts library.

from pinneapple_design.bricks import Assembly, Ground, analyse_assembly

a = Assembly(ground=Ground("table", [(-1000, 0, -1000, 1000)]))   # a table that ends at x = 0
a.add("brick_1x8", -4, 0, 0, colour="blue")                         # half of it past the edge
a.add("brick_1x8", 0, 0, 3, colour="yellow")                        # on top, reaching 64 mm further
r = analyse_assembly(a)
print(r.status, r.explanation)                                      # mechanism: where the centre of mass left

docs.title: The parts
docs.text:
quantity value source stud pitch 8.0 mm (20 LDU) LDraw unit system plate / brick height 3.2 mm / 9.6 mm (8 / 24 LDU) LDraw unit system stud 4.8 mm diameter, 1.6 mm high LDraw stud.dat primitive part width 8 n - 0.2 mm (0.1 mm clearance per side) StableLego configuration (7.8 mm unit) brick masses e.g. 2x4: 2.16 g, 1x8: 3.03 g StableLego brick library (Liu et al. 2024) plate masses shell model fitted to the brick masses (worst residual +28 % on the 1x1 brick) parts.fit_mass_model

The catalogue (parts.CATALOG) holds rectangular bricks and plates with their LDraw part numbers. Assemblies live on the stud grid (x, y in stud pitches, z in plate heights). Two parts are joined where the top of one overlaps the bottom of the other: each overlapping cell is one stud-tube contact. Assembly.validate() reports overlaps and parts with no contact path to the ground; the ground is a table (smooth) or a baseplate (studs), optionally limited to regions such as a table edge or two banks.

docs.title: The physics
docs.text:
Statics (statics.analyse). Every part is a rigid body. Every contact patch carries compression at its four corners, and a stud joint also carries a clutch tension at each stud (at most JointModel.clutch_n) and a horizontal force at each stud; smooth contacts carry Coulomb friction. A linear programme finds the force distribution with the smallest peak stud utilisation. If one exists within the clutch, the build stands (the lower-bound theorem of plasticity); if none exists even with unbreakable studs, the build is a mechanism and the report says which support polygon the resultant left and by how much. capacity gives the largest factor on the external loads, and progressive_failure releases the critical joints round by round.

Joint model. The clutch is 0.98 N per stud, the friction capacity reported for the StableLego analysis (Liu, Deng, Wang, Liu, IEEE RA-L 9(11) 2024) and reused by BrickGPT (Pun et al., arXiv:2505.05469). No uncertainty is published, so the sensitivity study scales it by an assumed 0.5x to 1.5x. Limits of the model:

  • tension only: a joint fails when its pull-out force exceeds the clutch;
  • horizontal stud forces are unbounded by default (as in StableLego); JointModel(shear_n=...) caps them;
  • a single stud is a pivot about the vertical (no torsion);
  • rigid parts and no joint compliance: the force distribution is the most favourable one, so the verdict is optimistic for brittle clutch;
  • side-by-side parts do not push on each other (there is a 0.2 mm gap);
  • contact forces act at least edge_inset_mm (0.5 mm, assumed) inside a patch edge. Without it the search drives builds onto a knife edge (centre of mass exactly over a table edge), which the statics accepts with zero margin and Newton tips; the closed-form checks use sharp edges (edge_inset_mm=0).

Dynamics (dynamics.replay). NVIDIA Newton replays a build: every cluster held together by intact studs is one rigid body made of its boxes, released joints become box-box contacts with friction, tables have edges and a floor below, and vertical loads are dead weights. Newton has no breakable joints, so the statics decides which joints let go and Newton shows what happens next.

FEA (fea.solve). The voxelised build as one Hex8 solid (incompatible modes), for load paths and stresses in the plastic. It is an upper bound on stiffness: joint compliance is not modelled.

docs.title: The loop
docs.text: search.evolve and search.surrogate_search mutate builds with plain edits (add, remove, move, swap, rotate, recolour) and grammar rules that read the last evaluation (extend toward the goal, add a counterweight, brace the joint that failed, widen the base, mirror a half of a span). Every candidate is simulated; duplicates are looked up. Evolution selects survivors with NSGA-II and Deb's constraint handling on the goal's objectives (for example reach and part count). The surrogate search proposes eight times more children than it can afford, ranks them with a Gaussian process trained on every build simulated so far (upper confidence bound on a penalised score) and simulates only the best. search.compare runs both with the same evaluation budget and seeds.

docs.title: Visuals
docs.text:
• visuals.evolution_timeline + timeline_scene(...).export(folder): the twin3d three.js viewer plays the evolution generation by generation. Build frames are coloured by stud utilisation (the load path); rejected candidates are replayed by Newton with the joints that let go in red. Serve the folder over http.
  • visuals.render_frames, write_gif, write_mp4: the same frames from the software renderer.
  • visuals.render_blender, turntable_blender: Blender Cycles renders (pip install bpy).
  • visuals.write_instructions: step images per layer, a part list and an LDraw file with one STEP per layer.

docs.title: LDraw files and the parts library
docs.text: ldraw.write_ldr / write_mpd write builds; ldraw.read_ldr reads .ldr and .mpd files (sub-models expanded, quarter-turn rotations; parts off the grid or outside the catalogue are listed in skipped). ldraw.fetch_parts_library() downloads the LDraw parts library at run time into a cache folder; it is licensed CC BY 2.0 ("LDraw.org Parts Library") and is not copied into this repository. ldraw.PartsLibrary(root) triangulates real parts for renders.

docs.title: The experiment
docs.text:
python examples/bricks/self_modifying_bricks.py --full       # 5 seeds x 400 evaluations per strategy and goal
python -m pinneapple_lab sweep bricks -g case=cantilever,bridge,tower

docs.title: Results of the full run
docs.text:
5 seeds, 400 physics evaluations per run and strategy (examples/bricks/_out/report.md has every number, summary.json the raw values).

Closed forms. All nine checks pass (trust report APPROVED): the LP reproduces the harmonic stacking limit and the single-block limit exactly, the stud-cantilever tension and the tower tipping push to 1e-16, the beam reactions to 1e-15; the voxel FEA beam deflection is within 0.4 % of Timoshenko (1.4 % above Euler-Bernoulli alone, which leaves out shear). Newton agrees with harmonic stacking at 0.9x to 0.99x (stands) and 1.01x to 1.05x (falls). It disagrees at exactly 1.00x, the neutral equilibrium of the closed form, where it tips the stack.

Statistic: the median of the best score over the 5 seeds, a seed that found no feasible build counted as the worst, and in brackets the range over the feasible seeds (the same rule as comparison.png and the report).

goal evolution surrogate-guided best build cantilever, reach past the edge with 8 parts 111.9 mm (95.9 to 135.9), 5/5 feasible 103.9 mm (71.9 to 127.9), 5/5 135.9 mm, 34 % of the clutch bridge over 96 mm carrying 1 N, parts 5 (3 to 5), 5/5 feasible 8 (3 to 8), 3/5 feasible 3 parts, carries 1.46 N tower that survives a 10 mN push, height 118.4 mm (57.6 to 144.0), 5/5 115.2 mm (70.4 to 153.6), 5/5 153.6 mm, 16 parts, 1.64 x the push

Evolution has the better median on all three goals and is the more reliable on the bridge (the surrogate-guided search found no bridge in 2 of 5 seeds), but the margins are smaller than the range over seeds and the surrogate-guided search found the tallest tower, so 5 seeds do not separate the two strategies. For reference, unconnected blocks of the same length reach (L/2) H_8 = 86.7 mm (harmonic stacking), so the stud clutch buys 57 % more reach (135.9 mm), still far below the 255 mm centre-of-mass bound.

Sensitivity. The best cantilever and tower stand over the whole assumed clutch band (0.5x to 1.5x) and with stud shear capped at 0.3 N; the best bridge fails at 0.5x clutch (0.49 N per stud, load factor 0.80) and stands from 0.75x, so its verdict depends on the joint strength.

The three best builds stand in Newton under their goal loads (the bridge with its 1 N dead weight, the tower with the 10 mN push): largest displacement 0.00, 0.00 and 0.03 mm in 0.6 s, no tilt.

Statics against Newton (searched candidates, every joint intact, dt = 0.25 ms): agreement 90 % on cantilevers, 100 % on bridges, 75 % on towers; every disagreement is a statics "mechanism" that Newton keeps standing:

  • cantilever (2 cases): the centre of mass is 0.2 and 0.5 mm past the inset support, inside the 0.5 mm edge inset that the statics assumes and Newton's sharp boxes do not;
  • tower (5 cases): no equilibrium in the statics although the resultant is inside the support; Newton shows a slow drift of 0.1 to 0.8 mm without tilting, which points to sliding at the friction limit. The single-stud torsion assumption explains 2 of 40 tower mechanisms; the rest is not explained.

XPBD friction creeps under a sustained sideways load: the best tower drifts 0.23 mm at dt = 1 ms and 0.03 mm at 0.25 ms in 0.6 s while the statics says friction holds, so the cross-check uses the small step.

Limits. The verdicts rest on the cited 0.98 N clutch, which has no published uncertainty, on rigid parts and the most favourable force distribution (optimistic for brittle clutch), on unbounded stud shear and on an assumed friction coefficient. Nothing here was compared with physical builds.

docs.title: PINNeAPPle from any coding agent: the MCP server
docs.text:
pinneapple-mcp is a Model Context Protocol server (stdio, built on the official MCP Python SDK, 1.x or 2.x). Any MCP client, such as Gemini CLI, Claude Code, Cursor, Codex or Antigravity, can then solve, benchmark and validate physics problems with PINNeAPPle, and every result comes back with its physics checks. For agents that read files instead of calling tools, the repository's AGENTS.md covers the same ground as a guide.

pip install "pinneapple[mcp]"
pinneapple-mcp --help            # or: python -m pinneapple_mcp

docs.title: Tools
docs.text:
Tool What it does Runs as capabilities version, device, optional APIs present (benchmark, zoo, datasets, geometries), limits, working directory call list_methods solve methods by kind, and the method catalog with each item's validation status call describe_method options of a solve method (pinn, fem, ...) or code, references and evidence of a catalog item (S2, ...) call list_presets problem presets call solve a problem (preset or JSON box problem) by one method; metrics against the reference, physics checks, trust card, prediction.npz, field.png job trust_card physics checks of any field (inline values or a .npz / .npy / .csv file): finite values, PDE residual, boundary conditions, conservation, maximum principle, reference error, applicability (OOD); decision APPROVED / REVIEW / REJECT call design design from a plain-language goal: out_of_scope (with what would be needed) or needs_input (the questions) at once, otherwise the design package: verdict with probability, design, margins, full-solver verification, operating window, bill of materials, files (guide) call / job reason, reason_library, reason_check the chain of whys of a design (pinneapple_reason): from a naive concept, computed failure modes, countermeasures and checks until every requirement passes, with the explanation, the trust decision and the report files; the library of failure modes and countermeasures; one failure mode on given parameters (guide) job / call / call benchmark several methods with the same training budget (epochs, collocation points, seeds), scored on the same grid against one reference; table.md and a trust card per run job zoo_list, zoo_predict, zoo_validate pre-trained, verified models of pp.zoo and the datasets of pp.datasets; predictions with the rows outside the validity range flagged; the model's trust report call job_status, list_jobs, cancel_job follow, list and stop jobs call

Every input is described by a JSON schema (from the typed signatures), and every tool returns a JSON object. solve and benchmark return a job_id at once: poll job_status (or pass wait_seconds). Results are written under the working directory, and their paths are in the result.

A box problem in JSON (expressions use the coordinate names, pi, e and NumPy functions; they are parsed, never eval-ed):

{"name": "plate", "domain": {"x": [0, 1], "y": [0, 1]}, "fields": ["T"], "pde": "laplace",
 "bcs": [{"kind": "dirichlet", "field": "T", "on": "y_max", "value": "sin(pi*x)"},
         {"kind": "dirichlet", "field": "T", "on": "y_min", "value": 0},
         {"kind": "dirichlet", "field": "T", "on": "x_boundary", "value": 0}],
 "exact": "sin(pi*x)*sinh(pi*y)/sinh(pi)"}

or a preset: {"preset": "burgers_1d", "preset_kwargs": {"nu": 0.0032}}.

docs.title: Safe defaults
docs.text: Setting Default Change with working directory ./pinneapple_mcp_work --workdir, PINNEAPPLE_MCP_WORKDIR wall time per job 600 s (the job process is killed) --max-seconds, PINNEAPPLE_MCP_MAX_SECONDS memory per job 8192 MB of address space --max-memory-mb, PINNEAPPLE_MCP_MAX_MEMORY_MB concurrent jobs 2 --max-jobs, PINNEAPPLE_MCP_MAX_JOBS network inside jobs off (non-local connections raise) --allow-network, PINNEAPPLE_MCP_ALLOW_NETWORK=1 files trust_card may read the working directory and the directory the server started in, up to 200 MB --roots, PINNEAPPLE_MCP_ROOTS, PINNEAPPLE_MCP_MAX_FILE_MB training epochs, checked grid points 20000, 250000 PINNEAPPLE_MCP_MAX_EPOCHS, PINNEAPPLE_MCP_MAX_POINTS

docs.title: Plug it in
docs.text: The command is the same everywhere: pinneapple-mcp (add --workdir /path/to/results to choose where results go). If the console script is not on the agent's PATH, use python -m pinneapple_mcp with the interpreter of the environment where PINNeAPPle is installed.

docs.title: Gemini CLI
docs.text:
~/.gemini/settings.json (or .gemini/settings.json in the project):

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "pinneapple": {"command": "pinneapple-mcp", "args": ["--workdir", "pinneapple_results"], "timeout": 600000}
  }
}

Then /mcp in Gemini CLI lists the tools.

docs.title: Claude Code
docs.text:
claude mcp add pinneapple -- pinneapple-mcp --workdir pinneapple_results

or, for everyone working in a repository, a .mcp.json at its root (this repository ships one):

{"mcpServers": {"pinneapple": {"command": "python", "args": ["-m", "pinneapple_mcp", "--workdir", "pinneapple_mcp_work"]}}}

docs.title: Cursor
docs.text:
~/.cursor/mcp.json (global) or .cursor/mcp.json (project):

{"mcpServers": {"pinneapple": {"command": "pinneapple-mcp", "args": ["--workdir", "pinneapple_results"]}}}

docs.title: Codex, Antigravity and other clients
docs.text:
Any client that launches stdio MCP servers takes the same command. For Codex, in ~/.codex/config.toml:

[mcp_servers.pinneapple]
command = "pinneapple-mcp"
args = ["--workdir", "pinneapple_results"]

docs.title: A Colab or Jupyter cell
docs.text:
The tools are plain Python functions, so a notebook can call them directly:

!pip install -q "pinneapple[mcp]"
from pinneapple_mcp import tools
st = tools.solve({"preset": "burgers_1d"}, "pinn", {"epochs": 2000}, wait_seconds=600)
print(st["status"], st["result"]["decision"], st["result"]["metrics"])

or drive the real server through an MCP client in the same process (MCP SDK 2.x; with 1.x, use mcp.shared.memory.create_connected_server_and_client_session(server._mcp_server)):

from mcp import Client
from pinneapple_mcp import build_server

async with Client(build_server()) as client:          # top-level await works in Colab / Jupyter
    print([t.name for t in (await client.list_tools()).tools])
    r = await client.call_tool("list_methods", {"category": "solver", "validated_only": True})
    print(r.structured_content["catalog_counts"])

docs.title: What an agent should do with a result
docs.text: Read decision and trust_cards before anything else. REJECT means a critical check failed (PDE residual, a boundary condition or the reference): report the failing checks, do not report the numbers as a result. REVIEW means a non-critical check failed or too few checks could run (for example no reference and no boundary data): say which. The checks are listed with their values and limits in the card, and in trust_card_<field>.md next to the prediction.

docs.title: Unstructured mesh generation
docs.text:
pinneapple_design.geometry.mesh.generate.generate_mesh makes a triangle mesh (2-D) or a tetrahedral mesh (3-D) with gmsh. In 3-D it can add prism layers at the walls. It rates every element and can write the mesh and a 3-D view of its quality. The Flow node geometry.unstructured_mesh calls it. The structured grid of geometry.mesh is unchanged.

from pinneapple_design.geometry.mesh.generate import generate_mesh

out = generate_mesh("cylinder", [0.5, 1.0], h=0.08,
                    boundary_layer={"first_layer": 0.01, "n_layers": 3, "growth": 1.2}, out_dir="mesh")
out["element_counts"], out["sicn_min"], out["volume"]     # {'tetra': 6678, 'wedge': 6066}, 0.017, 0.7810 m3

More pictures are in docs/assets/mesh/: a box, a sphere, local refinement, 2-D meshes with wall layers, an STL part, and the SICN histograms with the measured numbers. python scripts/mesh_generation_gallery.py makes them all, this figure included.

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: input meaning geometry One of five primitives or a file. Primitives: box, cylinder, sphere, rectangle (2-D), disk (2-D). Files: .stl, .step / .stp, .iges / .igs. dimensions Primitive sizes in m: box [lx, ly, lz], cylinder [radius, height] (axis +z), sphere [radius], rectangle [lx, ly], disk [radius]. origin Where the primitive goes, in m: the corner of a box or rectangle, the centre of a sphere or disk, the base centre of a cylinder. h Target element size, in m. scale Converts a file's length unit to metres; 1e-3 for millimetres. refine Balls of smaller elements, [{"center": [x, y, z], "radius": r, "h": h_local}]. The size grows back to h over one radius. boundary_layer {"first_layer": m, "n_layers": n, "growth": g}. In 3-D, prisms are extruded inward from the surface. In 2-D, layers of triangles line the boundary. out_dir Where to write the files: mesh.msh (gmsh), mesh.vtu (ParaView), quality.glb and quality.json. Nothing is written anywhere else. max_input_mb Largest geometry file accepted, checked before the file is opened. Default: PINNEAPPLE_MESH_MAX_INPUT_MB, else 100 MB. max_elements Largest mesh, estimated before meshing. Default 2,000,000. Above it, the error names the smallest acceptable h.

docs.title: File inputs
docs.text:
• STEP / IGES: read through OpenCASCADE, gmsh's OCC kernel.
  • STL without a boundary layer: meshed by the existing mesher_3d.mesh_from_surface.
  • Open STL: refused. An STL with open or non-manifold edges raises ValueError with the count of each edge kind; the check is pinneapple_data.cae.quality.surface_checks.

docs.title: Guards
docs.text:
These protect an app that runs the tool on untrusted input.

  • Local files only. A URL is refused; nothing is downloaded.
  • File size. A file above max_input_mb is refused before it is opened.
  • Mesh size. The mesh size is estimated before meshing, from the volume or area over h^d with measured densities: 6 tetrahedra per V/h^3 and 2.5 triangles per A/h^2. The estimate also counts the refinement balls and one prism per wall triangle per layer. Files are estimated from their bounding box. The estimate is 1.0 to 1.35 times the count gmsh makes (tested).
  • Missing gmsh. The error says pip install gmsh.

docs.title: Fixed settings
docs.text:
• Algorithms: Frontal-Delaunay in 2-D and Delaunay in 3-D.
  • One thread, so the element order is deterministic.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
The names, types and units are declared in the module's X_OUTPUTS, which the Studio reads.

output meaning dim 2 or 3. n_nodes Number of nodes. n_elements Number of elements of the mesh's dimension. element_counts Elements per type (for example tetra and wedge). sicn_min, sicn_mean [-] gmsh minSICN: the signed inverse condition number of the Jacobian. 1 is the ideal element; ≤ 0 is inverted. Below 0.1 the node logs a warning. gamma_min, gamma_mean [-] gmsh gamma: inscribed / circumscribed radius, normalised to 1 for the ideal element. aspect_ratio_max, aspect_ratio_mean [-] Longest / shortest edge of each element, from pinneapple_data.cae.quality.element_metrics. volume [m3] Volume of a 3-D mesh; null in 2-D. area [m2] The 2-D area, or the boundary area of a 3-D mesh (faces owned by one element). h_min, h_mean, h_max [m] Edge lengths. files Paths of the written files. backend How the mesh was made.

docs.title: Quality view
docs.text:
The view is pp.viz.field_view on the mesh. It has three cell fields: sicn, gamma and aspect_ratio.

  • quality.glb is the glTF. Fields are stored as vertex attributes _F0, _F1, _F2.
  • quality.json is its meta, with schema pinneapple-field-view/v1.
  • Apps open both with /shared/fieldview3d.js.

In the Flow, the node shows the view as ctx.view("scene", {"glb", "meta"}).

docs.title: Flow node geometry.unstructured_mesh
docs.text:
• Input: geometry, optional. With shape = domain, it meshes the rectangle or box of the connected geometry.domain.
  • Output: mesh, of port type unstructured_mesh. It is its own type, so it cannot be wired by mistake into the finite-difference solvers that read the structured grid. The value is {geometry, summary, files}.
  • Report:
  • metrics n_nodes, n_elements, sicn_min, gamma_min, aspect_ratio_max, h_* and the volume or area;
  • tables quality (min / mean / max and threshold) and elements;
  • the 3-D view;
  • the files as artifacts.
  • Files: read only from the data folder (PINNEAPPLE_FLOW_DATA).

docs.title: Measured (gmsh 4.12.1 from Debian, one thread; tests/test_mesh_generation.py)
docs.text:
These numbers come from the Debian gmsh used for development. The tests also pass with the pip wheel, gmsh 4.15.2.

case h [m] elements result unit box 0.2 / 0.1 / 0.05 734 / 4943 / 37043 n ~ h^-2.83; SICN min 0.304 / 0.295 / 0.289; volume 1 exactly unit square 0.2 / 0.1 / 0.05 66 / 248 / 944 n ~ h^-1.92; SICN min 0.904 / 0.884 / 0.866 cylinder r = 0.5, H = 2 0.2 / 0.1 / 0.05 1033 / 7626 / 58346 volume error -1.98 % / -0.51 % / -0.12 % (facets inside the circle, ~h^2) sphere r = 0.5 0.1 / 0.05 2571 / 19514 volume error -1.44 % / -0.36 % disk r = 0.5 0.05 755 area error -0.17 % unit box, 3 layers from 0.01 m 0.2 730 tetra + 1224 prisms volume 0.999995; shortest edge 0.0100 m; SICN min 0.051 cylinder r = 0.5, H = 1, 3 layers from 0.01 m (figure) 0.08 6678 tetra + 6066 prisms volume -0.56 %; SICN min 0.017 STL of the unit box 0.2 1217 tetra volume 1.0, area 6.0 STEP box in mm, scale = 1e-3 0.1 volume 0.125 m3, area 1.75 m2

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Thin prisms at sharp edges. Prism layers are extruded along averaged normals. Where the wall turns sharply (the rim of a cylinder), the prisms flatten: SICN 0.017 in the figure. Where layers would overlap, gmsh stops, and generate_mesh raises a ValueError asking for a thinner layer or a larger h.
  • STL refinement. refine on an STL works only with a boundary layer, because without one the existing mesh_from_surface meshes it and takes no size field. For local refinement, use STEP / IGES.
  • Linear elements only. Elements are first order.
  • No named boundary groups. The .msh has no physical groups for inlet, wall and so on.

docs.title: Metamorphic tests: checking a surrogate without ground truth
docs.text:
Most physics gives relations between inputs and outputs that hold whatever the true answer is: mirror the geometry and the flow mirrors; keep the Reynolds number and the dimensionless answer stays; add heat and the peak temperature does not fall; double the source of a linear problem and the answer doubles. These are metamorphic relations, and they test a surrogate where no reference solution exists. pinneapple_analysis.validation.metamorphic runs them on any callable model (NumPy arrays or dicts of columns in, arrays or dicts out).

from pinneapple_analysis.validation.metamorphic import box_sampler, check_relations, relations_from_spec

def peak(x):                                       # any model: here the exact peak temperature of a heated slab
    return {"T": x["T0"] + x["q"] * x["L"] ** 2 / (8 * x["k"])}

relations = relations_from_spec([
    {"name": "more-heat-hotter", "kind": "monotonic", "input": "q", "output": "T", "direction": "increasing"},
    {"name": "better-conductor-cooler", "kind": "monotonic", "input": "k", "output": "T", "direction": "decreasing"},
    {"name": "same-q-L2", "kind": "invariant", "inputs": {"q": "4 * q", "L": "L / 2"}, "output": "T", "tol": 1e-9},
])
box = box_sampler({"q": (1e3, 1e5), "L": (0.01, 0.1), "k": (1, 400), "T0": (250, 350)})
report = check_relations(peak, relations, box, n=64, search="hypothesis")
print(report.summary())
assert report.passed

docs.title: Relations
docs.text:
Relation Class / spec kind Holds when Geometric symmetry Symmetry / symmetric f(T x) = S(x, f(x)); reflect_field, rotate_field for gridded inputs Similarity scaling Similarity the dimensionless output is unchanged when the dimensionless groups are (same Re at another size, Darcy with a and f scaled together) Invariance Invariance / invariant an input change that must not matter does not move the output Monotonicity Monotonicity / monotonic more of an input gives no less (no more) of an output; the violation is the wrong-way move over the spread of the output, default tolerance 1e-3 Superposition Superposition / superposition f(a + b) = f(a) + f(b) and f(2a) = 2 f(a) for linear problems (affine=True subtracts f(0)) Resolution consistency ResolutionConsistency an integral of an operator's output is the same with the input at another resolution

Violations are relative: to the RMS of the output over the samples (default), to each sample's own output (per_sample, for positive quantities) or to a fixed scale such as the model's accepted error. The worst sample is returned as the counterexample. With search="hypothesis" (and the hypothesis package installed) a property-based search for a violating sample runs as well; without the package the report says it used random search only.

docs.title: Zoo models
docs.text:
pinneapple_hub.zoo.relations.check_zoo_relations(model) runs the relations each zoo model's physics implies:

Model Relation Worst violation (128 samples) Tolerance airfoil_cst_rans_mlp mirror camber and angle of attack: lift flips 0.83 x accepted Cl error (0.01) 2 moment flips 0.91 x accepted Cm error (0.002) 2 drag unchanged 1.4 % 4 % lift grows with angle of attack (-2 to 8 deg) 0 1e-3 heatsink_forced_mlp resistance falls with air speed; pressure drop grows with it; resistance falls with conductivity 0 1e-3 resistance independent of power (air speed 2-6 m/s, per sample) 1.1 % 2 %

The mirror tolerance is twice the card's accepted mean error because both sides of the relation are predictions. The power invariance is not tested below 2 m/s: there the physics engine that generated the training data is not power-linear either (its resistance rises 6.5 % when the power doubles at 0.6 m/s), and the model follows it.

docs.title: In pinneapple check
docs.text:
Declare relations on a [[model]] with a domain (rule PC303):

[[model]]
name = "peak-temperature"
path = "surrogates/peak_temperature.py:predict"
inputs = ["q", "L", "k", "T0"]
outputs = ["T"]
domain = { q = [1e3, 1e5], L = [0.01, 0.1], k = [1, 400], T0 = [250, 350] }
relations = [
  { name = "better-conductor-cooler", kind = "monotonic", input = "k", output = "T", direction = "decreasing" },
]

docs.title: How it was checked
docs.text:
tests/test_metamorphic.py, with the finite-volume Darcy solver (operator_benchmarks.darcy_2d) as the reference:

  • the solver obeys superposition in the source to 4.7e-16, reflection and 90-degree rotation of (a, f) to round-off, and u(c a, c f) = u(a, f); the mean pressure on a 32² grid and its 16² cell average agree to 1.6 %;
  • an FNO trained on the same map (FNO2d, test error 10.8 %) violates superposition by 0.68 of the output scale;
  • a model that ignores the source fails similarity scaling, a tilted Darcy solution fails reflection, an airfoil model with a 0.03 lift offset fails the camber mirror (about 6 x the accepted error), and a slab model with a unit slip in k fails monotonicity; each reports its counterexample;
  • the zoo models pass the relations above.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• A relation only tests what it states. A model can satisfy every relation and still be wrong by a constant factor that the relations do not constrain; use it alongside residual and reference checks.
  • Random and property-based search find violations, they do not prove their absence.
  • Tolerances must come from the physics and the model's stated accuracy. A relation that does not hold for the real physics in part of the box (the heat sink's power invariance at low air speed) is restricted to where it holds, not loosened.

docs.title: Pre-trained models and datasets (pp.zoo, pp.datasets)
docs.text:
PINNeAPPle ships a small set of pre-trained surrogates and ready-made datasets. You can load each one in one line, then test, evaluate, validate, benchmark and fine-tune it.

Only items that passed a quality gate are included:

  • Models: the held-out error against an independent reference is documented and reproducible, the physics checks of the trust report pass, and the validity range is recorded.
  • Datasets: they were generated by a verified solver with convergence evidence, or come from a public source with a compatible licence; their schema, splits and provenance are documented.

The zoo catalogue lists every model and dataset with its metrics, size and Hugging Face link. The candidates that did not pass, and why, are listed in docs/dev/model_dataset_inventory.md.

Model What it predicts Held-out error (reference) Valid for airfoil_cst_rans_mlp Cl, Cd, Cm of a CST airfoil, with ensemble uncertainty Cd 0.54 % and Cl ±0.003 on 15 unseen shapes (OpenFOAM RANS); Cd 2.8 % vs XFOIL α −2…14°, Re 4·10⁶, CST bounds heatsink_forced_mlp Plate-fin heat-sink resistance (K/W), pressure drop (Pa), 95 % upper bound R 0.71 %, ΔP 1.0 % on 900 designs (verified physics engine) Ducted air, 0.5–6 m/s, 10–400 W heatsink_natural_mlp Plate-fin heat-sink resistance (K/W) in natural convection, 95 % upper bound; trained with monotonicity constraints R 0.47 % mean, 1.5 % p95 on 750 designs (verified physics engine) Free air, vertical fins, 1–80 W rover_contact_grc1_viper (v1.1.0) Drawbar pull, normal load, torque of a rover wheel on lunar regolith Fx 0.22 N, Fz 0.47 N RMSE (ranges 1.4 and 1.4 kN), Wong–Reece with slip-sinkage Slip −0.4…0.9, sinkage 2–60 mm Dataset Content airfoil_rans_cst_re4e6 436 OpenFOAM RANS runs, the grid study and an XFOIL polar heatsink_forced_convection, heatsink_natural_convection 6000 and 5000 heat-sink designs solved by the physics engine rover_contact_grc1_viper Wong–Reece contact forces over slip × sinkage single_wheel_tests Published single-wheel testbed points (validation data) burgers_1d_li2021 1-D viscous Burgers, ν = 0.1: 1200 trajectories on 1024 points, t = 0…1 (Li et al. 2021 input distribution); Hub-only, 55 MB darcy_2d_li2021 2-D Darcy flow: 1200 piecewise-constant permeability / pressure pairs on 128 × 128 (Li et al. 2021); Hub-only, 71 MB navier_stokes_2d_li2021_nu1e-3 2-D Navier–Stokes vorticity, ν = 10⁻³: 1200 runs on 64 × 64, t = 0…50 (Li et al. 2021); Hub-only, 12 shards, 919 MB thermal_channel_cfd Actuated heated channel (2-D incompressible flow + heat, Re 100): 82 trajectories of u, v, p, T on 128 × 32 × 101 snapshots, with two unseen actuation families for testing; Hub-only, 8 shards, 360 MB airfoil_rans_cst_re4e6_fields The cell fields (p, Ux, Uy, nut on the 20064-cell O-grid) of the 436 OpenFOAM runs of airfoil_rans_cst_re4e6, same splits; Hub-only, 5 files, 186 MB cylinder_wake_lbm Confined cylinder wake (lattice Boltzmann, blockage 0.2): 720 vorticity snapshots of 9 saturated runs at Re 20–100, labelled by regime, Strouhal number and wake amplitude; Hub-only, 3 files, 64 MB

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text: The complete script is examples/model_zoo/quickstart.py.

docs.title: 1. Browse
docs.text:
import pinneapple as pp

pp.zoo.list()        # ['airfoil_cst_rans_mlp', 'heatsink_forced_mlp', 'heatsink_natural_mlp', ...]
pp.datasets.list()   # ['airfoil_rans_cst_re4e6', 'heatsink_forced_convection', ...]

card = pp.zoo.info("airfoil_cst_rans_mlp")      # a ModelCard
card.task, card.inputs, card.outputs            # names and units
card.validity_range["alpha_deg"]                # [-2.0, 14.0]
card.validation_metrics["test/Cd_mape_pct"]     # 0.545
print(card.to_markdown())                       # the full card: training data, licence, citation, trust report

docs.title: 2. Load and predict
docs.text:
model = pp.zoo.load("airfoil_cst_rans_mlp")     # weights checked against the manifest's SHA-256
naca2412 = dict(T0=0.169591, T1=0.144959, T2=0.131433, M0=0.024922, M1=0.071088, M2=0.058960)
out = model.predict(**naca2412, alpha_deg=[0, 2, 4, 6])
out["Cl"], out["Cd"], out["Cl_std"]             # ensemble mean and spread

predict takes named columns (keyword arguments or a mapping) or an (n, n_inputs) array in model.input_names order. It warns with pp.zoo.OutOfRangeWarning for rows outside the validity range. model.in_range(...) returns the mask.

docs.title: 3. Compare with the reference
docs.text:
ev = pp.zoo.evaluate("airfoil_cst_rans_mlp")
ev["matches_card"]                              # True: the card's metrics are reproduced
ev["metrics"]["xfoil_naca2412/Cd_mape_pct"]     # 2.8 -- against XFOIL, an independent solver

xfoil = pp.datasets.load("airfoil_rans_cst_re4e6", split="xfoil_naca2412")
pred = model.predict({k: xfoil[k] for k in model.input_names})

evaluate(name, dataset) also accepts any of the following, and reports the share of cases outside the validity range:

  • a dataset name with split=;
  • a DatasetSplit;
  • an (inputs, outputs) pair;
  • a mapping of columns.

docs.title: 4. Validate
docs.text:
report = pp.zoo.validate("airfoil_cst_rans_mlp", inputs={**naca2412, "alpha_deg": [4.0, 18.0]})
report.decisao                  # "REVIEW": alpha = 18 deg is outside the validity range (and a warning is raised)
print(report.to_markdown())     # card metrics reproduced, acceptance limits, physics checks

The physics checks are model-specific:

  • Airfoil: lift slope against thin-airfoil theory, Cl monotone below stall, symmetric-airfoil antisymmetry, Cd > 0.
  • Heat sink: monotonic effects of airflow, conductivity and source size; positivity.
  • Rover:
    • load grows with sinkage;
    • pull grows with slip before its peak;
    • the Mohr–Coulomb limit holds;
    • My ≥ R·Fx.

docs.title: 5. Benchmark
docs.text:
res = pp.zoo.benchmark("airfoil_cst_rans_mlp", budget_s=30, seeds=3)
res.table(); print(res.to_markdown())

This runs pp.benchmark (the equal-budget benchmark API) on the model's own dataset. It compares the shipped model with the same architecture trained from scratch on the same training split under the same compute budget, and evaluates both on the same held-out test set. The run includes pp.benchmark's gates, determinism check, report and trust card. It needs pinneapple_analysis.benchmark.

docs.title: 6. Fine-tune, with a held-out guard
docs.text:
new = pp.datasets.load("airfoil_rans_cst_re4e6", split="naca_reference")   # or (X_new, Y_new), or a dict of columns
ft = pp.zoo.finetune("airfoil_cst_rans_mlp", new, epochs=50, lr=1e-5)
print(ft.summary())             # guard metrics on the ORIGINAL test set, before -> after
ft.save("my_airfoil")           # refused (FinetuneRejectedError) if any got worse by > 2 %, unless force=True
pp.zoo.load_dir("my_airfoil")

How the fine-tune works:

  • It trains a copy of the model; the original is never modified.
  • By default (replay=True) the original training split is mixed in, to limit forgetting. NaN targets (e.g. a missing Cm) are ignored.
  • save_to= / registry= (a pinneapple_registry.ArtifactRegistry) save in the same call, and are refused the same way.
  • A forced save records the regression in the new card's data_lineage["guard"].

The guard is not a formality. Fine-tuning this airfoil model on 36 extra NACA runs makes it worse on the 15 held-out shapes, and the guard refuses to save it.

docs.title: 7. Check each query, export to ONNX, run in a browser
docs.text:
validate judges a model as a whole. query_checks judges one input. It answers four questions:

  • Is the input inside the validity range?
  • Are the outputs physical?
  • Does the ensemble agree as well as it did on held-out data?
  • Do the model's physics checks hold at this point?

Each check carries the rule ID that pinneapple check uses: PC601 (out of range), PC602 (sparse region), PC402 and PC403 (unphysical or non-finite output), and PC302 (model residual). The verdict is the worst status among them:

  • fail: the query is outside the range, so the answer is an extrapolation.
  • warn: use the answer with caution.
  • pass: every check holds.

Design constraints, such as the airfoil's t/c ≥ 11 % and |Cm| ≤ 0.10, are reported but never change the verdict.

r = pp.zoo.query_checks("airfoil_cst_rans_mlp", T0=.17, T1=.15, T2=.13, M0=.02, M1=.07, M2=.06, alpha_deg=16)[0]
r["verdict"]["status"]                                # 'fail': alpha 16 deg is beyond the trained range
[(c["id"], c["status"], c["detail_text"]) for c in r["checks"] if c["status"] != "pass"]
pp.zoo.check_spec("airfoil_cst_rans_mlp")             # the declarative spec: values, limits, templates, verdicts

export_onnx writes one ONNX graph that takes the card's physical inputs and returns its physical outputs. The graph includes the pre-processing (CST encoding, log features, normalisation) and the post-processing (exp, ensemble mean and spread, conformal bound).

The export is refused if the graph differs from the PyTorch model by more than 1e-5. The comparison runs on every held-out and independent-reference input of the zoo. With checks=True, the graph also takes a query input and returns the values of the query checks, so any ONNX runtime gives the same verdict as Python.

info = pp.zoo.export_onnx("heatsink_forced_mlp", "heatsink.onnx", checks=True)
info["parity"]                                        # 1.6e-06, against PyTorch on the 900 held-out designs
pp.zoo.onnx_parity("heatsink_forced_mlp", "heatsink.onnx")

For the browser, python -m pinneapple_hub.zoo.web data/web/zoo writes each model's graph and a JSON file. The JSON holds the model card, the check spec and the reference data to plot. The same command writes the CST airfoil geometry graphs from pinneapple_design.aero.geometry_onnx.

The JS runtime that reads these files ships with the package in pinneapple_hub/zoo/web/:

  • onnx.js, a dependency-free ONNX interpreter;
  • zoo.js, with loadModel, loadAirfoilGeometry and evaluate. evaluate is the JS twin of pinneapple_hub.zoo.checks.evaluate.

tests/js/zoo_web.test.mjs checks the runtime against Python. The Playground is built on it.

docs.title: Datasets
docs.text:
info = pp.datasets.info("heatsink_forced_convection")
print(info.to_markdown())                       # splits, columns with units, provenance, verification, licence
test = pp.datasets.load("heatsink_forced_convection", split="test")
test["r_base_k_w"], test.columns, test.n_rows
X, Y = test.xy(["base_width_mm", "power_w"], ["r_base_k_w"])
test.to_pandas()

The zoo datasets are also registered in pinneapple_data.datasets.DatasetRegistry as zoo/<name>.

docs.title: Operator-learning benchmarks
docs.text:
burgers_1d_li2021, darcy_2d_li2021 and navier_stokes_2d_li2021_nu1e-3 are the standard problems of Li et al. (2021, the Fourier Neural Operator paper), with the input distributions of that paper. They are generated by PINNeAPPle's own verified solvers (pinneapple_simulation.numerical_solvers.operator_datasets). Each dataset card gives:

  • the resolution and time-step study (discretisation error 4e-12 for Burgers and about 8e-4 for Darcy, in relative L2);
  • the solver checks: the Cole–Hopf exact solution for Burgers, a manufactured solution with second-order convergence for Darcy;
  • the seeds and the 1000 / 200 train / test split.
train = pp.datasets.load("darcy_2d_li2021", split="train")      # downloads ~59 MB once
a, u = train["a"], train["u"]                                    # (1000, 128, 128) each

docs.title: Airfoil flow fields
docs.text:
airfoil_rans_cst_re4e6_fields holds the cell fields of the same 436 OpenFOAM runs as airfoil_rans_cst_re4e6, regenerated with pinneapple_design.aero.dataset (the coefficients match the campaign; only runs flagged unsteady differ, within their oscillation). Each row is one run: CST weights, angle of attack, coefficients, status, and the cell centres and p, Ux, Uy, nut at the 20064 cells (free stream U = 1, chord 1). The grid moves with the shape, so x and y are stored per run. The test split holds the 15 shapes held out by the airfoil surrogates.

test = pp.datasets.load("airfoil_rans_cst_re4e6_fields", split="test")    # one 26 MB file
steady = test["status"] != "unsteady"
p, x, y = test["p"][steady], test["x"][steady], test["y"][steady]           # (n, 20064) each

docs.title: Heated-channel digital twin
docs.text:
thermal_channel_cfd is the actuated heated-channel problem of PINNeAPPle-Benchmark experiment 05, generated by the library's 2-D incompressible solver (pinneapple_simulation.numerical_solvers.thermal_channel_datasets). The inlet velocity U(t) and the heater flux Q(t) vary in time; each trajectory stores the fields, the actuators and the quantities of interest (outlet temperature, maximum temperature, pressure drop, heat balance). The card gives the solver checks (Poiseuille, Nusselt number 5.388 vs 5.385), the three-grid GCI of the dataset grid (1–4 %) and the split plan: 48 / 8 / 12 trajectories of random steps and ramps, plus 8 chirped-sinusoid and 6 edge-step trajectories from actuation families never seen in training.

test = pp.datasets.load("thermal_channel_cfd", split="test_unseen_sinusoid")   # one 37 MB file
fields = test["fields"]                                   # (8, 101, 4, 128, 32): u, v, p, T every 0.4 time units

docs.title: Hosting, cache and offline use
docs.text:
Every file is listed in pinneapple_hub/zoo/manifest.json with its SHA-256, size, version and its Hugging Face Hub location (huggingface.co/PINNeAPPle-Labs/<name>, tag revision: v<version>, or v<version>.postN when the same files were republished with a new card or derived formats; the loader then falls back to v<version> while the new tag does not exist yet, and checks the SHA-256 either way). A file is resolved in this order:

  1. Bundled with the package. This applies only to small items (under about 2 MB each). Larger datasets are Hub-only: one <split>.npz per split, possibly sharded into <split>-NN.npz, and pp.datasets.load(name, split=...) downloads only the files of the requested split.
  2. The cache. $PINNEAPPLE_ZOO_CACHE, by default ~/.cache/pinneapple/zoo.
  3. The Hub. The file is downloaded once with huggingface_hub (or plain HTTPS), checked and cached.

Each step can fail with a specific error:

  • A checksum that does not match raises pp.zoo.ChecksumMismatchError. A corrupt cache entry is fetched again when online.
  • With PINNEAPPLE_OFFLINE=1 (or HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1), nothing is downloaded, and a file that is not available locally raises ArtifactUnavailableError.
  • An item the Hub does not have yet raises ArtifactNotPublishedError, which says how to publish it.

pp.zoo.status(name) and pp.datasets.status(name) show where each file resolves from, without downloading it.

docs.title: Versions and the physics a model was trained on
docs.text:
A new release of a model keeps the old one: the manifest lists it under superseded, with its files, their SHA-256, its Hub tag and the reason it was superseded. pp.zoo.versions(name) lists every release, and pp.zoo.load(name, version="1.0.0") loads an old one (from the Hub, with a SupersededModelWarning that gives the reason).

A surrogate is only a surrogate of the physics it was trained on. The rover contact model records that physics in its card (data_lineage.physics) and its config.json: the full WongReeceModel.physics_config(), i.e. the soil and all its parameters, the wheel, gravity and the model options. ZooContactSurrogate(pp.zoo.load(...)) .check_physics(model) lists what differs from the model it is used with and raises a PhysicsMismatchWarning; vehicle.dashboard.vehicle_dashboard does this and notes any difference on the PINN chart. A test fails when the library's GRC-1, the VIPER wheel or the Wong-Reece options change without a new zoo release.

rover_contact_grc1_viper v1.0.0 was trained before slip-sinkage was added to GRC-1 (n1 = 0). Against the current Wong-Reece model it errs by up to ~200 N at high driving slip. v1.1.0 is trained on the current physics (n1 = 0.8) with the same held-out protocol (2000 Latin-hypercube states, seed 1000, disjoint from training). With slip-sinkage the pull need not grow with slip at a fixed sinkage, so its gate checks that dFx/ds has the sign of the recorded reference instead of dFx/ds ≥ 0.

docs.title: On the Hugging Face Hub
docs.text:
What each repo holds besides the manifest's files, so the Hub's own tools work:

  • Datasets: Parquet for the dataset viewer and datasets.load_dataset. The npz files stay the source of truth (the library reads them, SHA-256 checked). pinneapple_hub.zoo.parquet.write_dataset derives Parquet files from them, deterministically, under data/<config>/<split>-NNNNN.parquet. Scalar columns are plain columns; array columns are fixed-size list columns of their shape (List(List(float32, length=128), length=128); use with_format("numpy")). A sample larger than 512 KiB whose arrays share a leading axis (Navier-Stokes vorticity in time, the heated-channel fields in time) is stored as one row per step, with sample and step columns, so the viewer can show every row. Shards stay below 256 MiB uncompressed and row groups below 16 MiB. Splits with other columns (a grid, a convergence study, an XFOIL polar) are separate configs. The README's YAML (configs with the data_files of each split, dataset_info features and split sizes, licence, task category, size category, tags) is written by pinneapple_hub.zoo.hub_cards.dataset_card, with the columns, units, provenance and both ways of loading. pinneapple_hub.zoo.parquet.read_parquet puts a split back together; a test checks the round trip npz -> Parquet -> arrays bit for bit.
  • Models: safetensors, ONNX and an honest card. Next to weights.pt the repo holds model.safetensors (the same tensors; pinneapple_hub.zoo.export.load_safetensors), model.onnx (pre- and post-processing in the graph, parity with PyTorch within 1e-5) and example.json (a held-out case, the model's outputs for it and the verdicts). The card says library_name: pinneapple, pipeline_tag: tabular-regression and inference: false: no Hub inference provider can run these models with their encoding, ensembles and validity checks, so the widget is off. Its "How to use" code prints the numbers of example.json, and the publishing workflow runs it.
  • The demo Space PINNeAPPle-Labs/zoo-demo, linked from every model card, replaces the widget. It is a static Space (no server, free for the organisation): pinneapple_hub.zoo.demo.export_space computes, from the models published on the Hub, every model's prediction along a sweep of each input with its ensemble spread or conformal bound and the verdict of its query checks at every point, and writes them with each model's ONNX graph (prediction and query checks in one graph) and the browser runtime (pinneapple_hub/zoo/web). The page (apps/zoo_space, UI only, with the Playground's charts) plots a sweep, shades where the checks warn (yellow) or fail (red), and shows the checks at the chosen input and the model's trust decision. Evaluate in your browser runs the graph on the visitor's own inputs. tests/js/zoo_space.test.mjs runs every precomputed sweep again through the browser runtime and requires the same numbers and the same verdicts as Python.

To publish (maintainers):

  1. Add a repository secret HF_TOKEN with write access to the PINNeAPPle-Labs organisation.
  2. Run the Publish zoo to the Hugging Face Hub workflow. It also runs on every push to main that changes the zoo.

Hub-only items are not in the repository. To upload them, put their files on a branch as <name>/<file> (for example the output of scripts/zoo/operator_data.py generate) and run the workflow by hand with staging_ref set to that branch. Every staged file must match the SHA-256 in the manifest. Runs without staging_ref convert the Hub-only datasets from the copy already on the Hub (downloaded, SHA-256 checked) and upload only their Parquet files and card.

After the upload the workflow checks, anonymously, what the Hub serves, and fails when something is wrong:

  1. every manifest file at the tag (SHA-256);
  2. the dataset viewer of every dataset: datasets-server is-valid (preview and viewer, retried while the Hub processes the push), splits (every split of the manifest is listed) and first-rows of every split;
  3. every model: loaded from the Hub with the bundled copy ignored, its card metrics reproduced on the stored reference, the card's example reproduced by the PyTorch, safetensors and ONNX copies, the card's front matter, and its "How to use" code run;
  4. the Space reaches RUNNING and serves its page, index.json and every model's sweeps.

To republish files that did not change (a new card, new derived formats), bump the item's revision to the next v<version>.postN: the old tags stay as they are, so code pinned to them keeps working. Inputs of the manual run: only (some items), tags=false (upload to main without creating the tags, e.g. to try a branch; the model checks then wait for the tagged run) and space.

Without the secret, the workflow checks the manifest and skips the upload with a warning. python scripts/zoo/publish_to_hub.py --dry-run builds the derived files and cards and lists the uploads; --verify-viewer, --verify-models and --verify-space run the checks from any machine that reaches the Hub.

docs.title: Forecasting near-random series without overfitting
docs.text:
Some series are almost random: chaotic systems observed with noise, noise-driven physical systems, financial returns. A flexible model always finds something in them on its training data. This guide gives measured answers to four questions:

  1. Is there anything predictable at all, and how do you know before fitting a model?
  2. How far ahead can each model family forecast before its skill falls back to a baseline?
  3. Which training choices actually prevent overfitting, and by how much?
  4. How do the point and probabilistic scores compare once the differences are tested for significance?

Everything here comes from two scripts: examples/near_random_forecasting/run_study.py runs the study and render_visuals.py draws the visual pack from its results. Their results are committed in examples/near_random_forecasting/results/: one JSON per series, the overfitting studies, and tables.md, from which every table below is copied. The figures are in examples/near_random_forecasting/figures/. The library pieces live in pinneapple_systems.time_series (predictability, synthetic, forecast_lab, metrics_ext, validation, datasets.public) and are tested in tests/test_near_random_forecasting.py and tests/test_near_random_visuals.py.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
from pinneapple_systems.time_series.predictability import predictability_report
from pinneapple_systems.time_series.forecast_lab import presets
from pinneapple_systems.time_series.forecast_lab.study import run_zoo

c = presets.case("double_well", n=1500)                       # series, protocol and model zoo
report = predictability_report(c.data.y, horizons=c.protocol.horizons, dt=c.data.dt, n_surrogates=19)
print(report["surrogate_tests"]["npe_iaaft"]["p_value"])      # more structure than a linear Gaussian process?
res = run_zoo(c.data, c.specs[:6], c.protocol, budget=2)      # baselines + gradient boosting, purged CV tuning
print(res["models"]["gbm"]["test"]["skill_rmse"], res["models"]["gbm"]["skill_horizon_vs_best_baseline"])

Your own series: wrap it in SeriesData(obs, target=0, dt=...), pick horizons for a Protocol, and list ModelSpec(name, family, factory, grid) entries. Every forecaster implements fit(data, train_origins, val_origins, horizons) and predict(data, origins) -> Forecast (a mean plus a Gaussian standard deviation or ensemble samples).

docs.title: The protocol
docs.text:
The same rules for every series and every model (forecast_lab.study):

  • Test period fixed first. The last 20 % of each series is the test period. It is set before any tuning and touched once, by the final fitted model. Every forecast is made from an origin t using data up to t only, and targets t + h for each horizon h. Forecasts are direct (one output per horizon), not iterated.
  • Validation block, purged. The last 15 % of the development part (everything before the test period) is the validation block. It is used for early stopping, for calibrating the predictive spread of point forecasters, and for choosing each family's representative. Training origins stop at least max(h) samples before it, so no training label falls inside it (purge = largest horizon). Validation labels never reach the test period.
  • Purged walk-forward tuning. Each tuned model gets the same budget: 4 configurations drawn from its grid (presets.BUDGET). Each configuration is scored on 3 walk-forward folds of the development part (2 for sunspots). Each fold has a purged inner block for early stopping. The score is the mean over horizons of RMSE / RMSE(persistence), so all horizons weigh the same. The best configuration is refitted once on the final split.
  • Same origins for everyone. All models of a series start at the same first origin (the longest input window in the zoo), and are scored on the same test origins (every second one, every one for the sunspots; 51 to 687 per series).
  • Scores (study.evaluate), per horizon:
  • MAE and RMSE, and skill = 1 − RMSE / RMSE(reference).
  • CRPS: closed form for Gaussian forecasts, the fair ensemble estimator for ensembles; skill against climatology.
  • Coverage of the central 50, 80 and 95 % intervals, and the PIT histogram with its mean absolute deviation from flat (0 = flat).
  • A point forecaster gets a Gaussian predictive distribution whose standard deviation at each horizon is its RMSE on the validation block. Physical models with filters or SDEs produce their own distributions: Kalman, EnKF and Euler–Maruyama ensembles.
  • Tests. One-sided Diebold–Mariano tests on squared errors (HLN small-sample correction, long-run variance up to the overlap of h-step errors) against persistence and against the best baseline: at each horizon, the baseline with the lowest validation RMSE, so the reference is not picked on the test period. The p-values are Holm-adjusted across all non-baseline models at each horizon (family-wise error 5 %), and Benjamini–Hochberg q-values over all model × horizon tests are stored too.
  • "Last horizon with skill" is the largest h such that, at every horizon up to h, the skill is positive and the Holm-adjusted p-value is below 0.05.

The zoo per series, defined in forecast_lab.presets:

family models baseline persistence, climatology (training mean and std), AR(p) by AIC, ARIMA(p ≤ 2, d ≤ 1, q ≤ 1) by AIC, simple exponential smoothing, seasonal naive (the value whole periods before the target) and phase-aligned mean cycle (PhaseClimatology: the training cycle, re-aligned to the phase of each origin by least squares over the last 1 or 3 periods; tuned). The period is the highest peak of the training periodogram. data gradient boosting on lags (scikit-learn histogram GBM, one per horizon), MLP, LSTM (time_series.models.LSTMForecaster), TCN (TCNForecaster), transformer (pinneapple_neural VanillaTransformer) data + physics GBM with physics features (the fitted vector field or drift at the origin state, or the Kalman-filtered state and energy); MLP with a physics-residual loss on the predicted path (fully observed ODEs; λ ∈ {0, 0.01, 0.1, 1} tuned) physical the governing ODE / delay ODE with parameters fitted by multiple shooting on the training data, deliberately misspecified versions (Lorenz-63 without the −xz term, Mackey–Glass with delay 14 instead of 17, an OU model of the oscillator and of the double well), SINDy, EnKF (40 members) on the fitted ODE, Kalman-filtered linear SDEs (OU, damped oscillator), SDE drift regression with Euler–Maruyama ensembles hybrid physical forecast + GBM correction (correct and misspecified physics), UDE: misspecified Lorenz-63 + neural closure trained through the integrator, linear drift + neural drift closure for the double well

Prior knowledge given to the physical models (assumptions): the structure of the equations, initial parameter guesses 20–30 % off, the Mackey–Glass delay (17) and exponent (10), the Lorenz-96 dimension. Physical models never see the true parameters.
