The largest Lyapunov exponents come from the equations (Benettin two-trajectory method, synthetic.largest_lyapunov_benettin, natural logarithm per unit time): * 0.893 for Lorenz-63 (Sprott 2003, Chaos and Time-Series Analysis, gives 0.906); * 0.0049 for Mackey–Glass (synthetic.mackey_glass_lyapunov, a perturbation of the whole delay history, 50 000 time units at step 0.1); * 1.677 for Lorenz-96.

One Lyapunov time (LT) is 22 samples for Lorenz-63, 68 for Mackey–Glass and 12 for Lorenz-96.

The Mackey–Glass value was checked for convergence (pipeline.lyapunov_study, results/lyapunov_mackey_glass.json; three seeds each, which change the initial history and the perturbation direction):

step 10 000 time units 50 000 200 000 0.1 0.00481 ± 0.00056 0.00498 ± 0.00017 0.00501 ± 0.00015 0.05 0.00509 ± 0.00033 0.00504 ± 0.00003 0.00516 ± 0.00003
  • At 10 000 time units (the first version of this study used one such run, 0.0046) the seed alone moves the estimate by about ±10 %.
  • With longer runs the estimate settles at 0.0050 (step 0.1) to 0.0052 (step 0.05). The 3 % dependence on the step is presumably the integration error of the delayed term, which is interpolated linearly at the half step.
  • The value used for the LT axes (0.0049) is within 5 % of the finest estimate.
  • Unverified comparison. A reviewer quoted 0.006 to 0.007 for τ = 17 from Farmer (1982, Physica D 4:366) and Wolf et al. (1985, Physica D 16:285). Neither paper could be opened from this environment (publisher sites and arXiv were not reachable), so their values, units and settings are not checked here. Our converged value is 13 to 29 % below that range.
  • Hypothesis, not a finding: if those values are in bits per unit time, they would be 0.0042–0.0049 in natural log, consistent with ours. This was not verified.

docs.title: 1. Is there anything to predict?
docs.text:
predictability_report(y) runs before any model. It fits an AR model (order by AIC, in-sample one-step R²), computes the permutation entropy (order 5, 1 = i.i.d.) and the sample entropy (m = 2, r = 0.2 std), and estimates the Rosenstein exponent on a delay embedding. It then runs surrogate tests with 99 surrogates each:

  • The statistic is the out-of-sample error of a nearest-neighbour predictor (NPE, one-sided) and the time-reversal asymmetry (TRA, two-sided).
  • Shuffled surrogates test for any temporal structure.
  • IAAFT surrogates test for structure beyond a linear Gaussian process seen through a monotone transform.
  • A series with an AR(1) coefficient above 0.99 is tested on its differences.

The verdict column reads "nonlinear structure" if either IAAFT test rejects at 5 %, "linear structure only" if only the shuffle test rejects.

series AR order (R² 1-step) perm. entropy sample entropy Rosenstein λ (true λ) NPE / std p shuffle p IAAFT p TRA IAAFT verdict Lorenz-63, noise 0.01 std 14 (0.99) 0.43 0.44 0.89 (0.893) 0.13 0.01 0.01 0.53 nonlinear structure Lorenz-63, noise 0.1 std 13 (0.95) 0.67 0.72 0.73 (0.893) 0.21 0.01 0.01 0.75 nonlinear structure Lorenz-63, noise 0.3 std 14 (0.80) 0.91 1.38 0.64 (0.893) 0.42 0.01 0.01 0.97 nonlinear structure Mackey-Glass, noise 0.01 std 20 (0.99) 0.59 0.62 0.01 (0.005) 0.03 0.01 0.01 0.04 nonlinear structure Mackey-Glass, noise 0.1 std 20 (0.94) 0.64 0.86 0.01 (0.005) 0.14 0.01 0.01 0.09 nonlinear structure Mackey-Glass, noise 0.3 std 19 (0.81) 0.83 1.50 0.01 (0.005) 0.39 0.01 0.01 0.39 nonlinear structure Lorenz-96 (K=40), noise 0.1 std 8 (0.95) 0.74 0.82 0.76 (1.677) 0.30 0.01 0.01 0.01 nonlinear structure Ornstein-Uhlenbeck 2 (0.80) 0.94 1.41 0.14 0.50 0.01 0.76 0.84 linear structure only Noise-driven damped oscillator 14 (0.97) 0.68 0.87 0.17 0.24 0.01 0.86 0.26 linear structure only Double-well (regime switching) 6 (0.93) 0.95 0.91 0.20 0.30 0.01 0.08 0.89 linear structure only White noise 0 (0.00) 1.00 2.20 0.00 1.05 0.81 0.76 0.88 no structure found Random walk 0 (0.00) 1.00 2.20 -0.00 1.05 0.71 0.67 0.98 no structure found (tested on differences) USD/EUR daily log-returns 0 (0.00) 1.00 1.97 0.00 0.90 0.01 0.01 0.15 nonlinear structure Sunspots (yearly) 9 (0.86) 0.60 0.84 0.03 0.60 0.01 0.84 0.01 nonlinear structure

What this says:

  • The tests call every control correctly. White noise and the random walk (tested on its increments) show no structure: permutation entropy 1.00, AR order 0, no rejection. OU and the oscillator show linear structure only. All chaotic series reject the IAAFT null.
  • The double well (IAAFT p = 0.08) is called linear at 5 %. At this sampling step and noise level, its regime switching is not distinguishable from a linear Gaussian process by these two statistics.
  • The USD/EUR returns reject both nulls, but the entropy is 1.00 and the AR order is 0. The structure is in a nonlinear statistic, not in the mean. Volatility clustering of returns is the usual explanation; that is an interpretation, which this study did not test. As section 2 shows, no model forecasts the mean return better than the baseline. A rejected surrogate test says there is structure, not that the structure is forecastable.
  • The sunspots reject the time-reversal null (p = 0.01): cycles rise faster than they decay.
  • The Rosenstein exponent is unreliable. It gives 0.20 for the (non-chaotic) double well and 0.14 and 0.17 for the linear OU and oscillator. For Lorenz-96 it gives 0.76, against the true 1.68: a scalar embedding of a 40-dimensional system does not recover it. For Mackey–Glass it is 1.1 to 1.7 times the Benettin value (0.0052 to 0.0085, against 0.0049). The estimate also depends on the fit window of the divergence curve; the default here is samples 5–30, and tests/test_near_random_forecasting.py only asks for 0.6–1.3 on noise-free Lorenz-63 (true 0.906). Use it only next to a surrogate test, never alone.

The surrogate-trained twins check whether a model learned more than the linear correlations. The same GBM is trained once on the real development data and once on an IAAFT surrogate of it (and on a shuffled one), then both are scored on the real test period. The table gives the RMSE skill against persistence, averaged over horizons.

The real-trained model beats its IAAFT twin only on the chaotic series (by 0.12 to 0.42 for Lorenz-63 and Mackey–Glass) and, slightly, on the double well (0.04) and the sunspots (0.05). On OU, the oscillator, the noise controls and USD/EUR the difference is 0.00 to 0.01: whatever the GBM learned there, a linear Gaussian process with the same spectrum teaches it too. On white noise and USD/EUR, the 0.28 skill against persistence is just the gain of forecasting the mean instead of the last value; the shuffled twin gets the same 0.28. Lorenz-96 seen through a single variable (0.03) is nearly linear-looking: the univariate GBM cannot use the other 39 variables. The random walk's shuffled twin (−14.95) is meaningless: shuffling the levels of a random walk destroys it. It is kept to show what a broken surrogate looks like.

  • Against persistence everything looks good, up to the longest horizon on most series, because persistence is a poor forecast once the horizon passes the correlation time (figure). Against the best baseline (chosen on validation at each horizon: AR or ARIMA, and on Mackey–Glass the phase-aligned mean cycle from h = 16 on) the picture is honest:
  • Lorenz-63: 1.4 LT for every family at noise 0.1, and at noise 0.3 except the hybrid (0.7 LT). At noise 0.01 the EnKF and the hybrid reach 2.9 LT and the data models 1.4 LT.
  • Mackey–Glass: 1.9 LT for the data, data + physics and hybrid families at noise 0.01. At noise 0.1 it is 1.9 LT for data + physics and hybrid and 0.9 LT for the data family. At noise 0.3 it is 0.5 LT for all three. The fitted delay equation alone stops earlier: 0.9, 0.5 and 0.2 LT.
  • Lorenz-96: 2.7 LT for the EnKF, 1.3 LT for the hybrid, 0.7 LT for the data and data + physics families.
  • Linear stochastic series: no family beats the linear baseline at any horizon. That is the correct answer. The fitted Kalman models recover the true parameters:
  • OU: θ = 0.994, σ = 0.990 (true 1, 1).
  • oscillator: ω = 0.995, ζ = 0.059, σ = 0.308 (true 1, 0.05, 0.3).

They are then equal to ARIMA, not better, because a linear SDE sampled at a fixed step is an ARMA process. * Double well: no significant skill over ARIMA for any family. The mean gains are at most 0.05. The drift regression recovers the cubic drift shape, 0.80 x − 0.92 x³ against the true x − x³: the coefficients shrink towards zero because of the observation noise, as stated in the assumptions. * Noise controls and USD/EUR returns: nothing beats the baseline, at any horizon, for any of the five data-driven models. That is the correct answer, and the protocol reports it as "none". * Sunspots (51 test origins from 1947, targets up to 2008): only the data + physics and hybrid representatives beat the best baseline (AR(18)), and only one year ahead. The fitted oscillator alone has a period of 2π/0.637 = 9.9 years and ζ = 0.32, and it is worse than the best baseline at every horizon.

Misspecified physics, measured (Lorenz-63, noise 0.1, skill against the best baseline at h = 1, 2, 4, 8, 16):

model skill ODE without −xz 0.36, 0.30, 0.10, 0.00, −0.01 + GBM correction 0.49, 0.69, 0.80, 0.70, 0.53 UDE closure 0.47, 0.68, 0.79, 0.66, 0.30 correct ODE + EnKF 0.54, 0.73, 0.84, 0.79, 0.65

Both repairs work at short horizons. The UDE falls below the baseline after about 1 LT (−0.09 at h = 32). With a wrong delay (noise 0.01), the Mackey–Glass model's skill against persistence swings between −0.64 and +0.75 across horizons. A GBM correction brings it to 0.60–0.99 at every horizon.

docs.title: 3. What prevents overfitting, measured
docs.text:
Ten training variants (eight on the series without physics) were run on three series. Each was trained on the final split and scored by:

  • its error on its training origins, on the validation block and on the untouched test period;
  • the cross-validation estimate of four schemes (for the deliberately overfit models and two regularised references): shuffled k-fold, walk-forward without purge, purged walk-forward, and purged k-fold with an embargo of max(h).

  • The train–test gap is the detector. The deliberately overfit models have gaps of 0.21 to 0.57 (wide MLP, no early stopping) and 0.44 to 0.93 (GBM with 255 leaves, which drives its training error to 0). Every early-stopped model has a gap of 0.054 or less.
  • Early stopping on a purged validation block is the single most effective choice. The same 546k-parameter MLP goes from a test error of 1.159 to 0.908 (double well), 0.919 to 0.723 (USD/EUR) and 0.476 to 0.423 (Lorenz-63) when it stops on the validation block.
  • Model size matters less than stopping. A 16-unit MLP (357 to 920 parameters) and an early-stopped 546k-parameter MLP score within 0.015 of each other on the double well and USD/EUR. On Lorenz-63 the large one is better (0.423 against 0.504), so smaller is not automatically safer.
  • Weight decay 1e-2 plus dropout 0.2 on top of early stopping changes the test error by −0.015 (USD/EUR), +0.001 (double well) and +0.131 (Lorenz-63, where it under-fits).
  • A 5-member ensemble improves on its single member by 0.002 to 0.018.
  • The physics-residual loss changes nothing measurable here: 0.447 with λ = 0.1 against 0.446 without, on Lorenz-63. In the zoo, the tuner picked λ = 0 at noise 0.01, 0.1 at noise 0.1, 0.01 at noise 0.3 and 1 on Lorenz-96.
  • Which CV scheme to trust. For the regularised models (MLP 64x2, GBM with 7 leaves), the four schemes agree within 0.04 of each other and of the test error. For the overfit MLP they differ: shuffled k-fold gave the lowest (most optimistic) estimate of the four in all three series. Double well: 0.990 shuffled against 1.159 on test. USD/EUR: 0.862 against 0.919. Lorenz-63: 0.438 against 0.476. The purged walk-forward estimates were 1.205, 0.921 and 0.468, closer to test in each case. Walk-forward with and without purge gave nearly the same numbers here (largest difference 0.005). With h ≤ 128 samples and several thousand training origins, the purge removes few samples; it matters more with long horizons and short series.

docs.title: 5. A real daily series: YouTube trending
docs.text:
Data. "Trending YouTube Video Statistics" (Kaggle, user datasnaek; listed there as CC0 1.0 public domain). The Kaggle page itself could not be opened from this environment; the licence is taken from the search-engine listing of that page, so treat it as stated by the source, not checked here. The US file (USvideos.csv) is fetched from a GitHub mirror at a pinned commit and checked against its SHA-256 (datasets.public.PINNED["youtube_trending_us"]); two independent mirrors serve byte-identical files. No API key is needed.

load_youtube_trending_us aggregates it per trending day: 205 days from 2017-11-14 to 2018-06-14, 196 to 200 entries per day. Eight calendar days are missing from the source (2018-01-10, 01-11 and 04-08 to 04-13); they are skipped, so one step is one trending day. Two series, horizons 1, 2, 3, 5 and 7 days, the baselines plus the data-driven zoo (there is no physical model for this):

  • log10 total daily views: trends upward over the period.
  • Entertainment slots per day: 36 to 63 of the ~200 entries (mean 48.6).

Predictability (results/tables.md):

series AR order (R² 1-step) NPE / std p shuffle p IAAFT p TRA IAAFT verdict log10 total daily views 10 (0.97) 1.78 1.00 1.00 0.03 nonlinear structure Entertainment slots 1 (0.80) 0.81 0.01 0.45 0.37 linear structure only
  • The surrogate tests assume a stationary series. On the trending views series the NPE is larger than the standard deviation and the shuffle and IAAFT tests give p = 1.00: the original is less predictable by nearest neighbours than its surrogates, presumably because test points late in the trend have no neighbours at that level. The "nonlinear structure" verdict rests on the time-reversal test alone and should not be read as evidence of exploitable nonlinearity.
  • The Entertainment count has linear (AR(1)) structure and nothing beyond it.

Forecasts (test period 34 days, 2018-05-06 to 2018-06-08):

series best baseline (val) best data model (val) its RMSE skill vs persistence, h = 1 2 3 5 7 significant vs best baseline (Holm) log10 total daily views exp_smoothing transformer -0.00 0.02 -0.12 -0.43 0.02 none Entertainment slots ar lstm -0.13 -0.12 -0.17 -0.13 -0.08 none

No model of the zoo is significantly better than the best baseline on either series at any horizon. With 34 test days the DM tests have little power, so this says the gain, if any, is too small to detect on this sample.

The surprise calendar below shows the same comparison day by day.

docs.title: Visual pack
docs.text:
examples/near_random_forecasting/render_visuals.py draws four 3-D scenes with Blender Cycles (bpy from PyPI, in process, CPU; pinneapple_blender.cycles) and two 2-D figures from the committed case results. Every number on them is in results/visuals.json. The scenes are built by forecast_lab.renders, which also returns the data drawn.

Predictability landscape. One tile per series: x is the horizon (log10 Lyapunov times for the chaotic series, log10 samples otherwise), y the four families, and height the RMSE skill of the family's best model (chosen on validation) against the best baseline, floored at -0.5. The translucent plane is skill 0. The chaotic series peak at 0.44 (Mackey–Glass, noise 0.3) to 0.98 (Lorenz-63, noise 0.01) and are back at 0.05 or less at their longest horizon (3.8 to 5.7 LT). Sunspots peaks at 0.20; every other series stays at 0.06 or less. On white noise, USD/EUR and the YouTube series only the data family was run.

Forecast cone. The same gradient-boosting forecaster refitted at every horizon 1 to 48 (so every step of the cone is a real forecast, not an interpolation) on Lorenz-63 (noise 0.1) and white noise. On Lorenz-63 the cone starts narrow and widens; on white noise it is as wide at h = 1 as at h = 48. Over all 576 test origins and horizons the 90 % band covered 89.0 % (Lorenz-63) and 89.4 % (white noise) of the outcomes, and the 50 % band 62.3 % and 50.4 %. A 3-second clip draws the cone step by step: figures/visuals/forecast_cone.mp4.

Attractor vs surrogates. Lorenz-63 x (noise 0.01), delay-embedded in three dimensions with delay 7 samples, next to its IAAFT surrogate (same spectrum and value distribution) and a shuffled surrogate. The nearest-neighbour prediction error relative to the standard deviation is 0.13, 0.29 and 1.05: the surrogate keeps the linear part of the predictability, the shuffle keeps none.

Ensemble divergence. 50 members started from one state perturbed by 1 % of the attractor standard deviation, integrated with the true equations. Mean spread (in units of the standard deviation) at the start, at 1 LT and at the end:

system start 1 LT end Lorenz-63, 5 LT 0.011 0.018 0.747 Mackey–Glass, 5 LT 0.009 0.052 0.944 noise-driven oscillator, 150 steps (all members share one forcing path) 0.009 – 0.001

The chaotic spreads grow 67 times (Lorenz-63) and 110 times (Mackey–Glass) over 5 LT, to about one standard deviation of the attractor; the damped linear oscillator forgets the initial difference and the members converge. Its unpredictability comes from the forcing, not from the initial state.

Memorise vs learn. The over-parametrised MLP of the overfitting study (512 × 3 units, 32 lags, no early stopping) against the regularised one (64 × 2, early stopping), refitted. The figure shows the last 150 training and the first 150 test origins; the one-step RMSE is over the whole training and test sets:

series variant params train test double well overfit 546 312 0.166 0.350 double well 64 × 2 + early stopping 5 768 0.245 0.248 Lorenz-63, noise 0.1 overfit 579 080 0.613 1.145 Lorenz-63, noise 0.1 64 × 2 + early stopping 7 816 0.861 0.913

The overfit network follows the training noise and is worse on the test period.

Surprise calendar. One cell per day of the test period, coloured by log2(|error of the best model| / |error of the best baseline|) at h = 1, both chosen on validation (blue: model closer; red: baseline closer). The model was closer on 68 % of the 34 days for YouTube views (transformer vs exponential smoothing), 38 % of 34 days for the Entertainment count (LSTM vs AR) and 50 % of 687 days for USD/EUR returns (MLP vs AR). None of these differences is significant in the DM tests above.

docs.title: What to use when
docs.text:
• Always first: run predictability_report.
  • If the shuffle test does not reject, forecast the mean (climatology) and stop.
  • If only the shuffle test rejects, an AR or ARIMA model is the forecast. In this study nothing beat it on the linear series, with or without physics.
  • If IAAFT rejects, nonlinear models may help, but check with the surrogate-trained twin. USD/EUR rejected both nulls and still nothing beat the mean.
  • Compare against the best baseline chosen on validation, not against persistence. Persistence is beaten by the climatological mean on every mean-reverting series. Skill against persistence alone would have credited the noise controls with +0.3.
  • Near-periodic series need a periodic baseline. On Mackey–Glass, the phase-aligned mean cycle keeps 0.58 to 0.61 skill against persistence at h = 256 samples (3.8 LT), more than AR's 0.39. With it in the baseline set, every family's skill horizon dropped (see section 2). Without it, the first version of this study credited the learned models with skill to 3.5 LT at every noise level. On the sunspots, seasonal naive (period 11) matches AR at 5 years (0.61) but is not better on validation, and on the oscillator AR stays the best baseline.
  • Chaotic system, known equations, fully observed: fit the parameters on the training data and assimilate with an EnKF. It had the longest or joint-longest skill horizon on Lorenz-63 and the longest on Lorenz-96. Calibrate its spread separately; here it was under-dispersed.
  • Known equations that may be wrong: add a statistical correction (physics + GBM). Across all series and horizons it was at most 4.2 % worse in RMSE than its physics alone, and up to 43 % better. It repaired a misspecified Lorenz-63 and a wrong-delay Mackey–Glass. A UDE closure repaired the short horizons too, but was worse after 1 LT.
  • No equations, chaotic series: a GBM on lags did as well as the neural forecasters at a fraction of the cost. On Lorenz-63 and Mackey–Glass, its skill against the best baseline (mean over horizons) was the best of the five data models or within 0.05 of it. On Lorenz-96 (40 inputs, 3000 training windows) it was the best data model (0.15), and the LSTM and TCN were worse than AR (−0.10 and −0.14).
  • Training: early stopping on a purged validation block; the size of the network mattered less than that. Ensembles help a little. Use purged walk-forward (or purged k-fold) cross-validation, never shuffled k-fold, and report the train–test gap.
  • Report significance. Many small skill differences in the tables (double well, OU, oscillator: ±0.03) are not significant after Holm adjustment across the zoo.

docs.title: Limits: what was not tested, and why
docs.text:
• One realisation per synthetic series and one seed per model. The spread across realisations and seeds is not measured. The DM tests account for the sampling error of the test period only.
  • Tuning budget: 4 configurations per model, at most 60 epochs (neural forecasters), at most 3000 training windows per neural model. Larger budgets could change the ranking between neural architectures (not between families on the linear and noise series, where all are at the baseline).
  • Forecasts are direct, at fixed horizons. Iterated one-step models, sequence-to-sequence decoders and probabilistic neural heads (quantile or distributional outputs) were not tested. Neural and GBM spreads are Gaussian, calibrated on the validation block.
  • No foundation models. Chronos and TimesFM wrappers exist in time_series.foundation_models but need packages and weights this environment could not download.
  • Kuramoto–Sivashinsky was not run. Lorenz-96 is the only high-dimensional case.
  • Data assimilation only where the state is observed. The EnKF was run on Lorenz-63 and Lorenz-96 (all variables observed), not on Mackey–Glass, whose state is a delay history. Kalman filtering was used for the linear SDEs.
  • SINDy only on the fully observed ODEs. It has no delay or stochastic library. The UDE was only tested on Lorenz-63; the double well has a neural drift closure instead.
  • Volatility models (GARCH) were not part of the zoo. USD/EUR is tested for forecasting the mean return only.
  • Real data: one financial series, one physical series and two series from one YouTube dataset. The sunspot test period has 51 origins and the YouTube one 34, so their DM tests have little power.
  • The Rosenstein exponent was computed with one embedding (dimension 4, delay from the autocorrelation) and one fit window. As shown above, it is sensitive to both.

docs.title: The PINNeAPPle Observatory
docs.text: A 3-D web app that shows the sky and the solar system as they are now from the visitor's location, with satellites, astrophysics analyses and a physics-informed orbit surrogate shown with its trust checks.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
pip install -e ".[sky]" -r apps/observatory/requirements.txt
cd apps/observatory && uvicorn observatory.api:app --port 8094

Open http://localhost:8094, press ⌖ (or pick a city). Drag to look around, scroll or pinch to zoom, click an object. Solar system flies out from your position to the planets; Sky flies back. URL parameters make views reproducible: ?lat=-23.55&lon=-46.63&t=2026-10-13T22:05:00Z&az=250&alt=16&fov=72 (view=system, tab=engine, panel=0).

docs.title: Languages
docs.text:
The interface is in English and Brazilian Portuguese (EN / PT in the top bar). The default follows the browser language; the choice is kept in the URL (#lang=pt) and in local storage. Every string the page shows comes from the message catalogues apps/observatory/observatory/static/i18n/en.json and pt.json (menus, panels, tooltips, check names, verdicts, units, API error messages); numbers and dates follow the locale (Intl.NumberFormat, Intl.DateTimeFormat, decimal comma in Portuguese). Constellations use their Portuguese names (pinneapple_physics.astro.stars.constellation_names, e.g. Cruzeiro do Sul, Escorpião); stars keep their IAU names; the Sun, Moon and planets are translated. Server errors carry a message code (X-Error-Code) so the page shows them in the visitor's language.

tests/test_observatory_i18n.py fails if a key is missing from one catalogue, if a placeholder differs, or if interface text is hard-coded in static/*.js or index.html (a lint over the string literals); the browser test apps/observatory/tests/e2e/i18n.spec.js switches to Portuguese, checks that the main panels have no English left and switches back (cd apps/observatory && npm ci && npx playwright test).

docs.title: Observing session
docs.text: The Observe tab reproduces an observing night. Plan: pick the Moon, a planet, a bright star or a Messier object and get its altitude curve for the next 24 h with the dark hours shaded, rise / transit / set, astronomical night, the Moon and the best window (air mass, Moon separation, sky brightness); a target that never rises from your place is flagged. Telescope: an 80 mm refractor, a 200 mm Newtonian, an 8" SCT, binoculars or your own aperture and focal length, with an eyepiece or a camera: magnification, true field, exit pupil, Dawes / Rayleigh resolution, limiting magnitude and image scale. Slew: an alt-azimuth or German equatorial GoTo mount moves at a realistic rate (trapezoidal profile per axis, horizon limit, meridian flip). Track: the eyepiece view stays on the target while time runs at 1x to 3600x; the field turns on an alt-az mount (field rotation, shown), stars dim and redden with air mass, the sky brightens with twilight and moonlight, seeing blurs the view. Weather: "Real sky" uses the Open-Meteo cloud forecast and clouds hide the view; "Perfect sky" removes the weather, so any target can be observed on any night. The session log keeps notes, snapshots and the conditions. Deep-sky fields use DSS2 colour cut-outs from CDS hips2fits (cached on the server and credited in the view); without network the field is drawn from the star catalogue. The physics is in pinneapple_physics.astro.observing, checked in tests/test_astro_observing.py: rise / transit / set of the Sun, Moon and three bright stars within a minute of Skyfield at São Paulo and Tromsø, air mass from Kasten & Young (1989), the optics formulas, and the field rotation against the parallactic angle.

docs.title: Space journey
docs.text: Journey (top bar, or "Fly there" on a Learn card) flies from your place on Earth to the selected planet, moon, the Sun or a star. You lift off from your latitude and longitude, leave the atmosphere and cross the Solar System with the planets where they are on the chosen date; stars are reached through interstellar space at their parallax distance, with the real neighbouring stars drawn in 3-D around the path. The speed control is logarithmic, and the scale markers (Moon distance, 1 au, heliopause, 1 light-year, nearest star) are announced as you pass them. The counters show the distance travelled and left, the light time, how long the trip would take walking, by airliner, at New Horizons' or Voyager 1's speed and at light speed, and the target's apparent size and magnitude as it grows. On arrival you can look around (drag) and the info card opens; at a star, "Look back home" turns you around and the Sun is a faint star of the right magnitude (about +0.5 from Alpha Centauri, +1.9 from Sirius). The geometry is in pinneapple_physics.astro.journey (plan, scene), checked in tests/test_astro_journey.py.

docs.title: Learn mode
docs.text: The Learn tab (and the end of the Object tab) shows an info card for the Sun, planets, Moon, dwarf planets, major moons, the brightest stars, the 88 constellations, the 110 Messier objects and the ISS, Hubble and Tiangong: what it is in one sentence, key numbers with everyday comparisons (size against the Earth, light time, length of day and year), how to see it tonight from your place, three to five curiosities, a short history and missions, and a short quiz for classrooms. Search works with names in English or Portuguese. Every number carries its source (numbered marks, with the list at the end of the card); the dataset is pinneapple_physics/astro/data/facts/ and the library pinneapple_physics.astro.facts (card, search, quiz, tonight, validate).

docs.title: What is computed where
docs.text: The server (apps/observatory/observatory/api.py) calls pinneapple_physics.astro for every position, event and analysis and returns samples a few minutes apart; the browser interpolates them, rotates the J2000 star catalogue with the server's precession-nutation matrix and the sidereal time, and draws (three.js r169, vendored with the library). Refraction and extinction of the stars are applied in the vertex shader with the same formulas as the library.

docs.title: Checking it
docs.text: pytest tests/test_astro_accuracy.py tests/test_observatory.py runs the accuracy checks (table) and every API endpoint offline (a local TLE file stands in for CelesTrak).

docs.title: PINNs, neural networks and ML in the app
docs.text:
Every model carries a trust card: its verdict, its checks against an independent reference, and a short "how this was computed, how much to trust it". The numbers are in the astronomy page.

  • Satellites → Orbit decay: a PINN integrates the drag decay of the ISS-like orbit through the NRLMSIS 2.0 thermosphere for the solar flux and geomagnetic activity you set, with a Monte-Carlo envelope of the inputs; it is compared with a Runge-Kutta integration and with SGP4's own drag model.
  • Analyses → Asteroids and close approaches: Apophis, Phaethon, Ceres and 67P from JPL SBDB elements, propagated in the field of the Sun, planets and Moon; the Apophis flyby of 13 April 2029 is reproduced within JPL's 3σ range. A PINN can be trained for the selected body (Kepler orbit plus a network for the planetary perturbations, about a minute) and is checked against the integrator. A learned propagator (one network for many near-Earth asteroids) is shown with its errors on unseen bodies and is rejected by its own gate.
  • Analyses → Space weather and aurora: Kp now and 3 h / 24 h ahead with calibrated 80 % intervals, and the chance of seeing the aurora overhead or low on the horizon at your geomagnetic latitude.
  • Analyses → Observing conditions: P(clear sky), cloud quantiles, transparency and a seeing proxy from the Open-Meteo ensemble (marked not verified until it is calibrated against observations).
  • Analyses → Stellar ML: the HR diagram clustered without labels, and the luminosity / spectral classes predicted from colour and absolute magnitude, cross-validated against the catalogue.
  • Analyses → Black hole: a thin accretion disc around a Schwarzschild black hole, traced along exact null geodesics and lensed in front of the part of the sky you are looking at (Doppler beaming on or off). The far side of the disc appears above and below the shadow, with the photon ring inside.

docs.title: Physics checks in CI
docs.text:
pinneapple check is a linter for physics. It reads simulation results and Physics-AI models and fails when they violate physics: conservation of mass, energy or momentum, the governing PDE, boundary and initial conditions, bounds, units, the training range of a model, a stored reference, or the integrity of the files. It works like ruff or pytest: zero configuration to start, readable output, exit codes, and SARIF/JUnit for CI. The GitHub Action in this repository turns a violation into a failed check with an annotation on the line that caused it.

The lid speed of a cavity case changed from 1 to 2 m/s in 0/U: the boundary condition, the stored reference and the wall rule fail, and the annotation sits on the movingWall entry. Rendered from the real output of pinneapple check examples/physics_check/fail.

docs.title: Add it to a repository in three lines
docs.text:
# .github/workflows/physics-check.yml (steps of a job with `security-events: write`)
- uses: actions/checkout@v4
- uses: PINNeAPPle-Labs/PINNeAPPle@main      # pin a tag or a commit SHA

and a pinneapple-check.toml at the root (or nothing: see zero configuration). A complete workflow is in examples/physics_check/workflow.yml.

Locally:

pip install "pinneapple[check]"
pinneapple check                 # or: python -m pinneapple.check

docs.title: What it checks
docs.text:
Target Read with Checks OpenFOAM case folder polyMesh, the latest time (and the one before, and 0), phi when written mass balance from the solver flux, divergence, momentum or heat residual with the case's own Gauss-linear operators, boundary values per patch, initial fields, wall velocity, bounds, units from dimensions .npz / .h5 on a grid 1-D coordinate arrays x, y, z, t and fields of shape (len(x), len(y), ...) second-order finite differences: residual, divergence, boundary balances over the box, conserved totals in time, boundary and initial values .vtu / .vtk, point tables (.csv, .npz, .h5) meshio, x, y, z columns; a point set on a lattice becomes a grid least-squares derivatives for residual and divergence; bounds and units .csv of quantities of interest name,value[,unit] rows, or one row with a column per quantity regression against a reference with relative or absolute tolerances Model: file.py:function any framework behind a NumPy function (N, n_inputs) -> (N, n_outputs) PDE residual and divergence by central differences at sampled points, balances on a grid over its domain, boundary and initial conditions, bounds, training range of the queries, reference points Model: .pt checkpoint + architecture (a pp.list_models() name) scanned first, then torch.load(weights_only=True); training range from metadata.domain_bounds the same, plus PC803 Model: zoo = "name" (a pp.zoo.list() name) the pre-trained, verified model; inputs, outputs and validity range from its model card the same; without a full domain, predictions are checked at the queries Model: hub = "org/name" pinneapple_hub.from_pretrained; training range from the model card the same Artefacts [integrity]: manifest, public key, signed globs; sha256 = ... on a target hashes, signatures, untracked files

Physics: incompressible-flow (div u = 0; du/dt + (u.grad)u + grad p/rho - nu lap u = 0, p kinematic unless rho is given), heat (rho_cp dT/dt = k lap T + q, or alpha for the diffusivity), elasticity (div sigma + f = 0, E and nu, plane strain in 2-D), conservation (dq/dt + div F = S, with flux = { q = "F" }).

Every number is relative, so one default tolerance works across units and scales: a residual is RMS(residual) / RMS(sum of the absolute terms), a balance is |net flow| / total absolute flow through the boundary, a boundary deviation is a fraction of the field scale. Defaults are in the table at the end; override per target.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
pinneapple-check.toml (or the same tables under [tool.pinneapple.check] in pyproject.toml; paths are relative to the file):

[check]
select = ["ALL"]                  # ruff-style prefixes: "PC1", "PC201"
ignore = ["PC203"]
fail-on = "error"                 # error | warning | never
baseline = ".pinneapple-check-baseline.json"
severity = { PC502 = "error" }    # change the level of a rule

[[result]]
name = "cavity"
path = "cases/cavity"             # OpenFOAM case
physics = "incompressible-flow"
parameters = { nu = "0.01 m2/s" } # a number (SI) or "<number> <unit>": the dimension is checked (PC504)
units = { U = "m/s", p = "m2/s2" }
ic = { U = [0, 0, 0] }
reference = { path = "reference/cavity.npz", fields = ["U"], rel-l2 = 1e-3 }
tolerances = { residual = 0.05 }
[result.bc.movingWall]            # a patch name; on grids "x=min", "y=max" or "x=0.5"
U = [1, 0, 0]

[[result]]
path = "fields/heat_plate.npz"
physics = "heat"
parameters = { k = "10 W/(m*K)", q = "1000 W/m3" }
[result.bc."x=max"]
T = "300 + 25*(1 - y**2)"          # an expression of x, y, z, t (numpy functions, pi)

[[result]]
path = "qoi/airfoil.csv"
[result.reference]
path = "reference/airfoil.csv"
qoi = { Cd = { rel = 0.02 }, Cl = { abs = 0.005 } }

[[model]]
name = "pinn"
path = "models/pinn.py:predict"
inputs = ["x", "y"]
outputs = ["u", "v", "p"]
physics = "incompressible-flow"
parameters = { nu = 0.025 }
domain = { x = [-0.5, 1.0], y = [-0.5, 1.5] }   # where to sample (default: train-range)
method = "E10"                                  # id in the method catalog (PC901)

[[model]]
name = "surrogate"
path = "models/surrogate.py:predict"
inputs = ["Re", "aoa"]
outputs = ["Cd"]
train-range = { Re = [1e5, 1e6], aoa = [0, 10] }
train-samples = "models/training_points.csv"    # for the data-gap rule PC602
queries = "models/queries.csv"                  # the inputs the model will be asked about

[integrity]
manifest = "models/manifest.json"   # python -m pinneapple_security manifest models -o models/manifest.json
public-key = "keys/release.pub.json"
signed = ["models/*.pt"]            # each needs a valid <file>.sig

Wrapping a model of another framework is two lines:

# models/pinn.py
def predict(X):                       # X: (N, 2) array of x, y
    return net(torch.as_tensor(X, dtype=torch.float32)).detach().numpy()   # (N, 3): u, v, p

docs.title: Zero configuration
docs.text: Without a configuration file, pinneapple check [paths] looks for OpenFOAM case folders and .vtu, .vtk, .npz, .h5 files, infers incompressible flow from U and p, and runs what needs no declaration: finite values, physical admissibility from field names (absolute temperature and density positive, alpha.* and mass fractions in [0, 1], k, epsilon, omega, nut non-negative), mass balance, divergence and wall velocity.

docs.title: Command line
docs.text:
pinneapple check [paths] [--config FILE] [--select PC1,PC201] [--ignore PC5] [--extend-select ...]
                 [--format text|json|sarif|junit|github|summary] [--output FILE]
                 [--sarif FILE] [--junit FILE] [--json FILE] [--summary FILE]
                 [--baseline FILE] [--write-baseline] [--no-baseline]
                 [--fail-on error|warning|never] [--exit-zero] [--show-passed] [--no-fixes]
                 [--list-rules] [--explain PC101] [--arena-cases [FILE ...]]

--arena-cases replays the regression cases of the validation arena: the stored escapes must still be rejected and the stored false alarms still accepted (without a file: the cases shipped with the library).

Exit codes: 0 nothing to report (warnings allowed with --fail-on error), 1 violations, 2 a configuration or usage error. Inside GitHub Actions the default format is github (annotations followed by the readable log).

examples/physics_check/fail/cases/cavity/5/U:432:1: PC201 [error] U on patch 'movingWall': max deviation from the declared (1 0 0) is 1 (0.623 of the field scale > 0.001); found e.g. (2 0 0)
  = help: Fix the boundary condition in the case (the patch is named in the message and the annotation points at its entry), or raise the boundary-loss weight of the model.
examples/physics_check/fail/models/queries.csv:6:1: PC601 [error] query 5 of examples/physics_check/fail/models/queries.csv is outside the training range of drag-surrogate: Re=2.50e+06 not in [1.00e+05, 1.00e+06]
  = help: Restrict the queries to the training range, retrain on a range that covers them, or route those queries to the solver (a fallback).

Found 27 errors and 7 warnings in 19 targets (97 checks passed).

Annotations point at the line that explains the violation: the patch entry in the OpenFOAM field file, the row of the queries file, the header of a CSV, the file that changed after its manifest, or the declaration of the target in pinneapple-check.toml.

docs.title: Adopting it on a repository with existing violations
docs.text:
pinneapple check --write-baseline          # records today's violations in .pinneapple-check-baseline.json

Commit the file and set baseline = ".pinneapple-check-baseline.json". Violations recorded there are reported as baselined and do not fail the job; a new one does. The fingerprint is (rule, target, subject), not the value, so a baselined violation that gets worse stays baselined: remove its entry once it is fixed.

docs.title: The GitHub Action
docs.text:
action.yml at the root of this repository is a composite action. Inputs:

Input Default paths . files or folders, separated by spaces config configuration file version pinneapple release from PyPI; empty installs the source of the action's own ref, so @v0.8.0 or @<sha> pins the checker python-version 3.11 torch false CPU torch, only to load .pt checkpoints select, ignore, fail-on, baseline, args as on the command line annotations true annotations on the changed lines sarif true upload to code scanning (security-events: write); a failed upload never fails the job sarif-category pinneapple-check one per job when the action runs several times summary true a table per target with its trust card in the job summary

Outputs: exit-code, errors, warnings, report (JSON with every check) and sarif-file. The pip cache is keyed on the version, and only the checker's dependencies are installed (NumPy, SciPy, pandas, meshio, h5py, cryptography; no torch unless asked), so a run takes well under a minute.

This repository runs the action on itself (.github/workflows/physics-check.yml): the passing fixtures must give no violation, and the failing fixtures must break exactly the rules listed in examples/physics_check/fail/expected.json.

docs.title: Evidence, not just a red cross
docs.text:
The JSON report (--json) groups the checks of each target by the six stages of the trust card used by pinneapple_lab (data and geometry, model, physical constraints, benchmark, uncertainty, decision): a stage is answered when its checks passed, failed, partial (warnings only) or open when nothing checked it. An open stage is reported as open, never as passed.

pinneapple_check.evidence.guardrail_checks(report, target) returns the checks in the form pinneapple_veriphysics.applicability.build_applicability_map(guardrail_checks=...) reads (pde_residual, conservation_*, reference_data_match, dimensional_analysis), so a CI run feeds the Decision Record directly.

What is reused rather than rewritten: the OpenFOAM, VTK and point-table readers and the face geometry of pinneapple_data.cae; units and quantity ranges from pinneapple_data.physical_units; the training envelope of pinneapple_physics.physics_audit (range and nearest-sample distance); field metrics from pinneapple_analysis.validation.field_metrics; the method catalog and its validated/tested status; pinneapple_security for manifests, Ed25519 signatures and pickle scanning. None of these imports torch, and the checker loads them without the package __init__ files that do, so it starts in a fraction of a second.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• The residual of stored fields carries the discretisation error: on OpenFOAM meshes the operators are the same Gauss-linear ones as the solver's, so a converged case gives about 1e-4; on coarse grids, near singular corners or with other schemes, raise residual for that target rather than globally.
  • Elasticity residuals are computed on grids, point clouds and models; on OpenFOAM meshes only the force balance (PC104) is planned, not implemented yet.
  • Decomposed OpenFOAM cases (processor*) are not reassembled: reconstruct first.
  • A model is checked where it is sampled (n-points, default 1024, fixed seed): a violation confined to a small region can be missed. Raise n-points for decisions that depend on it.
  • The out-of-range rule checks a box (and the distance to training samples when given), not the full shape of the training distribution.

docs.text:
pinneapple check --list-rules prints this table, pinneapple check --explain PC101 one entry.

The model's method is not validated in the method catalog

docs.title: PC001
docs.text:
unreadable-target (error). The file or folder named in the configuration does not exist, has an unsupported format, or failed to parse. Nothing else can be checked for this target, so this is always an error.

Fix: Check the path (relative to the configuration file) and the format: an OpenFOAM case folder, .vtu/.vtk, .npz, .h5/.hdf5, a .csv of quantities of interest, a Python callable file.py:function or a checkpoint.

docs.title: PC002
docs.text:
nothing-checked (warning). No rule could run on this target: no physics was declared or inferred, no bounds, no reference. A linter that checks nothing passes everything, so this is reported.

Fix: Declare physics = "incompressible-flow" | "heat" | "elasticity" | "conservation", bounds, boundary conditions or a reference for the target.

docs.title: PC101
docs.text:
mass-imbalance (error). For an incompressible (or steady) flow the volume flux entering the domain must leave it. The check sums the flux through every boundary face (from phi when the solver wrote it, else from the face velocity) or, for a model, integrates u.n over the faces of the domain box, and divides the net flux by the total absolute flux. A non-zero value means a leaking boundary condition, an unconverged run or a model that creates or destroys mass.

Fix: Look at the inlet/outlet patches named in the message; check that the run converged (residuals) and that the outlet is not a fixed-value velocity. For a PINN, add a mass-balance or divergence penalty, or use a divergence-free architecture (stream function).

docs.title: PC102
docs.text:
divergence (error). Incompressible flow requires div(u) = 0 in every cell. The check computes the discrete divergence (finite volume on OpenFOAM meshes, finite differences on grids, least squares on point clouds, central differences on a model) and reports its RMS relative to the RMS of the velocity gradients, a number between 0 and 1.

Fix: Converge the pressure-velocity coupling further (more correctors, tighter p tolerance). For a model, raise the weight of the continuity residual or sample more collocation points where the message says the divergence is largest.

docs.title: PC103
docs.text:
energy-imbalance (error). For steady conduction the conductive flux k dT/dn through the boundary plus the heat generated inside must be zero. The check reports the net heat flow relative to the total absolute boundary heat flow.

Fix: Check the thermal boundary conditions (a fixed temperature on all walls with a source has no steady solution only if the flux cannot leave), the source term and the conductivity; converge further.

docs.title: PC104
docs.text:
momentum-imbalance (error). For static elasticity the tractions on the boundary plus the body force must sum to zero (Newton's second law with no acceleration). The check reports the norm of the resultant relative to the total absolute traction.

Fix: A missing support, a load applied twice or wrong material constants. Check the declared Young's modulus and Poisson ratio and the displacement boundary conditions.

docs.title: PC105
docs.text:
conserved-total-drift (error). For a generic conservation law on a closed domain (or with the boundary flux declared) the integral of the conserved quantity must stay constant. The check compares the total at every stored time with the first one.

Fix: Use a conservative discretisation, reduce the time step, or declare the boundary flux column so the balance accounts for it.

docs.title: PC201
docs.text:
boundary-condition (error). The value of a field on a boundary patch (or a model's prediction on a boundary of its domain) differs from the value declared in the configuration by more than the tolerance (relative to the field scale).

Fix: Fix the boundary condition in the case (the patch is named in the message and the annotation points at its entry), or raise the boundary-loss weight of the model.

docs.title: PC202
docs.text:
initial-condition (error). At the first time (stored snapshot, or t = t0 for a model with a time input) the field must match the declared initial condition.

Fix: Check the initial field written by the pre-processing, or the initial-condition loss of the model.

docs.title: PC203
docs.text:
wall-velocity (warning). On a patch of type wall the fluid sticks to the wall (no-slip). A non-zero face velocity on a wall usually means a moving wall that was not declared, or a slip condition by mistake.

Fix: If the wall moves (a lid, a rotating part), declare its velocity under [result.bc.<patch>]; otherwise set noSlip on the patch.

docs.title: PC301
docs.text:
pde-residual (error). The governing equation of the declared physics is evaluated on the stored fields and its RMS residual is divided by the RMS of the sum of the absolute values of its terms: 0 means the equation holds exactly, 1 means the terms do not balance at all. Discretisation error makes it non-zero on coarse meshes, so the default tolerance is loose.

Fix: Converge the solver, refine the mesh where the residual is largest, or check the declared parameters (viscosity, conductivity, source) match the ones used in the run.

docs.title: PC302
docs.text:
model-residual (error). The model is evaluated at sampled interior points of its domain and the PDE residual is computed with central differences. Reported as the relative residual described for PC301.

Fix: Train longer, add collocation points where the residual is largest, or check that the declared parameters match the ones the model was trained with.

docs.title: PC303
docs.text:
metamorphic-relation (error). A declared metamorphic relation does not hold for the model's predictions: more of an input moves an output the wrong way (monotonic), a change that must not matter moves the output (invariant, e.g. a similarity group kept fixed), a mirrored input does not give the mirrored output (symmetric), or a linear model is not linear (superposition). These hold whatever the true answer is, so they test a surrogate where no reference solution exists. The worst sample found is reported as the counterexample (pinneapple_analysis.validation.metamorphic, guide: Metamorphic tests).

Fix: Look at the counterexample: a sign error, an input swapped or in the wrong unit, or a fit that is not constrained in that region. If the relation does not hold for the real physics there, narrow its box or remove it rather than loosening the tolerance.

docs.title: PC401
docs.text:
out-of-bounds (error). A value is outside the range declared under bounds in the configuration.

Fix: Check the solver limiters (e.g. MULES for a phase fraction), the time step, or the model's output activation (a sigmoid keeps a fraction in [0, 1]).

docs.title: PC402
docs.text:
unphysical-value (error). Some quantities have hard physical limits whatever the problem: absolute temperature and density are positive, phase and mass fractions lie in [0, 1], turbulent kinetic energy, dissipation and eddy viscosity are non-negative. The quantity is inferred from the field name (T, rho, alpha., Y, k, epsilon, omega, nut) and its unit.

Fix: Bound the solution (positivity-preserving schemes, bounded limiters, a softplus on the model output) or, if the name is misleading, declare bounds for the field explicitly.

docs.title: PC403
docs.text:
non-finite (error). NaN or Inf in a stored field or a model prediction. Every other check on that field is unreliable.

Fix: The run diverged or the model was evaluated outside its numeric range; inspect the time step and the residual history.

docs.title: PC451
docs.text:
dataset-physics (error). Samples of a dataset ([[dataset]]) differ from the solution of their own discrete problem (or their boundary values or flux balance are off), or rows break a relation declared between columns. A model trained on such data inherits the error, and model-level checks may never see it (NVIDIA/physicsnemo#2036: Darcy data generated with a wrongly scaled cross term). Guide: Dataset physics audit.

Fix: Regenerate the data with the documented equation and discretisation; the failing samples are listed in the evidence.

docs.title: PC452
docs.text:
dataset-diversity (error). The effective number of distinct samples (participation ratio of the principal components) collapses, or samples are exact or near copies of each other (NVIDIA/physicsnemo#2035: every Fourier coefficient of a permeability sample shared one value).

Fix: Check the sampler: independent random coefficients per mode and per sample, a fresh seed per sample.

docs.title: PC453
docs.text:
dataset-leakage (error). A test sample's nearest training sample is closer than a thousandth of the typical spacing between training samples: the held-out error measures memorisation, not generalisation.

Fix: Split before deduplicating, split by case or geometry rather than by row, and drop the flagged pairs.

docs.title: PC501
docs.text:
unit-mismatch (error). The unit written in the file (OpenFOAM dimensions, a CSV header T [degC], an HDF5 units attribute) does not match the unit declared in the configuration: either a different dimension (m/s versus Pa) or the same dimension on a different scale (degC versus K).

Fix: Convert the data, or correct the declared unit.

docs.title: PC502
docs.text:
unit-missing (warning). Neither the file nor the configuration gives the unit of a field that a physics check uses, so its magnitude cannot be checked against the parameters.

Fix: Declare it: units = { T = "K", U = "m/s" } under the target.

docs.title: PC503
docs.text:
implausible-magnitude (warning). The values are far outside the typical range of the quantity in the declared unit, which is the usual sign of a unit slip: temperatures around 20 declared in kelvin, pressures in bar declared in Pa.

Fix: Check which unit the data is really in and declare that one.

docs.title: PC504
docs.text:
parameter-unit (error). A parameter given with a unit (nu = "1e-5 m2/s") has a dimension different from the one the declared physics needs (kinematic viscosity, thermal conductivity, Young's modulus...).

Fix: Give the parameter in a unit of the right dimension; nu is kinematic (m2/s), mu dynamic (Pa s).

docs.title: PC601
docs.text:
out-of-range-query (error). At least one query (a row of the queries file) has an input outside the range the model was trained on. The training range comes from the configuration (train-range), the checkpoint metadata (domain_bounds) or the model card. A surrogate extrapolates silently: its answer there is not evidence.

Fix: Restrict the queries to the training range, retrain on a range that covers them, or route those queries to the solver (a fallback).

docs.title: PC602
docs.text:
sparse-training-region (warning). The query is inside the training box but far from every training sample (more than three typical spacings, on standardised inputs), so the model interpolates over a hole.

Fix: Add training samples near the reported query, or treat its answer as an extrapolation.

docs.title: PC701
docs.text:
field-regression (error). Relative L2 error between the field and the reference (same points, or the reference interpolated on them) is above the tolerance.

Fix: If the change is intended, regenerate the reference and commit it with the change; otherwise find the commit that moved the result.

docs.title: PC702
docs.text:
qoi-regression (error). A quantity of interest (drag, lift, a peak temperature...) differs from its reference value by more than its relative or absolute tolerance.

Fix: Same as PC701: update the reference deliberately, or fix the regression.

docs.title: PC703
docs.text:
reference-unusable (warning). The reference file is missing, unreadable, lacks the field, or has a shape that cannot be matched to the result.

Fix: Regenerate the reference with the same mesh/points and field names, or give fields to compare.

docs.title: PC704
docs.text:
spectral-bias (warning). Energy in the high-wavenumber band of the field differs from the reference's by more than the tolerance (E_pred / E_ref - 1 over the top third of the resolved shells). A smoothed field has a small relative L2 error and still misses the small scales that carry heat transfer, mixing or loads; added noise shows up as a positive bias. Computed on grid results with the same shape as the reference (pinneapple_analysis.validation.spectral). In the failing fixture fields/mixing_c.npz the field is blurred by one cell: relative L2 0.18 % (PC701 passes), high-band energy 0.5 % of the reference's.

Fix: Check the model's spectral bias (more Fourier modes, a finer output grid, a loss on gradients or spectra), or raise tolerances.hf-bias deliberately if the small scales do not matter for the use.

docs.title: PC801
docs.text:
hash-mismatch (error). The SHA-256 of a file differs from the one in the integrity manifest (or a listed file is missing): the artefact changed after it was recorded.

Fix: If the change is intended, rebuild the manifest (python -m pinneapple_security manifest <dir>) in the same commit; otherwise restore the file.

docs.title: PC802
docs.text:
bad-signature (error). The detached signature (<file>.sig) does not verify with the configured public key, or is missing when signatures are required.

Fix: Re-sign the artefact with the release key (python -m pinneapple_security sign), or check that the configured public key is the right one.

docs.title: PC803
docs.text:
unsafe-checkpoint (error). The pickle stream of the checkpoint imports callables outside the allow-list, so torch.load would run them. The checker does not load such a file.

Fix: Re-save the weights only (torch.save(model.state_dict(), ...)) or as safetensors.

docs.title: PC804
docs.text:
untracked-artefact (warning). A file in a folder covered by the manifest is not listed in it, so a change to it would go unnoticed.

Fix: Rebuild the manifest so it includes the file.

docs.title: PC901
docs.text:
unvalidated-method (warning). The method id declared for the model (method = "S12") has status tested or untested in the PINNeAPPle method catalog: no reference test checks it against a known solution.

Fix: Prefer a validated method for decisions, or add a reference test for this one.

docs.title: Default tolerances
docs.text: Key Default Used by mass 1e-3 PC101 divergence / model-divergence 1e-2 / 5e-2 PC102 (stored fields / model) energy 1e-2 PC103 momentum 1e-2 PC104 total-drift 1e-3 PC105 bc / ic 1e-3 / 1e-2 PC201 / PC202 wall-velocity 1e-6 PC203 residual / model-residual 5e-2 / 5e-2 PC301 / PC302 rel-l2 / qoi 1e-2 / 1e-2 PC701 / PC702 hf-bias 0.25 PC704 (|high-band energy ratio - 1|) fraction-slack 1e-6 PC402 (fractions)

docs.title: The fixtures
docs.text: examples/physics_check/ holds a passing and a failing case for every rule: real icoFoam runs (lid-driven cavity, channel; the failing cavity has the lid speed typed as 2 m/s), analytical fields with known physics (conduction with a source, a block under its own weight, a diffusing conserved quantity, a cooling plate, a VOF phase fraction) with one deliberate defect each, a stand-in PINN for Kovasznay flow (the failing one creates mass), a drag surrogate queried out of range and in a gap of its data, an unsafe checkpoint and a tampered artefact. python examples/physics_check/generate.py rebuilds them.

docs.title: Physics Design Optimizer (app, day 23)
docs.text:
Optimise parametric designs with explicit objectives, constraints and physics models, gradient-aware, and compare gradient, evolutionary and Bayesian methods on the same problem and budget. Live at https://design.pinneapple.org; source in apps/physics_design.

Designs plate-fin heat sink (six geometry parameters; neural surrogate of the FVM engine, differentiable; the FVM engine verifies), CST airfoil (six shape weights and the angle of attack; zoo ensemble trained on OpenFOAM runs) Methods gradient through autograd, SLSQP with finite differences, NSGA-II, differential evolution, Bayesian optimisation, Latin-hypercube baseline; same budget and seeds for each Output per method: evaluations, wall time, hypervolume, evaluations to 95 % of the best, converged or still improving; Pareto fronts and convergence curves; candidates from the best front over all methods with their verification status, margins and geometry; STL / STEP / CSV

The same comparison in Python:

from pinneapple_design.design_optimizer import compare_methods, presets

problem = presets.heatsink_problem("surrogate", objectives=("mass_g", "pressure_drop_pa"))
cmp = compare_methods(problem, ["gradient", "nsga2", "bayesian", "random"], budget=80, seeds=(0, 1))
print(cmp.table())

Limits. Gradients are those of the surrogate; every candidate is verified like any other. Airfoil candidates stay "only surrogate" (no CFD in the app). One seed does not rank methods: use several.

docs.title: Detect false data injection with physics residuals
docs.text:
An attacker who rewrites a sensor stream in a plant keeps every value plausible on its own and close to its own history. That is exactly what a purely data-driven detector learns, so it is what such a detector checks. What the attacker cannot keep without a model of the plant is the physics that ties several sensors together: a tank level must integrate the measured in- and outflows, a valve passes q = sqrt(a + b * dh) for the head across it.

pinneapple_security.cps turns those laws into residual channels, identifies their constants from trusted data (a grey-box twin: no hand-tuned coefficients), and raises alarms with a per-channel CUSUM calibrated to a false-alarm budget. It is a defensive tool: it reads sensor data and reports which balance broke.

docs.title: The three-tank example
docs.text:
reservoir --pump Fp--> T1 --valve F12--> T2 --valve F23--> T3 --demand Fd--> consumers

from pinneapple_security.cps import FlowLaw, MassBalance, PhysicsResidualDetector, episode_metrics
from pinneapple_security.cps_bench import inject, simulate_three_tank

train = simulate_three_tank(7, seed=0)            # dict of sensor columns, one sample per minute
calib = simulate_three_tank(7, seed=1)            # clean data the detector does not fit on
test = simulate_three_tank(10, seed=2)

det = PhysicsResidualDetector(components=[
    MassBalance("h1", ["Fp"], ["F12"], dt=60, window=1),   # area identified by least squares
    MassBalance("h2", ["F12"], ["F23"], dt=60, window=1),
    MassBalance("h3", ["F23"], ["Fd"], dt=60, window=1),
    FlowLaw("F12", "h1", "h2", midpoint=True),             # q^2 = a + b (h1 - h2), a and b identified
    FlowLaw("F23", "h2", "h3", midpoint=True),
]).fit(train)
det.calibrate(calib, false_alarms_per_day=1.0)

attacked = inject(test, "bias", [(3000, 3240)])            # F12 meter reads 4 % high for four hours
out = det.detect(attacked)
out["first_alarm"], out["channels"][:3]                    # time of the first alarm, balances blamed
episode_metrics(out["alarms"], [(3000, 3240)], len(test["h1"]))

Your own plant needs only the column names and the laws that hold between them. Any object with name, fit(D) and residual(D) -> array is a component, so an energy balance of a heat exchanger, a pump curve or a state-estimation residual of a power network plugs in the same way.

docs.title: Choices that matter
docs.text:
• window=1 for storage balances when the flow meters report averages over the sample interval: the residual is then white noise, which is what the CUSUM assumes. Longer windows reduce level noise but make the residual autocorrelated, and the calibrated threshold grows.
  • midpoint=True for flow laws with averaged flows and levels read at the start of the interval. Without it the law is evaluated at the wrong head and the residual carries a bias that changes with the operating point.
  • Calibrate on clean data the detector was not fitted on, at least as long as the attack episodes you care about. calibrate bisects the threshold to meet the budget exactly on that trace.

docs.title: Benchmark: physics against data-driven detectors
docs.text:
python examples/security/02_physics_residual_fdi.py --seeds 0 1 2 fits four detectors on a trusted week, calibrates each to one false alarm per day on another clean week, then injects six attacks in 20 four-hour episodes of a ten-day test trace. The same CUSUM alarm rule is used for every detector, so the comparison measures the residuals, not the alarm logic. Baselines: a linear autoregressive twin of all sensors (three lags, ridge), PCA of sensors and increments (Q statistic), and an isolation forest.

Mean of three seeds. AUC is episode-level (largest statistic in each attack episode against every clean window of the same length); "det" is the fraction of episodes detected, "delay" the median delay in minutes, "loc" the fraction of detections whose blamed channel contains the attacked sensor.

Nominal operating regime (false alarms per day on clean test data: physics 0.63, AR twin 0.63, PCA 0.80, isolation forest 0.50)

attack physics AUC / det / delay / loc AR twin PCA isolation forest bias (F12 +4 %) 1.000 / 1.00 / 8 / 0.98 1.000 / 1.00 / 16 / 0.03 0.490 / 0.10 / 122 0.497 / 0.03 / 152 ramp (h2, 0 → 8 cm) 1.000 / 1.00 / 108 / 0.93 1.000 / 1.00 / 82 / 0.57 0.497 / 0.10 / 119 0.504 / 0.05 / 148 stuck (h3) 1.000 / 0.98 / 9 / 0.93 1.000 / 0.98 / 10 / 0.76 0.815 / 0.67 / 89 0.368 / 0.03 / 202 delayed (F23, 24 h old) 1.000 / 0.97 / 1 / 1.00 0.994 / 0.90 / 3 / 1.00 0.877 / 0.77 / 51 0.592 / 0.10 / 148 scaling (Fd −8 %) 1.000 / 1.00 / 4 / 0.90 1.000 / 1.00 / 6 / 0.07 0.632 / 0.25 / 137 0.499 / 0.08 / 144 coordinated replay 0.986 / 0.97 / 0 / – 0.990 / 0.97 / 0 / – 0.496 / 0.13 / 96 0.463 / 0.05 / 94

Shifted operating regime (25 % more demand, pump band 1.4–2.2 m instead of 1.0–2.5 m; nothing refitted). False alarms per day on clean test data: physics 0.47, AR twin 84.4, PCA 32.0, isolation forest 1.07.

attack physics AUC / det / delay / loc AR twin AUC PCA AUC isolation forest AUC bias 1.000 / 1.00 / 6 / 0.98 0.670 0.562 0.454 ramp 1.000 / 1.00 / 128 / 0.95 0.733 0.560 0.439 stuck 1.000 / 0.90 / 16 / 0.71 0.697 0.689 0.339 delayed 1.000 / 0.83 / 5 / 0.77 0.552 0.662 0.521 scaling 1.000 / 1.00 / 4 / 0.70 0.669 0.611 0.431 coordinated replay 0.901 / 0.83 / 0 / – 0.538 0.551 0.480

What the numbers say:

  • In the regime it was trained on, a good data-driven twin (the AR model) detects as well as the physics: both reach AUC 1.0. Physics is faster on the bias (8 vs 16 min) and slower on the slow level ramp (108 vs 82 min: a level drift barely moves a storage balance until the valve laws see it), and it points at the right sensor far more often (0.98 vs 0.03 for the bias, 0.90 vs 0.07 for metering fraud).
  • When the plant moves to an operating point the data never covered, the data-driven detectors flood the operator (84 and 32 false alarms per day) while the physics residuals stay calibrated (0.47 per day) and keep AUC 1.0. This is the practical argument for physics: plants change set-points, seasons and demand far more often than anyone refits a detector.
  • The isolation forest and PCA, which only look at the joint distribution of the readings, miss most attacks that keep values in range.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Coordinated replay of every sensor is physically consistent. Both residual detectors catch it here only because the splice from the live to the replayed recording is a discontinuity (delay 0). An attacker who aligns the splice, or one who knows the plant model and injects consistent data (a stealthy attack in the sense of Liu, Ning and Reiter 2009), is invisible to any residual test. Pair the detector with anomaly.replay_score, with signed data paths (pinneapple_security.signing) and with physical watermarking where the control loop allows it.
  • The benchmark is simulated (seeded, reproducible). Public ICS datasets either need a signed request (SWaT, WADI) or were not reachable when this was written; an adapter for BATADAL is on the roadmap.
  • Attacks rewrite the reported readings only; the controller here acts on the true T1 level, so no attack changes the physical trajectory.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• E. S. Page, "Continuous inspection schemes", Biometrika 41 (1954).
  • Y. Liu, P. Ning, M. K. Reiter, "False data injection attacks against state estimation in electric power grids", ACM CCS 2009.
  • A. A. Cárdenas et al., "Attacks against process control systems: risk assessment, detection, and response", ASIACCS 2011.
  • D. I. Urbina et al., "Limiting the impact of stealthy attacks on industrial control systems", ACM CCS 2016.
  • J. Giraldo et al., "A survey of physics-based attack detection in cyber-physical systems", ACM Computing Surveys 51(4) (2018).
  • R. Taormina et al., "The battle of the attack detection algorithms (BATADAL)", J. Water Resour. Plann. Manage. 144(8) (2018).

docs.title: PhysicsNeMo trains, PINNeAPPle says when to trust
docs.text:
PhysicsNeMo trains the models. PINNeAPPle checks whether their predictions can be trusted, without the reference solution. The two complement each other: nothing below retrains or replaces a PhysicsNeMo model. The example is examples/vs_physicsnemo/07_physicsnemo_trains_pinneapple_checks.

The animated version alternates the two exported samples of each regime: physicsnemo_darcy_trust.gif.

docs.title: Where each model works, and why
docs.text:
The orange maps show where each prediction errs, estimated from its PDE residual alone, with no reference: - estimated_error: the error of u; - estimated_flux_error: the error of the flux a grad u.

The badges under each prediction say which use it can serve (use_verdicts, limits fixed a priori): - interior field: values of u at least 8 cells from the walls, OK if the estimated interior error is ≤ 5 %; - walls & fluxes: values and gradients next to the walls and boundary flow rates, OK if the estimated error in the 2 cells next to the walls is ≤ 5 % and the flux balance is ≤ 2 %; - inputs: the coefficient inside the training envelope; - CI: what pinneapple check returns for that prediction.

Regime Model interior error, estimated / true (median) wall-band error, estimated / true interior field OK walls & fluxes OK inputs as in training test set FNO 2.3 % / 1.3 % 32 % / 19 % 99 % of samples 0 % 95 % test set MeshGraphNet 22 % / 15 % 32 % / 23 % 0 % 0 % 95 % contrast FNO 85 % / 41 % 392 % / 65 % 0 % 0 % 0 % contrast MeshGraphNet 688 % / 77 % 529 % / 81 % 0 % 0 % 0 % length scale ÷3 FNO 3.1 % / 1.6 % 34 % / 21 % 94 % 0 % 61 % length scale ÷3 MeshGraphNet 21 % / 15 % 37 % / 28 % 0 % 0 % 61 %
  • FNO: use it for the field away from the walls, not for wall gradients or boundary fluxes. Its error is about 1 % in the interior and about 20 % in the 2 cells next to the walls. Its flux also errs along the jumps of a. The net outflow it implies is off by 14 % (median) against the reference. This holds for the shorter length scale too: the interior is still about 2 %, although 39 % of those coefficients are outside the training envelope.
  • MeshGraphNet: not usable at this budget, for fields or for fluxes. Its error is spread over the whole domain, and its flux errs along every jump of a. In the same CPU hour it did 3.7 epochs (the FNO did 41), and its 15 message-passing steps reach 15 cells of a 128-cell grid, which is little for an elliptic problem.
  • Contrast {1, 20}: neither model. The inputs are outside training, and the error is large everywhere.

How much to trust the estimate. It is not a certificate: - It tracks the true error map; correlation 0.79 (FNO) and 0.85 (MeshGraphNet) on the test set. - It over-estimates by 1.4 to 2.7× (the certified bounds below are the guarantee). - Its use verdicts agree with the same verdicts computed from the true error on 94 to 100 % of the samples in every regime. Every disagreement is conservative: 6 % of the FNO's length-scale samples, and 1 % of its test samples, are called "not OK" in the interior although they are.

docs.title: Set-up
docs.text: Problem -div(a grad u) = 1 on the unit square, u = 0 on the boundary, a ∈ {3, 12} (Li et al. 2021) Data zoo dataset darcy_2d_li2021: 1000 train / 200 test pairs on 128 × 128 cells, each solved on 512² and averaged Models PhysicsNeMo 2.2.2 FNO (4 layers, 12 modes, width 32, 2.37 M parameters) and MeshGraphNet on the 128 × 128 grid graph (15 message-passing steps, hidden 32, 0.15 M parameters; PyTorch Geometric) Budget ComputeBudget(wall_s=3600) each, 4 CPU threads (Xeon 2.8 GHz), Adam, cosine learning rate, relative L2 loss Training reached FNO 5144 steps = 41 epochs (train loss 0.012); MeshGraphNet 1828 steps = 3.7 epochs (train loss 0.15) Regimes test split (100 samples for calibration, 100 for evaluation); contrast a ∈ {1, 20}; length scale 3× shorter (tau = 9), 100 samples each, solved with the same reference solver (operator_datasets.darcy_set) Time data 4 min, training 2 × 60 min, evaluation 5 min, checks 2 ms per sample

docs.title: The checks (no reference solution)
docs.text:
pinneapple_physics.darcy_checks uses the reference solver's own discretisation: cell-centred finite volumes, harmonic-mean faces and half-cell Dirichlet faces. The solver's solution passes every check to round-off.

Check What it measures energy bound residual_error_bound: ‖r‖ in the dual norm of the constant-coefficient operator (one fast sine transform), over √min a and ‖u‖_A. A guaranteed upper bound on the relative energy-norm error, i.e. the error of the flux field a grad u, against the discrete solution. L2 bound residual_l2_bound: the same certificate through the discrete Poincaré inequality. A guaranteed upper bound on the relative L2 error of u itself. boundary condition RMS of u extrapolated to the boundary, over max |u| flux balance |net outward flux − ∫f| / ∫f positivity most negative u / max |u| (maximum principle) inputs a inside the training envelope: values, contrast, high fraction, interface density (CoefficientEnvelope)

Use profiles (PROFILES). The limits are the library's fixed engineering tolerances, grouped by the quantity a use depends on, each with its reason in the code. None was chosen from a model's values.

Profile For Limits (reason) fields maps and point values of u L2 bound ≤ 0.05 (the 5 % the library applies to a reference comparison); u = 0 ≤ 0.02 (Dirichlet tolerance of pp.trust_card); positivity ≤ 0.01 (its max-principle tolerance) fluxes boundary flow rates, wall gradients, Darcy velocity energy bound ≤ 0.10; flux balance ≤ 0.02 (the reference solver reaches 0.01)

Each profile verdict is over the batch (90th percentile of each metric), with the graded ratio value / limit of the worst metric: 1 is at the limit. vs validation (calibrate_tolerances) compares the same metrics with the model's own 99th percentiles on the 100 held-out in-distribution calibration inputs. Only inputs are needed, never labels. This layer is a drift monitor: it says whether the model is less physical here than where it was validated. inputs is the envelope check.

docs.title: Certified checks: use profiles (strict)
docs.text:
Regime Model rel. L2 (median) fields: verdict, ratio (worst metric value / limit) fluxes: verdict, ratio (worst metric value / limit) vs validation inputs test set FNO 1.4 % REJECT, 9.5× (L2 bound 0.48 / 0.05) REJECT, 18× (flux 0.36 / 0.02) APPROVED APPROVED test set MeshGraphNet 15.3 % REJECT, 44× (L2 bound 2.2 / 0.05) REJECT, 11× (energy bound 1.07 / 0.10) APPROVED APPROVED contrast FNO 40.9 % REJECT, 211× REJECT, 148× (flux 2.95) REJECT REJECT contrast MeshGraphNet 76.8 % REJECT, 467× REJECT, 27× (energy bound 2.69) REJECT REJECT length scale ÷3 FNO 1.8 % REJECT, 12× REJECT, 20× (flux 0.40) REJECT (marginal) REJECT (39 % outside) length scale ÷3 MeshGraphNet 15.0 % REJECT, 53× REJECT, 12× (flux 0.23) REJECT (marginal) REJECT (39 % outside) test set reference solver — APPROVED, 0.71× APPROVED, 0.48× — — contrast reference solver — REJECT, 4.0× APPROVED, 0.90× — —

The profiles judge the whole field with guaranteed bounds, so they are strict. They answer "can this prediction be certified for this use as a whole?"; the section above answers "where can it be used?". What this shows:

  1. Neither model meets the engineering limits of either profile at this 60-minute CPU budget. The physics layer does not separate the two models by verdict; it grades them. On fields the FNO is 4.6× closer (9.5× against 44× the limit). On fluxes the MeshGraphNet is 1.7× closer (11× against 18×): its flux balance (0.21) is better than the FNO's (0.36), although its L2 error is 10× larger.
  2. The FNO is the better model at equal budget by error. On CPU it does 11× more epochs per hour (41 against 3.7) and ends with a 10× smaller test error. The MeshGraphNet is undertrained. With 15 message-passing steps it also sees at most 15 cells in each direction on a 128-cell grid, which is little for an elliptic problem.
  3. A 1.4 % L2 error can still have a 22 % flux error. The FNO's predicted net outflow differs from the reference solver's by 22 % (median over the first 40 test samples, 42 % at p90). Its relative error in the two cells next to the walls is 19 %, against 1.7 % inside. Its true energy-norm error is 18 %, and the bound gives 29 %. 58 % of its test predictions go below −1 % of their maximum near the walls. The fluxes profile rejects it for a reason the reference confirms.
  4. The fields certificate is conservative. The certified L2 bound is about 30× the FNO's true L2 error (median 0.41 against 0.014) and 12× the MeshGraphNet's. For the contrast regime (min a = 1) even the reference solver's own solution fails it (4× the limit). A field-map use therefore cannot be approved by this certificate alone at these limits. The energy bound is much tighter (1.7× the true energy error for the FNO).
  5. Out of distribution, the label-free checks see the degradation. For contrast {1, 20} the FNO's ratios grow from 9.5× / 18× to 211× / 148×, while its error goes from 1.4 % to 41 %. The drift and input layers reject, for both models.
  6. A shorter length scale degrades the models moderately, and the drift layer flags it only just. The true energy-norm error rises by about 25 % for both models (FNO 0.167 → 0.208, MeshGraphNet 0.86 → 1.09). The FNO's L2 error rises from 1.4 % to 1.8 %; the MeshGraphNet's does not change. The drift monitor fails on the residual bound for 11 % (FNO) and 34 % (MeshGraphNet) of the samples, so the batch verdict is a marginal REJECT. The input envelope flags 39 % of these coefficients (interface density), a conservative alarm given how little the FNO degrades.
  7. Cost. On this CPU the reference finite-volume solve at 128² takes 0.07 s. FNO inference takes 0.037 s per sample and MeshGraphNet 0.55 s. For a 2-D problem this size the surrogates' speed advantage is small; the case is here to show the trust layer, not to argue for surrogates.

docs.title: In CI: pinneapple check and the GitHub Action
docs.text:
run.py evaluate exports two predictions per model and regime (check/predictions/) and the configuration (check/pinneapple-check.toml, written with darcy_checks.check_config_entry). Each target declares: - physics = "darcy"; - bounds and envelope of a: the training coefficients (CoefficientEnvelope.to_check_config); - as tolerances, its model's validated limits.

pinneapple check runs darcy_checks.sample_checks on each prediction: PC301 (energy and L2 bounds), PC101 (flux), PC201 (u = 0), PC402 (positivity), PC401 (envelope). The verdicts shown in the figure come from the same function, on the same files.
