    ablations={"airfoil": {"pinn": {"lr1e-3": {"lr": 1e-3}, "lbfgs": {"lbfgs": 0.3}}}})   # changes to the best config

budget_study trains the best configuration again at each listed budget (seed 0, on the problem's study instances) and adds those points to the seed-0 runs of budget_levels: a table per instance and figures/budget_study.png. ablations trains the best configuration with each change at the full budget on the problem's audit instance and puts it next to the unchanged run (the Setup audit table). Both only add jobs: adding budgets, problems, methods or variants to them reuses an existing out_dir; changing or removing an entry is refused like any other configuration change (it would reinterpret cached runs).

docs.title: Example: what the gates and the advisor said on PINNeAPPle-Benchmark experiment 09
docs.text:
Experiment 09 is five problems and seven methods through pp.benchmark. From its report:

  • error [airfoil/pinn_rans] Did not converge: the error is no better than a trivial prediction. Evidence: mean velocity rel. L2 on the held-out runs = 0.96 (>= 0.9). Suggestion: check the nondimensionalisation, the loss weights and the collocation density near walls and leading edges; consider more budget or a formulation with fewer stiff terms. With the training gate "no divergence" failing in 2 of its 29 runs, the row is INVALID. The budget study (budget_study: 1 h, 4 h) and the setup audit (ablations: learning rate, Adam -> L-BFGS) show neither more compute nor those settings help: the PINN collapsed to the zero-flow solution of its own equations.
  • warning [airfoil/mgn] Still improving at the full budget: velocity rel. L2 0.368 at 1/3 of the budget, 0.169 at the full one (54 % lower for 3x). Edit: problem_budgets.airfoil.wall_s: 900 -> 2700.
  • warning [darcy] The OOD set is not clearly outside the training data: 9 % of the OOD inputs outside the training distribution (threshold 50 %), 1 of 100 outside the applicability envelope. Suggestion: move the OOD inputs further out. (Its OOD column is read as a second test set.)
  • The setup audit of the potential-flow PINN found that wall and Kutta weights of 1 instead of 10 lower its velocity error from 0.81 to 0.51: a wider search would have helped it.

The gates also caught problems in the benchmark itself before it was published (a preflight that did not know freestreamPressure, a y+ estimate fed the wrong argument, a convergence metric a potential-flow model fails by construction); each was fixed with a test.

docs.title: Your own problem or method
docs.text:
Wrap your arrays (inputs and outputs on a grid) and FNO and DeepONet apply at once; pass pinn_setup to add PINNs:

prob = pp.benchmark.ArrayProblem("my_flow", train=(X_tr, Y_tr), val=(X_va, Y_va), test=(X_te, Y_te),
                                 ood=(X_ood, Y_ood), data_cost_s=3600.0)
pp.benchmark.run(problems=[prob], methods=["fno", "deeponet"], budget=pp.ComputeBudget(wall_s=120), out_dir="r")

Or register new ones (they are then usable by id, in YAML and in parallel workers):

@pp.benchmark.register_method("my_net")
class MyNet(pp.benchmark.Method):
    title = "My net"
    def supports(self, problem): return isinstance(problem, pp.benchmark.FieldOperatorProblem)
    def space(self, problem): return {"lr": [1e-3, 3e-3], "width": [64, 128]}
    def train(self, problem, prepared, cfg, seed, budget, final=True, **job):
        ...  # train under `budget` with pinneapple_analysis.cost.train_within_budget; return a result dict
    def architecture_checks(self, problem, prepared, cfg): ...  # your gates (shapes, overfit, ...)

@pp.benchmark.register_problem("my_problem")
class MyProblem(pp.benchmark.FieldOperatorProblem):
    def generate(self, split, n, n_workers): ...   # (inputs, outputs, solver core-seconds)
    def verify_solver(self): ...                   # checks of your solver against a known answer

The built-in problems: burgers, darcy, navier_stokes (the operator-learning standards), airfoil (the aero app's RANS airfoil; needs OpenFOAM), inverse_heat (h from sensors). Methods: pinn, fno, deeponet, mgn, mlp, mlp_fields, pinn_rans. See Choosing a method for what the published benchmark found.

docs.title: Choose a model by the scale of the question
docs.text: This guide shows how to make an adaptive ensemble respect scales: declare what each model resolves, ask each question at a scale, check closures, and let the ensemble escalate to a finer model when needed. The concepts are in Multiscale ensembles: scales, filters and closures.

docs.title: 1. Declare the scales of every model
docs.text:
from math import pi
from pinneapple_physics.multiscale import Filter, ScaleProfile

L, h = 2 * pi, 2 * pi / 64
profiles = [
    ScaleProfile("fno", Filter("gaussian", 2 * h), h, re_range=(150, 300), fidelity=0),         # surrogate
    ScaleProfile("les", Filter("sharp", pi / 16), L / 48, closure="dynamic Smagorinsky", fidelity=1),
    ScaleProfile("dns", Filter("sharp", 0.0), L / 128, re_range=(0, 6000), fidelity=2),          # resolved
]

Declare the filter the model's output actually carries:

  • a surrogate trained on Gaussian-filtered data carries that Gaussian;
  • a dealiased spectral LES on n points carries a sharp cut-off at k = n/3;
  • a resolved solver carries no filter.

docs.title: 2. Ask each question at a scale
docs.text:
from pinneapple_physics.multiscale import ScaleQuery, ScaleAwareRouter

router = ScaleAwareRouter(profiles, query_fn=lambda case: ScaleQuery(case["filter"], re=case["re"]))
print(router.route(ScaleQuery(Filter("sharp", h), re=3000)))     # only the DNS resolves this
print(router.route(ScaleQuery(Filter("gaussian", 8 * h), re=200)))  # the surrogate is enough

docs.title: 3. Bring every output to the requested filter
docs.text: Use refilter(output, profile.filter, query.filter), not apply_filter(output, query.filter). Filtering an already-filtered output again gives a wider filter than the one asked for. refilter applies only the part of the requested filter that the model's own filter has not applied yet.

docs.title: 4. Check closures without a reference
docs.text:
from pinneapple_physics.multiscale import closure_health, DynamicSmagorinsky, VorticityNS2D

h = closure_health(w_les, w0_les, kc=16, closure=DynamicSmagorinsky(), solver=VorticityNS2D(48, nu))
h.ok, h.reasons      # enstrophy growth, spectral pile-up or collapse, Germano-identity error

docs.title: 5. Put it together
docs.text:
from pinneapple_physics.ensemble import PhysicsEnsemble

ens = PhysicsEnsemble(experts, mode="select", router=router,
                      prediction_checks={"les": lambda pred, case: les_health(case)},
                      error_tolerance=0.25, error_context=lambda case: case["filter"])
out = ens.predict(case)
out["active"], out["failed_checks"], out["escalated_by_checks"]

For every case the ensemble:

  • uses the lowest fidelity rung that resolves the requested scale;
  • skips models whose checks fail;
  • moves up a rung when the models on the current rung last missed the tolerance at this scale.

examples/physics_ensemble/multiscale_turbulence.py runs the whole comparison on 2-D turbulence.

docs.title: Science by area (pp.science)
docs.text:
pinneapple_science (pp.science) organises PINNeAPPle by area of science. Every experiment is a small, self-checking study: it computes a quantity by a numerical route (a field solution, a quadrature, a time integration, a fit to noisy readings) and compares it with a cited reference, in one or more dimensions. The atlas maps every area the module will cover, says which are available, which the rest of the library already covers in part, and which are planned, and points to that code instead of copying it.

import pinneapple as pp

pp.science.atlas()                                     # every area and subarea, with its status and pointers
pp.science.experiments(area="electromagnetism", dim="3D+t")
r = pp.science.run("em.faraday_induction")             # a magnet falling through a loop, 3-D in time
print(r)                                               # computed vs reference, physics checks, trust decision
r.save("out/faraday")                                  # result.json, figures, the animation (MP4 and GIF)

python -m pinneapple_science atlas --html atlas.html --check     # the atlas page; every pointer validated
python -m pinneapple_science list --dim 2D
python -m pinneapple_science run em.hall_effect
python -m pinneapple_science report all                          # rewrites examples/science/ (manifests, seals)

Flow Studio: node science.run (choose the experiment and the dimension) and science.atlas. Hub: the two nodes, the pp.science API and recipe, and one example entry per experiment folder (with its Lab seal), under Verification and convergence. Agents: the row and the example in AGENTS.md.

docs.title: What every experiment declares
docs.text:
field values area an atlas area id, e.g. physics.electromagnetism level academic: didactic, checked against a textbook value; research: configurable, with convergence and uncertainty kind theory: a numerical or symbolic derivation checked against a closed form, a published value or a limit; practice: a virtual bench with instruments (noise, calibration error, resolution) and a fit with its uncertainty dims 0D (lumped elements, no spatial coordinate), 1D, 2D, 3D, 3D+t (three space dimensions and time). The same experiment runs in every dimension its physics allows.

Every result carries:

  • comparisons with references (closed_form, published, codata, limit, conservation, convergence or, for a bench, ground_truth), each with its source, the computed and reference values, the measured error and the tolerance;
  • physics checks (conservation, residuals of Maxwell's equations with pp.maxwell, convergence order, symmetry);
  • the trust report (pinneapple_analysis.trust.TrustReport): a failed reference comparison is critical (REJECT), any other failed check gives REVIEW;
  • figures and, for 3D+t, an animation of the 3-D field in time;
  • the Lab manifest experiment.json and the Lab seal stamped on the figures (python -m pinneapple_science report).

No number is typed in: values are computed by the run; references carry their citation.

docs.title: Electromagnetism (available)
docs.text:
Built on pp.em (pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics: statics, FDTD, Mie, media, waves) and pp.maxwell (pinneapple_physics.maxwell_checks). The committed results, with every comparison, are in examples/science/; each experiment folder has its README with the tables and sealed figures.

experiment dims what is computed reference em.coulomb_superposition 3D, 2D a charged ring and two finite line charges as sums of point charges ring potential (elliptic integral, Jackson 3.3); finite line (Griffiths ex. 2.2) em.gauss_law 3D, 2D flux through a cube / square by Gauss-Legendre quadrature; div E residual of a charge cloud Q_enc / eps0; pp.maxwell.gauss_electric em.parallel_plate_capacitor 2D, 3D C from the field energy of a finite-volume solution, Richardson-extrapolated Palmer (1937) strips; Kirchhoff (1877) discs; 3-D Cartesian vs axisymmetric em.biot_savart 3D wire (midpoint rule), loop (polygon), 400-turn helix Griffiths 5.37, loop elliptic integrals, finite solenoid em.ampere_law 2D, 3D circulation of B from a FV solution of lap A = -mu0 J; paths linking a square loop once, twice, never mu0 I_enc x linking number em.faraday_induction 3D+t flux of a falling magnet's field through a loop (Stokes, oint A.dl), EMF = -dPhi/dt; animation Maxwell's coaxial-circle formula; free-fall time of the sign change em.circuits_rc_rl_rlc 0D step responses by ODE integration; tau, omega_d, alpha measured from the waveforms RC, L/R, sqrt(1/LC - (R/2L)^2), R/2L; energy balance em.hall_effect 2D Hall bar with the Drude conductivity tensor; Hall coefficient at mid-length; geometric factor vs L/W R_H = 1/(n q) em.dipole_radiation 3D, 3D+t Poynting flux through spheres from kr = 0.3 to 30; energy per period from the real fields; 4-D Maxwell residuals; animation eta k^2 abs(I l)^2 / (12 pi), D = 1.5 em.lossy_plane_wave 1D FDTD in a conducting dielectric; alpha and beta fitted from the DFT field gamma = sqrt(j omega mu (sigma + j omega eps)) em.fresnel_snell 2D Bloch-periodic FDTD at oblique incidence; abs(r) for s and p; Brewster; transmitted angle from the phase gradient Fresnel, Brewster, Snell em.waveguide_modes 2D FD Helmholtz eigenproblem of a WR-90 cross-section, TE and TM f_c = c/(2 pi) sqrt((m pi/a)^2 + (n pi/b)^2) em.cavity_resonance 2D, 3D FDTD ring-down; spectral peaks matched to modes rectangular cavity formula em.mie_scattering 3D Mie series efficiencies BHMIE published sample; Rayleigh; optical theorem; Q_ext -> 2 em.bench_mu0_solenoid 3D bench: Hall probe, ammeter, caliper; mu0 from the slope of B(I) with a GUM budget; coverage of U checked by Monte Carlo CODATA 2022 em.bench_rc_discharge 0D bench: 8-bit oscilloscope with noise and time-base error; C = tau / R with its uncertainty; coverage by Monte Carlo the capacitor's true value (hidden from the fit)

docs.title: Research level
docs.text:
experiment dims what is computed reference / evidence em.research_fdtd_3d 3D+t a 3-D FDTD study configured by a dict (domain, cells per wavelength, sources, materials: spheres, boxes, cylinders of any medium); a Hertzian dipole on a refinement ladder, radiated power by the near-to-far-field transform; then the dipole beside a dielectric sphere on the same ladder closed-form dipole power and pattern, observed order, Richardson and Roache's GCI; for the configured case (no closed form) its own extrapolation and GCI against a declared target; Faraday, Ampere-Maxwell and Gauss residuals of a block of the field in x, y, z and t em.research_uq_waveguide 2D Monte Carlo of a, b, eps_r tolerances through the finite-difference eigen-solver: mean, std, 95 % interval of the TE10 and TE20 cut-offs first-order GUM propagation with closed-form sensitivities, tolerance from the sampling error of the std em.research_inverse_permittivity 1D eps_r and sigma of a slab recovered by least squares from a reflection spectrum measured by FDTD with receiver noise, with the Jacobian covariance; the model's bias is removed by simulating the instrument at the fitted point; repeated on noise realisations the truth the measurement was generated with (hidden from the fit); coverage (95 %) and centring of the stated u em.research_surrogate_hall 2D a Gaussian process of the Hall geometrical factor G(L/W, mu B) trained on solver runs (Latin hypercube), variance calibrated by leave-one-out on the training runs error on held-out solver runs; +-2 sigma coverage; the long-bar limit

The FDTD study writes the fourth dimension two ways: an MP4 / GIF of E_z r on the three central planes in time, and a single-file three.js page (the Studio viewer, pinneapple_tools.visualization.studio.web_viewer) with play, pause and a time slider.

from pinneapple_science.em.fdtd_study import FDTDConfig, run_fdtd

cfg = FDTDConfig.from_dict({"f0": 1e9, "size": 2.4, "cells_per_wavelength": 14,
                            "sources": [{"kind": "dipole", "component": "Ez", "at": [0, 0, 0]}],
                            "materials": [{"shape": "box", "center": [0.5, 0, 0], "size": [0.2, 0.6, 0.6],
                                           "eps_r": 6.0, "sigma": 0.01}]})
run = run_fdtd(cfg, snapshots=24)            # run.power (W at f0), run.pattern(theta), run.slices, run.volume

Limits stated by the experiments themselves: Palmer's and Kirchhoff's formulas are asymptotic (the capacitor experiment measures how Kirchhoff's error falls with a/d: +6.2 %, +2.3 %, +0.8 % at a/d = 2.5, 5, 10 in the committed run); the thin-plate edge limits the finite-volume order to about 1; the Fresnel comparisons use an absolute tolerance of 5e-3 on abs(r) at 40 cells per wavelength. The dipole beside a sphere converges at first order (staircase sphere with fill-fraction averaging), so its finest grid carries a GCI of a few percent; the surrogate's +-2 sigma band covers 80 % of the held-out runs, at the threshold the experiment declares.

docs.title: The atlas
docs.text:
The atlas is versioned data, pinneapple_science/data/atlas.json (schema pinneapple.science.atlas/1). The full table is examples/science/ATLAS.md and the navigable page examples/science/atlas.html (search, filters by status and by branch). Statuses:

  • available: pp.science experiments in every dimension listed, each checked against its reference;
  • partial: library code covers part of the area (a module, a problem preset or a Lab experiment the atlas points to); no pp.science experiment yet;
  • planned: mapped, nothing in the library yet.

Areas: classical mechanics; electromagnetism and optics; thermodynamics and statistical physics; fluid mechanics; continuum and solid mechanics; acoustics and waves; quantum mechanics; special and general relativity; nuclear and particle physics; condensed matter; plasma physics; astrophysics and cosmology; geophysics; chemistry; materials science; biology and biophysics; neuroscience; ecology and epidemiology; earth and climate sciences; applied mathematics and numerical methods.

pp.science.validate() (and tests/test_science.py) fails when a pointer names a module, preset or Lab experiment that does not exist, when an available subarea has no experiment, or when a registered experiment is missing from the atlas.

docs.title: Adding an area or an experiment
docs.text:
1. Map it. Add the area (or the subarea) to pinneapple_science/data/atlas.json with its status and the pointers to code that already covers it ({"module": ...}, {"preset": ...}, {"lab": ...}). Point to existing code; do not copy it. Bump version.
  2. Write the experiment in pinneapple_science/<area>/<topic>.py (new physics or numerics go in the library, in the package they belong to, with tests; the experiment calls them):
from pinneapple_science.core import Experiment, Reference
from pinneapple_science.registry import register

@register
class Pendulum(Experiment):
    name = "mech.pendulum_period"
    title = "Pendulum period"
    area = "physics.classical_mechanics"
    topic = "oscillators"
    level, kind, dims = "academic", "theory", ("0D",)
    references = ("Taylor, Classical Mechanics (2005), sec. 4.9",)
    params = {"L": 1.0, "theta0": 0.1}

    def _run(self, res, dim, p):
        T = ...                                   # integrate the ODE, measure the period from zero crossings
        res.compare("small-angle period", T, Reference(2 * 3.14159265 * (p["L"] / 9.80665) ** 0.5,
                    "Taylor eq. 5.12", "limit"), tol=1e-3, unit="s")
        res.figure("pendulum", fig)
  1. Register the module in pinneapple_science.registry.MODULES, list the experiment under its subarea in the atlas ({"experiment": "mech.pendulum_period"}) and in the Flow node list (pinneapple_flow/nodes/science.py, EXPERIMENTS), and set the subarea to available when every dimension it claims runs.
  2. Commit the results: python -m pinneapple_science report mech.pendulum_period writes examples/science/<area>/<experiment>/ with result.json, figures, the manifest and the sealed figures; then python -m pinneapple_science report all refreshes the catalogue. Run python -m pinneapple_lab reindex first in a fresh checkout so the curation sees every committed run.
  3. Test it: add the name to FAST in tests/test_science.py (with a quick parameter set that runs in seconds and still passes its references).

docs.title: Engineering Sensitivity Lab
docs.text:
Which parameters really control the result, and which can you freeze? Day 16 of the apps series: https://sensitivity.pinneapple.org (source: apps/sensitivity_lab).

Give a model (built-in benchmark, pp.zoo model or ONNX graph), runs done in your solver (OpenFOAM, CalculiX: download the Saltelli design, upload the results) or a dataset, the parameters with their ranges or distributions and the responses. The lab returns Sobol first-order, total and second-order indices with bootstrap intervals, Morris screening, main-effect and ICE curves, local derivatives (automatic differentiation for torch models) and the parameters you can freeze, each recommendation checked by re-running the model with them fixed.

On the Ishigami benchmark every estimated index is within 0.003 of the exact value and inside its 95 % interval. On the heat-sink design, fin count controls the thermal resistance (total index 0.54); ambient temperature and power can be frozen (total index < 2e-4) and fixing them changes the output variance by less than 0.1 %. From data alone (3,900 simulations) the app flags that the inputs are correlated (r = 0.66), so the first-order indices add up to more than 1.

Everything shown comes from pp.sensitivity (see Uncertainty and sensitivity studies on any model). Limits, methods and the API are in the app README.

docs.title: Spectral fidelity: what relative L2 does not see
docs.text:
Relative L2 error rewards smooth predictions. A blurred field can have a small L2 error and still miss the small scales that carry heat transfer, mixing or loads, and neural operators are known to under-predict them (spectral bias). pinneapple_analysis.validation.spectral measures what L2 hides. It is NumPy only and works on any field on a regular grid, from any code.

import numpy as np
from pinneapple_analysis.validation.spectral import spectral_fidelity

report = spectral_fidelity(pred, ref, ndim=2)          # arrays (..., ny, nx): leading axes are averaged
print(report.summary())                                # rel. L2, high-band energy ratio and bias, per-band table
print(report.passed)                                   # False when |bias| > tol (default 0.25)

docs.title: What is measured
docs.text: Quantity Function Meaning Energy spectrum E(k) energy_spectrum(u, ndim, periodic=..., window="hann") Shell-summed, integer radial wavenumbers k = rint(|m|), sum E = mean(u^2) for a periodic field. Non-periodic fields are mean-removed and Hann-windowed (unit mean square). Energy ratio per band, high-wavenumber bias spectral_comparison, high_wavenumber_bias E_pred / E_ref - 1 over the top third of the shells where the reference has energy: about -1 for a smoothed prediction, 0 for the reference itself, positive for added noise. Phase error and coherence per band spectral_comparison Energy-weighted mean phase difference [rad]; |sum P R*|^2 / (sum |P|^2 sum |R|^2) (1 = the same modes). Structure functions structure_functions(u, ndim, orders=(2, 3)) S_p(r) = <|u(x + r) - u(x)|^p> per axis, signed S_3, flatness S_4 / S_2^2 (3 for Gaussian increments; larger at small r for intermittent fields). Gradient errors gradient_metrics(pred, ref, ndim, spacing, vector_axis=..., walls=...) Error in grad u and |grad u|; for a velocity field, vorticity and strain-rate magnitude; for a scalar, the mean wall flux -k du/dn on chosen faces. Power-law slope fit_power_law(k, E, kmin, kmax) Least-squares slope in log-log.

docs.title: Where it is reported
docs.text:
• pinneapple check: rule PC704 spectral-bias on every grid result with a grid reference of the same shape (tolerance hf-bias, default 0.25).
  • pp.benchmark: field problems (Burgers, Darcy, Navier-Stokes) add an "HF energy bias" column next to the relative L2 error.
  • pp.validate: part of the validation report (once it lands, #696).

docs.title: How it was checked
docs.text:
tests/test_spectral_fidelity.py:

  • a synthetic field with a prescribed k^-5/3 spectrum: every shell within 1 % (the construction makes it exact to round-off) and the fitted slope within 1 %;
  • a 2-D decaying-turbulence velocity field from the pseudo-spectral solver (pinneapple_physics.multiscale.ns2d, 64², nu = 5e-4, t = 3, spectrum slope about -3.3): the field against itself has zero bias, zero phase error and unit coherence; a copy through a Gaussian filter of half a cell has a relative L2 error of 2.5 % and a high-wavenumber bias of -0.68 (flagged; -0.92 at 0.75 cell, where L2 is 4.9 %); 5 % white noise gives a positive bias above 0.25;
  • closed forms: S_2(r) of a linear field, flatness 3 of Gaussian noise, vorticity and strain of an analytic velocity field, and the wall flux of x^2 + y.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Small added noise is below the default tolerance: 2 % white noise on the turbulence field gives a bias of +0.19 (not flagged at 0.25), 5 % gives +1.09. Lower tol if noise matters for the use.
  • The bias compares energies, not positions: a field shifted by a few cells keeps a zero bias. The phase error and coherence catch that.
  • The band edges are fractions of the resolved range of the reference. A reference with almost no energy at high wavenumbers (smooth solutions) gives a short high band; the check is most informative for multi-scale fields.
  • Non-periodic fields are windowed, which spreads energy across neighbouring shells (leakage). Ratios are robust to it because prediction and reference get the same window; absolute spectra of non-periodic fields are approximate.

docs.title: PINNeAPPle Studio: every tool, example and app in one place
docs.text:
pinneapple_studio turns the whole library into a catalog of tools and the repository's examples into a gallery you can run. It is the library side of the PINNeAPPle Studio: the full web interface lives in the Engineering API and reads this package; pinneapple studio serves a local version (the Flow Studio UI plus the Studio API).

pinneapple studio summary                          # tools per category and status, gallery per state
pinneapple studio search "dissipador de calor com aletas" --category executable
pinneapple studio tool preset:water_hammer_valve_closure
pinneapple studio gallery --state blocked          # what cannot run here, and the command that fixes it
pinneapple studio run-tool preset:water_hammer_valve_closure --inputs '{"t_close": 2.0}'
pinneapple studio run example:lbm                  # the quick configuration of the example's flow
pinneapple studio                                  # http://127.0.0.1:8765, API under /api/studio

docs.title: The catalog of tools
docs.text:
Every public class and function of every pinneapple* package is a tool (pinneapple_studio.catalog.load()), plus the industrial presets (preset:<name>) and the science experiments (experiment:<name>). Nothing is skipped: tests/test_studio.py checks that each public symbol gets a category. The category comes from the code, with the reason stored next to it:

category rule in the Studio executable every required input has a type a form can hold (numbers, text, booleans, lists and dicts of those, Literal choices, paths, numeric arrays as lists, dataclasses of those as nested forms); a class also needs a method that does the work (run, solve, predict, ...) a card with a form generated from the signature, a Run button (a job in the sandbox) and the result with its evidence composite it takes or is an object other tools build (a tensor, a model, a problem, a callable, an input without a type annotation), or it is a layer, a loss, a callback or an adapter a block of a pipeline: the card shows the examples and modules that use it reference exceptions, type definitions, entry points (CLI, servers), internal, deprecated or placeholder modules, plain data records shown with its description and the reason it is not a tool

Each tool carries:

  • its signature, parameters with annotations and defaults, and the docstring;
  • the Portuguese prose of the map, whole (docs/pt/_mapa/prosa);
  • its status and the evidence behind it;
  • the tests and the examples that use it;
  • its tasks, physics areas and products;
  • related tools from the import graph;
  • its outputs (outputs: name, type, unit and description of each value) and where they were read (outputs_source).

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
pinneapple_studio.outputs reads what a tool returns from the code. Nothing is guessed. The sources, from the strongest:

outputs_source where declared a module-level X_OUTPUTS = {"tool_name": [{"name": ..., "type": ..., "unit": ..., "description": ...}]} written by the author, or the outputs of a preset's card annotation the return annotation: a NamedTuple or dataclass gives one output per field (units from the docstring entries with the same names, or the class's Attributes), a plain type gives one unnamed output, -> None gives none docstring the Returns section, numpy (tau : float [s]) or Google (float [s]: the time constant) style none nothing says what it returns; outputs is empty

When there is no record class, the docstring's entries name the outputs, and a plain annotation fills the types the docstring leaves out. A unit is read only in brackets after the type, preceded by a space. Brackets glued to a name (list[float]) are part of the type, and brackets holding a comma ([0, 1]) are not a unit.

prose_unmatched lists prose whose symbol is no longer in the code. A symbol without prose shows none; nothing is generated.

docs.title: Input ranges
docs.text:
An author declares the input box a function is valid for by assigning a literal after it, at the top level of the module:

def pfr_conversion_ktau(k: float, tau: float) -> dict[str, float]:
    ...


pfr_conversion_ktau.x_ranges = {"k": (0.0, 10.0), "tau": (0.0, 1e4)}

The catalog reads it without importing the module. Each (lo, hi) becomes the form's minimum / maximum for that input, with "x-ranges-source": "declared"; None leaves a side open. A name that is not a numeric input, or a default outside its range, is listed in the tool's form_problems. Preset inputs take their ranges from the preset's card.

docs.title: Status
docs.text:
The rules are those of the Engineering API's Capability Registry:

status rule verified a test that runs by default calls it and compares with a reference (validate() asserted, a reference / exact / analytic solution, a relative error); for a preset, its recorded validation.json shows every reference case passing tested a test that runs by default calls it, without a reference comparison discovered no test that runs by default calls it (examples and opt-in slow tests do not count)

docs.title: Navigation and search
docs.text:
pinneapple_studio.search.Index(catalog) runs BM25 over the name, module, docstring, prose and tags, in Portuguese or English:

  • accents are folded and names are split (HeatSink, heat_sink);
  • calor also finds heat, from a fixed table plus the glossary's terms in parentheses.

Filters cover category, status, task, area, product, package and kind. The tasks, areas and products are regular expressions in pinneapple_studio.taxonomy, and each tag keeps the words that matched.

docs.title: The gallery
docs.text:
pinneapple_studio.gallery.load() lists every example folder, every paper reproduction (examples/reproductions/*) and every app. Each entry's data sheet comes from experiment.json, the example flows of pinneapple_flow.examples (their measured runs and comparisons), the README and the prose.

The requirements are read from its scripts: packages with the pyproject.toml extra that installs them, external programs (OpenFOAM, FreeCAD, CalculiX, ParaView, Blender, Ollama), a GPU, the network and credentials. They are checked on this machine. An entry that cannot run is blocked, with each missing piece and its fix. A cost is shown only when a run was measured.

docs.title: Running
docs.text:
pinneapple_studio.runner.queue() is a pinneapple_core.service.jobs.JobQueue with two job kinds, tool and gallery. Each job runs in its own process:

  • with an environment from an allowlist, without tokens, keys, passwords or database URLs;
  • under memory, CPU and open-file limits;
  • with a time limit, logs, progress and cancel.

A gallery job runs the example's flow, quick by default, and compares it with the committed measurement. It never writes to measured.json. It can also run one of the example's scripts in its own process.

Every result carries an evidence record: parameters, versions, wall time, files with SHA-256, and verifications that are each pass, fail, inconclusive or not_run. The comparisons of an example flow and the checks of a preset or an experiment become those verifications. A tool that just returned a value has no verification, so its outcome is not_run.

docs.title: The API
docs.text:
pinneapple_studio.api.router(queue) is a FastAPI router. The app that mounts it brings the security: login, API keys and rate limits.

method path GET /summary counts, labels of every navigation, facets, gallery per state GET /tools?q=&category=&status=&task=&area=&product=&package=&kind= search with facets of the hits GET /tools/{id}, /compare?ids=a,b, /tree, /modules/{module}, /glossary cards, comparison, the package tree GET /gallery?kind=&state=&q=, /gallery/{id} entries and data sheets POST /jobs ({"kind": "tool" \| "gallery", "params": {...}}) 202 and the job id; a composite tool or a blocked entry is refused with the reason GET / POST /jobs/{id}, /jobs/{id}/logs, /jobs/{id}/cancel, /jobs/{id}/files/{name} status and result, logs, cancel, files

The inventory, catalog and gallery are generated per commit under ~/.cache/pinneapple/studio (PINNEAPPLE_STUDIO_CACHE) and never committed. PINNEAPPLE_ROOT points the Studio at a checkout when the package is installed from a wheel.

docs.title: Coverage
docs.text:
python -m pinneapple_studio coverage writes the coverage table (a page of the docs site, studio/COVERAGE.md) and exits 1 on a problem. The generated job of .github/workflows/tests.yml runs it.

  • Every public symbol has a category. There is no baseline for this.
  • Every executable tool has a valid form and one of:
  • a smoke run of its current code that returned;
  • a reason it is not run: it needs the network, a server, a screen, credentials or an LLM (a rule in pinneapple_studio.coverage), or a real cause stated in pinneapple_studio/tool_reasons.json;
  • a line in pinneapple_studio/coverage_baseline.txt.

The baseline holds the tools that had none of these when the gate came in. It only shrinks: a tool that gains a run or a reason must leave it, and a new tool cannot enter it. In the Studio and in the table, such a tool reads "ainda não roda: falta entrada de exemplo" (or the error of its failed smoke run), and it is never counted as ready. - Every example and reproduction runs from the Studio (a measured run of its flow, or a recorded run of its scripts) or says why: a missing requirement with its fix, or the flow inventory's stated reason.

A smoke run calls the tool from its form and records whether it returned. It is not a physics check: that is the status from the tests, and the verifications of a job. The tools run in batches, one interpreter per batch:

  • each in a disposable checkout (git worktree) with its own HOME, the job environment and no network (unshare -n);
  • after each tool the checkout is compared with its commit, the files the tool changed are recorded on the tool, and the copy is restored.

The inputs of tools with required fields come from pinneapple_studio/tool_inputs.json. pinneapple studio inputs fills that file from calls with literal arguments in the tests, examples and Hub snippets; calls expected to fail (pytest.raises) are skipped.

pinneapple studio inputs                       # harvest example inputs
pinneapple studio smoke                        # tools whose code changed or never ran (--all for every tool)
pinneapple studio examples                     # scripts of the examples without a flow
pinneapple studio coverage --record-history    # the table, the gate, and today's point on the baseline curve

The weekly workflow .github/workflows/studio-smoke.yml runs the same commands and uploads the records for a maintainer to commit.

docs.title: Surrogates from simulation results: study, regime arena, gateway
docs.text:
Three library pieces turn a table of simulation runs into a model that others can call, and say where it can be trusted:

Piece What it does pinneapple_analysis.surrogate.run_study trains every applicable method on the same splits and budget, measures on unseen data, picks one by validation error, packages it with its limitations and a trust report pinneapple_arena.regimes.run_regime_arena ranks methods per data regime (interpolation, few data, extrapolation, geometry change, steep fronts) over several seeds, with physics violations, solver baselines and a dataset audit pinneapple_registry.ModelGateway publishes versions, runs them behind one predict with the model's OOD policy (warn or refuse), logs every call, aggregates latency / counts / errors, exports TorchScript and ONNX

docs.title: A surrogate study
docs.text:
from pinneapple_analysis import surrogate as S

data = S.examples.airfoil_rans()             # 374 OpenFOAM RANS runs: 6 CST weights + alpha -> Cl, Cd
study = S.run_study(data, budget=3.0, seeds=2)          # 3 s of wall clock per training run
print(study.best, study.ranking("test"), study.ranking("shift"))
print(study.trust["decision"], study.limitations["concentration"])
out = study.model.predict({"T0": 0.15, "T1": 0.12, "T2": 0.13, "M0": 0.02, "M1": 0.05, "M2": 0.04,
                           "alpha_deg": [4.0, 30.0]})
print(out["outputs"]["Cl"], out["ood"][1]["reasons"])      # alpha 30 is flagged: outside the training range
study.model.save("airfoil_model")

Your own data: S.read_table(bytes_or_path, name) reads CSV, Parquet, JSON, HDF5 and NPZ; S.from_table(df, inputs, outputs, group=...) picks the columns. A field output is a set of columns u_0, u_1, ... (with grid_shape= and optionally coords=), or S.from_arrays({"X": ..., "Y": (n, *grid), "coords": ...}).

Which methods apply (S.applicable(kind, n_train, grid_shape, has_pde), each with the reason when not): polynomial ridge and an MLP always; a Gaussian process up to 2000 training samples (on POD coefficients for fields); gradient-boosted trees (XGBoost if installed, else scikit-learn) for scalars; FNO and DeepONet for fields; a PINN only for fields with a declared PDE (pde={"type": "burgers", "coords": {"x": "x", "t": "t"}, "coefficients": {"nu": "nu"}}; types in S.PDE_TYPES).

Equal budget. The iterative methods (MLP, FNO, DeepONet, PINN) train until the same ComputeBudget is spent (pinneapple_analysis.cost.equal_budget.train_within_budget) and keep the best of ten validation checkpoints; the one-shot fits (ridge, GP, trees) are fitted once and report the time they used.

Unseen data. S.make_splits carves out a distribution-shift set first (whole groups, the edge of the input space, or one end of an input) and then a random held-out test set. The model is selected by validation error; the test and shift sets only measure it.

Limitations (study.limitations): training-range validity bounds, the OOD gate (training range plus nearest-neighbour distance, the batched form of physics_audit.Envelope), the error per input quartile and where it concentrates, the worst samples, the extrapolation ratio, and for fields the mean error map and, with a declared PDE, the finite-difference residual of the predictions relative to the reference data.

Trust report (pinneapple_analysis.trust.TrustReport): held-out error against the target (0.10 nRMSE or 0.05 relative L2 by default), R² > 0 on every output (critical), shift error within 3x the held-out error, seed spread, and the PDE residual check for fields. A check that could not run says why.

docs.title: Regime arena
docs.text:
from pinneapple_arena.regimes import run_regime_arena

data = S.examples.burgers_fields()           # exact viscous Burgers fields for 96 viscosities
result = run_regime_arena(data, budget=3.0, seeds=3, baselines={"fdm": S.examples.burgers_fdm_baseline()})
print(result.rankings["extrapolation"], result.overall, result.baselines, result.audit["decision"])

The protocol is in result.protocol: one split for every method and seed (the model seed varies, the data does not), the same budget and stopping rule, default hyper-parameters (no per-method search), the dataset hash, the hardware and date. Physics violations are the share of predictions breaking the dataset's declared constraints (pinneapple_data.audit.constraint_mask, e.g. Cd > 0, the maximum principle abs(u) <= 1.005); the splits are audited by pinneapple_data.audit.audit_dataset (the checks behind pinneapple check PC451-PC453). Regimes the data cannot support (no groups, scalar outputs for steep fronts) are reported as unavailable with the reason; graph networks and R-OAMS are listed in NOT_IN_LIBRARY with why they are not run.

docs.title: Gateway
docs.text:
from pinneapple_registry import ModelGateway

gw = ModelGateway("./models")
v = gw.publish("airfoil-cl-cd", "airfoil_model", ood_policy="refuse")      # or a SurrogateModel
gw.publish("airfoil-zoo", "airfoil_cst_rans_mlp", kind="pinneapple.zoo")    # zoo models too
r = gw.predict("airfoil-cl-cd", [{"T0": 0.15, "T1": 0.12, "T2": 0.13, "M0": 0.02, "M1": 0.05, "M2": 0.04,
                                  "alpha_deg": 4.0}])
print(r["outputs"], r["ood"], r["latency_ms"], gw.metrics()["by_version"])
gw.export("airfoil-cl-cd", None, "onnx", "airfoil.onnx")                    # PyTorch surrogates only

Versions follow ModelStore (vYYYYMMDD_HHMMSS, stages, a REJECT trust report blocks staging and production unless an override reason is recorded). A caller may tighten a model's OOD policy (warn to refuse), never relax it. Surrogates are unpickled only after their sha256 matches their card: publish only directories you produced.

Other servers with the same API (the Surrogate Studio, the Benchmark Arena, any app built on gateway_router) are reachable from Python with pinneapple_registry.gateway_client.GatewayClient(base_url, api_key=...). A gateway can serve them too:

  • gw.publish(name, "https://host/v1/models/<model>", kind="remote") forwards to the remote model;
  • gw.publish_ref(model_ref) publishes from a ModelRef: zoo:<name>, or an http(s) URI whose input ranges become the validity bounds.

The front gateway enforces its own bounds and OOD policy, and logs and meters every call before forwarding.

docs.title: Topology optimisation
docs.text:
pinneapple_design.topology optimises the material layout on a fixed grid of elements (density method, SIMP): each element carries a density rho in [0, 1], a filter and a Heaviside projection turn the design variables into densities, and an optimiser (optimality criteria or MMA) updates them from adjoint sensitivities.

Piece API Density filter (cone weights, any radius), symmetry maps DensityFilter.grid(nelx, nely, r_min), SymmetryMap Heaviside projection with continuation heaviside, heaviside_derivative, DesignChain(n, filter, beta=...) Optimisers oc_update (optimality criteria), MMA (method of moving asymptotes, Svanberg 1987; dual solved with L-BFGS-B) Driver and gradient check optimize(problem, volume_fraction, filter, "oc" / "mma", ...), finite_difference_check Structural compliance on Q4 elements (MBB beam, cantilever) Compliance2D.mbb, Compliance2D.cantilever Thermal compliance ThermalCompliance2D Stokes flow with Brinkman penalisation (Borrvall-Petersson) StokesDissipation2D.double_pipe Rotor iron of an electric machine for torque pinneapple_design.topology.magnetic, on pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics (guide)

docs.title: What is verified
docs.text:
tests/test_topology_optimization.py asserts:

  • sensitivities through filter and projection against finite differences for compliance, thermal compliance and Stokes dissipation;
  • MMA against SciPy's SLSQP on the five-variable cantilever problem of Svanberg (1987): same optimum to 1e-8 relative (1.33995636);
  • OC and MMA reach the same MBB compliance, and the MBB result is a truss attached to the load and supports;
  • the double-pipe problem gives two pipes in a 1 x 1 domain and one merged channel in a 1.5 x 1 domain, the qualitative result of Borrvall & Petersson (2003);
  • the reluctance-rotor optimisation increases torque, and the torque-ripple objective's gradient.

Runs of the examples (2026-10-17, CPU):

Example Result 01_mbb_beam.py (60 x 20, volume 0.5) compliance 233.71 (OC, 146 iterations), 233.49 (MMA, 58 iterations); with projection 190.05, gray fraction 2.3 %; gradient check 1.0e-6 02_heat_and_stokes_flow.py thermal compliance 4.18e8 (uniform) -> 2.49e7; double pipe dissipation 136.4 -> 25.7 (1 x 1) and 179.3 -> 26.8 (1.5 x 1) 03_reluctance_rotor.py 1410 design variables; mean torque 38.10 N m with linear iron, 13.44 N m when the same rotor is re-evaluated with nonlinear iron; Maxwell stress 46.21 vs co-energy 47.07 N m at 5 degrees

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• The rotor optimisation uses linear iron; the nonlinear re-evaluation shows that a thin-featured rotor saturates, so the design should be optimised with the nonlinear B-H curve (the adjoint supports it; the example does not).
  • On thin-featured designs Maxwell-stress and co-energy torque differ by about 2 % (46.21 vs 47.07 N m above), more than on smooth geometries; refine the band and air gap before trusting single-angle torques.
  • Grids are structured and 2-D.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• K. Svanberg, The method of moving asymptotes, Int. J. Numer. Meth. Eng. 24 (1987) 359-373.
  • M. P. Bendsoe and O. Sigmund, Topology Optimization: Theory, Methods and Applications, Springer, 2003.
  • T. Borrvall and J. Petersson, Topology optimization of fluids in Stokes flow, Int. J. Numer. Meth. Fluids 41 (2003) 77-107.

docs.title: Physics checks during training (Lightning, PhysicsNeMo, Hugging Face)
docs.text:
Models trained outside PINNeAPPle are usually validated once, at the end, after the whole budget is spent. The callbacks in pinneapple_neural.callbacks run the checks of pp.validate on a fixed validation batch every N steps and log them to the framework's logger. They warn (or stop the run) when a physics metric worsens for K consecutive checks while the training loss improves, and write the validation report and trust card at the end. None of the frameworks is a dependency of PINNeAPPle.

from pinneapple_neural.callbacks import PhysicsMonitor

mon = PhysicsMonitor("darcy_2d", reference=(a_val, u_val), every=50, patience=3, action="warn",
                     report_path="runs/validation.json")        # + runs/validation.trust.json at the end

# PyTorch Lightning: logs to every logger of the Trainer (TensorBoard, W&B, MLflow, CSV)
from pinneapple_neural.callbacks import PhysicsValidationCallback
lightning.Trainer(callbacks=[PhysicsValidationCallback(mon)]).fit(module, loader)

# PhysicsNeMo training loop (PhysicsNeMo has no trainer class): one call per optimiser step
from pinneapple_neural.callbacks import PhysicsNeMoHook
hook = PhysicsNeMoHook(mon)
with LaunchLogger("train", epoch=epoch) as log:                 # physicsnemo.utils.logging
    ...
    if hook(model, step, loss, log=log):                        # True when action="stop" fired
        break
hook.finish(model)

# Hugging Face Trainer: metrics go through trainer.log, i.e. to its report_to integrations
from pinneapple_neural.callbacks import PhysicsTrainerCallback
PhysicsTrainerCallback(PhysicsMonitor(..., model_fn=lambda m: m.net)).attach(trainer)
  • Checks. The monitor accepts any problem pp.validate takes: "darcy_2d", a zoo card, a PINN problem ({"pinn": "burgers_1d"}, PINN validation), a rollout, a tabular spec. level picks the checks. Each check's value is logged as physics/<check id>, plus physics/n_fail and physics/n_warn.
  • model_fn. Maps the framework's module to the network to validate, e.g. when a LightningModule or a Hugging Face model wraps it.
  • Early warning. For each watched check (watch=, default all numeric ones; a lower |value| is better), it counts consecutive checks in which the metric worsened while the loss fell. At patience it emits a PhysicsWarning that lands in monitor.alerts and in the trust card's training_alerts. With action="stop" it also stops training.
  • Training-time losses. pinneapple_analysis.uncertainty.residual_bound.ResidualLoss is a differentiable physics loss ‖f − A u‖² / ‖f‖² in the discretisation of the reference solver (sparse, PyTorch). The tests train with it.

docs.title: Results (from tests/test_training_callbacks.py, CPU)
docs.text:
A PhysicsNeMo FNO (2 layers, 6 modes) on 64 Darcy samples at 16 × 16, validated every 40 steps on 8 reference solutions of operator_benchmarks.darcy_2d, 400 steps, loss = relative data MSE + w × ResidualLoss:

Run Result w = 0.01, trained in Lightning and in a PhysicsNeMo loop identical physics metrics at all 10 checks (to 1e-5); no alert; relative L2 0.09, energy-norm error bound 0.44 w = 0.01, Hugging Face Trainer 10 checks logged through trainer.log; no alert w = −0.01 (sign error: the residual is maximised) alert at step 160 of 400 on the energy bound, the flux and the reference error; this is the earliest step every=40, patience=3 allows. With action="stop", training stops there (also in the HF Trainer).

Observed but not asserted in the tests: with w = 0 (data loss only), the monitor flags conservation.flux at step 200. The boundary-flux imbalance rises from 0.22 to 0.37 while the data loss keeps falling. This is the kind of drift the callback is for.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• A check costs one pp.validate call on the validation batch. For Darcy at level="quick" with 8 samples at 16 × 16 it takes about 13 ms; at standard, which adds the spectral and symmetry tests, about 28 ms. Choose every accordingly.
  • The rule needs the loss at each check. In the Hugging Face Trainer it is the latest logged loss, so set logging_steps no larger than every.
  • Identical metrics across frameworks require identical training: the same initial weights, batch order and optimiser. The HF Trainer shuffles and uses its own optimiser, so its run is checked for logging and stopping, not for equality.
  • pp.validate could not run a PhysicsNeMo FNO given a field without a channel axis: PhysicsNeMo raises ValueError, not RuntimeError. This is fixed here.

docs.title: A latent surrogate that says when not to trust it
docs.text:
A latent reduced-order model encodes the solver's fields in a few coordinates (POD), regresses those coordinates on the design parameters, and decodes. It answers in a fraction of a millisecond, and answers just as fast where it is wrong. TrustedLatentSurrogate (in pinneapple_neural.architectures.rom) adds three checks to every answer, calibrated on designs the latent model never saw, and hands the result to the library's TrustReport:

check what it measures calibrated how in the report error bound latent predictive spread (Gaussian-process std, or a bootstrap ensemble of latent regressors) scaled to the relative L2 error of the field normalised split-conformal: covers the true error with probability 1 - alpha for queries drawn like the calibration set not critical: above the tolerance → REVIEW design envelope mean distance to the k nearest training designs conformal p-value against the calibration designs critical: p < alpha_envelope → REJECT physics residual the discrete governing equations evaluated on the decoded field (a sparse mat-vec, no solve) 1 - alpha_residual conformal quantile of calibration residuals critical → REJECT

The envelope check exists because conformal coverage only holds while queries look like the calibration data; out there the spread itself can be overconfident. The physics residual is independent of the data: it sees errors that every member of an ensemble agrees on.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
from pinneapple_neural.architectures.rom import ParametricPOD, TrustedLatentSurrogate

sur = TrustedLatentSurrogate(
    ParametricPOD(r=64, regressor="gpr", normalize=True),   # latent model; "rbf" uses a bootstrap ensemble
    alpha=0.1,                                              # 90 % error bound
    residual=lambda p, u: rel_residual(p, u),               # optional: ||L(p) u - f(p)|| / ||f(p)||
).fit(P_train, X_train, P_cal, X_cal)                       # calibration designs: never used for fitting

a = sur.assess(P_new, tol=0.02)        # X, error_bound, envelope_p, residual, decision per query
report = sur.trust_report(P_new[0], tol=0.02)
report.decisao, report.to_markdown()   # APPROVED / REVIEW / REJECT with the reasons

assess returns the same decision as the report: REJECT on an envelope or residual failure, REVIEW when the error bound exceeds the tolerance, APPROVED otherwise. A REVIEW or REJECT means "run the solver for this one", which is what a design loop or a digital twin should do with the answer.

docs.title: Experiment: every answer against the full solver
docs.text:
python examples/latent/trusted_latent_surrogate.py --seed 0 (also seeds 1 and 2). Full model: steady 2-D advection-diffusion-reaction of a Gaussian source on a 96 × 96 grid (upwind finite differences, sparse direct solve), four parameters (wind speed, direction, decay rate, source position). 150 training and 100 calibration designs from an envelope with a hole (a band of wind speeds and directions never simulated). Three test groups of 150: inside the envelope, inside the hole (inside the parameter box, so a box check passes them), and 5–30 % beyond the box in one parameter. Tolerance: 2 % relative L2 error. Mean of three seeds, [min, max] where it varies:

envelope hole beyond the box median / p95 relative error 0.84 % / 3.8 % 0.61 % / 1.4 % 4.9 % / 17 % nearest training design (baseline), median 17 % 20 % 31 % fraction with error > 2 % 15 % 2 % 90 % coverage of the 90 % error bound 0.92 [0.87, 0.96] 0.99 0.65 APPROVED / REVIEW / REJECT 58 / 39 / 3 % 71 / 28 / 0 % 6 / 18 / 76 % approved with error > 2 % 2.4 % 0.4 % 1.6 %

Detecting a wrong answer (error > 2 %) over all 450 queries, ROC AUC: error bound 0.980, physics residual 0.976, envelope p-value 0.943, box check 0.891. Spearman correlation with the true error: bound 0.95, residual 0.93.

As a gate, over the three seeds: the trust decision approved 607 answers, of which 20 (3.3 %) were wrong, the largest approved error being 1.2 %, 3.5 % and 5.3 % per seed. A box check approved the 900 in-box answers, of which 79 (8.8 %) were wrong, with largest approved errors of 7.4 % to 14.5 %.

Speed: full solve 45.6 ms; surrogate 0.71 ms per query in a batch (65 times faster), 2.5 ms per query with the three checks (18 times faster). A single query costs 11 ms (only 4 times faster) because scikit-learn's GP prediction has a fixed per-call overhead for each latent coordinate; batch the queries.

What the numbers say:

  • The latent model is genuinely useful here (0.8 % median error, 20 times better than the nearest design), and most of its failures are recognisable before anyone looks at the reference: the bound and the residual each rank wrong answers with AUC ≈ 0.98.
  • The hole turned out to be interpolable (0.6 % error), and the gate approved most of it: the envelope check flags distance, but the decision only rejects when the p-value is extreme, so the gate is not needlessly conservative.
  • Beyond the box the coverage of the bound drops to 0.65, which is why the envelope check is critical: it rejects three quarters of those queries.
  • The error bound is marginal over the calibration distribution, not conditional per query. With 100 calibration designs the coverage fluctuates by a few percent between seeds, and the approval rate inside the envelope varied from 33 % to 71 %: more calibration designs make both steadier.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• J. Lei, M. G'Sell, A. Rinaldo, R. Tibshirani, L. Wasserman, "Distribution-free predictive inference for regression", JASA 113 (2018).
  • A. N. Angelopoulos, S. Bates, "A gentle introduction to conformal prediction and distribution-free uncertainty quantification", arXiv:2107.07511.
  • V. Vovk, A. Gammerman, G. Shafer, Algorithmic Learning in a Random World, Springer (2005).
  • B. Peherstorfer, K. Willcox, "Data-driven operator inference for nonintrusive projection-based model reduction", CMAME 306 (2016).
  • J. S. Hesthaven, G. Rozza, B. Stamm, Certified Reduced Basis Methods for Parametrized PDEs, Springer (2016) (residual-based a-posteriori error estimators).

docs.title: Uncertainty and sensitivity studies on any model
docs.text:
Two questions every surrogate (or solver) raises before anyone uses its numbers: how far can I trust this prediction? and which parameters actually control it? PINNeAPPle answers both on any model that maps an (n, d) array of inputs to (n, m) outputs: a pp.zoo model, an ONNX graph, a solver wrapper or a closed form.

import pinneapple as pp
from pinneapple_analysis.study_models import StudyModel

model = StudyModel.from_zoo("heatsink_forced_mlp", outputs=["r_base_k_w"])   # also from_onnx(bytes), builtin("ishigami")
X_cal, y_cal = model.reference("cal")                                         # the model's own calibration split
X_test, y_test = model.reference("test")                                      # held out: never used to calibrate

study = pp.conformal_study(y_cal[:, 0], model.predict(X_cal)[:, 0], y_test[:, 0], model.predict(X_test)[:, 0],
                           alpha=0.1, scale_cal=model.predict(X_cal)[:, 0], scale_test=model.predict(X_test)[:, 0])
print(study.coverage, study.coverage_ci)            # measured on the 900 test designs, with its Wilson interval

docs.title: Uncertainty (pp.uncertainty)
docs.text:
Question API Interval with a coverage guarantee, measured on held-out data conformal_study(y_cal, pred_cal, y_test, pred_test, alpha, scale_cal=, scale_test=, group_by=) Uncertain inputs with distributions distributions.as_space([...]): uniform, normal, truncnormal, lognormal (median, gsd), triangular Propagate them through the model propagate_space(fn, space, n, method="mc" / "lhs" / "sobol", limits=) (pp.propagate_uncertainty) Cheap moments and Sobol indices for a smooth model with few inputs polynomial_chaos(fn, space, degree) with its leave-one-out Q2 Is this input inside the data the model learned from? ApplicabilityDomain.fit(X_ref, names, bounds).assess(X): inside / sparse / outside Which cases need the high-fidelity solver? route_cases(status, pred, lower, upper, tolerance=, limits=) + routing_summary

Conformal intervals are valid on average over data like the calibration data. Two reports keep that honest: the reliability list (measured coverage at several nominal levels) and the per-group coverage (group_by= an input or the prediction), which shows where a constant-width interval under-covers. Normalised scores (a scale per point: the prediction itself for a relative error, an ensemble spread) make the width follow the error.

The applicability gate uses the declared validity range (a model card's) and the k-nearest-neighbour distance in standardised inputs: a point is sparse when its 5th neighbour is farther than for 99 % of the reference points themselves (a hole in the data inside the range). The routing rule sends a case to the high-fidelity solver when it is outside or sparse, when its interval is wider than the tolerance the decision needs, or when its interval contains a decision limit.

docs.title: Sensitivity (pp.sensitivity)
docs.text:
Question API Share of output variance per input, with confidence intervals sobol_indices(fn, space, n, second_order=True) (pp.sobol_indices) Same, from runs done elsewhere (OpenFOAM, CalculiX, a campaign) saltelli_design(space, n, seed=) → run → sobol_from_runs(space, n, run_ids, Y, seed=) From an existing dataset, no designed experiment first_order_given_data(X, y) Cheap screening of many inputs morris(fn, space, r): mu*, sigma, r (d + 1) evaluations Shape of each effect, interactions effect_curves(fn, space): partial dependence + ICE Local gradient local_derivatives(fn, x0, torch_fn=): autodiff for torch models, central differences otherwise Which inputs can be fixed? freeze_recommendation(indices, threshold) and the direct check verify_freeze(fn, space, frozen)

The estimators are Saltelli (2010) for first order, Jansen (1999) for total and Saltelli (2002) for second order, with percentile-bootstrap intervals. tests/test_sensitivity.py checks them against the exact indices of the Ishigami and Sobol' G functions (pinneapple_analysis.sensitivity.testfunctions). An input is recommended for freezing only when the upper bound of its total index is below the threshold for every output; an estimate below the threshold with a wider interval is reported as inconclusive (more samples needed), never as freezable.

docs.title: Apps
docs.text:
• Engineering Sensitivity Lab (sensitivity.pinneapple.org): Sobol, Morris, effect curves, derivatives and the freeze recommendation for a model, solver runs or a dataset.
  • Engineering Uncertainty Lab (uncertainty.pinneapple.org): intervals, applicability alerts, the routing rule and propagation for a model and its data.

docs.title: Engineering Uncertainty Lab
docs.text:
Know when a prediction is reliable, and when the case must go to the high-fidelity solver. Day 15 of the apps series: https://uncertainty.pinneapple.org (source: apps/uncertainty_lab).

Pick a model (a pp.zoo model or an uploaded ONNX graph), its reference data, the cases you want to decide on, the uncertain inputs and the decision limits. The lab returns:

  • split-conformal intervals with their coverage measured on held-out data (Wilson interval, reliability across levels, coverage per region and per applicability gate; the raw ensemble interval for comparison when the model has one);
  • applicability alerts: outside the validity range, or inside it where the reference data are sparse;
  • a routing rule per case (surrogate or high-fidelity solver, with the reasons), checked against the heat-sink physics engine where the library has it;
  • propagation of uncertain inputs (Monte Carlo, Latin hypercube, Sobol; polynomial chaos when cheap), with the probability of meeting the limits with and without the model's own error.

On the heat-sink example the 90 % intervals cover 91.0 % (95 % CI 89.0–92.7 %) of the 900 held-out designs. Of eleven screened designs, the only one whose engine value falls outside its interval is the corner of the design space, which the gate flags as sparse and routes to the solver. On the airfoil example the model's own ensemble interval covers 75 % of held-out OpenFOAM runs at a 90 % nominal level; the conformal interval on the same spread covers 88 %.

Everything shown comes from one library call, pp.uncertainty.uncertainty_study (see Uncertainty and sensitivity studies on any model). Limits, methods and the API are in the app README.

docs.title: Periodic unit cell: an FNO over frequency × scan, and an equal-budget benchmark against Bayesian optimisation
docs.text:
An infinite phased array (a tightly coupled dipole array, TCDA) or a frequency-selective surface is simulated as one unit cell with periodic boundaries carrying the phase of the scan angle and a Floquet port. The quantity a wideband array designer watches is the active reflection coefficient at the element port over frequency and scan angle. This guide runs a campaign of cells in EMerge, trains a Fourier neural operator (FNO) from the cell parameters to the whole (frequency × scan) map, measures its error on cells it never saw, and compares, at the same number of solver calls, two ways of minimising the worst-case active reflection: an FNO plus an optimiser (verified by the solver), and Bayesian optimisation calling the solver directly.

Everything lives in pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.periodic; the example examples/use_cases/antennas/unit_cell_benchmark.py only calls it.

pip install emerge
python examples/use_cases/antennas/unit_cell_benchmark.py --quick                 # 3 cells, budget 6 (~6 min)
python examples/use_cases/antennas/unit_cell_benchmark.py --cells 64 --budget 24  # the pilot below

docs.title: The cell (tcda.TCDACell, generic)
docs.text:
A square cell of side a (22 mm by default); the ground plane at z = 0 (the bottom face of the cell); a dipole strip of width w at height h, fed across a gap s by a lumped port (100 Ω); its arms stop g/2 from the cell edge, so neighbouring dipoles couple capacitively across g; an optional dielectric superstrate (er_s, t_s) at d_s above the dipole; air up to 0.35 λ above the stack and a Floquet port. check() refuses a cell that lets a grating lobe in at the highest frequency and scan (a ≥ λ/(1 + sin θ)). The default ranges of the campaign (benchmark.CELL_RANGES) vary h, w, g, t_s and er_s.

EMerge details that matter: the periodic boundary conditions exist only after mw._initialize_bc_data(), so the scan angle is set after it; one mesh then serves every scan angle of a cell (the angle changes only the boundary phases and the port), and solving the angles in sequence on one model gives the same S11 as solving each alone (test). SuperLU is used.

docs.title: Measured
docs.text:
Pilot on 4 CPU cores (EMerge 2.8.9, SuperLU, res 0.1 λ), generic cell ranges, 3.0–6.0 GHz in 7 steps × scan θ = 0, 15, 30, 45° in the E-plane, LHS of 64 cells (results/unit_cell/campaign.csv):

  • Cost per cell (one process: one mesh, 4 scan solves of 7 frequencies): median 93 s, 35–327 s, peak memory 2.04 GB; 64 cells in 7 490 s of process time, all solved. About half of the cells ran while another study shared the cores.
  • Mesh error at this resolution (default cell, broadside): |Γ| at 3/4/5/6 GHz is −3.53/−6.65/−10.69/−18.35 dB at res 0.1 λ, −3.13/−6.19/−10.29/−21.94 dB at 0.07 λ and −2.77/−5.73/−9.80/−26.83 dB at 0.05 λ (52 s and 462 s for that run): about 0.5 dB per step away from deep nulls, more in them. The pilot compares methods on the same solver settings; its absolute |Γ| carries this mesh error.
  • FNO (from the 5 parameters to the 7 × 4 map of |Γ| in dB, 60 s of training on one thread, the last 16 cells never seen):
training cells held-out RMSE, every (f, θ) max abs error RMSE of the worst case per cell 12 4.58 dB 26.0 dB 0.49 dB 24 3.11 dB 18.3 dB 0.27 dB 48 2.26 dB 14.6 dB 0.22 dB

The pointwise error is dominated by the deep resonant nulls (their depth moves with the parameters); the worst-case active reflection over the band and scans, the quantity optimised below, is predicted to 0.2–0.5 dB. * Equal budget, 24 solver calls each, minimising the worst-case |Γ| over the band and scans:

strategy (24 solver calls each) best worst-case |Γ| (solver value) reached at call LHS of 20 cells alone (random search) −3.10 dB 3 LHS of 20 + FNO + optimiser over 4 000 candidates + 4 verifications −6.54 dB 21 (first verification) Bayesian optimisation on the solver −6.72 dB 19

On this 5-parameter problem the two strategies end within 0.2 dB of each other; Bayesian optimisation got there two calls earlier. The FNO ranked well but was pessimistic: its predictions for the 4 verified candidates were −4.31 to −4.38 dB, the solver gave −4.56 to −6.54 dB. What the FNO buys is the rest of the map: one trained model predicts the whole (frequency × scan) response of any cell in milliseconds, for other objectives too, while the Bayesian run answers only the question it was run for. A single seed and a 24-call budget: the ranking between the two is not established by this pilot. The run was interrupted once by a machine restart and resumed from the saved results (CLISimulator(resume=True)), with the same designs and the same values.

A one-thread FNO matters: with four threads competing with each other (or with a solver) the same FNO took 26 steps in 20 s instead of 2 421; fit_fno trains on one thread by default.

docs.title: What it would take to run 1,000 cells
docs.text: Measured here: a median of 93 s per cell for 7 frequencies × 4 scans at res 0.1 λ on 4 cores, one cell per process (peak 2.04 GB). At that rate 1,000 cells are about 26 hours of one 4-core machine, and the cells are independent: the runner's one-process-per-cell layout spreads over as many machines (or preemptible instances) as are available, a cell lost to a preemption costing one rerun. A finer mesh (0.05 λ, 462 s for one broadside run of 4 frequencies) multiplies the cost several times. No cloud price is quoted here.

docs.title: API
docs.text:
from pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.periodic import benchmark as bm
from pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.periodic.tcda import TCDACell, simulate

simulate(TCDACell(h=9), [3, 4.5, 6], [(0, 0), (30, 0)])           # rows of active reflection
table, sim = bm.campaign(64, freqs, scans, "runs/")               # DOE of cells, one process per cell
X, Y, tags = bm.to_arrays(table, list(bm.CELL_RANGES), freqs, scans)
predict, info = bm.fit_fno(X[:48], Y[:48], wall_s=60)            # FNO over the (f, scan) map
bm.heldout(predict, X[48:], Y[48:])                               # error on unseen cells
bm.equal_budget(bm.solver_from(sim, names, freqs, scans), bm.CELL_RANGES, budget=24)

docs.title: Red team / blue team for the validation checks
docs.text:
The check power matrix measures the checks against a fixed list of defects, which only shows that they catch the defects someone already thought of. The arena (pinneapple_analysis.validation.arena, issue #707) adds an adversary. A red team searches for wrong outputs that pass every check (escapes) and for correct outputs that fail (false alarms). A blue team then calibrates the checks with a stated false-alarm rate and strengthens them until every stored escape is caught. Escapes and false alarms are stored as regression cases, and CI replays them.

import pinneapple as pp

rep = pp.validate.arena("darcy_2d", budget="small", alpha=0.05)      # = arena.run_arena(...)
print(rep.to_markdown())        # per round: escapes, false alarms, mutation score, ROC/AUC, min. detectable magnitude
assert rep.passed, rep.failures()
rep.save_cases("cases/darcy_2d.json")

pinneapple check --arena-cases                    # replay the cases shipped with the library
pinneapple check --arena-cases cases/*.json       # or your own; exit 1 on a regression
python examples/validation_arena/run_arena.py     # full size on Darcy 2-D and Burgers 1-D

docs.title: Red team
docs.text:
• Mutation operators. These are the fault library of #697 (bias, scale, smoothing, noise, wrong boundary values, sign flips, out-of-range use, stale models) applied at every magnitude. The mutation score is the share of the mutants that matter (true relative error ≥ 10 %) which the defence rejects. This is the test-adequacy measure of mutation testing for deep learning (DeepCrime, Humbatova et al. 2021; MuFF, arXiv:2501.09846), with the checks as the tests. A mutant that matters and passes is an escape.
  • Search-based evasion. Each generator is a parametrised family of outputs. The search maximises the true error against the reference solver while every check stays under its threshold, using differential evolution (SciPy), CMA-ES (written from Hansen's tutorial, arXiv:1604.00772) or finite-difference L-BFGS-B (method=).
  • Physics-consistent attacks. These outputs solve a nearby problem exactly, so the residual stays small:
  • Darcy: a smooth change of log a (coefficient_field) or of f (source_field);
  • Burgers: another viscosity (viscosity), the exact initial condition followed by the evolution of a smoothed one (hard_ic_evolution, what a hard-constrained PINN with spectral bias returns), or rescaled time (time_warp).
  • False-alarm search. The search runs over correct cases from the verified solvers, with coefficient contrast, feature size, amplitude, viscosity and solver resolution varied inside the training envelope, and maximises the largest margin of the defence. The result is the most suspicious-looking correct case, which counts as a false alarm when it is rejected.

docs.title: Blue team
docs.text:
• Calibrated combined test. The clean calibration cases are split in two halves, A and B. Each check's scale s_j is its split-conformal quantile on A (pinneapple_analysis.uncertainty.conformal.conformal_quantile), with a floor of 1 % of its own tolerance. The combined statistic is T = max_j value_j / s_j, and its threshold is the split-conformal quantile of T on B. The probability that a new clean case is rejected by any check is then at most alpha_cal (Vovk et al. 2005; Angelopoulos & Bates, arXiv:2107.07511). This is the family-wise rate, so false alarms do not grow with the number of checks.
  • alpha_cal = safety × alpha, with safety = 0.5 by default, so that the rate measured on a finite held-out set stays under the stated alpha.
  • The guarantee needs ceil((n_B + 1)(1 - alpha_cal)) ≤ n_B, and Defence.alpha_guaranteed reports whether that holds.
  • Hardening. Stored false alarms are correct cases, so the threshold is raised just above them; this can only lower the false-alarm rate. While a stored escape still passes, the blue team adds the check from check_library(problem) that rejects the most remaining escapes after recalibration. The log records what was added and why.
  • Regression cases. Every escape and false alarm is saved with its case seed, variation, generator and parameters, together with the hardened thresholds. pinneapple check --arena-cases regenerates each case and requires escapes to be rejected and false alarms to pass.

docs.title: Results (seed 0, alpha = 0.01, 2 rounds, full budget)
docs.text:
Full budget: 400 clean calibration cases, 300 held-out clean cases, 3 base cases × 160 evaluations per generator, and 4 random fields × 80 evaluations for the false-alarm search. Regenerate with python examples/validation_arena/run_arena.py --rounds 2.

Darcy 2-D Burgers 1-D round-0 defence (hand-set tolerances) FD residual, boundary condition, bounds, training envelope FD residual, initial condition, bounds, training envelope escapes found at round 0 (true error ≥ 10 %, every check passes) 15 16 worst escape coefficient_field: 87 % true error time_warp (s = 0.5): 50 % true error mutation score, before → after 67.3 % → 100 % (419 mutants) 75.5 % → 100 % (351 mutants) held-out false-alarm rate, hand tolerances → combined test 1.33 % → 0.00 % (0.67 % after round 1) 0.00 % → 1.00 % worst false alarm (most suspicious correct case) margin −0.11, accepted margin −0.03, accepted check added by the blue team conservative residual on the solver stencil one-step re-integration residual stored escapes rejected after blue 15/15 16/16 escapes ≥ 10 % found at round 1 against the hardened defence 0 (largest accepted error 4.9 %) 0

How to read these results:

  • Round 0 shows that the default checks have real blind spots. A Darcy output solved for the wrong permeability field, or a Burgers solution at the wrong time, has a small finite-difference residual and the right boundary or initial condition. Every check accepts it, yet it is wrong by 50-87 %.
  • The strengthened checks close these gaps because they use the solver's own discretisation.
  • No correct case was rejected by the hand-set tolerances in the search. The held-out set did contain 4 correct Darcy cases (out of 300) that the hand-set tolerances flag.
  • The calibrated test states its rate:
  • Darcy stays under 1 % with a margin.
  • Burgers is at the bound (3 of 300). Its one-step residual is calibrated on correct cases solved at finer resolution, so the tail is real.

The report also lists, for every check and fault, the detection rate, the false-alarm rate, the ROC AUC over fault magnitude and the minimal detectable magnitude, before and after the round.

docs.title: External models
docs.text: audit_model(problem, predict) runs any model through the hardened defence shipped with the library and compares each output with the reference solver. predict(inputs, params) returns the field on the problem's grid (Darcy a → u on 32 × 32 cells, Burgers u0 → u(t, x)). The result lists the escapes (wrong outputs the defence accepts) and the accurate outputs it rejects. This is the hook for the FNO and MeshGraphNet models of the PhysicsNeMo trust experiment: wrap their inference as predict (PhysicsNeMo is not a dependency of PINNeAPPle, so this is not run in CI).

docs.title: Scope and limits
docs.text:
• Two problems with verified solvers. A check is only as strong as the discretisation it shares with the reference: the conservative residual flags correct solutions computed on a different grid at the level of the discretisation error, which is why it is calibrated rather than set to round-off.
  • The evasion search is local to its budget. "No escape found" means none within the stated evaluations, not none at all; the report says which.
  • The data-level arena (datasets rather than single outputs) is measured by the fault-injection matrix with the dataset checks; the conformal calibration covers the case-level checks.

docs.title: Validation gallery: one worked example per model family and per physics
docs.text:
examples/validation/ shows how to validate your kind of model on your kind of physics. Every example has the same structure:

  1. Train or load the model, with data from the library's reference solvers or the zoo.
  2. Run pp.validate.
  3. Read the trust card. validation.gallery.conclude writes report.json, trust_card.json, report.sarif and failure.json to examples/_out/validation/<example>/.
  4. Run pinneapple check in CI.
  5. See one real failure the checks catch, on a broken variant of the same model.

Everything runs on a CPU. CI runs the whole gallery at smoke size (.github/workflows/validation-gallery.yml; under 3 minutes on a 4-core machine) and fails if an example stops catching its failure. Run one example with python examples/validation/<file>.py [--full].
