docs.title: What holds
docs.text:
• Exactness everywhere.
  • Exact condensation, block-wise or algebraic, reproduces the global solve to round-off on every operator tried:
    • symmetric conduction with conductivity contrasts up to 1e5, anisotropy 100 and 0.01, 1-µm layers, alternating pitch: 1e-9 to 6e-8 K;
    • non-symmetric advection–diffusion up to Pe_b = 1000: 1e-13;
    • Stokes saddle points with one pressure unknown per block: 1e-12;
    • Picard-linearised Navier–Stokes and conjugate heat transfer up to Re 100: 1e-14;
    • meshless matrices: 1e-9.
  • So the algebra is never the problem.
  • Reduced interfaces degrade gracefully with physics. Contrast, anisotropy and thin layers change the m = 12 error by at most 2.2×.
  • For advection–diffusion the modes needed for 1 % grow only from 2 (Pe_b ≤ 10) to 3 (Pe_b 100–1000).
  • For Stokes 2 modes suffice, and for the Re 100 cold plate 3.
  • Recirculation crossing block faces is real but small at these Reynolds numbers: 4.5 % of the face flux at Re 100.
  • Far field (T1).
  • At fixed m the error grows about 3× for every 4× more blocks: m = 12 gives 1.4 mK at 256 blocks, 16 mK at 1,024, 52 mK at 4,096 and 0.21 K at 16,384.
  • The m needed for 0.1 K went 6 → 12 → 12 → 24. That is exactly the pre-registered limit of 2×, on a coarse m grid.
  • The exact correction fixes it at moderate cost:
    • PCG iterations to 1 mK are 2, 8, 8 and 32;
    • time to 1 mK is 5 s against 481 s for one fine AMG solve at 4,096 blocks.

docs.title: What breaks, and why
docs.text:
1. Cost whenever blocks stop repeating (T4, T5, T6, T7, F1, F3).
  2. The method's advantage is reuse. With random variants the memoised hierarchy is slower than the flat condensation from V = 4 on (20 s against 4.9 s; 61 s against 6.6 s at V = 256), because almost no subtree repeats.
  3. With every block distinct (T4), the exact path costs more than the fine solve. At 32 × 32 it did not fit in memory: one dense block model per distinct block.
  4. Non-linear material laws make every block distinct at every Picard iteration: 4.4× (T6) and 4.5× (T7) slower than the fine non-linear solve, at the same accuracy.
  5. A numerically computed velocity field differs bit by bit between "periodic" blocks. Content-identical reuse then finds nothing (80 of 80, 44 of 44 blocks distinct), and condensed Picard is about 2× slower than the full one (F3).
  6. Cost against a sparse direct solver in 2-D (F2, M4).
  7. Even with 9 distinct of 288 blocks, condensing a 2-D Stokes system was 4.6× slower than one sparse direct solve.
  8. The factorisation of the separator dominates (its dense blocks fill in).
  9. In 2-D, nested dissection is already near-optimal, so there is little left to win for a single right-hand side.
  10. Sub-pitch features the modes cannot represent (T8).
  11. A single-cell power spike gives 1.66 K with 12 modes. The other adversarial maps (checkerboards, noise, corners) stay below 10 mK.
  12. The estimator is not fooled: its effectivity stays in 1.4–1.8. It flags the problem, and refinement or the exact correction has to act on it.
  13. Heterogeneous blocks with base-stack modes (T4).
  14. On a package where every block differs (voids, delamination ×30), the m-mode interfaces are off by 0.46 K at 16 × 16 blocks (0.68 K at 8 × 8). On uniform packages they are off by 2–16 mK.
  15. The learned-operator study of the track 1 report compared the learned path with all-exact blocks on the same m-mode interfaces, not with the fine solution. Its 4 mK agreement did not include this 0.68 K.
  16. The generic algebraic layer in 3-D (T6, T7, T10 at 16 × 16).
  17. The separator factorisation ran out of memory.
  18. The port-based block condensation of pinneapple_condense.substructure does not have this problem: it keeps faces separate.
  19. The generic layer is a correctness tool here, not a fast one.
  20. Meshless (M1–M4).
  21. RBF-FD converges for advection–diffusion but is 28–32× less accurate than FV at equal unknowns at low Pe. It is only competitive at Pe_b = 100.
  22. GFDM is unstable (errors up to 1e9).
  23. Collocated meshless Stokes does not converge reliably: RBF-FD goes 46 %, 50 %, 18 %; GFDM decreases but stagnates at 35 %.
  24. The FV-at-interfaces hybrid removes the interface failure of the report (its error is now spread over the band and the points alike), but stays 6–8× worse than FV everywhere. Its largest errors sit at the meshless points near the domain boundary and the band edge.
  25. Meshless blocks condense exactly and, with deterministic neighbour selection, are found identical. Condensation is still slower than one direct solve.
  26. Prior + exception patches on transport (E1).
  27. On advection-dominated fields the residual of a coarse prior is no better than random at choosing where to solve, and its selected blocks overlap the true top-error blocks by at most 0.69.
  28. The error of a coarse prior is carried downstream, away from where the residual is large.
  29. In the thermal case of track 1c (diffusive, local defects) the same method worked.

docs.title: Where the idea stands
docs.text:
Condensation is exact and robust as algebra. Its accuracy-per-mode survives contrast, anisotropy, thin layers, moderate Péclet and Reynolds numbers. Its growth with package size is real but controllable (m doubling per 16× blocks, or the exact correction).

Its speed comes only from repetition, and the campaign shows how fragile that is: - random variants; - non-linear material laws; - computed advection fields; - 2-D problems where sparse direct solvers are already efficient.

Each of these removes the gain, sometimes entirely. A practical method needs: - identical-up-to-tolerance block matching, not bit-identical (computed velocities, temperature-dependent k); - parametric block operators (the learned path, with interface modes trained for heterogeneity); - H-matrix arithmetic for the separators.

None of these is implemented here.

docs.title: Deviations from the pre-registration
docs.text:
Listed here instead of changing the hypotheses above.

  1. F0, Poiseuille. The pre-registered criterion expected an exact parabola (1e-6). The ghost-cell wall treatment is O(h²) for curved profiles; the observed order is 2. That sub-criterion is met (refuted) as written.
  2. F2 / F3 metric. The velocity inlet fixes the flow rate, so the pressure drop at that flow rate (the equivalent permeability measure) replaces the flow-rate error.
  3. T7 law. "β such that R_c doubles over the range" is implemented as a linear rise from R_0 at the coolest to 2 R_0 at the hottest interface temperature of the linear solution, saturating at 2 R_0.
  4. An unsaturated law ran away: R up → T up → R up.
  5. A first run took the range from the die-top cells instead of the interface the law is applied to. That made the law inert, and it was corrected and re-run.
  6. Reduced scales (memory).
  7. T4 at 16 × 16 instead of 32 × 32 (killed at 13 GB).
  8. T6, T7 and T10 at 8 × 8 instead of 16 × 16: the separator factorisation of the generic layer ran out of memory. Those failures are kept as results.
  9. T1 has no m = 48 point at 16,384 blocks (beyond 15 GB).
  10. T4 "exact path" is the condensation of every block followed by the PCG correction to the fine solution. The all-exact-blocks solve of the learned study still uses m-mode interfaces (item 4 of "What breaks").
  11. Implementation defects found and fixed during the runs; affected studies re-run.
  12. The block count of the algebraic partition counted unknowns on the far boundary as a new block (F1–F3 re-run; verdicts unchanged).
  13. The meshless k-nearest-neighbour search broke ties differently in different blocks. M4 first measured 16 of 16 blocks distinct and a speedup of 0.26; after the fix, 9 of 16 distinct and 0.16.
  14. E1 budgets select a fraction of blocks; with one ring of halo the solved fraction is larger. It is reported as such.

docs.title: Immersed analysis on raw geometry (issue #966)
docs.text:
The question: can PINNeAPPle analyse a part straight from its geometry (a signed distance, a voxel mask, an STL) without generating a conforming mesh, accurately enough and fast enough to matter? The earlier meshless attempt (RBF-FD and GFDM in condensation_falsification.md, M1–M4) lost to finite volumes at equal unknowns. This part tests the other well-established family: immersed / finite cell methods.

Every number below was measured in this container (4 cores, one thread per run, Python 3.13, NumPy / SciPy, pyamg 5.3, gmsh 4.15, CalculiX 2.21) by the commands given with each table.

docs.title: Method (pinneapple_simulation.immersed)
docs.text:
• Geometry: any level set phi(X) (negative inside). Sources: analytic SDFs and their CSG (ball, box, cylinder, torus, annulus, |, &, -), any vectorised SDF (e.g. pinneapple_design.geometry.gen.sdf_shapes), a voxel mask (VoxelGeometry: Euclidean distance transforms of material and void, interpolated), or an STL (STLGeometry). For the STL, the inside test is the generalised winding number (Jacobson et al. 2013) with a dipole tree (Barill et al. 2018), and the distance is the exact point-triangle distance to candidates from a KD-tree of surface samples. In the near band of a watertight, consistently oriented surface, the sign comes from angle-weighted pseudonormals (Bærentzen & Aanæs 2005); there it is identical to the winding number (0 mismatches on 200 000 points) and about 4× cheaper. A surface with holes uses the winding number everywhere.
  • Discretisation: uniform background grid, Q1 or Q2 Lagrange elements; unknowns only on the active cells.
  • Cut cells: adaptive octree, depth levels (default 2 for Q1, 3 for Q2). Leaves still cut are split into Kuhn simplices and clipped by the level set. The surface points are put on the true surface by regula falsi. The fine rule of each cut cell is compressed by moment fitting onto (2p+1)^d Gauss points, which is exact for the stiffness and mass integrands (Q_2p). The cut-cell matrices are then one matrix product.
  • Small cuts: ghost penalty on the faces of cut cells (Burman 2010; coefficient 0.1 for Q1, 0.01 for Q2), or the finite cell method's fictitious material α = 1e-6 (Parvizian, Düster & Rank 2007), or none. The condition number is computed on request (Lanczos plus shift-invert, raw and Jacobi-scaled).
  • Boundary conditions: Nitsche for temperatures. The penalty is β k / h with ghost penalty, or comes from a per-cell eigenvalue problem without it (Embar, Dolbow & Harari 2010). Heat flux and convection use surface quadrature on the clipped facets. Conditions are selected by where(X, n).
  • Checks returned with every solve: an energy balance (heat generated against heat leaving through each condition, using Nitsche's consistent flux) and, on request, the condition number.

docs.title: Sphere and cylinder in closed form
docs.text:
Uniform generation q, convection h on the surface. Sphere: T = T∞ + qR/3h + q(R² − r²)/6k. Finite cylinder with convection on the mantle and adiabatic caps: T = T∞ + qR/2h + q(R² − r²)/4k (Incropera et al., §3.5).

Case Order n Unknowns L2 rel H1 rel sphere Q1 6, 12, 24, 48 350 … 69 092 3.45e-3, 7.40e-4, 1.58e-4, 3.56e-5 2.12e-1 … 2.68e-2 (rate 1.0) sphere Q2 4, 8, 16, 24 879 … 74 231 7.32e-5, 1.92e-5, 4.74e-6, 2.10e-6 4.21e-4 … 2.15e-5 cylinder Q1 6, 12, 24, 48 L2 rates 2.31, 2.38, 1.59 H1 rates 0.97, 0.98, 0.99 cylinder Q2 4, 8, 16, 24 847 … 70 839 4.48e-4, 2.37e-4, 1.17e-4, 8.35e-5 1.63e-2 … 6.12e-3

Two measured limitations:

  • Geometry-limited Q2. The exact sphere field is quadratic, so Q2 can represent it exactly. What remains is the O((h/2^depth)²) error of the clipped surface, and the L2 rate is 2.0, not 3.
  • Sharp edges. On the cylinder, Q2 drops to an L2 rate of about 1. A manufactured Dirichlet field on the same cylinder also loses its rate at the finest grid (L2 rates 2.93, 0.76). The level set has a kink at the rim, the linear clipping inside a leaf chamfers it, and the facets of the chamfer take the mantle or the cap condition by their normal. Edge-preserving clipping (one level set per smooth face) is the known remedy; it is not implemented here.

docs.title: Small cuts and conditioning
docs.text:
2-D manufactured case on a disk (n = 10). The grid is placed so that the disk pokes offset × h past a grid line, which leaves slivers in the cells it enters. Command: verification.conditioning(order).

offset order smallest cut fraction κ, none κ, FCM (Jacobi-scaled) κ, ghost (Jacobi-scaled) L2 rel, none / FCM / ghost 0.1 Q1 3.3e-04 1.1e+09 1.2e+08 (3.9e+01) 3.3e+02 (2.5e+01) 9.8e-03 / 9.8e-03 / 1.2e-02 0.01 Q1 4.1e-06 3.8e+13 8.5e+08 (6.1e+01) 3.1e+02 (2.4e+01) 9.5e-03 / 9.5e-03 / 1.2e-02 0.001 Q1 4.2e-08 2.3e+18 2.2e+09 (2.8e+01) 2.8e+02 (2.4e+01) 9.6e-03 / 9.6e-03 / 1.2e-02 0.0001 Q1 4.2e-10 singular 4.4e+09 (2.8e+01) 2.6e+02 (2.4e+01) 9.6e-03 / 9.6e-03 / 1.2e-02 0.1 Q2 3.3e-04 singular 2.7e+08 (1.7e+05) 3.7e+04 (2.6e+02) 3.1e-04 / 3.1e-04 / 4.3e-04 0.01 Q2 4.1e-06 singular 1.2e+09 (3.5e+05) 6.3e+04 (2.8e+02) 3.1e-04 / 3.1e-04 / 4.4e-04 0.001 Q2 4.2e-08 1.8e+23 5.7e+09 (8.6e+03) 6.4e+04 (2.9e+02) 3.1e-04 / 3.1e-04 / 4.5e-04 0.0001 Q2 4.2e-10 singular 1.5e+10 (5.2e+02) 6.2e+04 (2.9e+02) 3.1e-04 / 3.1e-04 / 4.5e-04

Without stabilisation, Q2 is numerically singular. The finite cell method keeps the solution accurate, but the raw condition number grows to 1e8–1e10. The ghost penalty keeps it bounded and independent of the cut: about 3e2 for Q1 and 6e4 for Q2 (2.4e1 and 2.9e2 after Jacobi scaling). Its cost is the error: 25 % above FCM for Q1, 40–45 % for Q2.

The two coefficients were chosen together. For Q2 a ghost coefficient of 0.1 gives about 4× the FCM error. With 0.01 and the Nitsche penalty β = 40, the matrix was indefinite at offset 0.01 (two negative eigenvalues), because the weak ghost penalty no longer controls the gradient on the sliver. β = 100 is positive definite at every offset from 0.3 to 1e-4 (tests/test_immersed.py::test_ghost_nitsche_matrix_stays_positive_definite_on_slivers). The Q2 defaults are ghost 0.01 and β = 100. Every Q2 table in this report was measured with them; the convection cases have no Nitsche term and do not depend on β.

docs.title: Other geometry inputs
docs.text:
Sphere with convection, Q1 and Q2 at h = R/8 (tests/test_immersed.py, measured once here):

Input Volume error L2 rel (Q1 / Q2) Quadrature time (Q1 / Q2) SDF −2.3e-4 3.8e-4 / 4.7e-6 1.2 / 5.3 s STL (icosphere, 20 480 triangles) −7.7e-4 (faceting) 4.2e-4 / 4.4e-5 8.3 / 32.4 s Voxels (R/40) −5.7e-4 1.1e-3 / 9.7e-4 0.7 / 4.2 s

The STL and voxel errors are dominated by the input itself: the facets of the icosphere, and the staircase of the voxels smoothed over one voxel. STL quadrature is 6× slower than the SDF because every level-set value is a nearest-triangle query. In the near band the pseudonormal sign brought it down from 116 s to 32 s for Q2; the winding number alone was 27 of 36 s in a Q1 profile.

docs.title: Equal accuracy against conforming FEM
docs.text:
Command: python -m pinneapple_simulation.immersed.compare --parts sphere_mms sphere --out DIR. Raw rows are in immersed/compare_results.json. Same part, same exact field, one thread.

  • Conforming: P1 / P2 tetrahedra from gmsh (P2 nodes on the CAD sphere), solved by the same Python assembly and the same linear solver: SuperLU up to 3e5 non-zeros, otherwise CG with smoothed-aggregation AMG. CalculiX 2.21 (C3D10) runs on the identical P2 mesh. It agrees with the internal P2: L2 3.0e-5 against 2.8e-5 at h = 0.2. Its error stops falling near 1e-6 at the two finest meshes, which looks like the output precision of the .frd file.
  • Times: each method's geometry phase (cut-cell quadrature for immersed, gmsh meshing and optimisation for conforming) plus assembly and solve. The energy-balance check is left out for both methods.
  • Equal accuracy: log-log interpolation between measured runs only; targets outside the measured range are not reported.

docs.title: Verdict (part 1, steady heat)
docs.text:
Measured on two parts, a sphere with a smooth field and a sphere with generation and convection.

Immersed wins where: - Unknowns, smooth non-polynomial fields: Q2 reaches 1e-4 with 1.73e4 unknowns against 3.27e4 for conforming P2. The Cartesian grid spends fewer nodes on the same volume. - Raw geometry: an STL (winding number), a voxel mask or an SDF is solved directly, with no meshing step and no meshing failure mode. A surface with 10 missing triangles still gets the right inside test. - Conditioning: with the ghost penalty, κ stays at 3e2 (Q1) / 6e4 (Q2) for cut fractions down to 4e-10. - Matching low order: Q1 vs P1 at 1e-3 on the convection sphere is a draw (0.50 s vs 0.66 s, similar unknowns).

Immersed loses where: - Wall time at equal accuracy on clean CAD: 1.2–1.8× slower than conforming P2 on the smooth field (6.45 vs 5.50 s at 1e-4, 1.38 vs 0.77 s at 1e-3). No meshing time is saved there: the Python cut-cell quadrature took as long as gmsh's compiled meshing (3.3 s vs 2.6 s). - Fields conforming P2 represents exactly: on the quadratic sphere field, immersed Q2 is geometry-limited (L2 rate 2.0). It needs 3.5× the unknowns and 7× the time of P2 or CalculiX to reach 1e-5. - Sharp edges with a change of boundary condition: on the cylinder rim, Q2 falls to L2 rate ≈ 1 (8.4e-5 at 7e4 unknowns). Meshing is not the bottleneck there; edge-preserving clipping would be needed. - STL input cost: 6× the SDF quadrature time (32 s for Q2 at h = R/8 on a 20 480-triangle sphere).

Parts whose meshing is not trivial (an STL heat sink and an STL bracket), elasticity and transient heat: below.

docs.title: Part 2: linear elasticity and two STL parts
Elasticity verification
docs.text:
immersed.solve_elasticity reuses the discretisation, the stabilisation and the Nitsche machinery. Displacements can be imposed on all components or a subset; loads are tractions, pressures, or a total force spread over the area the selector finds (Force). Every solve returns an equilibrium check: applied loads against the reactions computed from Nitsche's consistent flux. Commands: verification.elastic_convergence(verification.elastic_manufactured(dim), order, ns) and verification.solve_elastic_case(verification.lame_sphere(), n, order).

docs.title: Two parts given only as STL: a heat sink and a bracket
docs.text:
immersed.parts builds both parts in gmsh's OpenCASCADE kernel and writes them as STL. The STL is the only geometry either method sees: - the immersed solver reads it with STLGeometry (winding number); - the conforming solver turns it into a volume mesh with gmsh (tet_fem.occ_stl: classify the facets, rebuild the surfaces, mesh).

Each run is compared with a fine conforming P2 run on the same STL, at 3000 interior points (≥ 0.3 mm inside) and at one probe point. Command: parts.study(name, plan, reference, out_dir). The study is checkpointed: each run is appended to <name>.jsonl, and an interrupted study resumes. Raw rows: immersed/heat_sink.jsonl and immersed/bracket.jsonl. Times are one thread; compute = geometry phase (quadrature, or gmsh meshing from the STL) + assembly + solve.

  • Heat sink. Aluminium (k = 205 W/m K): a 40 × 40 × 4 mm base with 7 fins, each 1.5 mm thick and 20 mm high. A 15 × 15 mm chip under the centre puts in 20 W (HeatInput, spread over the area each method finds there). Every other surface has h = 25 W/m² K to air at 25 °C. Reference: P2 at 1 mm (139 630 unknowns).
  • Bracket. Steel L-bracket, two 60 × 40 × 6 mm flanges with a 4 mm inner fillet. Two 6 mm bolt holes are clamped, and 500 N pulls down on the arm's end face (Force). Reference: P2 at 1.5 mm (217 131 unknowns).

Both selectors had to apply exact totals. With per-point selection, the rounded edges of the end face lost 8 % of the bracket load (461 N instead of 500 N). With per-face selection, the conforming meshes changed the chip power from mesh to mesh, and their errors did not converge.

  • Locking. Linear elements lock in bending on a 6 mm plate, conforming P1 and immersed Q1 alike (12–49 % error).
  • Q2 vs P2. Q2 removes the locking but needs 4× the unknowns and 20× the time of P2. A uniform grid spends cells on the bracket's bounding box, and its 3-D Q2 couplings (125 nodes) make the matrix much denser than P2's.

docs.title: Part 3: transient heat
docs.text:
immersed.transient.solve_transient_heat: ρc ∂T/∂t − div(k ∇T) = f with the θ scheme (θ = 1 backward Euler, θ = 1/2 Crank–Nicolson). The steady operator and loads are reused; the mass matrix comes from the same cut-cell rule. With the ghost penalty, a mass ghost term γ_M ρc h² (γ_M = 0.01) controls small cuts. Time-dependent sources f(X, t) and conditions bcs(t) are supported. The matrix is factorised once.

  • Initial field. The first version projected T0 in L2. That left round-off-sized noise on small-cut unknowns, which Crank–Nicolson never damps: the error stayed at 1.4e-3 for every Δt without the mass ghost term, and at 1e-5 with it. Nodal interpolation removed the floor.
  • Manufactured solution in time. 2-D disk, Q2, n = 80, t ∈ [0, 0.5], u = e^{−t} sin 2x cos 3y + x², Dirichlet:

docs.title: Verdict (all parts)
docs.text:
Measured on a sphere, a cylinder, a torus, a Lamé shell, an STL heat sink and an STL bracket.

Immersed wins: - Raw geometry in, no meshing failure mode. An SDF, a voxel mask or an STL is solved directly. An STL with holes still gets a robust inside test. No geometry here failed for either method, but gmsh's high-order optimiser did abort the whole process on one coarse STL mesh, which the immersed path cannot do. - Smooth parts and smooth fields: fewer unknowns than conforming P2 at equal accuracy (sphere, manufactured field: 1.73e4 vs 3.27e4 at 1e-4), with optimal rates in L2 and H1 for heat, elasticity and time stepping. - Small cuts: with the ghost penalty, the conditioning stays bounded whatever the cut (κ ≈ 3e2 / 6e4 for Q1 / Q2 down to cut fractions of 4e-10).

Immersed loses: - Wall time, everywhere measured: 1.2–1.8× on the smooth sphere, about 7× when P2 represents the field exactly, 20× on the bracket and more than 50× on the heat sink at equal accuracy. - Meshing time saved is negative here. The Python cut-cell quadrature took as long as or longer than gmsh's meshing of the same geometry in every case: 3.3 s vs 2.6 s on the sphere; 9–52 s vs 1–3 s on the STL heat sink. - Sharp edges: - with a change of condition across them (cylinder rim), Q2 drops to L2 rate ≈ 1; - with convection on all of them (heat sink), the chamfered edges remove 1.3 % of the area and the temperature plateaus near 1 %; the error converges only like h/2^depth. - Thin-walled parts in bending: Q1 locks (as P1 does). Q2 works but needs 4× the unknowns of P2, because a uniform grid cannot grade towards thin walls.

What would change the verdict, and was not built here: - edge-preserving clipping (one level set per smooth face, or exact clipping by the STL triangles); - local or adaptive grid refinement (hanging nodes, an octree background); - compiled quadrature, since the Python octree is the time sink.

On the measurements here, conforming P2 is faster and at least as accurate on every part that gmsh can mesh. The immersed path's remaining case is input that cannot be meshed well or at all: voxel data, defective STL, geometry sweeps that change topology. None of these was measured here; the evidence for them is the method's design (no mesh to fail), not a benchmark.

docs.title: Adaptive Physics Condensation: geometry-independent thermal models of chip packages
docs.text:
Research line, track 1 of 3 (condensation). Tracks 2 (a physics query engine) and 3 (verification of what a PINN has actually learned) build on this one and are reported separately.

Code: pinneapple_condense. Benchmark: examples/physics_condensation. Every number below was measured in this repository's CI container (4 cores, 15 GB RAM, no GPU). Each comes from results/*.json of that example. Each study ran in a fresh Python process, and peak memory is that process's peak resident set size. Nothing below is quoted from another source unless it carries a citation.

docs.title: 1. The question
docs.text:
A 2.5D/3D package has 10^4 to 10^6 microbumps, TSVs and C4 bumps, and a fab-resolution CAD model has up to 10^9 polygons. An engineer asks only a few questions of it:

  • the peak junction temperature;
  • the temperature of each junction;
  • how the heat divides between the lid and the board, and through each bump;
  • the thermal resistance.

Can the cost of answering them track the physical complexity of the package rather than its element count:

  • how many distinct kinds of structure it has;
  • how far heat spreads;
  • how many independent power patterns it sees?

Three objects get confused here:

what it is what drives its size geometry the solids and their materials number of features (bumps, vias, layers) discretisation the unknowns a solver needs to resolve the geometry and the fields features x cells per feature fields / observables temperatures and fluxes, and the few numbers asked of them the physics: diffusion length, sources, contrasts

A fine mesh couples all three. The cost of a direct solve grows with the discretisation even when 10^5 bumps are identical and the answer is a handful of numbers. Homogenisation (Keff) cuts the discretisation by replacing the geometry with averages. It also erases whatever happens below the averaging scale, and Section 4.6 measures what it erases. This work keeps the exact fine operator and condenses it:

  1. every repeated block is reduced once to its interface operator;
  2. identical blocks, and identical arrangements of blocks, share that work;
  3. interior fields are rebuilt only where they are asked for;
  4. an error estimate decides where the reduction has to be undone.

docs.title: 2. Related work
docs.text:
How the references were checked. The network in this container blocked direct access to publisher pages, DOI resolvers, arXiv, patent offices and the vendor's site; only a web-search tool worked. Each reference below was checked against search-result records of publisher, repository or index pages. Where a field could not be confirmed it is marked.

Homogenisation and multiscale methods. Periodic homogenisation gives effective coefficients from cell problems (Bensoussan, Lions and Papanicolaou 1978). For two-phase composites, the Hashin–Shtrikman bounds bracket the effective conductivity (Hashin and Shtrikman, J. Appl. Phys. 33 (1962) 3125, doi:10.1063/1.1728579). Our Keff baseline uses the lower bound in plane and the parallel rule through the layer. Multiscale finite elements (Hou and Wu, J. Comput. Phys. 134 (1997) 169, doi:10.1006/jcph.1997.5682) and the heterogeneous multiscale method (E and Engquist, Commun. Math. Sci. 1 (2003) 87) keep fine-scale information in coarse basis functions or local solves.

Substructuring and component mode synthesis. - Static condensation onto interfaces and component mode synthesis go back to Hurty (AIAA J. 3 (1965) 678; DOI from citing lists only) and Craig and Bampton (AIAA J. 6 (1968) 1313, doi:10.2514/3.4741). - Characteristic constraint modes reduce the interface itself (Castanier, Tan and Pierre, AIAA J. 39 (2001) 1182; DOI not confirmed). - The closest prior work to ours is the static-condensation reduced basis element method. Huynh, Knezevic and Patera (ESAIM: M2AN 47 (2013) 213, doi:10.1051/m2an/2012022) and Eftang and Patera (Int. J. Numer. Methods Eng. 96 (2013) 269, doi:10.1002/nme.4543) introduce port reduction with a posteriori error estimation. - Our reduced interfaces with a residual-based estimate follow the same idea. The differences are the port basis (load-informed POD, Section 3.3), the nested memoised hierarchy, and the learned-operator fallback. - Load-dependent Ritz vectors (Wilson, Yuan and Dickens, Earthquake Eng. Struct. Dyn. 10 (1982) 813; details from a citing list) motivate building interface modes from loads rather than from an eigenproblem.

Fast direct solvers. - Nested dissection orders a mesh so that elimination proceeds through separators (George, SIAM J. Numer. Anal. 10 (1973) 345, doi:10.1137/0710032). - Hierarchical matrices (Hackbusch, Computing 62 (1999) 89, doi:10.1007/s006070050015) and HSS multifrontal solvers (Xia, Chandrasekaran, Gu and Li, SIAM J. Matrix Anal. Appl. 31 (2009) 1382, doi:10.1137/09074543X) compress the dense separator Schur complements, whose off-diagonal blocks have low numerical rank. - The fast multipole method exploits the same far-field smoothness for particle interactions (Greengard and Rokhlin, J. Comput. Phys. 73 (1987) 325, doi:10.1016/0021-9991(87)90140-9). - Our hierarchy is nested dissection on reduced interfaces, with memoisation of identical subtrees. Section 4.4 measures the off-diagonal ranks of its top operator, but the H-matrix arithmetic is not implemented.

Model reduction. Projection-based parametric model reduction is surveyed by Benner, Gugercin and Willcox (SIAM Rev. 57 (2015) 483, doi:10.1137/130932715). Hyper-reduction of nonlinear terms uses the empirical interpolation method (Barrault, Maday, Nguyen and Patera, C. R. Math. 339 (2004) 667, doi:10.1016/j.crma.2004.08.006) and DEIM (Chaturantabut and Sorensen, SIAM J. Sci. Comput. 32 (2010) 2737, doi:10.1137/090766498). The learned block operator of Section 3.5 is a parametric POD of the operator entries with a Gaussian-process regression, the existing pinneapple_neural.architectures.rom.parametric.ParametricPOD.

Chip thermal models and neural operators. - Compact thermal models such as HotSpot (Skadron et al., ISCA 2003, pp. 2–13, doi:10.1109/ISCA.2003.1206984) and 3D-ICE (Sridhar et al., ICCAD 2010, pp. 463–470, doi:10.1109/ICCAD.2010.5653749) use coarse grids or layer-homogenised resistances. - Neural operators learn the map from power maps to fields: - FNO (Li et al., ICLR 2021, arXiv:2010.08895); - DeepONet (Lu et al., Nat. Mach. Intell. 3 (2021) 218, doi:10.1038/s42256-021-00302-5); - for 3D ICs, DeepOHeat (Liu, Li, Hu, Yu, Shiau, Ai, Zeng and Zhang, DAC 2023, arXiv:2302.12949); - physics-enforced networks for full-chip thermal analysis (Chen, Lu, Jin and Tan, ICCAD 2023; DOI not confirmed). - These learn the whole field map, so their error is not bounded by a solver. Here learning is confined to block operators, inside an exact algebraic assembly with a check against the exact operator.

PINN failure modes (they motivate track 3): spectral bias and stiffness of the loss landscape (Wang, Teng and Perdikaris, SIAM J. Sci. Comput. 43 (2021) A3055, doi:10.1137/20M1318043; Wang, Yu and Perdikaris, J. Comput. Phys. 449 (2022) 110768, doi:10.1016/j.jcp.2021.110768), and failures at higher coefficients (Krishnapriyan et al., NeurIPS 2021, arXiv:2109.01050). PINNs: Raissi, Perdikaris and Karniadakis, J. Comput. Phys. 378 (2019) 686, doi:10.1016/j.jcp.2018.10.045.

Reference company (ideas only). Vinci (getvinci.ai; formerly Vinci4D) sells physics AI for semiconductor packaging, thermal and thermo-elastic. What search-result text of their pages and press releases says (the pages themselves could not be loaded from this container):

  • "up to 1000x faster than conventional simulation tools" (Business Wire, 2 Dec 2025);
  • a homepage table of 20 s against 2 h for a commercial FEA solver at 117,440,512 DOF;
  • no manual meshing;
  • research notes that report results both without homogenisation and with per-layer Keff tensors.

These are the company's own claims; they are not verified here and are not compared with our numbers. The brief for this work names a patent application, WO2026064513A1, as theirs, describing:

  • a latent encoding of geometry and a separate topology representation;
  • boundary conditions, materials and sources as inputs;
  • a field-prediction model;
  • verification or correction by the governing equations or a solver.

We could not retrieve the document: patent offices were unreachable and searches returned no record. Title, applicant and claims are therefore not verified. The design here was not taken from it: there is no geometry latent and no learned field predictor. Learning is confined to block operators inside an exact assembly. Whether this work is free to operate against that application, or anything else, needs an IP specialist; nothing here is a freedom-to-operate opinion.

docs.title: 3.1 Benchmark and reference solver
docs.text:
pinneapple_condense.package builds a synthetic multilayer package from bottom to top:

layer thickness contents organic substrate 200 µm — C4 bumps in underfill 60 µm — silicon interposer with copper TSVs 100 µm — microbumps in underfill 20 µm — die 100 µm power on its bottom cell row (flip chip) TIM 30 µm contact resistance 5e-6 m²K/W on both faces copper lid 500 µm Robin cooling h = 2e4 W/m²K on top
  • The board side has h = 1e3 W/m²K. Laterally the package is a square array of 40 µm unit cells (blocks), each with one microbump, one TSV and one C4 bump, all square in plan.
  • Materials are representative: Si k = 148, Cu k = 401, solder 58, underfill 0.5, TIM 4, substrate 0.8 W/m/K. The copper values match Incropera et al.'s Table A.1 (as transcribed); the silicon value is a handbook value (Wikipedia gives ~149). The package is synthetic and is not a product.
  • One block is 8 x 8 x 23 = 1,472 cells.
  • Power maps are a uniform background (40 %) plus Gaussian hotspots, at a mean of 1e6 W/m² (100 W/cm²).
  • The reference (fv) is a cell-centred finite-volume scheme: harmonic face conductances and contact resistances in series. It is solved by sparse LU up to 6e4 unknowns and by AMG-preconditioned CG (pyamg) to a relative residual of 1e-11 above that.
  • With all heat generated on the active row and non-negative power, the discrete maximum principle for this M-matrix scheme puts Tmax on that row (Varga, Matrix Iterative Analysis, 2nd ed., Springer 2000; Ciarlet and Raviart, Comput. Methods Appl. Mech. Eng. 2 (1973) 17, doi:10.1016/0045-7825(73)90019-4). Every reference run checks it.

docs.title: 3.2 Block condensation (exact)
docs.text:
Each block is a voxel box with one port node per lateral boundary face. Each port is joined to its cell by the half-cell conductance; eliminating a shared port gives exactly the fine scheme's harmonic face conductance. The fine problem is therefore the assembly of blocks through their ports, and nothing is approximated. Eliminating the cells gives

S = K_pp − K_pc K_cc⁻¹ K_cp,     g = W p,  W = −K_pc K_cc⁻¹ E,     T_c = Z p − Y t

Blocks with the same variant (materials, a voided bump, a missing bump, a degraded contact) share S, W, Y and Z, which are cached. A test checks this path against the reference to 1e-7 relative.

docs.title: 3.3 Reduced interfaces, error estimate, refinement
docs.text:
A face has 8 x 23 = 184 port nodes, and its trace is restricted to m modes: the constant, then the leading POD modes of two equally weighted sets of exactly solved traces.

  • Local: the interior faces of a 4 x 4 patch under every unit active-cell load. These are the near-field traces any power map can produce.
  • Global: the interior faces of an exactly condensed 16 x 16 package under 24 random hotspot maps. These are the far-field traces, where the lid, die, interposer and substrate spread heat laterally at different rates.

The POD comes from the eigenvectors of the 184 x 184 Gram matrix. The snapshot set is built once per stack (about 2.5 min) and cached on disk.

The global problem is then a Galerkin restriction, with two consequences:

  • the error is the energy-norm best approximation over the chosen interface space;
  • with the constant in every basis, the global heat balance holds to round-off.

The global set is what lets reduced interfaces work at scale (Section 4.2): with local snapshots only, the error grew with the package size. The textbook choice, characteristic constraint modes (the softest eigenvectors of the face Schur complement), fails outright here: its soft modes localise in the low-k underfill and substrate and miss the vertical temperature profile.

Interiors are exact, so the fine residual lives only on port nodes. The per-face estimate is η_F² = r_Fᵀ S_FF⁻¹ r_F. Refinement marks the faces holding half of Σ η² (Dörfler marking) and either doubles their modes (p) or restores their full port field (full).

Exact correction. Condensed.correct makes the reduced model exact. It solves the unreduced interface problem by conjugate gradients, preconditioned by the reduced model (two-level additive Schwarz: a coarse solve on the interface modes, plus face-block Jacobi) and started from the reduced solution. The iterations needed, not the final accuracy, depend on m.

docs.title: 3.4 Hierarchical condensation with memoised subtrees
docs.text:
hierarchy.Hierarchy splits the array in halves recursively. Each merge eliminates the shared faces of two children: dense Schur complements on reduced ports, that is, nested dissection. A node's operator depends only on its shape and its children's operators, so nodes are memoised by that key:

  • a uniform 2^L x 2^L array needs 2L merges;
  • a few variants add a few per level;
  • the build cost follows the number of distinct subtrees, plus the dense algebra of the top separators, which grows with the array side.

A power map goes up the tree as condensed loads; ports come down. The downward pass can be restricted to the path to one block, which is what a point query needs (track 2).

docs.title: 3.5 Learned block operators with verification
docs.text:
When blocks differ continuously (a void fraction, TIM degradation, TSV quality), each block would need its own factorisation. learned.LearnedBlocks learns the reduced operator (S_r, W_r, O_t, O_p) as a function of the block parameters θ from 48 exact condensations (Latin hypercube). It uses POD of the entries, taken as a correction to the operator of the centre block, plus a GP regression. solve_adaptive then runs four steps:

  1. Blocks outside the training box, or with a large predictive deviation, are condensed exactly.
  2. The global problem is solved.
  3. The hottest blocks and a random audit sample are compared with their exact operator at the solved state. The check uses the local junction discrepancy and the global effect of the heat-flow residual they inject, A⁻¹ r_b, computed with the already factorised global matrix.
  4. Failing blocks are replaced by their exact operator and the problem is solved again. The audit gives an additive estimate for the blocks never checked.

docs.title: 3.6 Transient
docs.text:
transient.CBTransient applies Craig–Bampton to the heat equation:

  • per block, static constraint modes, the exact static response to the block's own power, and k slowest fixed-interface modes;
  • interface modes from steady and Laplace-shifted (K + sC) traces, because steady traces miss early-time profiles (Section 4.7);
  • implicit Euler at a fixed step, against the fine reference at the same step.

docs.title: 3.7 Meshless (track 1b)
docs.text:
meshless.point_cloud places nodes from the implicit description only: layers are z intervals and inclusions are square prisms. There is no volume mesh.

  • Interior nodes: a jittered lattice per material region. The spacing is min(cap, thickness / 3) per layer, and at least 4 nodes span each inclusion within a band around its walls. Rows are aligned with the heated layer's step.
  • Surface nodes: lattices on each surface. Interfaces carry node pairs, one per side. Plane spacing follows the layers on both sides.

meshless.assemble collocates the equations with RBF-FD (PHS r^3 plus degree-2 polynomials, Flyer, Fornberg, Bayona and Barnett, J. Comput. Phys. 321 (2016) 21) or GFDM (weighted least squares, Benito, Ureña and Gavete, Appl. Math. Model. 25 (2001) 1039, doi:10.1016/S0307-904X(01)00029-4). The generic n-D weights live in pinneapple_simulation.meshless.stencils.

  • Inside a region, k ∇²T + q = 0, using same-region stencils only.
  • At the top and bottom, Robin conditions.
  • Each interface pair gets flux continuity and the contact law from one-sided stencils.
  • interface="naive" keeps one node per interface point, lets stencils cross materials, and imposes no interface condition.

Instabilities found and fixed on the way, each measured on an exact solution (tests/test_condense.py):

  1. Neumann side walls collocated at nodes: the error grew under refinement. The fix treats the adiabatic sides as mirror planes, so stencils near a side use reflected images of the nodes.
  2. Interface-plane stencils whose nodes were all coplanar made the local systems singular. The fix allows at most n/3 nodes in a surface node's own plane.
  3. Row scales spanned 12 orders of magnitude (k/h² against 1), and the factorisation lost the small rows. The fix equilibrates the rows.

Oversampled least-squares collocation (Tominec, Larsson and Heryudono, SIAM J. Sci. Comput. 43 (2021) A1441, doi:10.1137/20M1320079) is implemented as an option.

docs.title: 3.8 Prior + exception patches (track 1c)
docs.text:
exceptions.run takes four steps:

  1. Prior. It builds a cheap field (the Keff solution copied to the fine cells, or the 1-D column of each block).
  2. Residual. It computes the prior's finite-volume residual K T_prior - f on the fine grid (one sparse product) and ranks blocks by its norm, or picks them at random for the baseline.
  3. Patches. It solves the fine problem on each selected block plus a halo, with the prior as Dirichlet data around the patch.
  4. Correction. It blends the patch solutions into the prior and adds alpha * phi (phi: the response to a uniform map) so that heat out equals heat in.

docs.title: 4. Results
docs.text: All figures are in examples/physics_condensation/figures/. Tables are rounded from results/*.json.

docs.title: 4.1 Reference solver and mesh convergence
docs.text:
Joint refinement on 8 x 8 blocks, at 4 / 8 / 16 cells per block side with 1 / 2 / 4 times the vertical rows (from 23.5 k to 1.5 M cells):

quantity observed order error of the default mesh (8 cells, 1 x rows) Tmax 0.49 0.37 K of 66.5 K mean junction T 0.89 0.048 K die/TIM heat 1.13 5e-5 W (0.05 %)
  • Error measure: errors are against the Richardson extrapolation.
  • Energy balance: every reference run balances to better than 1e-9.
  • Maximum principle: Tmax always sits on the heated row, as the discrete maximum principle requires; checked on every run.
  • Why Tmax converges slowly: it is a pointwise maximum of a field heated in a thin row.
  • The yardstick: 0.37 K is the discretisation error every reduction below must be compared with.

docs.title: 4.2 Reduced interfaces: accuracy against the number of modes
docs.text:
package m interface dofs Tmax err worst junction err die/TIM heat per-bump heat effectivity 12 x 12 6 1,872 0.10 K 0.13 K 0.42 % 8.7 % 1.03 12 x 12 12 3,744 2.4 mK 2.5 mK 0.012 % 0.87 % 1.38 12 x 12 24 7,488 1e-5 K 2e-5 K 1e-3 % 0.019 % 1.23 32 x 32 6 12,672 0.76 K 0.88 K 2.2 % 20 % 0.98 32 x 32 12 25,344 27 mK 44 mK 0.03 % 3.2 % 1.12 32 x 32 24 50,688 3.5 mK 6.8 mK 0.1 % 0.25 % 0.89 64 x 64 12 — 0.37 K 0.50 K 0.46 % 5.1 % —

How to read the table: - Effectivity is the error estimate divided by the true energy-norm error. It stays between 0.9 and 1.6 for m ≥ 4. - Energy balance holds to 2e-10 for every m, as the constant mode guarantees. - The 64 x 64 row is the hierarchy on a single-hotspot map, against two 6.1 M-cell reference solves (Section 4.5).

What failed along the way: 1. Characteristic constraint modes stay at 19 K error for m = 2, 8 and 24. Their estimate effectivity is 0.07, so the estimator does not see the failure either. 2. POD of local traces only (the first version) gave 0.23 K at 12 x 12 but 8.8 K at 64 x 64 with m = 6, and 0.25 K still at m = 48. - Projecting the exact 32 x 32 traces showed the cause: six local modes miss the substrate and lid "plane" temperatures that spread independently in the far field. - Two alternatives made things worse, because they short-circuit the low-k layers vertically or laterally: one constant per layer (77 K at 64 x 64) and one per z row (83 K). - Adding the global snapshot set fixed it: 0.37 K at m = 12 and 0.25 K at m = 16 on that case, about the mesh error of Section 4.1.

docs.title: 4.3 Error-driven refinement and the exact correction
docs.text:
Refinement (a negative result). On 12 x 12 blocks with a sub-pitch hotspot, refining the faces flagged by the estimate does not beat adding modes everywhere: - doubling the modes of the marked faces reaches an energy error of 0.29 at 836 dofs; - un-reducing the marked faces reaches 0.19 at 25 k dofs; - uniform m = 16 reaches 0.014 at 5 k dofs.

The estimator is not the problem: it tracks the error at effectivity 0.6–0.7. The reduction error is global, spread over all faces, so any local marking pays a lot for each face it touches. Face refinement only pays when the error is local.

Exact correction. On 32 x 32 blocks, 1.5 M cells, a single hotspot at 4x power (Tmax 307 K), CG on the unreduced interfaces, preconditioned by the reduced model:

start after 10 its after 40 its to 1e-9 residual fine AMG solve m = 6 (5.1 K error) 27 mK, 1.3 s 1.8 mK, 5.4 s 234 its, 26 s, 3e-8 K 71 s m = 12 (0.13 K error) 1.9 mK, 1.3 s 0.29 mK, 4.9 s 184 its, 25 s, 3e-8 K 71 s

The reduced model is therefore never the last word. When a query needs the fine answer, ten iterations bring it to the millikelvin level for about the cost of one more solve.

docs.title: 4.4 Cost against package size
docs.text:
examples/physics_condensation/results/scaling.json. Each point ran in a fresh process; the peak memory is that process's. All points use the same package family: uniform 40 µm unit cells, hotspot power, 1,472 fine cells per block.

blocks fine cells fine FV reference (AMG) flat condensation, m=12: build / solve / RAM hierarchy, m=12: build / solve / RAM hierarchy, m=6: build / solve / RAM 16 2.4e4 2.2 s 0.49 s / 0.4 ms / 0.19 GB 0.32 s / 1 ms / 0.19 GB 256 3.8e5 53 s, 0.35 GB 0.34 s / 3 ms / 0.19 GB 0.63 s / 7 ms / 0.19 GB 1,024 1.5e6 86 s, 1.0 GB 1.1 s / 15 ms / 0.38 GB 0.67 s / 0.20 s / 0.28 GB 2,304 3.4e6 213 s, 2.2 GB 4,096 6.0e6 5.8 s / 76 ms / 1.0 GB 2.3 s / 0.25 s / 0.67 GB 0.76 s / 0.10 s / 0.28 GB 16,384 2.4e7 47 s / 0.42 s / 4.1 GB 8.5 s / 0.88 s / 2.0 GB 1.9 s / 0.27 s / 0.65 GB 65,536 9.6e7 44 s / 3.4 s / 7.6 GB 5.5 s / 1.2 s / 2.1 GB 262,144 3.9e8 40 s / 4.0 s / 7.7 GB

Accuracy along the curve. - Where the fine reference fits (up to 1,024 blocks), the m=12 hierarchy's Tmax is within 16 mK of it. The flat and hierarchical condensations give the same Tmax to 1 mK at every size: they solve the same reduced problem. - m=6 is not accurate at scale, and its error grows with the package. Its Tmax departs from m=12 by −0.97 K (4,096 blocks), −2.96 K (16,384) and −6.03 K (65,536). The 262,144-block point shows that the method runs at that size in 7.7 GB. It does not show an accurate answer there: from that trend the error is likely 10 K or more, and nothing here measures it. - The m=12 error grows with size too, more slowly. Against the fine reference it is 2.4 mK at 144 blocks, 27 mK at 1,024 (Section 4.2) and 0.37 K at 4,096 (Section 4.5, two maps). - So the 65,536-block m=12 point (44 s build, 3.4 s per map) has an error that is not measured, likely above 1 K given that trend. The cost table is a cost result, not an accuracy result beyond 4,096 blocks. - The far-field snapshots cover 16 x 16 blocks (Section 3.3). Larger packages have longer-range interface modes that 12 modes do not hold. More modes for larger packages, or the exact correction (Section 4.3: 0.13 K to 1.9 mK in 10 iterations at 1,024 blocks), are the measured ways to control it.

Cost. - The hierarchy's build grows about 4–5× per 4× blocks (2.3 → 8.5 → 44 s), dominated by the dense merges at the top separators. Thanks to memoisation there are only 15–17 distinct merges. - The flat condensation grows faster, about 8× per 4× (5.8 → 47 s), dominated by the sparse factorisation of the interface system. It was not run beyond 16,384 blocks. - The fine AMG reference grows about linearly in cells, but with a large constant: 213 s at 3.4e6 cells. - A new power map costs one up-and-down pass: 3.4 s at 65,536 blocks, against a build of 44 s.

Compressibility of the top operator (results/root_ranks.json, 64 x 64 blocks, m=12, 3,072 root ports, 768 per side, singular values above 1e-8 of the largest): - coupling between adjacent sides: rank 74 of 768 (10%); - coupling between opposite sides: rank 16; - a quarter of a side against the far half: rank 10 of 192.

The top blocks are therefore strongly data-sparse, which is the case for H-matrix or HSS arithmetic (Section 2). It would remove the cubic growth of the top merges, but it is not implemented here.

docs.title: 4.5 Cost to build against cost per configuration
docs.text:
On 64 x 64 blocks (6.1 M fine cells, m = 12):

step time build: block condensation, modes from the cached snapshots, memoised merges 6.5 s each of 20 new power maps (1 to 5 hotspots) 0.29–0.98 s (median 0.48 s) one fine reference solve (AMG-CG) 386 s

On the two checked maps, the errors against the reference were: - Tmax 0.37 K and 0.32 K; - junction field relative L2 0.4 %; - die/TIM heat 0.46 %; - per-bump heat 5 %; - energy balance 2e-10.

The one-time snapshot build (about 2.5 min per stack) is not in the 6.5 s. It is cached on disk and shared by every package built on that stack.

docs.title: 4.6 What Keff homogenisation erases
docs.text:
All three cases are on 12 x 12 blocks. The condensed (m = 12) column is the same metric as the Keff Tmax error.

case Keff Tmax err Keff worst block-peak err lost intra-block spread Keff per-bump heat err condensed (m=12) Tmax err smooth power −0.14 K 0.41 K 0.65 K 14.5 % 2.4 mK sub-pitch hotspot (+20 % of P in one cell) −4.59 K 4.59 K 6.7 K 22.5 % 96 mK voided microbumps at the hotspot −0.12 K 0.43 K 0.70 K 15.1 % 8 mK
  • Speed: Keff takes 0.02 s against 9–11 s for the fine reference.
  • Bulk quantities survive: it keeps the die/TIM heat (0.1 %) and the energy balance.
  • What it erases: the junction structure under each bump (0.65 K of spread even with smooth power) and the share of heat each bump carries (14–22 % error).
  • Sub-pitch sources: a hotspot smaller than the pitch costs 4.6 K. Voided bumps are a variant of the block, so Keff averages them in too.

docs.title: 4.7 Transient (Craig–Bampton)
docs.text:
6 x 6 blocks (53 k cells), 150 implicit-Euler steps of 0.2 ms, with the power map switching every 10 ms:

m, k dofs max Tmax err max junction err die/TIM heat err run fine run 8, 8 960 86 mK 0.11 K 1.3 % 0.13 s 10.3 s 16, 16 1,920 23 mK 34 mK 1.6 % 0.17 s 32, 32 3,840 1.9 mK 5.3 mK 0.21 % 0.37 s
  • Interface modes for transients: they need the Laplace-shifted snapshots. With steady modes the m = 6 error was 1.3 K and did not fall with k.
  • Exactness: with every mode the model matches the fine run to 1e-8 (a test).
  • Build cost: the first build (216 s) includes the shifted snapshots, which are then cached.

docs.title: 4.8 Learned block operators with verification
docs.text:
All blocks differ (smooth fields of microbump voiding, TIM contact degradation and TSV quality), with four defect blocks outside the training box (two nearly open bumps, two delaminated TIM contacts):

blocks training learned + verified all exact Tmax err (verified) Tmax err (learned only) exact blocks 256 48 samples, 36 s 24.6 s 113 s 2.2 mK 2.2 mK 4 (OOD) 1,024 48 samples, 14 s 9.4 s 417 s 4.4 mK 4.4 mK 4 (OOD) 1,024 6 samples, 4 s 97 s 1,198 s 0.13 K 0.70 K 250 4,096 48 samples, 14 s 51 s 1,991 s 0.06 mK 0.06 mK 4 (OOD)

At 4,096 blocks the learned and verified solve is 39 times faster than condensing every block exactly. Of its 51 s, 37 s are verification: the 24 audited blocks and the A⁻¹ r effect estimate, which bounds the unchecked blocks additively at 64 mK. The 64 x 64 run shared the 4 cores with a PINN training run (Section 6), so both of its times are pessimistic by the same load.

The 6-sample case shows the fallback doing its job: - the predictive deviation flagged 227 blocks and the out-of-box rule 4; - the verification rounds replaced 4–5 more blocks each round, until the 5-round limit; - the error went from 0.70 K (learned only) to 0.13 K; - the additive estimate for the unchecked blocks was 4.4 K, which is conservative.

The defects themselves change the junction temperature by up to 0.17 K (16 x 16, exact with against without them).

docs.title: 4.9 Meshless (track 1b)
docs.text:
The package is 2 x 2 blocks. The reference is FV with 5,888 cells, solved in 0.09 s, with Tmax 65.87 K. Point generation takes 0.02–0.09 s for every cloud.

method interface nodes Tmax err die/TIM heat energy balance solve GFDM pairs 46 k −65.6 K −36 % −121 % 5.8 s RBF-FD pairs 46 k singular GFDM pairs 72 k +6.1 K +3.4 % +10.4 % 10.8 s RBF-FD pairs 72 k −1.9 K −2.8 % −2.8 % 10.7 s GFDM pairs 121 k +2.1 K +2.3 % +3.6 % 36 s RBF-FD pairs 121 k +6.2 K +9.4 % +9.5 % 39 s both naive 40–114 k −58 to −102 K −100 % −84 to −174 % both pairs + least squares 72 k −65.6 K −134 % 456–554 s, 9.4 GB

What the table shows: - Naive collocation across materials loses most of the heat, at every resolution. - Interface pairs turn that into an erratic 3–10 % error. Nothing converged in the range the container allows, and every run is worse than the 5,888-cell FV model. - The error map of the best run (RBF-FD, 72 k) is a near-uniform −1.5 to −2 K offset: a conservation error, not a local one. - Least-squares collocation is exact and stable on a smooth interface (the test: below 1e-3 relative across refinement). Its residual concentrates at the re-entrant corners of the bump/underfill frame, where it fails. - Where meshless wins here: there is no meshing step (the geometry is evaluated, not meshed), and a geometry change is a new point cloud in milliseconds. - Where it loses here: multi-material interfaces (k ratios up to 800), conservation (no discrete balance), conditioning (row-scaled 1-norm condition estimates of 1e8–3e9 at 40–46 k nodes) and cost.

Meshless block + Schur reuse was not built. A meshless block would need about 18 k nodes, against 1,472 FV cells for a more accurate block, so condensing it cannot be cheaper at equal accuracy. The hybrid (meshless bulk, conservative FV at the interfaces) is a next step.

docs.title: 4.10 Prior + exception patches (track 1c)
docs.text:
On 12 x 12 blocks (1.7 M cells; fine solve 22–24 s), with a 1-block halo:

case prior alone residual-selected patches random patches, same budget sub-pitch hotspot 4.59 K 0.35 K at 6.9 % of the cells solved; 0.14 K at 21.5 %; 0.07 K at 59 % 4.59 K up to 69 % of the cells; 0.06 K at 89 % smooth power 0.14 K 0.12 K at 24 %; 0.075 K at 61 % 0.14 K at 39 %
  • Energy: the correction closes the balance to 2e-16 in every run.
  • Per-bump heat improves little (22.5 % to 13–19 %). The prior's error is everywhere, and patches with prior boundary data cannot fix a far-field error.
  • The 1-D column prior is off by 266 K and 1,985 K on the same cases: it ignores lateral spreading, which carries most of a hotspot's heat away.

The method is a one-shot defect correction (a two-level Schwarz step) on a homogenised coarse level, like the local corrections of multiscale FEM. What this work adds is selecting the patches by the prior's residual, which beats random selection by more than 10x at equal budget when the error is local. It does not help when the error is spread out. Hotspots on an interface are the default here, since the heated row sits on the microbump interface.

docs.title: 5. Limitations and next steps
docs.text:
The benchmark - It is synthetic: square bumps, one microbump, TSV and C4 per pitch, layers the size of the die, isotropic representative materials, linear conduction, Robin cooling. - It has no lid overhang, warpage, or temperature-dependent k.

Track 1 (condensation) - Dense algebra on the top separator grows as the array side cubed. H-matrix or HSS compression of those blocks is measured (Section 4.4) but not implemented. - Interface modes are built per stack from snapshots. A stack with very different layers needs new snapshots; the "global" set covers 16 x 16 blocks of far field. - Local refinement did not pay. The exact correction is the robust way to reach the fine answer.

Track 1b (meshless) - It did not converge reliably on this multi-material benchmark. - Next: interface-enriched stencils or the hybrid with FV at the interfaces, and RBF-FD-LS with corner-weighted rows.

Track 1c (exception patches) - It works for local defects only. A prior with the right far field, and a fine correction only near features, is what condensation does exactly.

Falsification campaign. condensation_falsification.md pre-registered 23 hypotheses, each with a kill criterion, and tested them. Each verdict is computed from the measured results.

What holds: - Exactness held on every operator tried: contrast 1e5, anisotropy, thin layers, advection to Pe 1000, Stokes, Picard Navier–Stokes and CHT to Re 100, and meshless matrices. - Reduced interfaces needed only 2–3 modes per face for 1 % on the CFD cases.

What was refuted: - The far-field error grows about 3× per 4× blocks at fixed m. - The speed gain vanishes without repetition: random variants, non-linear k(T) and R_c(T), computed velocity fields, and 2-D Stokes against a sparse direct solve. - A single-cell power spike gives 1.7 K with 12 modes. - The meshless and hybrid discretisations stay several times less accurate than FV. - The residual of a coarse prior does not find the regions that need solving in transport problems.

Freedom to operate. This work did not examine any patent, including WO2026064513A1, beyond the brief's description. An IP specialist must review freedom to operate.

docs.title: 6. Physics learning verification (track 3)
docs.text:
Question. A low training loss and a low held-out error do not show that a learned thermal model has learned the physics. Can a check independent of the training loss tell which relations a model has learned, under the changes an engineer will make (power, source position, conductivity, contact resistance, cooling), and at which points?

Case. A 2-D die / TIM / lid cross-section (silicon 100 µm, TIM 30 µm, copper lid 500 µm, 2 mm wide), heated by a Gaussian line source at the bottom of the die. It has Robin cooling on top and adiabatic sides and bottom (pinneapple_analysis/validation/physics_learning_cases.py). The reference is the finite-volume scheme of pinneapple_condense.fv on 200 × 36 cells. One solve takes milliseconds, so every expected response comes from solving the physics, not from a rule.

Verifier (pinneapple_analysis/validation/physics_learning.py, verify(model, case)). It uses only model evaluations and reference solves, never the model's loss.

  • Structural checks at the solved state:
  • the discrete FV residual of the model's field at selected cells (heat created or destroyed, relative to the heat through the cell);
  • interface flux continuity;
  • boundary conditions: source flux, Robin top, adiabatic sides (as a cell balance), and the side gradient itself;
  • global energy balance;
  • consistency between neighbouring points;
  • mirror symmetry;
  • linear scaling with power.
  • Interventions: power ×2, source moved, source outside the training box, TIM conductivity ×2 and /2, cooling ×2, and a contact resistance added. Each model response is compared with the reference response to the same change.
  • Scope: an intervention on a parameter the model does not take is out of scope. It is reported, but it is not a defect.
  • Sufficiency: whether the model's inputs cover every parameter that moves the answer by more than 2% over its plausible variation.
  • Informative points: chosen near interfaces, the source and the boundaries (select_points).
  • Provenance: a check that still passes with untrained weights is credited to the architecture. A check that only the trained model passes is credited as learned.
  • Trust report: the result is a TrustReport with the decision APPROVED / REVIEW / REJECT.

Defective models. Seven deliberately defective models, each accurate on the training distribution by the usual metrics and wrong in one physical respect:

  1. interfaces smoothed over 25 µm × severity;
  2. frozen outside the training box;
  3. reversed TIM response;
  4. cooling learned from power, because the training data had h = 100 P;
  5. 3% × severity heat created in the lid;
  6. heat leaking through the adiabatic sides;
  7. saturating power response.

They run at severities 0.25, 0.5, 1 and 2. There are also seven controls: the reference, and the reference times 1 + a cos(2πjx/L) for a = 0.1% and 0.3%, j = 1, 2, 3.

The baselines are held-out relative L2 on 6 cases × 200 points of the training distribution, and the mean squared discrete residual. Both are flagged above 1%.

docs.title: 6.1 Detection against the usual metrics
docs.text:
examples/physics_learning_verification/results/detection.json, 7 s for the whole study on one core:

verifier physics loss > 1 % held-out L2 > 1 % defective models detected (22) 22 (100 %) 12 (55 %) 5 (23 %) controls flagged (7) 3 1 0
  • The physics loss misses all causal defects (out of distribution, reversed response, spurious correlation) and the scaling defect.
  • Held-out L2 misses every defect except large energy and scaling errors.
  • Each defect is flagged by the check that names it (tests/test_physics_learning.py::test_the_right_check_fails).

The three flagged controls are not false alarms in the physical sense. They are the higher-wavenumber errors: mode 3 at 0.1%, and modes 2 and 3 at 0.3%.

  • The residual these controls leave grows with the square of the wavenumber: the worst cell creates or destroys 9% (0.1%, mode 3), 12% (0.3%, mode 2) and 27% (0.3%, mode 3) of the heat through it. The passing controls stay at 1–4%. Most of this sits in the copper lid, where a small temperature error carries a large flux.
  • The mean squared residual shows the same ranking: 3.3e-3, 5.9e-3 and 3.0e-2, against at most 6.5e-4 for the passing controls.
  • The verifier's residual tolerance (5% of the heat through a cell) is therefore a statement about heat, not about temperature. A model can be 0.1% accurate in temperature and still fail it. Whether that is a defect depends on whether the user needs fluxes.
  • The CI test uses the controls that are small in heat-flow terms.

Informative against random points. At equal budgets the informative points detect every defect from 4 points. Random points detect 82% at 4 points, 95% at 8, and 100% from 16 (right panel). The verifier itself takes a median of 25 ms per model with 48 points.

docs.title: 6.2 Real learned models
docs.text:
results/models.json:

model train held-out rel. L2 physics loss decision what failed POD-GPR, correlated training data (h = 100 P) 48 solves 9.5e-5 2.2e-4 REJECT 5 interventions (cooling ×2: response off by 121 %, power ×2: 91 %), scaling 45 % POD-GPR, independent samples 48 solves 6.0e-3 1.6e-3 REJECT residual 13 %, source flux 18 %, TIM ×2 16 %, source outside the box 61 % PINN, soft side conditions 97 s, loss 2.8e-4 0.29 0.076 REJECT residual 51 %, interface flux 56 %, energy balance 29 % PINN, hard adiabatic sides 105 s, loss 2.0e-4 0.084 0.075 REJECT residual 76 %, interface flux 75 %, energy balance 8.4 %
  • The first row is the case the brief describes. Its held-out error is 0.01%, yet the verifier rejects it because it learned the correlation between cooling and power in its data, not the physics.
  • Both PINNs are rejected; their low training losses do not mean the solution is right.
  • The PINNs take only the nominal case, so every intervention is out of scope and reported as such.
  • Their losses are small because the loss is non-dimensional and dominated by the die, while the copper lid and the TIM jump carry the heat.
  • Interface flux is learned worst, consistent with the reported PINN failure modes at material jumps (Section 2).
  • Architecture against learned for the hard-constraint PINN:
  • the side gradient passes with untrained weights, so it is credited to the architecture;
  • neighbour consistency is credited to the architecture for both PINNs (a smooth network);
  • symmetry is learned.
  • The adiabatic-sides cell balance still fails (0.14): it involves the interior flux next to the wall, which the architecture does not constrain.
  • The PINNs ran 3,000 Adam steps on one core alongside the condensation benchmark. A longer schedule would lower the errors; the point measured here is that the verifier separates loss from physics, not how far a PINN can be trained.

docs.title: 6.3 Limitations (track 3)
docs.text:
• The case is 2-D and steady. Transient checks (heat capacity, time causality) are not implemented.
  • The expected responses need a reference solver. Here it is cheap; for a full package it is the condensed solver of track 1, which the verifier does not call yet.
  • Thresholds are fixed and relative: 5% for residual and boundary, 1% for energy, 10% for interventions. A calibrated threshold per quantity of interest would turn REVIEW/REJECT into an error bar.
  • The defects are synthetic and each has one cause. Real models mix them; the per-check report still names each failure, but the defect-type attribution has not been tested on mixtures.

docs.title: 7. Physics query engine (track 2)
docs.text:
Question. An engineer asks about a quantity at a place, under conditions, to an accuracy. Can a system answer with the cheapest method that is valid, and say: - the value and units; - the uncertainty; - under which conditions the answer holds; - where it came from; - whether it read a solved state or predicted an unsolved one?

Interface. pinneapple_query: Engine.query(quantity, where, time=None, conditions={}, accuracy=None, rigorous=False) returns an Answer: - value, unit, uncertainty; - kind: read, predicted or solved; - method, validity, provenance, seconds; - rigorous, and interval when the bound is guaranteed.

Locations are stable physical references, not mesh nodes: die@u,v (junction under a point), die@u,v,w (height fraction through the die), region:die[i0:i1,j0:j1], ubump[I,J], tsv[I,J], interface:die/tim, lid:top. They survive a change of mesh or of the number of interface modes.

Planner. Every method makes an Offer: expected cost, error bound, rigorous or not, valid or not. The planner takes the cheapest valid offer whose bound meets the target. With no target, it takes the default target (0.1 K for temperatures) or, for heat, the most accurate offer. With rigorous=True it takes only guaranteed intervals.

Methods on the chip package (pinneapple_condense.query), from cheapest to most expensive: - Read a stored state. Its uncertainty is that of the solve that made it: |T_m − T_2m| for a condensed solve, per observable. - Superposition of solved states. Conduction is linear in the power, so the coefficients come from least squares on the power maps. The uncertainty is the residual map's effect plus the states' own uncertainties weighted by |c|. - Monotone bound. The FV matrix is a nonsingular M-matrix, so its inverse is entrywise non-negative (Berman and Plemmons, Nonnegative Matrices in the Mathematical Sciences, SIAM, 1994, ch. 6). Any map with p_min ≤ p ≤ p_max is therefore bracketed by the uniform-map solutions, which for identical blocks are one block with adiabatic sides. This gives a rigorous interval for one block solve, ever. - Condensed solve with the memoised hierarchy at m and 2m. It returns the 2m value with |T_m − T_2m| as its uncertainty and stores the state for later reads. - Fine FV reference, only where it fits.

docs.title: 7.1 Measured demo
docs.text:
examples/physics_query/run_demo.py, results/query_demo.json.

The package has 48 x 48 blocks (3.4 M fine cells). Building the engine takes 11.9 s: the hierarchies at m = 12 and 24, plus a calibration solve of the package's own map.

There are 5,115 queries. Every answer is compared with a fine FV solve of the same conditions, which takes 190–218 s each (AMG-CG), and the process peaks at 2.9 GB.

phase queries method picked kind latency (median) error vs fine FV (max) error ≤ stated uncertainty own map, junction points 2,000 cached read 0.10 ms 26 mK 2,000 / 2,000 own map, die-interior points 100 cached (block rebuilt on its root-to-leaf path) read 56 ms 26 mK 100 / 100 own map, Tj_max, die/TIM heat, lid heat, one bump 4 cached read 0.9 ms 20 mK; heat within its stated uncertainty 4 / 4 0.5 P0 + 0.3 P1 + 0.2 P2, junction points 500 superposition predicted 4.1 ms 35 mK 500 / 500 same map, regions and interfaces 4 superposition predicted 5.0 ms 16 mK 4 / 4 unseen single-hotspot map, rigorous interval asked 501 bound predicted 0.2 ms interval half-width ≈ 2,550 K 501 / 501 inside same unseen map, target 0.5 K 2,004 condensed once (3.4 s), then cached solved, then read 0.12 ms (reads) 15 mK (solved point), 0.17 K (reads) 2,004 / 2,004

What this shows. - Reading against predicting is explicit. A read costs 0.1 ms. A prediction from superposition costs 4 ms and is labelled predicted, with its uncertainty and the states and coefficients it used. A new map with a tight target costs one condensed solve (3.4 s, against 190–218 s for the fine solve), after which the same map is read. - Stated uncertainties held: 5,113 of 5,113 non-rigorous answers were within them, and 501 of 501 rigorous intervals contained the fine value. - This needed a fix found by the demo. In the first run, superposition answered heat queries with an uncertainty of 1e-15 W. It treated linear combination as exact and ignored the error of the condensed states it combined; 3 of 4 heat answers were outside their uncertainty. - States now carry per-observable uncertainties. - Superposition and reads propagate them. - tests/test_query.py::test_heat_from_condensed_states_carries_their_uncertainty fails without the fix.

docs.title: 7.2 Limitations (track 2)
docs.text:
• The monotone bound is rigorous and useless for hotspot maps. Its width is set by p_max / p_min over the map: 2,550 K for a single hotspot at 1.3 times the nominal power. It is informative only for near-uniform maps. A tighter rigorous bound needs a decay estimate of the Green's function, which is not implemented.
  • Uncertainties are estimates, not bounds. |T_m − T_2m| is an estimate. It held on every query here, but Section 4.4 shows the reduction error growing with package size, and the estimate has not been tested beyond 2,304 blocks.
  • Conditions are only the power map. Changes of material, contact resistance or cooling invalidate every stored state (they are different keys) and need a new condensed solve. A parametric learned operator (Section 3.5) would be the cheaper method to offer there, and it is not wired in.
  • Steady state only. The time argument is accepted but no transient method is registered (Craig–Bampton, Section 3.6, would be the one).

docs.title: Security audit: the PINNeAPPle web apps and their deployment
docs.text:
Scope: the FastAPI apps under apps/ (34 apps plus the static Playground and Zoo space), the shared glue apps/_shared/appkit.py and the library code it runs (pinneapple_core.service, the parsers and solvers the apps call), the Lab catalogue server (pinneapple_lab/server.py), and the deployment in apps/deploy (Docker Compose, Caddy, the app Dockerfiles). Reference: OWASP Top 10 (2021) and ASVS 4.0 levels 1–2. Audit date: 2026-10-18, commit ee4b770b (main).

Method: an inventory of every app's routes, uploads, process calls, deserialisation, path handling and outbound requests, read from the code (summarised below), plus the tools in the next section. Every finding marked measured was reproduced by a test or a scan; the others were read from the code and are marked as such.

docs.title: Tool results (baseline, before any change)
docs.text:
Tool Scope Result bandit 1.8 apps/, pinneapple_security/, pinneapple_core/service/ 24 findings: 2 high (B324 SHA-1, used for design IDs), 5 medium (3× B608 SQL built from a fixed list of ? placeholders, B610, B301 pickle of a server-written cache), 17 low semgrep 1.181 (semgrep-rules: python lang, fastapi, jwt, requests, cryptography, dockerfile) apps + the evaluators they call 241 findings: 52 error (32× dockerfile missing-user, 16 useless-inner-function, …), 116 warning (incl. 4× eval-detected, 2× avoid-pickle, 2× SHA-1), 73 info pip-audit 2.9 union of apps/*/requirements.txt, resolved to current releases 0 known vulnerabilities gitleaks 8.21 whole git history (502 commits) 39 hits, all false positives: the placeholder curl -u USER:PASSWORD in three app UIs and key="axial_compressor_stage_3d" in pinneapple_veriphysics/example_cases.py. No committed secret found hadolint 2.12 35 app Dockerfiles 37: 33× DL3013 (unpinned pip), 3× DL3008 (unpinned apt), 1 info trivy 0.69 config apps/ 33 high: DS-0002, image runs as root (all app Dockerfiles but the Simulation Runner and the GUI agent) trivy 0.69 image base images python:3.11-slim: 0 critical, 46 high (2 with a fix); caddy:2: 0 critical, 4 high; caddy:2.8.4-alpine (Playground): 7 critical, 86 high, 92 % fixable

Not run here: Trivy on the built app images. download.pytorch.org (the CPU torch wheel every app image installs) is blocked from this environment and the CUDA wheel from PyPI exceeded the disk; the base images and the resolved Python dependencies were scanned instead, and the Security workflow's weekly image job builds and scans one app image in CI.

docs.title: Inventory
docs.text:
Shared to every app (apps/_shared/appkit.py, before this change):

  • Login: optional HTTP Basic (<PREFIX>_USER / <PREFIX>_PASSWORD, plain text in the environment, constant-time compare); with neither set, every route is open. Any login is admin. No lockout, no rate limit.
  • Caller identity (job and upload ownership, monthly quotas): API key, else login, else ip: + the last X-Forwarded-For entry, believed from any peer.
  • Runtime (install_runtime): SQLite job queue (thread or process executor, optional time limit, no resource limits), API keys (random, stored as SHA-256, scopes stored but not enforced), usage metering, uploads (streamed size cap, name reduced to [A-Za-z0-9._-], suffix allow-list, stored under the data volume, not the web root).
  • Static files: /vendor (three.js), /studio, /shared, each app's /static. No security headers, no CORS middleware anywhere (browsers default to same-origin), no CSRF protection, no session cookies (Basic auth and X-API-Key only).
  • Errors: FastAPI's default 500 has no trace; many routes return f"{type(e).__name__}: {e}" with 422; job logs carry the last 40 traceback lines to the job owner.

Per app (prefix · runtime · uploads · expensive work and its limit · process calls · deserialisation · outbound):

urls are recorded, not fetched guiagent GUIAGENT workflow zip, self-hosted mode only (50 MB) FreeCAD/OpenFOAM runs: job queue zip checked per member; LLM picks among committed workflows heatsink_sizer HSS none BusyLimiter HSS_MAX_SIZING — identifiability_lab IDENT table (runtime cap) job queue, row/parameter caps — interop_hub IOP files/zips (500 MB) BusyLimiter zips via cae.upload.expand (count and size caps, no ratio, no name check); pickle of a server-written cache (sid.isalnum()) inverse_heat IHL none PINN training threads, IHL_MAX_JOBS jobs without owner (random 48-bit ids) inverse_studio INVS table job queue — mesh_quality MQA files/zips (200 MB) BusyLimiter zips via expand meshless_lab MESHLESS point cloud (20 MB) job queue, node and budget caps user formulas → sympy.sympify behind a string blacklist model_gateway MDL onnx/zip/json (100 MB) inference, metered surrogate zip → pickle.load, "sha256-checked" against a card in the same zip (admin only);
